A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed just south of the Clay-Effingham county line, producing damage at a farmstead along the county line east of 1800th Street. At this location, metal from the top of a silo was blown off, and a barn was damaged with roof pieces blown off to the northeast for about a half mile. The tornado was in Clay County for less than a minute, before continuing northeast into Effingham County where it produced tracks through corn stubble in fields. It dissipated northwest of the intersection of East 200th Avenue and County Road 2200. This tornado had a maximum intensity of EF-0, and its total lifespan was 11 minutes.

As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Northeast Shelby County near the James community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm impacted the Lower Kobuk Valley, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 0431AKST on February 20 through 2059AKST on February 22, 2026. The Robert Curtis Memorial Airport AWOS (PFNO) in Noorvik first reported visibilities reduced to one-half mile in snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty-nine miles per hour gusting to thirty-five miles per hour at 0739AKST on February 21. During the peak of the event, the station measured sustained winds of twenty-three miles per hour with a peak gust of thirty-five miles per hour and one-half mile visibility in snow and freezing fog. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 0739AKST on February 21. Hazardous conditions, including blowing snow and reduced visibilities, persisted until the warning was downgraded on February 22. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. Pre-frontal vertical mixing allowed for these stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface across much of the northern mountains of NM as early as just prior to midnight March 14th into the predawn and early morning hours of March 15th. Further high winds followed the backdoor and Pacific portions of a surface cold front during the late morning and early afternoon across central and eastern NM. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common with a peak gust of 81 mph being recorded at the Raton Airport. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. Winds began to taper off in the mid-to-late afternoon as the strong portion of the jetstream exited into TX and the surface cold fronts advanced to southern NM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The LANL5 mesonet station saw a 68 mph wind gust, while several other LANL stations and the KLAM AWOS saw gusts of 58 to 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. Although isolated showers skimmed across southeast Ohio on the 19th, more robust showers and storms did not arrive until late that night. A few strong to severe storms that developed overnight produced gusty winds and penny size hail. The majority of activity shifted east across the Ohio River before daybreak on the 20th, then drier conditions took hold for the rest of the day. Rainfall amounts for this event generally totaled around an inch or less.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were downed on Route 218 near Route 7 south of Gallipolis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system from the west moved over Maine, late on 02/10 into 02/11. Occluded front moves over the state, bringing precipitation in the form of snow from west to southeast. Low began to slow down over eastern Maine, and alongside a surface low developing, heaviest snowfall occurred over eastern Maine. Warning criteria snowfall occurred in central and costal Washington county, with accumulations around 7-9 inches during the afternoon of the 11th. Storm total accumulations around 6-8 inches in southern Aroostook. Northern and eastern Aroostook, alongside Hancock county, had accumulations around 3-5 inches. The rest of the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Bangor region received about 2-4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system tracking through the Great Lakes lifted a series of fronts through eastern New York, resulting in widespread precipitation from Friday, February 20 through Saturday, February 21, 2026. Most of this precipitation fell in the form of snow, though some higher terrain areas received minimal accumulations of freezing rain and sleet with some lower-lying areas conversely receiving some plain rain. ||The highest accumulations of snow fell across portions of the Southwest Adirondacks and Upper Hudson Valley where 6 to nearly 10 inches were measured. Elsewhere, a couple of tenths up to 5 inches were common with the highest of these reported across the Catskills, Helderbergs, and Taconics. Fortunately, freezing rain accumulations were more apparent based on radar products rather than in ground-truth observations so little in the way of impacts occurred due to ice accretion. ||Key impacts: school delays and traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 7.1 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dynamic storm system brought unseasonably warm temperatures and rounds of severe weather to eastern Kentucky on February 19th and 20th. Near record warmth, combined with intense wind shear, fueled both discrete supercells and a subsequent overnight line of showers and thunderstorms.||The primary threat focused along the Mountain Parkway corridor during the afternoon of the 19th, where thunderstorms produced up to quarter-sized hail (1.00). As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Dodge County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 in fall 2025, the county experienced a period of mid-winter improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels on January 13. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 11 weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the original fall onset, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions (D2���D3) developed and intensified across portions of the New Orleans/Baton Rouge WFO area during February 2026, driven by persistent precipitation deficits and limited meaningful rainfall events. Early in the month, only isolated areas of severe drought (D2) were present across the northwestern parts of the region, but conditions steadily worsened as rainfall remained below normal, with precipitation deficits of roughly 2 to 4 inches observed across much of the region by the end of February. As a result, D2 drought expanded significantly across southern and southwestern portions of the forecast area, while pockets of extreme drought (D3) developed, particularly near coastal Louisiana. By late February, over 30 percent of the area was classified in D2 drought and more than 10 percent in D3, reflecting a rapid degradation in soil moisture and hydrologic conditions. The expansion of drought was most pronounced south of the Interstate 10 corridor, while areas farther north experienced more gradual degradation, generally remaining in D0 to D1 conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Prolonged D2 to D3 drought effected portions of Pointe Coupee Parish for the entire month of February.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of 6 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the southern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 23 to 28 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around three-quarters of a mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A developing 970 mb low over the north west Gulf of Alaska, sent an occluded front into the panhandle with the associated triple point tracking over the northern inner channels the afternoon and evening of March 6th. This caused winds through the inner channels to increase out of the south, reaching high wind criteria in Skagway until after the low center jumped into the Yukon and weakened. The following day, another low tracked in but was slightly further south and Skagway saw peak gusts just below warning criteria.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Marine Exchange of Alaska observation at the Skagway Ore Dock measured the first high wind gust as winds shifted suddenly out of the south with a peak of 56.4kt (65mph) at 230pm on the 6th. The Skagway Airport ASOS measured a peak gust of 55kt (63mph) at 415pm and the Marine Exchange station at the harbor measured a peak gust of 51.8kt (60mph) at 714pm. High wind gusts continued into the night at the Airport until 1104pm and at the Ore Dock until 123am.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Relatively clear early-day skies on February 12 led to isolated convection with rain and snow showers across portions of western Colorado. Some valleys were already saturated or near-saturated due to periods of precipitation over the prior days. As such, in spite of dense cloud cover lingering overnight and lacking radiational cooling, saturated surface conditions paired with weakening winds were capable of producing areas of dense fog on the morning on February 13.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread dense fog developed within the Yampa River Basin during the morning of February 13. The KCAG ASOS at the Craig-Moffat County Airport reported two prolonged periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog and freezing fog, once before sunrise and once after. Several hours of reduced visibility above 1/4 mile due to mist and fog were also observed during the morning. The KEEO ASOS at the Meeker Coulter Field Airport observed almost three hours of 1/4-mile visibility due to freezing fog prior to sunrise. The KHDN AWOS at the Yampa Valley Regional Airport also reported several prolonged periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog and freezing fog both before and after sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak remnants of an atmospheric river arrived to the Four Corners region during the afternoon of February 11 and overnight into the morning of February 12. Primarily virga showers dominated as the plume of moisture first arrived. Surface moisture eventually caught up near the Abajo Mountains around midnight and coinciding with brief rain showers. The mid-level atmosphere dried out again prior to sunrise, promoting radiational cooling amidst clearing skies and the development of sparse, yet dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief and localized dense fog developed near the Abajo mountains during the early morning period of February 12. The KU64 AWOS at the Monticello Airport reported about one hour of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following multiple days of rain and snow showers, drier northwesterly flow on the backside of a shortwave trough brought clearer skies on the evening of February 13 into the morning of February 14. With ample surface moisture still in place from the prior days' precipitation and strong radiational cooling from clear skies, dense fog developed across many valleys.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed within the eastern Uinta basin during the morning of February 14. The KVEL ASOS at the Vernal Regional Airport reported two roughly 15-minute periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to freezing fog prior to sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

Strong mid-upper level trough ejected into the Plains early on February 17 which led to a rapid deepening of a surface cyclone. Strong winds developed behind the cold frontal passage, leading to numerous high wind reports across central and western Kansas. Large wildfires spread quickly as a result of the strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ranger Road fire was a large wildfire that began in Beaver County, OK during the early afternoon hours of February 17th. Fueled by strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity, the fire spread quickly into Kansas. Evacuations were ordered for the town of Englewood, Ashland, and all of southern Clark County. Two firefighters were injured battling the blaze in the county. It was reported by local ranchers that hundreds of cattle perished in the fire. The exact acreage burned in Clark County is unknown, but the total acreage burned from the fire was 283,383. The fire was controlled February 24.

An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning. ||While individual event narratives are not included for Cotton, Harmon, Harper, Jefferson, Love and Tillman Counties, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of sleet and snow during this event, producing 4 to 7 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (7 inches) was reported near Chickasha. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system in the southern Bering Sea moved northeast over the Aleutian Islands bringing widespread snow showers and gusty north/northeast winds to much of southeast Alaska and parts of the Western Interior. The front on the leading edge of the Bering Sea low initiated the first waves of snowfall in the southeast Interior, while gusty north/northeast winds strengthened on the western side of the low. Falling snow and gusty winds created long-lasting blizzard conditions to coastal areas along the Lower Yukon. The strongest winds settled over St. Lawrence Island and along the Norton Sound coastline as the low moved further inland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Gambell AWOS (PAGM) site first met high wind criteria on 1/5/26 at 04:42L reporting 49 mph sustained winds, gusting at 59 mph. The AWOS site reported a peak observation at 04:56L on 1/5/26 of sustained winds at 47 mph, gusting to 63 mph. Wind gusts were in the upper 50 mph range for over 10 hrs as of 15:00L on 1/5/26.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A blockbuster winter storm that impacted millions across the lower 48, bringing a combination of ice; sleet; snow; rain; and strong winds, brought widespread heavy snowfall accumulations to all of eastern New York from January 25-26th, 2026. ||An arctic blast made for dangerously cold conditions across eastern New York from January 23-24, creating a requisite cold airmass that supported snow as the primary precipitation type with this storm. The connection of the northern and southern stream flow regimes then steered a potent, Gulf-originating low pressure system to the northeast. Strong to anomalous low- to mid-level dynamics drove impressive moisture transport from the Gulf and western Atlantic in and across the region the morning of the impending storm, Sunday January 25th. Snow began Sunday morning, initially with a large dendritic growth zone courtesy of persistent arctic air being filtered into the region from northerly flow about a nearby surface high to the northeast. However, as the storm tracked closer, its associated warm nose modified the thermal profile and shrunk and lifted the dendritic growth zone into the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere by the afternoon. Snowfall rates that initially looked to reach up to 2-4 per hour within laterally translating snow bands therefore became limited to 1-2 per hour courtesy of the disconnect between the best low-level forcing and the dendritic growth zone. Still, a widespread 10-20 of snow fell across the region between Sunday, January 25th and Monday, January 26th. ||The expansive impacts that this storm had on New York State as a whole led Governor Kathy Hochul to declare a widespread State of Emergency which encompassed all of our portion of eastern New York. NWS Albany received reports of numerous school and road closures in addition to traffic accidents across eastern New York. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency declarations, road closures, school closures, travel restrictions, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 12.4 inches.

Moisture pooled within valleys and lingered into the morning of March 4, at which point a transient ridge moved overhead, clearing skies and calming winds. This prompted dense fog to develop within the Yampa River Basin which persisted beyond sunrise.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread dense fog developed within the Yampa River Basin during the morning of March 4. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Northeast Shelby County near the James community.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines downed along FM Road 225 between Cushing and Douglass.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of March continued the trend of much above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation that characterized the winter of 2025-2026. Very little precipitation fell across the region, with all ten climate sites finishing the month with below normal totals. Likewise, temperatures were well above normal, with mean temperatures running 8-10 degrees above normal. As a result, drought remained, and worsened significantly in many locations. And in areas that had, to this point, remained drought free, drought developed and worsened rapidly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of March, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering approximately 40% of Colorado Zone 004 - Elkhead and Park Mountains. The remaining 60% of the zone was under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. With the 3/11 US Drought Monitor update, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to cover approximately 80% of the zone, with the remaining 20% under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. With the 3/24 update, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed, now covering 40% of the zone, with the remaining 60% under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. With the 3/31 update, the entire zone came under Exceptional (D4) Drought. No reports of impacts or losses relating to the drought conditions in the zone have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Banks County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Munson Ridge SNOTEL reported a snow depth increase from 40 inches at 16:00L on 2/18 to 50 inches at 16:00L on 2/19. The storm total snow amount for this event was 10 inches within 24 hours. This values exceeds the snowfall criteria threshold of greater than 8 inches falling in 24 hours for this forecast zone. Additionally, radar data showed frequent snow squalls over the area between the hours of 14:00L and 17:00L on 2/19. These snow squalls created winter storm conditions of blowing snow, wind gusts greater than 35 mph, visibilities at or below 1/4 miles, and whiteout conditions for multiple hours in the afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mostly scattered small limb debris but a few limbs larger than 3 inches in diameter were broken.

On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured at 2.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold upper level trough along with deep moisture and southeasterly winds allowed heavy rainfall to develop over the Koolau mountain range of Oahu, over Kauai, and over windward portions of Maui. On Oahu, the heavy rain developed and remained persistent for several hours, which led to flooding and flash flooding over the eastern and northern portions of the island. Particularly the Koolau Mountain Range was impacted. Portions of Maui and Kauai also experienced flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain began falling over the Koolau mountain range early in the morning and became anchored through most of the day. Widespread flooding occurred over much of the Koolau Mountains and eastern areas of Oahu. The following event summary includes a list of impacts that the flooding caused. A man in Kaneohe reported forty inches of water in his backyard with twenty inches of water in his house along the Keeahala Stream. The Kokokahi Gymnasium was reportedly flooded according to the broadcast media. Flood waters reportedly inundated homes in the neighborhoods bordered by the Likelike and Kamehameha Highways downstream of the Hoomaluhia Botanical Gardens. A business was flooded on Kamehameha Highway at the confluence of Opaeula Stream and Helemano Stream. The Likelike off ramp from the H3 Kaneohe-bound was closed due to flooding, and cars were flooded up to their windows. As a result, residents had to be rescued from their vehicles. A family on Kaneohe Bay Drive reported that rapid flood waters washed away the stairs leading up to their home. According to the City and County of Honolulu, a wastewater spill at the Ahuimanu Preliminary Treatment Facility occurred due to heavy rainfall and resulting inflow and infiltration into the wastewater system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. A strong portion of the jetstream overshot northern and eastern NM through Sunday, March 15th. While there was some blowing dust, visibility only fell to 5 to 7 miles in a few areas to include the Albuquerque metro area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The historically poor snowpack across Colorado through the 2025-2026 Winter season allowed for a shallow, weak snowpack to develop in the accident location. Recent fresh snowfalls in the weeks prior to the event allowed for a layer of soft, fresh snow to develop atop a stronger layer of storm snow, which was itself on top of the weakened initial snowpack. Strong winds in the days leading up to the fatal avalanche also provided wind-loading issues, continuing to weaken the overall snowpack conditions. Avalanche conditions in the Vail Pass area, where the fatal avalanche occurred, were rated at Considerable (3/5) at and above treeline, and at Moderate (2/5) below treeline.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: All information paraphrased from the Colorado Avalanche Information Center report on the incidence. The fatal avalanche was triggered by a solo backcountry skier in an area known locally as Boss Basin, in the area of Vail Pass, CO. Boss Basin is comprised of a series of northeast-facing slopes that are low-angled at the top, descending into steeper slopes below, ending at a flat bench. Conditions in the Vail Pass area on the accident day were rated by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center at Moderate (3/5) near and above treeline, with a Considerable (2/5) rating below treeline. The main concern was listed as Persistent Slab Avalanches, favoring slopes northwest through north to northeast facing at all elevation bands. The likelihood was listed as Likely, and size expected listed as Large to Very Large (up to D3), meaning these avalanches would be capable of burying, injuring, or killing a person as well as potential bury cars and break trees.  The avalanche forecast also included wording stating that humans could easily trigger avalanches where [they] find more than about 10 inches of snow, that avalanches that break on buried weak layers would be difficult to survive, and that remote triggering of avalanches would be possible. The backcountry skier that triggered the fatal avalanche, referred from here on as Skier 1, started the day at approximately 7AM local time in the Vail Pass Winter Recreation Area. Skier 1 used a snowmobile to access various terrain through the morning before heading toward Boss Basin around 1:15 PM local time, parking his snowmobile at the top of a nearby ridge. Skier 1 successfully made one descent and climbed back up the slope for a second. On the second descent, Skier 1 triggered the avalanche and was caught and buried near the toe of the avalanche with only the tip of one ski visible. As Skier 1 was alone, no rescue action was taken until family members noticed they were overdue at approximately 11:30 PM local time that evening. Members of Summit County Rescue Group searched through the night, finding the accident location by 6:00 AM local time the next morning. Two rescuers and a search dog were at the avalanche location by 8:00 AM, and the dog quickly alerted on an area of interest. In this location, the rescuers located Skier 1, now deceased, with their head buried approximately 1 foot below the snow surface. Skier 1 was dug out and eventually removed from the location by helicopter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Record warmth, coupled with little to no rainfall in March, led to rapid expansion of drought conditions across all of western and north central Nebraska. By the end of the month, areas of moderate (D1) drought conditions expanded to severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of March. North Platte saw its 3rd warmest, and Valentine had its warmest March on record. Valentine had its 9th driest and North Platte 19th driest March on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded to extreme (D3) drought conditions over the southern half of Sheridan County by the end of March. Over the northern half of the county, moderate (D1) drought conditions, deteriorated to severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The cooperative observer at Gordon 6N reported 0.59 inches of precipitation for March. This was 0.59 inches below the normal of 1.18 inches.

Storm total accumulations around 6-8 inches in southern Aroostook. Northern and eastern Aroostook, alongside Hancock county, had accumulations around 3-5 inches. The rest of the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Bangor region received about 2-4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 6 to 8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed eastern New York during the morning hours on February 7, 2026, ushering in an arctic air mass which remained in place through the morning hours on February 9, 2026. Localized strong winds occurred with the frontal passage during the early morning into the afternoon hours on February 7 which included a 66 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Voorheesville, a 55 mph wind gust at the Albany International Airport and a 53 mph wind gust at the New York State Mesonet site near Herkimer.||The combination of gusty winds and air temperatures falling below zero (as low as 20 degrees below zero in spots) resulted in wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) to fall to between 15 and 35 degrees below zero for many areas during the afternoon or evening hours on February 7 into the morning hours on February 8.||Despite less wind, cold conditions persisted once again during the overnight hours on February 8 into the morning hours on February 9 with air temperatures falling below zero once again (as much as 20 to 30 degrees below zero across some higher elevations) leading to wind chill values (feels-like temperatures) between 10 and 30 degrees below zero.

A low pressure system moving through Nevada on the 19th had a strong jet on the southern side of the low. This strong jet led to strong westerly surface winds across southeastern California, with peak gusts around 40-50 mph in many locations to as high as 66 mph in the southwest corner of Imperial County. California Highway Patrol (CHP) temporarily closed a portion of Interstate 8 to high profile vehicles in southwest Imperial County the night of the 19th through early morning on the 20th. There was a CHP incident report of a semi-truck on its side and blocking one lane of I-8, with one injury, but it was unconfirmed if the cause of the accident was strong winds. Wind gusts measured by the Mountain Springs Grade RAWS station, located along I-8 near the Imperial and San Diego county border, was reaching 50-60 mph from mid afternoon on the 19th through the early morning of 20th and peaked a couple of times at 66 mph, including around the time of the reported semi-truck accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol (CHP) temporarily closed Interstate 8 to high profile vehicles, due to high winds, from East Willows to Ocotillo beginning around midnight and the closure lasted until around 0800PST on the 20th. Around 2230PST, CHP had an incident report about a semi-truck on its side and blocking one lane of I-8, with one injury, but the report did not confirm if the accident was due to wind. Wind gusts measured by the Mountain Springs Grade RAWS station was reaching 50-60 mph from mid afternoon on the 19th through the early morning of 20th and peaked a couple of times at 66 mph, including around the time of the reported semi-truck accident. No damages or injuries reported due to wind being unconfirmed as a cause of the semi-truck accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: March 31, 2026, was a red-letter day for the southern tip of Texas in terms of drought.  Months of dry, top-five to ten warmest, low humidity, and breezy weather took its toll - and by the 31st, all areas were at Severe (D2) or higher, with 95% of the region at Extreme (D3) or higher, and a whopping 54.79% at Exceptional (D4) conditions.  Soon after, on Easter Weekend, the worst drought in 13 years would begin to crack with the start of spring rains, which continued through at least the end of May. ||Still, there were likely notable crop production/harvest losses in the Valley, and cattle herd production losses across the ranchlands, who had the longest duration of D3 and D4 conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Persistent dryness, heat, wind, and low humidity during the final week of March were enough to push Exceptional (D4) Drought into a large portion of the crop-rich sections of southern Hidalgo County.  Extreme (D3) conditions continued from Weslaco to Mercedes, and west of McAllen.  Unknown as of this writing are dollar damage/production losses to citrus and dryland crops that were struggling; planting had been delayed until rains came - which happened less than a week later.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Troup County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. Following the initial onset of D2 on October 21, 2025, the county experienced a brief period of mid-winter marginal improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels in late January. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 12 weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

There have been no reports of damage, fatalities, or injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Helen Wildfire ignited during the afternoon of March 3rd, quickly growing to over 1,000 acres on private land in Mora County west of Wagon Mound, NM. While NM 120 was temporarily closed to allow firefighters access to the wildfire, there were no other reports of damage, fatalities, or injuries. The fire reached a final size of 1,180 acres by March 5th before activity subsided.

With a strong wind field aloft already in place, showers and thunderstorms developed and formed into a line that moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland. This convective line brought damaging wind gusts and a tornado to the Eastern Shore.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm survey determined straight line wind damage near Millington Road with estimated maximum wind speeds of 80 to 90 mph. Along Coleman Road, the start of significant wind damage occurred as multiple trees were uprooted and large tree branches were snapped. A farm outbuilding also experienced removal of metal roofing that was scattered to the east into an open field. As the swath of wind damage continued, there was additional farm outbuilding damage near Mud Ford Lane as the roof of an outbuilding was removed with the debris being scattered to the east up to half a mile away. It was at this point that the damage path width was at its widest, with about one mile from the damage on Coleman Road to the damage on Mud Ford Lane. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tin roofing material removed from a fishing camp. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. A broad, positively tilted trough extending from the Central Plains into the Desert Southwest emerged on January 23rd. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. Liquid QPF values averaged over 3 inches, which led to crippling ice accumulations, especially from Oxford through Blue Mountain into Corinth. Widespread tree and scattered property damage occurred along with power outages that lasted several weeks in some locations across northeast Mississippi. Heavy sleet and snow resulted in transportation difficulties for up to two weeks across northwest Mississippi and widespread school cancellations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet accumulation of 1/2 to 1 inch, followed by 1/2 to 1 inch of ice.

Wind chills were as low as -1 at Greenville, 2 at Golden Triangle Airport, 3 at Louisville, 4 at Natchez; 5 at Columbus AFB, Hawkins Field in Jackson, and Vicksburg; 6 at Cleveland, Crystal Springs, Jackson, Meridian, and Starkville; 7 at Madison, 8 at Philadelphia, and 9 at Canton and Laurel. At least 278 residences and nine businesses were damaged or destroyed in the Mississippi portion of our forecast area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. Mandatory evacuations were issued for the community of Tyrone and surrounding areas on February 17th and were lifted on February 21st, and US Highway 54 was closed between Hooker and Tyrone during the height of the fire due to smoke and emergency equipment. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: No observations within the county. Estimated maximum wind gusts of 58 mph based on surrounding observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Southwest Grant Parish just north of the town of Boyce.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed near the intersection of Highway 126 and Highway 34 east of Dodson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mackinac Bridge was closed for winds and whiteout conditions, and county and state offices were proactively closed for the 16th, with a travel warning issued by emergency management on the evening of the 15th. Snowfall totals as high as 29 inches were reported in St. Ignace by CoCoRaHS observers. Blizzard conditions were observed at the Mackinac Island airport, KMCD, for several hours on the 15th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

The month of March continued the trend of much above normal temperatures and below normal precipitation that characterized the winter of 2025-2026. Very little precipitation fell across the region, with all ten climate sites finishing the month with below normal totals. Likewise, temperatures were well above normal, with mean temperatures running 8-10 degrees above normal. As a result, drought remained, and worsened significantly in many locations. And in areas that had, to this point, remained drought free, drought developed and worsened rapidly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of March, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering approximately 20% of Colorado Zone 005 - Upper Yampa River Basin, with the remainder of the zone under Severe (D2) Drought. With the 3/11 US Drought Monitor update, Extreme (D3) Drought expanded to cover 100% of the zone. With the 3/24 update, Exceptional (D4) Drought conditions developed, covering approximately 45% of the zone, with the remaining 55% under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. With the 3/31 update, Exceptional (D4) Drought expanded to cover 100% of the zone. No reports of impacts or losses related to the drought conditions in the zone have been received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Storm Survey team determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 105 mph embedded in a line of storms touched down just north of the Ascension/Assumption Parish line shortly after midnight on February 15th. This tornado started by snapping large branches and uprooting a tree on Te Nom Landry Rd and Highway 308 south. It continued moving east-northeast over open fields until reaching the intersection of Highway 3089 and Highway 70. Here, the tornado strengthened to EF-1 intensity where a power pole and tree trunk were snapped. This tornado maintained intensity as it continued moving to the east-northeast where it snapped a series of powerlines off of Baxter Rd on the south side of the CF Industries complex. The tornado then started to intensify to peak intensity as it crossed into St. James Parish while moving through mainly open fields before it hit a series of powerlines in an open field, snapping 4 lines. It maintained strength as it crossed another open field along Badger Rd before snapping another series of powerlines along Highway 18. The tornado appeared to weaken as it continued to move east-northeast across the Mississippi River. When the tornado reached Highway 3125, it partially snapped/bent another powerline. The tornado then moved into the marsh north of Highway 3025 before reaching Highway 61 where it uprooted another tree. The last damage point for this tornado is along I-10 where it snapped more large branches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted the White Mountains and High Terrain South of the Yukon River, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1200AKST on February 24, 2026. The storm produced heavy snow and significant blowing and drifting snow, leading to the closure of Eagle Summit on the Steese Highway starting at 0952AKST on February 22. Local Storm Reports confirmed the hazardous travel conditions and extensive drifting. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 0952AKST on February 22. Conditions gradually improved over the following days, and the final verification for the event was marked when Eagle Summit was safely reopened to traffic at 1054AKST on February 25. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lincoln County averaged 3.44 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.67 inches below normal, marking the 3rd driest start to the new year. It was the driest June through March stretch on record with deficits near a foot. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident on I-57 southwest of Watson, resulting in one indirect injury.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East Texas through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 0.50-1.75 inches, which was less than half of the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded farther southeast from Red River, Franklin, and Titus Counties to start the month into Western Bowie, Morris, and Camp Counties.

A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 8 Ball Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately 12 miles west of Clarendon, or ten miles west of Howardwick, along the US 287 corridor in Armstrong County. The fire was fueled by freeze-cured tall grasses and brush, driven by critical fire weather conditions including wind gusts up to 45 mph and low humidity. It exhibited rapid growth initially, spreading from a reported 200 acres to thousands of acres within the first 24 hours. Forward progress of the fire was stopped on the evening of February 18th but was contained on February 21st. In total, Eight Ball Fire burned 13563 acres across Armstrong and Donley counties.  There were evacuations in the Howardwick area on February 17th, which were lifted later on February 18th. US Highway 287 was closed from Goodnight to Ashtola for a couple of hours. Highway 70 was also briefly closed. The fire threatened approximately 1,100 homes and critical infrastructure. At the peak of the event, roughly 400 homes were evacuated.  The cause of the fire is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure trough digging southward down the west coast along with a 180 kt jet stream allowed a significant surge of Atmospheric River moisture along with strong southwest winds to advect into eastern Utah and western Colorado. This allowed for significant mountain snowfall across most mountains in eastern Utah and western Colorado where one to two feet of snow fell. Snowfall transitioned from a heavy wet snow with lower snow ratios in the early stages to an efficient power like snow with higher snowfall ratios due to the drastically changing temperatures. Some favored southwest slopes received up to three or more feet of snow as well. The strong jet allowed for strong winds and blowing snow in addition to the heavy snow falling with gusts in the 45 to 60 mph range on average across the mountains with some localized higher gusts above 70 mph. Due to the warm airmass, most lower valleys received rain or a mix limiting accumulations except the southwest Colorado valleys that saw a combination of heavy snow and blowing snow due to the wind once they received the colder air with a second shortwave and strong cold front towards the latter half of this three day storm event.  There were also some snow squalls in some areas due to the combination of heavy snow, wind and low visibility at times with the passage of the strong cold front toward the latter half of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 11 to 20 inches of snow fell across the area with 11.5 inches reported at Steamboat Springs 2.0 ESE. Winds gusted in the 55 to 75 mph range at Storm Peak Lab with a peak wind gust of 78 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
