A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS storm survey with additional support from a local storm report has confirmed an EF-1 tornado occurred west of Liberty, MS in Amite County. This tornado began near Berwick Cassels and Smylie Rd where minor tree damage was identified. Additional patches of increasingly more notable tree damage as wide as 175 yards occurred as the tornado tracked northeast along Smylie Rd. The tornado reached peak intensity with maximum sustained winds near 100 mph as it approached Enterprise Rd and Lower Liberty Gloster Rd where it snapped tree trunks and uprooted numerous trees. A manufactured observed minor roof damage. More tree damage from this tornado was identified where it crossed MS Hwy 24, moving northeast. A local storm report identified additional notable tree damage with a few uprooted/snapped medium to large pine trees near Rattlesnake Ln. This tornado evidently lifted near the Amite River just before reaching Old 24 Compromise Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of active winter weather, much of central Indiana remained entrenched in a cold, arctic air mass as the 19th began. While ambient temperatures were not as deep into the negatives as previous events, a tightening pressure gradient across the region resulted in significantly higher wind speeds, which served as the primary driver for hazardous conditions.||West-northwest winds gusting to around 25-30 mph across central Indiana ushered in the cold by mid-morning on the 19th, with ambient lows holding steady at mainly single digit degrees across the impacted northern and central zones. These intense breezes led to a primary period of criteria wind chills for several counties, including Warren, Montgomery, Clinton, and Tipton. Wind chills fell to -20 to -25 within the 19th 0800-1100 EST period, with the most severe conditions observed in Montgomery County where the combination of single digit air and 25 mph sustained winds produced a -25 wind chill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions,  Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural  activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred, despite a significant snow event, which produced little changed in drought conditions through the month leaving Severe (D2) drought and Moderate (D1) drought conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the region late on January 24th into early January 25th, followed by a surge of very cold Arctic air at the surface. As this shallow cold air mass advanced southward, it undercut lingering moisture and a warm layer aloft associated with departing precipitation.  During the early morning hours of January 25th, a brief period of freezing rain developed across portions of southeast Louisiana where surface temperatures fell below freezing while rain continued. This resulted in a light glaze of ice, generally less than one quarter inch, primarily on elevated surfaces such as trees and vehicles.  The freezing rain was short-lived, lasting approximately 3 to 6 hours before drier air aloft eroded the precipitation and ended the freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper level trough situated across the eastern Bering and Southwest Alaska helped support the development of a deep low pressure center south of the Alaska Peninsula during the second week of January 2026.  This low pushed a strong warm front into the Gulf of Alaska as the low center shifted eastwards with time, spreading widespread precipitation into Southcentral Alaska between January 9th and 10th.  The heaviest snowfall was observed through Thompson Pass, where over two feet of snowfall accumulation and whiteout conditions were observed due to strong northeasterly winds combined with the heavy snowfall rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Thompson Pass Department of Transportation reported total snowfall accumulations between 18 and 30 inches between 1/9 and 1/10/26.  Blowing snow and blizzard conditions were noted through the pass during mainly the onset of the event when gusty northeast winds were strongest during the evening to overnight hours on 1/9 to early 1/10.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of strong winds and light snow just the day prior, many locations saw a second cold front move through the region, producing gusty winds and light snow from the morning of the 18th through the morning of the 19th. Since there was little to no snowpack on the ground, any reductions in visibility depended on how heavy the falling snow was and how strong winds were. Conditions were generally worst in open, rural areas where the snowfall was able to blow around easier.||Winds gusted up to 45 mph in parts of western and southern Minnesota, and generally under an inch of snow fell across the region. Visibilities dropped to 1/4 mile in several locations, though it was often brief due to the showery nature of the snowfall. The snowfall was heaviest before the strongest winds developed, limiting overall impacts from this event.||The strongest measured wind gusts from January 18-19 were:|46 mph at KULM in New Ulm, MN.|45 mph at KBDH in Willmar, MN.|44 mph at KAXN in Alexandria, MN.|44 mph at KDXX in Madison, MN.|44 mph at KJYG in St James, MN.|43 mph at KMOX in Morris, MN.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds gusting to 35 mph and scattered snow showers resulted in periodic reductions in visibility as low as a 1/4 mile at times, though generally remained around 1 to 2 miles. The worst conditions were during the afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th daytime, temperatures were as low as -3F, while breezy winds were sustained up to around 10 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

A strong upper-level trough and an intensifying coastal low off the Eastern Seaboard combined to produce a fluffy snowfall event across southeastern Kentucky from January 30th through January 31st, 2026. The system was characterized by a persistent west-to-east oriented frontogenetic snow band that developed south of the Mountain Parkway. As the coastal system intensified into a powerful Nor'easter, the band pivoted and became nearly stationary along the Kentucky-Virginia border, leading to an extended period of light to moderate snowfall.||The highest accumulations were concentrated in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Harlan counties, where totals reached 4.0 to 5.0 inches. Because of the extremely cold Arctic airmass in place, snow-to-liquid ratios were high, ranging from 14:1 to 19:1, resulting in a very dry, powdery snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Impactful snowfall reached warning criteria across portions of Pike County. At 0855EST on the 31st, the State Police Post in Coal Run estimated 4.0 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system in the Gulf of Alaska pushed a strong frontal boundary northward into central Alaska bringing widespread snowfall and blizzard conditions. Winds strengthened ahead of the front, producing gusty winds through Alaska Range Passes and Dalton Highway Summits. Snowfall moved through the Interior from southeast to northwest, with the highest accumulations across the Alaska Range. Blizzard conditions developed in areas where falling snow and gusty winds were present. Effects from this storm were seen as far south as the Alaska Range, to as far north as the central/eastern Brooks Range.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Brevig Mission AWOS (PFKT) first met blizzard criteria at 12:56L on 1/10/26 reporting 1/4 mile visibility and winds gusting to 47 mph. The AWOS site continued to report reduced visibilities between 1/4 mile to 1/2 mile, and 40+ mph winds for over 36 hours as of 12:19L on 1/11/26.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure began to develop over the Southeast on the morning of the 22nd. By the evening it had moved to a position off the Carolinas and was deepening rapidly. Between 7 pm on the 22nd and 7 am on the 23rd, central pressure in the storm dropped from 991 mb to 966 mb. The intense low pressure combined with high pressure around 1045 mb building into Quebec to produce a strong pressure gradient across the region. The result was strong wind gusts through much of the day on the 23rd. While the heaviest snowfall remained largely over southern New England, the edge of the heavy snow did move into southern New Hampshire. The combination of the two produced blizzard conditions and near-zero visibility at times. While winds continued to gust into the evening, snowfall tapered off in the late afternoon hours on the 23rd. Key Messages: blizzard conditions, heavy snow, strong wind gusts, dangerous travel, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow managed to lift into parts of southern New Hampshire. The heaviest snowfall was on the morning of the 23rd into the early afternoon before tapering off. Though it was not frequent, Manchester-Boston Regional Airport did observed blizzard conditions intermittently into the early afternoon. Snowfall totals ranged from 5 to 9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.

High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.

Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totals as high as 28 inches at DeTour Village, with reports of as much as 34 inches on Drummond Island.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. A wide array of high winds in the 60 mph range affected the majority of the Texas Panhandle and some locations even experienced wind gusts over 70 mph. Damage to homes, structures, and overturned semi-trucks occurred during the afternoon as a result of these stronger winds. Blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions were also present thanks to the strong winds and several wildfires occurred across the Texas Panhandle as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Lavender Fire ignited on February 17, 2026, approximately five miles south of Boys Ranch in Oldham County. The fire began along the U.S. Highway 385 corridor. The fire was fueled by critically dry, waist-high grass and extreme wind conditions. It exhibited rapid growth initially, pushed by strong west winds with gusts reaching 50-60 mph. The fire quickly crossed key roadways, including FM 1061 (Tascosa Road), and spread toward the Canadian River. In total, the Lavender Fire burned 18423 acres across Oldham County and into Potter County.  Mandatory evacuations were issued for the Valley De Oro community and areas between Tascosa Road (FM 1061) and U.S. Highway 287 in north-central Potter County during the afternoon of February 17th. The Ady neighborhood was also evacuated on February 18th. FM 1061(Tascosa Road) at US Highway 385/281 was closed due to fires during the afternoon of February 17th and was reopened during the evening of February 18th. The Texas Department of Public Safety also shutdown Highway 287 on February 17th and US 87 was closed in both directions from FM 1719, just north of Amarillo to SH 354, south of Dumas. Approximately 250 people and homes were affected.  Incident report noted 40 homes saved, and 7 homes lost. In addition, Xcel Energy implemented a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) to reduce wildfire risk, which affected thousands of customers and resulted in some schools closing for the day due to lack of electricity and ability to feed students. The cause of the fire is undetermined.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry weather continued on February 18th and 19th. Winds were gusty but remained below high wind thresholds. Southwesterly sustained winds of 25-35mph occurred with gusts up to 45 or 55mph. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Somerset County averaged 2.62 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.43 inches below normal. Since June the precipitation deficits grew to over 8 inches. The USDM on March 31st had 78% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 22% in Extreme Drought (D3).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widspread tree and infrastructure damage across the county, with radial ice accretion of around 0.25 inches, resulting in nearly half the county's utility customers being without power by the morning of the 16th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado touched down along August Ln, just west of Polo Rd, where it damaged trees and a roof of a residence. It moved east along Polo Rd with sporadic tree damage. The heaviest tree damage occurred along Spirit of the Forest Ln and River Trace Rd where more than a dozen very large trees were uprooted or snapped. Periodic tree and large limb damage occurred along the remainder of the path until the tornado lifted in the Merrywood Estates subdivision. Path length was 9.3 miles. Max width was 75 yards. Estimated maximum winds around 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second week of February saw the first of 3 back to back major winter storms move across Alaska's West Coast and Interior. The week began with abnormally cold readings across the all of Northern and Central Alaska. By Monday a very strong storm system entered the Bering Sea and proceeded to move northeastward across the West Coast and the Interior of Alaska over the next several days. Initially the storm brought heavy snow and strong winds from the Bering Strait coastline down to the Yukon Delta region which resulted in blizzard conditions. As the storm moved deeper into the Interior the storm produced heavy snowfall and occasional snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began along the Bering Strait Coast shortly after midnight on the 11th and picked up in intensity as the night wore on. By mid morning the visibility reported by the Brevig Mission AWOS (PFKT) had dropped to 1/4 mile with wind gusts exceeding 35 mph. Shortly after midday full on blizzard conditions were occurring with blowing snow and the visibility dropping further to near 1/10 mile. During this time frame a max wind gust of 51 mph was re corded. By late afternoon conditions began to improve a bit, but the visibility stayed well below one mile for several more hours as strong wind gusts in excess of 40 mph continued.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A verified storm spotter on Old Murphy Dome Road reported a snow depth change of 17.7 inches between 2/17 and 2/19. This report was in direct correlation of radar observed snow squalls that occurred across the Middle Tanana Valley between the hours of 12:20L on 2/19 through 18:15L on 2/19. A peak observation was recorded at the Fairbanks ASOS site (PAFA) at 14:53L on 2/19 with sustained winds of 22 mph gusting to 36 mph, light snow, blowing snow, mist, and visibility at 1 mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An Arctic cold front ushered in the coldest air mass of the season to Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley with widespread cold temperatures between January 25-27, 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river brought snow followed by high winds, warming temperatures and heavy rain to the panhandle January 8th and 9th. A low pressure center developed along a triple point front as it tracked NE across the western Gulf of Alaska on the 9th. The low center deepened to 960mb as it approached the northern Gulf and the frontal system brought a period of high winds to the central and southern panhandle. This system brought with it heavy snow across the north, followed by a significant warm-up, heavy rain, localized flooding due to previous heavy snow blocking drainages, and avalanches. The flooding falls into the advisory level, but the rain was an additional impact due to the added weight of the snow on structures. Disaster declarations were expanded to more communities across the northern panhandle after this storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The mesonet station at the Annette Island Packing Company measured high winds during the afternoon and early evening of the 9th, including peak gusts of 68mph at 410pm. Other peak gusts across the island included 60mph at the Weather Service Office at 502pm, 86mph at the elevation site of Yellow Hill, 109mph at the elevation site of Chester Lake, and 63mph at the Walden Point mesonet station near the ferry terminal at 910pm.

Snow accumulations of 2 to 4 inches occurred across Knox and Stark counties, with lesser amounts to the south and east. Strong westerly wind gusts of 40-50 mph led to blowing snow and reduced visibility at times from Sunday evening through the day on Monday, March 16. Conditions gradually improved into the evening of Monday, March 16, as the winds weakened.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from September through December 2025 led to the development of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of Red River County Texas from the second week of January through the end of the month. During this time, rainfall amounts ranged from 4-7 inches, which was only around 25% of normal, resulting in considerable hardships from area agricultural producers. Pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires was also noted especially as lower humidities to end the year accelerated the drying of fuels. These conditions only accelerated during December as only a tenth up to a half inch of rain fell during the month throughout the county. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

Low pressure began to develop over the Southeast on the morning of the 22nd. By the evening it had moved to a position off the Carolinas and was deepening rapidly. Between 7 pm on the 22nd and 7 am on the 23rd, central pressure in the storm dropped from 991 mb to 966 mb. The intense low pressure combined with high pressure around 1045 mb building into Quebec to produce a strong pressure gradient across the region. The result was strong wind gusts through much of the day on the 23rd. While the heaviest snowfall remained largely over southern New England, the edge of the heavy snow did move into southern New Hampshire. The combination of the two produced blizzard conditions and near-zero visibility at times. While winds continued to gust into the evening, snowfall tapered off in the late afternoon hours on the 23rd. Key Messages: blizzard conditions, heavy snow, strong wind gusts, dangerous travel, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow managed to lift into parts of southern New Hampshire. The heaviest snowfall was on the morning of the 23rd into the early afternoon before tapering off. Though it was not frequent, neighboring Manchester-Boston Regional Airport did observed blizzard conditions intermittently into the early afternoon. Snowfall totals ranged from 5 to 9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of wintry weather impacted eastern Kentucky from February 22 into February 24, 2026, as a deep upper-level trough over the eastern United States funneled a moist, modified polar airmass into the region. This setup established a persistent northwesterly upslope flow regime, resulting in scattered to numerous snow showers. These showers were frequently cellular in nature and produced squall-like conditions at some locations.||Accumulations varied significantly across the region due to the convective and orographic nature of the event. While many locations near and west of Pottsville Escarpment saw only a dusting to an inch, higher terrain in the southeast experienced much more substantial totals. The heaviest totals were generally concentrated near the Pine and Black Mountains in the far east, where persistent upslope forcing maximized snowfall. However, isolated similarly heavy swaths were also noted upstream of these higher mountains over portions of Lee and Owsley counties, where convective snow bands persisted for extended periods. Despite high snow-to-liquid ratios of 15:1 to 40:1 for most locations, leading to dry, fluffy snow, the intensity of the showers caused slick and hazardous travel conditions on untreated roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Upslope snow was most significant along the ridges. Law enforcement estimated 4.0 inches of snow on top of Pine Mountain along US-421 at approximately 2,600 feet elevation. Big Black Mountain received an estimated 2.5 inches of accumulation, as per KYTC. Meanwhile, in the lower valleys, the local KSP Post at Harlan reported an estimated 2.0 inches. A member of the public at Lynch measured 2.0 inches and and emergency manager estimated 3.0 inches at Coldiron.

As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.

A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Wales AWOS site (PAIW) first reported blizzard conditions at 20:10L on 2/16 and continued through 17:39L on 2/17. Blizzard conditions were met at 23:10L on 2/16. Winds were consistently greater than 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 3 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 21:30L on 2/16 with 56 mph sustained winds gusting to 66 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and visibility less than 1/4 miles. Wind observations went down from 21:35L on 2/16 to 02:35L on 2/17, but winds were gusting well over 50 to 60 mph on each end of the outage. Additionally, blizzard conditions stopped briefly between the hours of 04:30L to 0800L on 2/17, but quickly started again shortly afterwards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began in Lauderdale County, Alabama and tracked into southern Middle TN. After the tornado crossed the Tennessee and Alabama state line, it traveled for ten more miles through Lawrence and Giles counties. In Bonnertown, many residences were impacted with several homes damaged. A few manufactured homes were moved off their piers, and a couple mobile homes were lofted or slid, but remained in tact. Other structural damage included missing awnings, removed shingles, carports thrown, and trees falling onto the structures. Several farm outbuildings were damaged. Numerous trees were snapped or uprooted. Beyond Bonnertown, the tornado continued east along Appleton Road, downing trees and destroying a chicken farm. The tornado then crossed into Giles County. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oxford County averaged 1.85 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 1.95 inches below normal, marking it the 3rd driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 75% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 25% in Moderate Drought (D1).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cooperative observer in Kalkaska reported at least 17 inches of snow; sleet also mixed in, resulting in difficulties traveling through and removing the snow. Around 0.1 to 0.2 inches of freezing rain accretion was also observed across the southern and eastern portions of the county.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Telfair County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 in fall 2025, the county experienced a period of mid-winter improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels on January 13. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 11 weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the original fall onset, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A record-breaking winter storm impacted the Northern Arctic Coast, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1145AKST February 20 through 2101AKST February 22, 2026. The ASOS located at Wiley Post-Will Rogers Memorial Airport (PABR) in Utqiagvik measured daily record precipitation on February 21 and February 22. Total liquid equivalent precipitation for the event exceeded three tenths of an inch, surpassing the entire monthly average for February of twenty-one hundredths of an inch. The storm produced hazardous conditions including periods of visibility reduced to one-half mile in snow and significant durations with visibility below one mile. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 1029AKST on February 21, when visibility at Utqiagvik dropped to one-half mile. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Bering Sea low moves into the Gulf of Anadyr, allowing for a strong front to move into Western Alaska. As the front approached the West Coast, strong east/southeast winds brought blizzard and whiteout conditions to much of the Seward Peninsula south. A secondary push of moisture brought by a shortwave system pushed off the Bering Sea low allowed for widespread heavy snow across St. Lawrence Island, the southern Seward Peninsula, and parts of the Western Interior. As the front pushed eastward across the state, snow squalls developed over portions of the Central Interior, leading to periods of heavy snowfall and gusty winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Kotzebue AWOS (PAOT) first reported blizzard conditions at 21:27L on 2/16 and continued through 02:15L on 2/18. Blizzard conditions were met at 00:30L on 2/17. Winds were consistently between 45 to 60 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 24 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 00:53L on 2/17 with sustained winds at 45 mph gusting to 70 mph, blowing snow, and visibility at 1/4 miles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful early season cold front spawned multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms. The first round occurred from late morning through mid afternoon, and focused mainly across northern Virginia into north-central Maryland producing scattered wind damage and a brief tornado. As the front itself crossed the region during the evening, a line of low-topped convection aided in the mixing down of an intense low-level jet, resulting in widespread 60 to 70 mph wind gusts near and east of the Blue Ridge and Catoctin Mountains.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down on Slacks Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper trough moved through the region in early February, spawning deepening surface low pressure offshore. A very steep pressure gradient resulted in strong winds across northeast North Carolina.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The C-MAN sensor at Duck Pier experienced strong winds as low pressure deepened offshore. Sustained winds were above 40 mph from midnight until 8:00 AM EST. Winds gusted above 40 mph from midnight through early afternoon with a peak gust of 59 mph measured at 6:42 AM EST.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Apparent temperatures dropped below zero degrees F during the morning of February 1. The sensor at Onancock, VA recorded a wind chill of -2 degrees F at 9:28 AM EST, while the ASOS at Wallops Island recorded a wind chill of -1 degree F at 7:54 AM EST. The AWOS sensor at Melfa, VA recorded a wind chill of -1 degree F at 6:35 AM EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened and became Severe (D2) during the month. A cooperative observed in Galesburg measured just 0.03 inches of precipitation during February, which was 1.84 inches below normal. Dating back to last September, the precipitation deficit for Galesburg was over 7 inches. The Severe Drought (D2) persisted through the end of the month. Streamflows and soil moisture values across the region ranged from well below normal to near record lows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two cold fronts associated with an elongated surface low pressure system swept across southwest Minnesota during the morning and early afternoon of February 18. Periods of sustained winds from 40 to 49 mph with gusts as high as 65 mph were reported across the area. Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of widespread wind gusts from 45 to 55 mph and light snow resulted in brief reductions in visibility to around one mile or less, resulting in difficult travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dangerous cold that began during the morning of the 31st across the South Carolina  Piedmont and foothills continued through the morning of the 1st. Winds gusting in the 20 to 35 mph range combined with air temperatures in the teens and single digits to result in minimum wind chills from -5 to 5 above across the area.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 42 mph at times at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Beresford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A coastal low stationed off the Tidewater of Virginia during the morning to afternoon hours of February 22, 2026 allowed for ample moisture influx from the Atlantic with light snow forming across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Light snow was mainly observed throughout the morning and afternoon hours with heavier snow beginning during the late evening hours and throughout the morning hours of February 23rd across portions of eastern Pennsylvania. This heavier snow was due to a combination of bombogenesis of the aforementioned area of low pressure and ample frontogenetic forcing that allowed for a heavy band of snowfall to form across portions of south-central Pennsylvania extending into the Susquehanna Valley. Winds associated with the pressure gradient of the rapidly deepening cyclone allowed for gusty winds, generally in the 30 to 40 mph range, across much of eastern Pennsylvania with highest gusts closer to the Atlantic Coast. Slick conditions and gusty winds from this system allowed for multiple accidents across eastern Pennsylvania, including one that resulted in one injury in Lancaster County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall began in Snyder County during the early morning hours with the heaviest snowfall falling during the evening hours of February 22nd and into the morning hours of February 23rd. Snowfall amounts in the county ranged generally between from two to four inches; however, a heavy snow band across western portions of the county allowed for localized accumulations between six and seven inches. Snowfall became lighter during the late morning hours of February 23rd before tapering off during the afternoon/evening hours. No incidents were reported due to this snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Gusty to strong west downslope winds developed along the east slope of the Front Range Mountains and Foothills during the morning of the 25th. Windy conditions spread east across the plains with gusts of 45 to 55 mph with a few local gusts reaching 65 mph. The strong winds combined very warm and dry conditions fuel two wildfires. One on the north Denver metro area and a second in northern Logan County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several wind gusts in the 58 to 62 mph range were recorded including a 62 mph wind gust in Briggsdale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The office received snowfall reports of up to 7 inches from the public, with the heaviest amounts estimated along the southwestern edge of the county. Measured wind gusts of 25 to 36 mph, combined with the heavy snowfall, reduced visibility to around one-quarter mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A highly anticipated, highly impactful Nor'easter struck eastern New York on the evening of Sunday, February 22 through the afternoon of Monday, February 23, 2026. Tracking along the East Coast and rapidly intensifying as it approached the 40 latitude/70 longitude benchmark, this system quickly gained national attention not only for its projected widespread blizzard conditions across many high profile, highly populated areas, but for the complexity of its forecast.||Confidence increased sufficiently for forecasters at National Weather Service Albany to upgrade prior issued Winter Storm Warnings to a Blizzard Warnings in Dutchess and Ulster Counties mere hours prior to snowfall onset. Once snow began, it didn't take long for rates to become moderate to heavy, particularly across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties, rapidly dropping visibility late in the evening of Sunday, February 22nd. As the core of the still strengthening storm drew closer, winds became gusty and reduced visibility further. The combination of heavy snowfall rates and frequent wind gusts between 25 to 40 mph made for on and off blizzard conditions, with visibilities falling below one quarter of a mile, from around 3 AM through nearly 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties. Snow finally began to gradually slow after 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 and eventually tapered off after 4 PM. The resulting snowfall totals across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties ranged from 7 to 18 inches.||As previously mentioned, this was a very complicated forecast. Model guidance in the days leading up to the event was highly variable in their depictions of the track and strength of the system. Ultimately, the track of the storm remained farther south and east than what was anticipated, leading to a fairly steep southeast to northwest gradient in snowfall totals. This also led to much lower snowfall totals than expected in many areas, including the immediate Capital Region, Taconic and Helderberg Mountains, Mohawk Valley, and Lake George-Saratoga Region. Outside of eastern Greene County, which ultimately received 7 to 17.5 inches of snow due to a combination of orographic enhancement and wrap around snow bands, snowfall totals within the Mid-Hudson Valley, Capital Region, Taconics, Helderbergs, Mohawk Valley, and Lake George-Saratoga Regions only amounted to about 0.3 to 6 inches.||Ahead of the event, the Governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, declared a State of Emergency for Albany, Columbia, Greene, Dutchess, Schenectady, Schoharie, and Ulster Counties in an attempt to keep residents off the roads. Consequently, many schools; local businesses; and roadways were closed, and there was a travel ban instated for all nonessential travel beginning at 9 PM on Sunday, February 22nd for Ulster and Dutchess Counties. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency, travel ban, road closures, traffic accidents, school closures, power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 6.7 inches and 3 to 5 hours worth of frequent wind gusts between 35 to 40 mph.

Once snow began, it didn't take long for rates to become moderate to heavy, particularly across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties, rapidly dropping visibility late in the evening of Sunday, February 22nd. As the core of the still strengthening storm drew closer, winds became gusty and reduced visibility further. The combination of heavy snowfall rates and frequent wind gusts between 25 to 40 mph made for on and off blizzard conditions, with visibilities falling below one quarter of a mile, from around 3 AM through nearly 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties. Snow finally began to gradually slow after 2 PM Monday, February 23, 2026 and eventually tapered off after 4 PM. The resulting snowfall totals across Dutchess and eastern Ulster Counties ranged from 7 to 18 inches.||As previously mentioned, this was a very complicated forecast. Model guidance in the days leading up to the event was highly variable in their depictions of the track and strength of the system. Ultimately, the track of the storm remained farther south and east than what was anticipated, leading to a fairly steep southeast to northwest gradient in snowfall totals. This also led to much lower snowfall totals than expected in many areas, including the immediate Capital Region, Taconic and Helderberg Mountains, Mohawk Valley, and Lake George-Saratoga Region. Outside of eastern Greene County, which ultimately received 7 to 17.5 inches of snow due to a combination of orographic enhancement and wrap around snow bands, snowfall totals within the Mid-Hudson Valley, Capital Region, Taconics, Helderbergs, Mohawk Valley, and Lake George-Saratoga Regions only amounted to about 0.3 to 6 inches.||Ahead of the event, the Governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, declared a State of Emergency for Albany, Columbia, Greene, Dutchess, Schenectady, Schoharie, and Ulster Counties in an attempt to keep residents off the roads. Consequently, many schools; local businesses; and roadways were closed, and there was a travel ban instated for all nonessential travel beginning at 9 PM on Sunday, February 22nd for Ulster and Dutchess Counties. ||Key Impacts: state of emergency, travel ban, road closures, traffic accidents, school closures, power outages.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Zone average snowfall of 8.3 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS on Beaver Island Airport in St. James reported near-blizzard to blizzard-like conditions all day on the 15th, with winds gusting as high as 61mph. This resulted in closure of many businesses on the Island due to conditions and trying to clear away significant amounts of snow. Cooperative observer was not on the island during the event, but reported total snow on the ground of 28 inches on the 17th with rumors of significantly more.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, drought conditions worsened and became Severe (D2) during the month. A cooperative observer in Olney measured 1.52 inches of precipitation during February, which was 1.05 inches below normal. Dating back to last September, the precipitation deficit for Olney was nearly 9 inches. The Severe Drought (D2) persisted through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
Low level frontogenesis developed ahead of a cold front, and an upper level shortwave provided lift to create a period of snow as it passed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The observer in Mack measured 1.1 inches of snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stacked surface low was located over northeastern MN. An area of deformation developed across the Dakotas and moved slowly into Minnesota. Forcing within the mid-levels allowed for moderate to heavy snow to fall across western MN. Additionally, due to the strength of the pressure gradient, wind gusts across much of western MN ranged between 35 to 50 mph. The rate of falling and blowing snow reduced visibility to whiteout conditions, making many roadways impassible. Snow lingered for several hours before finally dissipating the afternoon of the following day. Storm total snowfall ranged between a few inches up to 9.5 inches.||The highest measured snowfall totals from this event are:|9.5 inches ENE of Prior Lake (Scott)|8.5 inches in Shorewood (Hennepin)|7.7 inches in Waconia (Carver)|7.0 inches 1 E of Granite Falls (Chippewa)|7.0 inches 3 SSW of Elko New Market (Rice).||The strongest wind gusts measured from this event were: |50 mph at Canby Municipal Airport (Yellow Medicine)|48 mph at Redwood Falls Municipal Airport (Redwood)|48 mph at New Ulm Municipal Airport (Brown)|44 mph at Mankato Regional Airport (Blue Earth).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of mixed wintry precipitation fell at St. Cloud Regional Airport. CoCoRaHS observers measured an inch of snow 3 miles SSE of Big Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Garrett Fork exceeded its banks in places and flooded portions of Garrett Fork Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few large branches broken along North Factory Rd before LA 437.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought continued into March in northern and coastal Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. Frost depth at the beginning of March was roughly 27 inches at the Caribou office on March 9th, persisting to 26 inches on March 16th. Caribou had above average precipitation, but below average snowfall for the month of March. Bangor's climate site recorded below average precipitation and snowfall for March. At the end of February, northern Somerset, northwestern Aroostook, northern Piscataquis, southern Penobscot, and central and coastal Hancock counties, were included in severe drought. The Central Highlands region, eastern and southern Aroostook, far northern Hancock, and Washington counties were in moderate drought. In March, drought conditions remained status quo. No additional dry drinking well reports during March.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A lack of adequate precipitation in Interior Hancock led to prolonged drying conditions in February. Conditions were Severe Drought (D2) in late February and stayed in Severe Drought to the end of the month. Drought continued into April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong area of low pressure developed across the High Plains on the 17th and moved across the Dakotas on the 18th and into northern Wisconsin on the morning of the 19th. This led to a prolonged period of snowfall across the region. The track of this low was favorable for lake and terrain enhancement along the North Shore. Additionally, the strong low led to very gusty winds along the North Shore that led to a prolonged period of blizzard conditions that led to the closure of Minnesota Highway 61 for about 3 hours as crews were unable to keep up with the snowfall. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, New Hampshire remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 41% of New Hampshire were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. New Hampshire exhibited highly variable precipitation patterns in March 2026. While the state continued to observe below-normal accumulations and persistent hydrologic strain, central sections along the Merrimack valley and White Mountains experienced modest precipitation surpluses. The onset of seasonal thaw provided minor, superficial relief to shallow soil layers, but slow-responding deep groundwater tables remained severely depleted, with many monitoring locations lingering near or below the 25th percentile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coos County averaged 2.68 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.54 inches below normal, marking the 3rd driest June through March stretch on record with deficits over 8 inches. A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-0 tornado with maximum sustained winds estimated near 85 mph tracked across parts of southwest and central Washington Parish, south of Franklinton, LA. This tornado began near Sam Smith Rd where it snapped a rotted large hardwood tree. Additional tree debris and minor damage to skirting of a manufactured home was noted nearby. The tornado continued east-northeast where more abundant tree damage was identified including snaps of smaller tree trunks and branches along Daniels Rd, west of LA Hwy 25. This was where the tornado appeared to be at its strongest and widest, spanning about 75 yards wide. The tornado continued across the Bogue Chitto River, and additional minor tree damage was found by the survey team along LA Hwy 16, Tullos Rd, and Gene Williams Rd. Near Lee Rd and Thigpen Rd was where the last area of more concentrated minor tree damage was noted and this was the estimated end point of this tornado damage path. No additional damage was identified on Moore Rd nor LA Hwy 439, however, minor sporadic tree damage did continue farther east, north of Bogalusa, LA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On February 23rd, strong Nor'easter system moved northeast in the Atlantic, east of Cape Cod. It moved northeast through the Gulf of Maine, just south of Nova Scotia. Heavy snow fell during the morning into the evening of the 23rd for northern Hancock county, with totals roughly 4 - 8 inches. Bangor region roughly got 1 - 5 inches of snow.
