EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours.||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility of 0.5 mile reported at AWOS station KVIS Visalia Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a period of active winter weather, much of central Indiana remained entrenched in a cold, arctic air mass as the 19th began. While ambient temperatures were not as deep into the negatives as previous events, a tightening pressure gradient across the region resulted in significantly higher wind speeds, which served as the primary driver for hazardous conditions.||West-northwest winds gusting to around 25-30 mph across central Indiana ushered in the cold by mid-morning on the 19th, with ambient lows holding steady at mainly single digit degrees across the impacted northern and central zones. These intense breezes led to a primary period of criteria wind chills for several counties, including Warren, Montgomery, Clinton, and Tipton. Wind chills fell to -20 to -25 within the 19th 0800-1100 EST period, with the most severe conditions observed in Montgomery County where the combination of single digit air and 25 mph sustained winds produced a -25 wind chill.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures on the morning of the 19th were as low as 4F, while gusty winds were sustained as high as 26 mph...resulting in extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 16, 2026, gusty winds and snow squalls impacted eastern Nebraska. A shortwave trough pivoting across the Northern Plains drove an initial cold front and strong cold air advection (CAA) into the region. Behind a secondary cold front, enhanced atmospheric mixing tapped into higher winds aloft, transferring them to the surface. While widespread peak gusts ranged from 45 to 55 mph, isolated locations briefly recorded gusts of 58 to 62 mph. Additionally, horizontal convective rolls trailing the secondary front generated transient heavy snow showers, resulting in two distinct snow squalls. The intense winds within these bands caused localized blowing snow and rapidly reduced visibilities to 1/4 mile or less. The first squall moved through Cuming County during the late morning, followed by a second in Lancaster County during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KOMA ASOS measured wind gust of 62 mph at Omaha Eppley Airfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An open wave low pressure trough moved through Utah and formed a closed low near the Four Corners before pushing through southwest Colorado. Significant moisture ahead of this trough and cold air behind a strong cold front led to moderate to heavy snowfall across the mountains of western Colorado and southeast Utah, with the highest snowfall totals across the Uncompahgre Gorge area of the northwest San Juans due to favorable light northerly flow behind the closed low and temperatures within the dendritic growth zone.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 6 to 8 inches of snow fell across the area with 6 to 8 inches at both the La Sal Mountains and Abajo Mountains. A peak wind gust of 52 mph occurred at Abajo Peak.

Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall total at the cooperative observing station at North Central Michigan College was 29.0 inches, with 24.6 inches of this by the morning of the 16th. Other reports immediately near Little Traverse Bay were closer to 20 inches, with higher totals inland, especially toward Levering. Near-blizzard conditions reported at Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, on the 15th. Several reports of plow trucks getting stuck, and a greenhouse at Pellston Elementary collapsed due to the weight of the snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree fell onto power lines in Churchville.

A band of heavy snow, coupled with gusty winds and reduced visibility, impacted east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa beginning on the afternoon of February 19, 2026, and continuing into the early morning hours of February 20, 2026. The heaviest band of snow fell generally along a line from Lincoln, NE, to Omaha, NE, to Council Bluffs, IA, with a maximum snowfall of 10.3 inches measured 4 miles southeast of Bennington, Nebraska. Numerous snowfall reports in the 7 to 9-inch range were received across Lancaster, Douglas, Sarpy, Dodge, and Saunders counties in Nebraska, as well as Pottawattamie, Mills, and Harrison counties in Iowa.||The system was forced by a broad trough moving across much of the CONUS, accompanied by a potent shortwave trough that tracked into central Nebraska. As the system took shape, a surface low maintained impressive depth, progressing slowly across northern Kansas before deepening as it pivoted and ejected from northwestern Missouri toward Wisconsin. As the low passed to the south and east, strong height falls, warm air advection, elevated instability, and frontogenesis wrapped along its northern periphery, driving a narrow but potent band of snow into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Model soundings exhibited steep lapse rates, which supported convective snowband development and impressive snowfall rates across the area. This was coupled with wind gusts in the 25 to 35 mph range, frequently reducing visibility to below one-quarter of a mile in many locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.

An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Northeast Shelby County near the James community.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines downed north of Gladewater, reported via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted much of southeast South Carolina with significant snow accumulations on January 31st along with very cold wind chill temperatures persisting into late morning February 1st. The depth of cold air was sufficient to support snow as the primary precipitation type during afternoon and evening hours on January 31st. Snow accumulation ended by midnight on January 31st, but hazardous traveling conditions and very cold wind chill temperatures persisted through morning hours on February 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local criteria for an Extreme Cold Warning is temperature or wind chill of 10 degrees or less. A wind chill temperature of 10 degrees or less was ongoing at the Beaufort Marine Corps Air Station (KNBC), the Beaufort WeatherSTEM site (1190W) and the Beaufort Weatherflow site (XBUF) at 12 AM EST. The wind chill temperature first fell to 10 degrees or less at the Calibogue Sound Weatherflow site (XCLB) at 236 AM EST and at the Hilton Head Island Airport (KHXB) at 455 AM EST. The South Carolina Department of Public Health reported a fatality due to hypothermia associated with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Oglethorpe County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 on January 6, the county sustained 8 consecutive weeks at or above the D2 threshold as of the end of February. These conditions persisted into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blizzard conditions impacted Kivalina, where a Blizzard Warning was in effect from 0431AKST February 20 until 0843AKST February 22, 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Treutlen County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 in fall 2025, the county experienced a period of mid-winter improvement before conditions degraded back to D2 levels on January 13. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of 13 weeks at or above the D2 threshold since the original fall onset, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered small to medium branch debris. Some branches were 5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, drought conditions in Hall County intensified to D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions in February. Following the initial onset of D2 in January, the county sustained five consecutive weeks at or above the D2 threshold as of the end of February. These conditions persisted into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system tracked across the West Coast, North Slope, and Interior Alaska from February 20 through February 25, 2026. The episode began with widespread blizzard conditions impacting the West Coast and North Slope regions, where powerful winds and significant blowing snow reduced visibilities to near zero. As the system pushed inland, it transitioned into a heavy snow event for the Central and Eastern Interior. Notable snowfall reports included thirteen and one-half inches measured northwest of Ester and nearly nine inches reported by storm spotters in the Tanana Valley. Additionally, measurements from the Nenana Snotel indicated a seven-inch snow depth increase over a twenty-four-hour period during the height of the storm. These conditions created hazardous travel and significant impacts to infrastructure across the state. No fatalities or injuries were reported during this episode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm impacted the Southern Seward Peninsula Coast, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1104AKST on February 20 through 0900AKST on February 24, 2026. At 1710AKST on February 20, the Nome Airport ASOS (PAOM) reported one-quarter mile visibility in heavy snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty miles per hour gusting to thirty-two miles per hour. These conditions persisted through 1900AKST on February 20, with near-blizzard conditions occurring at times thereafter. The peak of the event occurred at 1818AKST on February 20, when the station reported one-quarter mile visibility in heavy snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty miles per hour and a peak gust of thirty-two miles per hour. FAA webcams and airport observations confirmed near-blizzard and whiteout conditions in Nome through the evening of February 20. The Rocky Point SNOTEL reported eight inches of snow accumulation between February 20 and February 21. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

A storm force low moved into the Bering on February 8. This low brought strong southeasterly winds to the Central Aleutians including Adak and Atka, which become more westerly by the afternoon. The strongest winds were observed during this time. Once the front pushed onshore by February 10, blizzard conditions were observed in the Kuskokwim Delta Coast for a time. Once the low approached the mainland, another period of blizzard conditions were observed in the Kuskokwim Delta on February 12.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bethel ASOS (PABE) saw blizzard conditions (less than or equal to 1/4 statute mile visibility, 45 to 50 mph gusts, and blowing snow) from 10:11 AM to 3:20 PM AKST on February 12.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of McCurtain County Oklahoma through the month of February. Rainfall amounts during February only tallied to 1.50-2.50 inches,  which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, extreme (D3) drought had expanded across the southern half of McCurtain County during the final few weeks of the month.

A drier than normal winter concluded with one of the driest Februarys on record across central and southeast Illinois. In Lincoln, only 0.08 inches of rainfall occurred during the month. Dating back to September 2025, precipitation deficits of 6 to 10 inches were common across the region. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought conditions worsened during February 2026, with a notable uptick in reported impacts and community restrictions (such as water rationing and burn bans). Streamflows, water levels, and soil moisture content ranged from well below normal to near record lows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to the Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was ongoing at the start of the month. Lincoln experienced their driest February on record, with the official observation recording just 0.08 of precipitation, which was 1.84 inches below normal. Dating back to last September, the precipitation deficit for Lincoln was more than 7 inches. Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across the county by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The beginning of February featured very cold temperatures and wind chills that began during late January across southwest Virginia. Temperatures as low as minus 8 degrees were recorded by a local cooperative observer in Clintwood during the first few days of the month, with similar temperatures observed in Buchanan County. The cold across this portion of the Appalachians was short-lived for the month, as temperatures quickly rebounded above freezing on February 3rd and once again by the middle of the month, where afternoon highs ranged in the 50s and 60s.

Southwest flow ahead of a deepening cutoff low over the Desert Southwest allowed for sufficient moisture to work into the area along a strong cold front. An additional low pressure system dropped in from the northwest, bringing colder air with it and pushing this cold front across the area. This resulted in moderate to heavy snowfall across the central and southern mountains of western Colorado and southeast Utah with the higher accumulations over the Uncompahgre Plateau and San Juan Mountains due to colder air and favorable orographics.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 10 to 16 inches of snow fell across the area with 11.9 inches of snow reported at Ouray 0.23NNW.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On January 9th, a surface low tracked northeast across the Central Great Lakes, into Ontario and then into Quebec. The occluded front associated with the system tracked across the Western and North Central New York areas on the afternoon of the 9th. Winds associated with the system started as strong downslope winds out of the southeast to south for the higher terrain near Lake Erie, but then shifted to the southwest where more winds were felt across a larger portion of Western New York. As the occluded front crossed the region during the afternoon, thunderstorms developed along the front as a line of showers came onshore from Lake Erie. While instability wasn't very favorable, there was a good amount of shear to support some severe thunderstorm potential. Severe thunderstorms were mainly confined to the Western Southern Tier up to the Western and Northern Finger Lakes. Between the strong to damaging winds from the system as a whole and the strong to severe winds from the thunderstorms, there was several reports received for wind related issues for the day.||Some of the notable winds associated with the system include: a 68 MPH at both the Niagara Falls Airport and at the New York State Mesonet in Batavia. A 64 MPH gust at Rochester Airport, 60 MPH gust at the Buffalo Airport and 59 MPH gust at the Dunkirk Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines downed in York.

Snow began falling during the early morning of the 31st and continued off and on for almost 24 hours, with periods of heavy snow becoming common during the afternoon. By the time the snow tapered off, 6 to 10 inch totals were reported across much of the area. An axis of around a foot occurred from east Charlotte to High Rock Lake and vicinity.

A series of passing frontal boundaries, surface lows and troughs during the week of January 18th resulted in yet another snowy period for Western and North Central New York. Most of the snow that fell was the result of lake effect, but periods of synoptic snow along with gusty winds at times resulted in primarily Winter Storm Warnings to be issued for this event. Lake Effect Snow Warnings were issued for two zones for later in this event, where snow was entirely lake effect. Snow squalls also occurred at times with the passage of frontal boundaries and troughs. ||Snowfall amounts of one to three and a half feet were common in the hardest hit areas, while widespread amounts of four to ten inches were common in most other areas across Western and North Central New York. Notable snowfall amounts include: 42.0 inches in Lacona, 36.0 inches in Lorraine and Mannsville, 29.2 inches in Eden, 26.0 inches in West Falls, 24.0 inches in Adams and Barnes Corners, 22.0 inches in Colden and Angola on the Lake, 19.5 inches in Elma Center and 19.1 inches in Copenhagen.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impactful and long-duration winter storm impacted Oklahoma and western-north Texas beginning on the evening of the 23rd and lasting into the morning of the 25th. A strong surface high, with origins across far northern latitudes, ushered in a very cold/sub-freezing airmass across the region by the morning of the 23rd. Over the coming 36 hours, increasingly strong west-southwesterly flow (and associated lift) fostered multiple waves of frozen precipitation across the forecast area. Initially, a mix of snow and sleet occurred, owing to a notable warm layer (i.e., warm nose) located between 700 and 800 mb. Eventually, by Saturday evening, continued mid-level cooling allowed for a transition to mostly snow with continued precipitation into Sunday morning.||While individual event narratives are not included for Clay County, with no direct surface observations reported during the event, at least 2 inches of snow/sleet accumulations and slick roadways likely occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The county received a combination of mainly sleet and some snow during this event, producing 1 to 4 inches of accumulation. The highest observed total (4 inches) was reported near Wichita Falls. Listed amounts reflect a synthesis of both remote sensing and direct observations.

Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum low temperature of -3 degrees Fahrenheit recorded with a minimum wind chill of -18 degrees Fahrenheit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter weather event impacted the Mid-South from January 23rd through January 25th, 2026, driven by a classic southern-stream cyclone interacting with entrenched Arctic air across the region. Downstream, strong surface high pressure was centered over the Midwest and Ohio Valley, promoting persistent cold air advection into the Lower Mississippi Valley and reinforcing a shallow subfreezing airmass.||Isentropic ascent intensified across the Mid-South beginning late January 23rd, as warm, moist air overran the shallow Arctic dome. This resulted in widespread precipitation developing from southwest to northeast across north Mississippi.||Thermal profiles across north Mississippi were marginal and vertically complex, with a well-pronounced warm nose between roughly 850���750 mb. This supported a mixed precipitation regime with crippling ice accumulations across portions of north Mississippi and large sleet accumulations across the Delta. ||The surface low that developed across Alabama was able to warm the surface in counties in closest proximity, resulting in mostly liquid precipitation in a few counties (Itawamba, Monroe, and Chickasaw), and there was even enough elevated instability for convective development. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Duck Creek below Whipple rose above a bankfull level of 12 feet on the afternoon of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest near 14.3 feet during the night. The creek then slowly receded back below bankfull level the afternoon of the 6th. While the creek was out of its banks, flooding of low sections of Route 821 below Whipple, the intersection of Kohl and Whipple Run Roads, Route 16 above Stanleyville, and fields next to the creek and around Whipple occurred.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line embedded supercell developed and tracked over north-central Maryland during the late morning into early afternoon hours on Monday, March 16, 2026. This storm was part of a much larger system that brought multiple rounds of severe weather to much of the eastern United States. Rotation was evident within the storm around 2000 to 3000 feet above ground on the KLWX WSR-88D radar, prompting a Tornado Warning as the storm moved from Frederick into Carroll County. The FAA TDWR TBWI showed this rotation quickly strengthen and lower to below 2000 feet just to the southeast of the mid-level mesocyclone being sampled by the KLWX WSR-88D. The tightened lower-level rotation persisted on TBWI for 1 to 2 minutes after the mid-level rotation on KLWX had notably weakened. It was beneath the tightening low-level rotation at around 12:02 PM EDT that the first evidence of tornadic damage was found. Several trees in a weakened state just southeast of the intersection of Hawks Hill Road and Beth Way snapped near the trunk, and fell toward the east, west, and north. The parent storm motion was northeast. The trees that fell were only around 100 feet apart at most, with an undisturbed landscape around it indicating an initially very narrow vortex perhaps no larger than about 25 to 50 yards in width. The tornado then crossed through open fields, lifting the south end of a long irrigation system and rolling it about 100 feet toward the north just east of Winters Church Road. After this, the circulation continued northeastward crossing several more fields and groves of trees, as well as Little Pipe Creek. The next visible and accessible damage was noted as the tornado approached and crossed MD-75 Green Valley Road near the intersection with MD-84 Union Bridge Road. Here, a couple dozen trees fell in opposing directions (southeast, northeast, east, northwest, and north). One large tree toppled onto power lines taking down a power pole and briefly trapping a motorist between the downed wires, pole, and downed trees. Several large pine trees at the intersection had their tops sheared off, falling toward the north, northeast, and east. Two trees on a hill just east of Mill Dale Lane fell toward the north-northwest, likely just outside the circulation but in its inflow as it passed across MD-84 Union Bridge Road. Meanwhile, an outbuilding just to the southwest of MD-75 Green Valley Road suffered a near total roof collapse, with the west-northwest facing walls partially collapsed inward. Similar to the trees off Mill Dale Lane, this outbuilding may have been just outside the tornadic circulation, with the damage a result of inflow winds into the vortex as it passed. It is at this point where the tornado reached its largest and strongest, with an estimated path width of 150 yards and peak winds of 80 mph. Despite the extent of the damage, only about one-third of the trees in its path at this point sustained visible damage, with no other visible damage to other outbuildings or the farmhouse at the nearby farm. A video taken from the Carroll County Emergency Operations Center showed a swiftly rotating lowering, likely the tornado in progress as it approached and crossed the intersection of MD-75 Green Valley Road and MD-84 Union Bridge Road, just northwest of their facility. Although trees in the foreground obstructed the view and could not confirm ground contact, the video was directly coincident with radar and the observed (convergent) damage. A few trees had their tops snapped off just northeast of MD-84 Union Bridge Road, but no visible damage was noted beyond this point. It is possible, based on the rotation signature on TBWI, that the tornado could have persisted for up to another mile over open fields, but the path length in this survey can only confidently conclude a path up to this point, approximately 1.68 miles in length. The National Weather Service Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office thanks Carroll County Office of Emergency Management for their assistance. Additionally, thanks to the trained spotters, media, and public that sent in reports of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

An upper level trough ejected east-northeast from the Desert Southwest into Northwest Texas and Western Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of February 14th, which resulted in the increase of very warm, humid air north across the region from the Gulf. In advance of this system, southwest flow aloft became established, with increasing instability at the surface and aloft coupled with strong wind shear and an approaching cold front enhancing large scale ascent across much of the Four State Region. As a result, showers and thunderstorms, some of which became severe over portions of East Texas and Central Louisiana, developed and spread east across the area during the late afternoon through the evening. Multiple reports of wind damage were received, with a brief, weak isolated tornado having been spawned in Southwest Grant Parish just north of the town of Boyce.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weak EF-0 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 75 mph briefly touched down just east of the Red River west of Highway 8 and Thompson Road in extreme Southwest Grant Parish just north of the town of Boyce. The tornado initially damaged a large hardwood tree where multiple branches were downed before also damaging a barn where a significant portion of the metal roofing was torn off and blown downstream towards the highway. Additional debris from the roof and some large branches were also found just east of Louisiana State Highway 8 before the tornado quickly lifted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Signficant tree and infrastructure damage across the county, with 0.2 to 0.4 inches of ice accretion reported over the area. Around 90 percent of utility customers in the county were without power by the morning of the 16th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. As an upper-level trough advanced into the Four Corners region, it induced southwesterly flow aloft and pushed a surface cold front through the local area. Convective development occurred in two distinct phases. Initially, surface-based supercells initiated along the advancing cold front in southwest Iowa, producing large hail. Later in the evening, a second round of elevated supercells developed behind the frontal boundary, affecting eastern Nebraska and extending back into portions of southwest Iowa. During the initial phase, storms in southwest Iowa produced measured hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Elliott. The subsequent elevated supercells produced even larger hail, highlighted by a report of 2.50-inch diameter hail near Laurel, Nebraska, along with numerous additional reports of 1.00 to 2.00-inch hail scattered across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public mPING report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

A potent low pressure system and cold front impacted a large part of the eastern United States on March 15 into the early morning hours of March 16, 2026. Ahead of this cold front, southerly non-thunderstorm winds strengthened across Middle Tennessee with 40 to 55 mph wind gusts common throughout much of the afternoon of March 15th. These winds caused several reports of downed trees and powerlines. The cold front along with a line of thunderstorms then approached from the west during the evening of March 15th and moved east through the early morning hours of March 16th. Damaging winds were the primary threat with this line of thunderstorms with many more reports of downed trees, tree branches, powerlines, and other damage received. This system was also responsible for three tornadoes, two of which were EF-1s. Fortunately, no injuries or fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado impacted portions of Clarksville. The tornado began in a neighborhood in Fort Campbell. Damage consisted of shingles off of roofs as well as some small tree limbs snapped. The tornado continued east toward Highway 41 where an overhang structure was blown down at a car wash. The tornado then moved northeast through additional neighborhoods and across Outlaw Airfield. Damage in the neighborhoods included rotten trees downed, tree branches snapped, downed fences, shingles blown off roofs, and occasional vinyl siding and metal fascia damage. The tornado crossed Outlaw Field and uprooted a few trees on a farm just northeast of the airfield. The tornado then continued northeast into a large residential neighborhood causing additional minor structural and roof damage to several homes and snapping small tree limbs. The tornado dissipated somewhere near the Tennessee and Kentucky state line in an open field south of Interstate 24 as no additional damage was found of Allen Road. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the evening of February 14, 2026, ahead of a cold front and moved eastward across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi overnight, maintaining organization as a QLCS with embedded circulations. The environment featured a moist and unstable airmass with increasing low-level shear, supporting the development of multiple brief tornadoes and widespread damaging winds. The first impacts occurred across southwest Mississippi late in the evening where several EF-1 tornadoes caused numerous snapped and uprooted trees, downed powerlines, and minor structural damage. As the line progressed into southeast Louisiana between late evening and the early overnight hours, additional EF-0 and EF-1 tornadoes were confirmed across East Feliciana, Ascension, St. James, Tangipahoa, Washington, Lafourche, and St. Tammany Parishes, generally producing tree damage with localized impacts to homes and infrastructure, including roof damage, a flipped RV, and snapped power poles. Widespread straight-line winds accompanied the convective line, with gusts frequently reaching 50 to 60 mph, resulting in numerous reports of downed trees, broken limbs, minor structural damage, and isolated industrial impacts, including damage to a fiberglass cooling tower in Ascension Parish. The line continued east into coastal Mississippi during the early morning hours of February 15, producing additional brief tornadoes and wind damage, while marine observations across adjacent coastal waters recorded thunderstorm wind gusts generally between 35 and 45 knots with isolated higher values.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Storm Survey team determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 105 mph embedded in a line of storms touched down just north of the Ascension/Assumption Parish line shortly after midnight on February 15th. This tornado started by snapping large branches and uprooting a tree on Te Nom Landry Rd and Highway 308 south. It continued moving east-northeast over open fields until reaching the intersection of Highway 3089 and Highway 70. Here, the tornado strengthened to EF-1 intensity where a power pole and tree trunk were snapped. This tornado maintained intensity as it continued moving to the east-northeast where it snapped a series of powerlines off of Baxter Rd on the south side of the CF Industries complex. The tornado then started to intensify to peak intensity as it crossed into St. James Parish while moving through mainly open fields before it hit a series of powerlines in an open field, snapping 4 lines. It maintained strength as it crossed another open field along Badger Rd before snapping another series of powerlines along Highway 18. The tornado appeared to weaken as it continued to move east-northeast across the Mississippi River. When the tornado reached Highway 3125, it partially snapped/bent another powerline. The tornado then moved into the marsh north of Highway 3025 before reaching Highway 61 where it uprooted another tree. The last damage point for this tornado is along I-10 where it snapped more large branches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Waldo County averaged 3.08 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.89 inches below normal, marking the third driest start to the new year, and the driest June through March stretch on record. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 7, a cold front approaching South Texas interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass already in place across the region, leading to the development of showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. Deep Gulf moisture transported northward by a strengthening low-level jet combined with strong upper-level dynamics and steep mid-level lapse rates to create an environment supportive of organized convection. Daytime heating ahead of the front further destabilized the atmosphere, with moderate to strong instability and strong deep-layer shear promoting storm development by late afternoon.||Storms moved into the region between approximately 4 PM and 6 PM, with conditions supportive of severe thunderstorms. The primary severe hazard was large hail, particularly across the Brush Country where lapse rates were steepest and instability was greatest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured quarter size hail near the intersection of Hahl Street and TX-16 with reports of power outages in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced continued dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) drought in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions intensified across north and central Georgia through February as the region's traditional recharge window began to close with significant deficits in place. While January saw a semi-active weather pattern, February was largely characterized by a more stagnant, dry pattern. Occasional cold frontal passages brought cooler air but failed to provide widespread, drought-improving rains across most of the area. This lack of meaningful precipitation caused the drought to not only persist but to expand further statewide.||Precipitation for February was markedly below normal for nearly the entire state. Widespread totals across north and central Georgia were limited to 1.5 to 4.5 inches (50 to 90 percent of normal), except in two swaths of higher totals. A stretch from Columbus to Macon to Swainsboro observed 4 to 7 inches of rain (110 to 200 percent of normal), as well as the Marietta to Snellville area in the Atlanta Metro which saw 5 to 7 (125 to 200 percent of normal). Despite the higher totals in some areas, streamflow and soil moistures struggled to revive following the waves of rainfall, and reports from agriculture partners maintained the dire grazing and pasture conditions. ||The U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) reflected a month of aggressive expansion of the D2 Severe Drought and D3 Extreme Drought areas. At the start of the month, 50.96 percent of north and central Georgia was D2 Severe Drought. By the end of the month, D2 or worse conditions covered 78.0 percent of the area. Most concerning was the rapid expansion of D3, which grew from roughly 2.9 percent to nearly 18.3 percent of the region. ||The drought persisted and intensified through March as dry conditions and lack of rainfall continued through what should be one of the wettest months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Hancock County remained under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions throughout February. By the end of February, the county had recorded a total of eight weeks at or above the D2 threshold, with drought conditions persisting into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The second week of February saw the first of 3 back to back major winter storms move across Alaska's West Coast and Interior. The week began with abnormally cold readings across the all of Northern and Central Alaska. By Monday a very strong storm system entered the Bering Sea and proceeded to move northeastward across the West Coast and the Interior of Alaska over the next several days. Initially the storm brought heavy snow and strong winds from the Bering Strait coastline down to the Yukon Delta region which resulted in blizzard conditions. As the storm moved deeper into the Interior the storm produced heavy snowfall and occasional snow squalls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began falling during the early morning hours of the 10th with the heaviest snow developing a few hours later. By midday strong winds and heavy snow had become established throughout the Lower Yukon Valley. The Marshall AWOS (PADM) began reporting blizzard like conditions with wind speeds exceeding 35 mph and the visibility lowering to around 1/4 mile around midday. By mid afternoon Blizzard conditions were ongoing and the visibility fell to around 1/10 mile as winds gusted as high as 47 mph. The blizzard subsided a few hours later, but heavy snow and strong winds kept the visibility at or below one mile well into the evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: March 31, 2026, was a red-letter day for the southern tip of Texas in terms of drought.  Months of dry, top-five to ten warmest, low humidity, and breezy weather took its toll - and by the 31st, all areas were at Severe (D2) or higher, with 95% of the region at Extreme (D3) or higher, and a whopping 54.79% at Exceptional (D4) conditions.  Soon after, on Easter Weekend, the worst drought in 13 years would begin to crack with the start of spring rains, which continued through at least the end of May. ||Still, there were likely notable crop production/harvest losses in the Valley, and cattle herd production losses across the ranchlands, who had the longest duration of D3 and D4 conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The March 31, 2026 Drought Monitor removed the last of Severe (D2) Drought along Padre Island National Seashore (barrier island, Kenedy County) and replaced it with Extreme (level 3 of 4, D3) conditions, except for the northeast corner.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Franklin County averaged 2.62 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.79 inches below normal. Since June, deficits grew to over 9 inches making it the driest stretch on record. The USDM on March 31st had 52% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 48% in Moderate Drought (D1).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slowly sinking cold front provided lift for thunderstorm development during the evening hours across north Mississippi. Partial clearing of skies prior to the frontal arrival resulted in moderate destabilization. Climatologically, February is cooler, which increases confidence in very cold air aloft. The lift from the front, an unstable environment, and cold air aloft raised a primary concern for large hail. Elevated MUCAPE values (up to 1500 J/kg) and steep lapse rates resulted in hail up to golf ball size to occur.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

A persistent polar airmass created a prolonged period of frigid conditions across eastern New York for the final days of January into the very beginning of February. Bitter cold air temperatures combined with periods of gusty winds and fresh, deep snowpack made for several days worth of dangerously cold conditions. ||The cold outbreak began early on January 29th where the most dangerously cold minimum wind chill values, or feels-like temperatures, were noted across the higher terrain areas of the Southern Adirondacks, Eastern Catskills, Mohawk Valley, and Taconics. However, by the following night, widespread dangerously cold temperatures overtook the region with minimum air temperatures ranging from -22 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit and minimum feels-like temperatures spanning -36 to -2 degrees Fahrenheit. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minimum wind chill of -31 degrees Fahrenheit recorded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant winter storm occurred across the southern, eastern, and northeastern United States during January 23-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved across Baja California toward the Desert Southwest and then across the southern to northeastern portions of the country during this time frame. This low pressure system was preceded by a strong arctic cold front, which dropped surface temperatures down to record breaking lows across portions of the southern United States, including the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Winter impacts were felt across nearly half of the country, with around an inch of freezing rain occurring at some areas across the southeastern US, inches of sleet across portions of north Texas, and up to one to two feet of snow for the Midwest into New England. This winter storm brought mostly snow to the region, but also there was some sleet mixed in across the southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle during the onset of precipitation across the region. Two to three day snow accumulation across the area ranged from just over an inch across the northwestern Panhandles to around nine to ten inches for the southeast Texas Panhandle. Frigid temperatures were also associated with this system and wind chill values dropped to as low as -20 to -25��F in the early morning hours during this time period. Temperatures remained below freezing across most of the Panhandles from early Friday morning behind the cold front passage until midday on Monday, January 26. The combination of the dangerously cold temperatures and impactful snowfall led to the closure of multiple school districts across the region as well as businesses and local government buildings. A few locations also saw infrastructure impacts such as pipes bursting in the region. Several counties also opened warming centers for the prolonged cold weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated one inch of snow fell around Boys Ranch. Overall the snow accumulation was minor across the county with most locations not seeing much over an inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The only winter weather event of the season occurred January 23-25. A mix of sleet and snow fell across the region, but sleet was the predominant precipitation type. The highest sleet and snow totals were north of Interstate 20, and the highest freezing rain totals were in our far eastern counties. In addition to the wintry precipitation, bitterly cold air accompanied the system meeting Extreme Cold Warning criteria through the 27th. Unfortunately 8 deaths were reported with this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sleet and snow totals between 1.2 and 2 inches were reported across Ellis County, along with reports of freezing rain accumulations up to 0.1 inches. The highest sleet and snow total was reported just southeast of Ovilla.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A historically damaging ice storm occurred across northeast Louisiana and the surrounding region. The corridor of heaviest ice accretion, with ice thickness measured at up to one inch, spanned from Richland Parish, including the area from Rayville to Delhi, northeastward through West and East Carroll parishes and the Lake Providence area. Tree damage in this region was tremendous, and several homes were damaged or destroyed by falling trees. Travel impacts persisted through Friday, January 30th in some areas. More than 143,000 customers in Louisiana lost power during the peak of the storm with thousands of power poles broken. Full power restoration took more than two weeks in the hardest hit areas, and it took more than one week for some customers in East Carroll, Franklin, Madison, Morehouse, Richland, and West Carroll parishes. Some meters remained unpowered for three weeks in the hardest hit portions of our area. The loss of electricity and the very cold temperatures that followed resulted in the loss of water in several communities.||Significant sleet accumulations, as high as 2 in Morehouse Parish occurred over parts of the area as well. In these areas, the weight of the accumulation resulted in the collapse of several sheds, carports, gas station awnings and the roofs of some buildings. Sleet remained on the ground across much of Morehouse Parish for an entire week.||Bitter cold conditions followed the storm, with temperatures as low as 10 to 15 degrees. Note: At several area weather stations, the lowest wind chill was unavailable because the anemometer was frozen and unable to record wind speed data.||One death due to hypothermia occurred in Franklin Parish.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain was observed across the parish with trace amounts of sleet mixing in concurrent with thunder. Trees and powerlines were brought down across the parish, and roads were hazardous with multiple vehicles having slid off the road. Freezing rain accumulation was estimated at 0.5 inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across the Ozarks but limited precipitation through the month allowed Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to develop across portions of far south central Missouri. Some expansion of drought conditions occurred through the month across portions of southwestern Missouri as well. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions,  Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural  activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred, despite a significant snow event, which produced little changed in drought conditions through the month leaving Severe (D2) drought and Moderate (D1) drought conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Duck Creek at Macksburg rose above a bankfull level of 13 feet on the morning of March 5th, then continued to rise to a crest around 14.5 feet that afternoon. The creek plateaued and then receded back below bankfull level the next morning. While the creek was out of its banks, flooding of the campground next to the gauge, Broad Street, Main Street, and fields and low-lying areas adjacent to the creek occurred.

A strong upper level weather system moved across the High Plains region and brought down very strong winds to the surface from the late morning to the late afternoon on February 17, 2026. Many locations across the Oklahoma Panhandle observed wind gusts o 60mph or greater. These strong winds brought blowing dust and extreme critical fire weather conditions as well. Several wildfires developed due to the dry grasses, low relative humidity and high wind gusts. One wildfire in Beaver County burned into Kansas and consumed over 200,000 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ranger Road fire ignited during the morning of February 17th near Highway 64, one mile southeast of Beaver, Oklahoma. This fire burned 283,283 acres across Oklahoma and Kansas. The fire was fueled by dormant, dry grasses and brush, driven by wind gusts of 60-70 mph and extremely low humidity (10-15%). These conditions created a fast fire environment, allowing the blaze to explode in size���growing from ignition to 15,000 acres in one hour to over 145,000 acres in just nine hours. It rapidly crossed the state line into Clark, Comanche, and Meade counties in Kansas. With strong wind gusts, this helped not only to spread the fire but limited aerial firefighting operations and complicated suppression efforts during the first stages of the fire's expansion. The cause is undetermined.  A firefighter was injured from being burned. In addition, a fire truck from Rosston Fire overturned in Beaver County and three fire fighters were injured, including one that suffered from 2nd and 3rd degree burns and broke his leg. There were 926 primary homes, 2 schools, and commercial/government buildings threatened. Evacuations: Mandatory evacuations for about 771 people that may have covered KS as well.  Gate and Knowles had evacuations on Feb 17th, and numerous outbuildings were destroyed in the fire.

Other notable amounts included 30 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL in Yellowstone National Park, 25 inches at the Burroughs Creek SNOTEL in the Absarokas and 24 inches over Togwotee Pass. High winds occurred along and East of the Divide as well as across Sweetwater County. Some of the more notable wind gusts included 82 mph along South Pass and 81 mph along the Chief Joseph Highway.
