EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful cold front spawned a narrow corridor of bowing line segments and line-embedded supercells, resulting in damaging straight-line wind gusts and tornadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A supercell thunderstorm moved through northern Montgomery and northwestern Howard Counties in Maryland during the evening hours of Wednesday March 11, 2026. The bow echo and associated downbursts/thunderstorm wind gusts caused sporadic tree damage from 60-80mph gusts, and created a brief EF-1 tornado, with focused tornadic damage near Cooksville in northwestern Howard County. On March 12, staff from the National Weather Service Baltimore/Washington Weather Forecast Office conducted a ground survey of the storm damage. The survey started near Damascus and extended through northwestern Howard County. There were numerous instances of trees uprooted or snapped, as well as damage resulting from downed trees. Tree fall was generally in the direction of the storm's easterly movement. Ground evidence suggested the thunderstorm produced scattered wind damage along its path from 60 to 80 mph wind gusts. However, as the storm continued east-northeastward, crossing the interchange of I-70 and MD-97, damage was observed 300 yards southwest of Old Frederick Road, crossing Old Frederick Road between Forsythe Road and Underwood Road. Here, along a treeline to the southwest of Old Frederick Road, approximately 50 trees were uprooted or snapped across an approximately 100 yard wide swath. Several of the uprooted trees fell at right angles to each other. Additional trees were snapped or uprooted near residences to the northeast of the road. The tornado appeared to have briefly lifted before touching down a final time at a residence on Underwood Road, where several trees were uprooted and snapped in multiple directions. This damage is indicative of a low-end EF-1 tornado. Additional to the ground survey, Doppler radar information from KLWX (Sterling VA radar) and TBWI (FAA BWI radar) was analyzed. Radar showed a powerful storm with broad rotation aloft along its path. From radar analysis coupled with ground observations, it was determined that an EF-1 tornado formed at 7:06pm and lifted at 7:08pm, with estimated winds up to 90 mph, a path length of 0.4 miles, and a maximum width of 100 yards. Special thanks to Howard County Office of Emergency Management for their assistance. Additionally, thanks to the trained spotters, media, and public that sent in reports of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Moderate (D1) drought to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

A line of storms swept across the state, producing scattered wind damage and eight tornadoes within the NWS Central Illinois coverage area.  The tornadoes occurred southeast of the I-72 corridor and all were rated EF-0 or EF-1. No injuries occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across the Ozarks with limited precipitation through the month. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri saw less amounts allowing Extreme (D3) Drought conditions to linger across far south central Missouri. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While some rainfall did occur, below the monthly average rainfall occurred for most of the county, which produced continued dry conditions. This allowed drought to remain Severe (D2) to Abnormally Dry (D0) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were blown down on Florida Court.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably warm temperatures, high wind, and low relative humidity combined with dormant fuels to promote conditions that supported the rapid spread of wildfire across portions of eastern Oklahoma in late February and early March. Large wildfires that began in late February continued into early March, with some additional wildfires beginning in the first few days of March. Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 10,000 acres in Latimer County, over 2500 acres in Pittsburg County, over 1600 acres in Pushmataha County, and more than 500 acres in Cherokee County and Le Flore Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drier and warmer than average conditions contributed to worsening drought across northeast Colorado during March 2026. D2 Severe Drought was introduced across Yuma county early in the month and persisted through the end of the month, with conditions deteriorating to D3 Extreme Drought by the last day of the month. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about one-half inch over far northwest portions of the county, to less than one-tenth of an inch over southeast portions. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from eighty-five hundredths to ninety-five hundredths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation for the month ranged from about one-half inch over far northwest portions of the county, to less than one-tenth of an inch over southeast portions. This was about three-tenths to eight-tenths of an inch below average. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about eighty-five hundredths to ninety-five hundredths across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

On the afternoon of March 6th, 2026, a lone supercell developed in La Porte County, IN and tracked northeast into Lower Michigan. The supercell moved through Cass, St Joseph, Branch, and Calhoun counties. NWS storm damage surveys from NWS Northern Indiana and NWS Grand Rapids found that the parent supercell spawned 4 tornadoes across Lower Michigan, ranging from EF-0 to EF-3 intensity. There were numerous reports called in to our office and videos posted on social media by storm chasers, broadcast media, trained spotters, and the public confirming tornado damage in Edwardsburg, Three Rivers, and Union City. The north side of Union Lake in Union City was one of the hardest hit areas with numerous homes taking on significant damage and trees sheared off. Several businesses in the city of Three Rivers also sustained notable damage. Unfortunately, there were multiple fatalities and injuries across Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photo received of hail up to a quarter in diameter. Photo taken on Marcellus Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from northeastern IN to north-central OH. Ahead of the cold front and within the warm sector, a line of multicell rain showers and thunderstorms generated sporadic straight-line convective wind damage in Wyandot and Marion Counties to Ashland County as the line persisted generally eastward in northern OH. Behind the line, a cluster of multicell rain showers generated a severe-caliber peak straight-line convective wind gust at the Lorain County Airport ASOS as the cluster of showers persisted generally northeastward. These showers and storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate effective bulk shear and weak MUCAPE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees downed in northwestern Crawford County, between Sycamore and Chatfield. Damage was caused by a line of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite drought improvement noted in February 2026, conditions deteriorated in March due to an abnormally dry month. Rainfall deficits for the month were over 3 inches with the least amount of rain measured across northwest Middle Tennessee. Clarksville in particular only measured 0.86 inches of rain during the entire month of March which was 3.46 inches below normal. By the end of March, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least the abnormally dry category. About 57 percent of the area was in at least moderate drought with about 7 percent of this area in severe drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions developed across Perry County in March 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. After initially only producing a few areas of wind damage, the line quickly intensified east of I-65. Around 1 AM CDT, several trees were downed across Coosa and Tallapoosa counties. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wide zone of tree and some structural damage was surveyed on the north side of Clayton and determined to be consistent with straight-line winds associated with a rear inflow notch and associated bow echo noted on KEOX radar. There were several areas of concentrated tree fall, particularly at a home on Highway 239 where at least 20 large pine trees were uprooted surrounding the home. A majority of the trees fell towards the east-northeast with the motion of the storm. The home itself sustained no obvious damage, but one tree did fall on a car in the driveway. Further west down 239, a large portion of the metal roof on the Barbour County Farm Center was blown into the parking lot, and several trees were also uprooted at the Barbour County Jail and Ventress Correctional Facility property along 239. A second area of concentrated tree damage was found further northeast on County Road 49, Kennedy Road, and Jacksonville Church Road. This damage appears to be associated with rear flank downdraft winds associated with a weak couplet noted on KEOX and KMXX radars. The vast majority of tree fall was oriented to the northeast or east-northeast, and the overall damage zone width on these consecutive roads was roughly one-half to one mile wide.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low in the Central Plains moved northeast into the Great Lakes late on Sunday the 15th. Ahead of its attendant cold front that passed later in the evening, a low level jet developed in the late morning and moved east. Daytime heating gave added energy to mix the lower levels of the atmosphere and bring strong winds from this feature to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and power lines were blown down across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous hail reports came out of southeastern DuPage County, mostly in the vicinity of Woodridge and Darien. Sizes ranged from 1 to 4 inches in diameter, though most of the reports were greater than 2.5 inches. Three separate reports of 4 inch hail were received out of this area.

Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced below average precipitation for the month of March, with some of the area receiving as little as 5 to 10 percent of monthly average rainfall amounts. Rainfall amounts ranged from only one quarter to one half inch across portions of Osage and Pawnee Counties, to as much as five to seven inches elsewhere. These dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand further in March. Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across all of Osage, Pawnee, Washington, Nowata, Creek, Tulsa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, Okfuskee, Okmulgee, and McIntosh Counties, and expanded across portions of Craig, Ottawa, Cherokee, Muskogee, Adair, Pittsburg, Sequoyah, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions affected portions of Choctaw, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

Critical fire weather conditions occurred on March 8th and 9th across the combined Panhandles. With continued lack of significant rainfall, grasses continued to be very dry and freeze cured across the region. With relative humidity values less than 10 percent and south to southwest winds of 15 to 20mph and gusts up to 40mph, this resulted in high fire danger across the region, and two fires that developed during this time. Fire weather conditions improved slightly on March 10th, where elevated conditions occurred. Winds were on the lighter side that day but did increase into the 10 to 20mph range and relative humidity values around 25 to 35 percent. However, any small spark continued to create wildfires given the dry nature of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Critical fire weather conditions occurred in Oldham County on March 8th as observed relative humidity values were around 6% at the Vega West Texas Mesonet. RFTIs of 5-8 were observed for nearly 6 hours that afternoon. The Maroon fire was sparked due to a passenger motorized RV. The fire was contained morning of March 9th with the total area burned being 745 acres. The fire did cause US Highway 385 to be closed between Channing and Boys Ranch for a period of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. However, well above normal precipitation occurred across the region during March. By mid-March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Clay County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rare strong and damaging downslope wind event started in the early morning hours of March 12th and continued through March 13th. Intense mountain wave activity was also a contributing factor to widespread wind gusts between 80 to 110 MPH across southeast Wyoming. Numerous reports of tree damage, power outages, and property damage including flipped over sixteen-wheeler tractor trailer trucks were reported to WYDOT and the National Weather Service. Areas of blowing dust also resulted in lower visibility on area roadways, which added to the already difficult travel scenario.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most observation sensors across northern Albany County reported strong wind gusts between 58 to 65 MPH. Peak gust of 65 MPH observed 12 miles northwest of Medicine Bow Wyoming.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front lifted northward through central Illinois on March 10th, allowing temperatures to soar into the upper 70s and lower 80s.  Record highs were established at Springfield (84 degrees), Peoria (83 degrees), and Lincoln (82 degrees)...all topping their previous highs set back in 1955.  As an upper-level disturbance tracked eastward out of the Plains and interacted with the departing front, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of a Macomb to Pontiac line during the late afternoon.  Some of these cells dropped giant hail (over 4 inches in diameter) across the southern part of the NWS Chicago County Warning Area (CWA).  Further south in the NWS Lincoln coverage zone, the storms spawned 3 tornadoes across parts of Knox, Stark, and Marshall counties.  After these initial cells tracked further northeast out of the area, a line of thunderstorms formed along an advancing cold front across the Illinois River Valley by late evening...with the storms eventually dropping south of the I-70 corridor toward daybreak on March 11th.  The line initially produced a downburst with 80-90mph winds in Havana in Mason County, as well as 2 tornadoes further east in rural Mason County.  Closer to sunrise, an additional tornado touched down near Yale in Jasper County before the storms exited into Indiana.

During the late morning through early afternoon of the 11th, an occluded surface low drifted eastward from near Green Bay to northwestern Lower MI. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward from northwest PA into southwestern NY, while the low's cold front swept eastward from northeastern IN to north-central OH. Ahead of the cold front and within the warm sector, a line of multicell rain showers and thunderstorms generated sporadic straight-line convective wind damage in Wyandot and Marion Counties to Ashland County as the line persisted generally eastward in northern OH. Behind the line, a cluster of multicell rain showers generated a severe-caliber peak straight-line convective wind gust at the Lorain County Airport ASOS as the cluster of showers persisted generally northeastward. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mansfield Airport ASOS recorded a peak straight-line wind gust of 66-mph from a line of rain showers.

Numerous wildfires occurred during this period, including ones that burned over 10,000 acres in Latimer County, over 2500 acres in Pittsburg County, over 1600 acres in Pushmataha County, and more than 500 acres in Cherokee County and Le Flore Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Fire initiated southeast of Angora Nebraska in eastern Morrill County during the afternoon hours of March 12th.  Aided by west-northwest winds, gusting over 50 MPH, fire raced to the east-southeast. By late evening on March 12th, the fire had tracked some 70 miles across Garden County into southwestern Arthur, far southwestern Grant, and northwestern Keith County. By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, 642,029 acres were consumed.  The Morrill fire was the largest fire on record in the state of Nebraska. One direct fatality occurred as a result of the fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire initiated during the early afternoon hours of March 12th east of Angora in Morrill County. Aided by 50 MPH winds, the fire tracked east of Garden County and spread across southwestern Arthur County. By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, approximately 64,590 acres of rangeland was consumed in the fire. The fire resulted in one fatality in southwestern Arthur County. One primary residence was destroyed, along with 6 outbuildings damaged in the fire. Two calf-cow pairs were lost in the fire in Arthur County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Damage was surveyed on Highway 26 on the eastern side of Hatchechubbee and determined to be consistent with a brief, EF0 tornado. The tornado tracked nearly parallel to Highway 26 where several softwood and hardwood trees were uprooted along various tree lines. The tornado ended near Colbert Road where some large branches were snapped.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions affected portions of Choctaw, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties during the month. A shortwave trough moved through the region on March 9, with a broken line of thunderstorms sliding east-southeastward across Central Alabama during the evening hours. These storms produced sporadic instances of wind damage across the northern half of Central Alabama, with the most concentrated area of damage being across Jefferson County. In addition to straight-line wind damage, an EF-0 tornado was confirmed in western Jefferson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service surveyed damage northeast of Haleyville from the Forkville area to the Ashridge community and determined it to be the result of straight-line winds. The most concentrated damage was observed at the intersection of Highway 195 and Little Crooked Rd around 5:35 pm CDT, where several structures were damaged. A furniture business sustained roof damage and had a glass door blown out, an open air hay shed was flipped onto an adjacent outbuilding, and a larger garage sustained roof and siding damage. In addition, a smaller three-car shed collapsed and fell into the larger garage. Just east of this, at least five trees were uprooted across Little Crooked Rd, with roofing tin from the garage blown into the fallen trees. This damage was all within 130 yards, with winds estimated up to 75 mph. No other notable damage was observed except for a few trees down along Jim Brown Rd approximately four miles to the southeast.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe Drought (D2) was in place at the start of the month. However, well above normal precipitation occurred across the region during March. By mid-March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Crawford County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a low wobbled east-southeastward from east-central NY to Atlantic waters east of Cape Cod and south of western Nova Scotia during the evening of the 22nd. This allowed the trailing surface cold front to sweep southward from mid-OH and toward the Middle Ohio River Valley while the upper-reaches of the front remained over northern OH. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches of the front released weak to moderate and elevated CAPE amidst steep mid-level lapse rates and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. As a result, scattered multicells and isolated supercells with small to severe hail developed over northern OH and persisted generally northeastward or eastward.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to penny-size about five-miles northeast of Millersburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent extreme to exceptional drought conditions continued across South Texas and the Coastal Plains throughout March 2026. The region experienced a prolonged period of below-normal precipitation, with many areas receiving little to no measurable rainfall and some locations reporting no significant rain since late summer. While isolated showers produced up to a few inches of rainfall in limited areas, these events were scattered and insufficient to provide meaningful drought relief. Above-normal temperatures, with daytime highs frequently reaching the upper 90s to near 100, combined with frequent windy conditions, exacerbated moisture loss and contributed to critically low soil moisture levels. Topsoil and subsoil moisture remained severely depleted, and environmental indicators such as lack of spring green-up, degraded rangeland, and diminished water sources highlighted the severity of the drought. Additionally, dry fuels and persistent winds led to elevated fire weather concerns. Overall, no significant improvement in drought conditions was observed during the period, with impacts continuing to intensify through the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced below average precipitation for the month of March, with some of the area receiving as little as 5 to 10 percent of monthly average rainfall amounts. These dry conditions, compounding on several months of dry weather, allowed the drought that developed across portions of the region in January to expand further in March. Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across all of Osage, Pawnee, Washington, Nowata, Creek, Tulsa, Rogers, Mayes, Delaware, Wagoner, Okfuskee, Okmulgee, and McIntosh Counties, and expanded across portions of Craig, Ottawa, Cherokee, Muskogee, Adair, Pittsburg, Sequoyah, Pushmataha, and Choctaw Counties. Extreme (D3) drought conditions affected portions of Choctaw, Delaware, Mayes, Wagoner, and Cherokee Counties during the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit, accentuated by one of the driest Februarys on record for central and southeast Illinois, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place across much of the region at the start of the month. However, a dramatic shift to a substantially warmer and wetter pattern during March resulted in considerable improvement in drought conditions. Most areas experienced rainfall amounts 2 to 6 inches above normal, and it was a top 5 wettest March for both Lincoln and Springfield. By the end of the month, the Extreme Drought (D3) was alleviated entirely, and areas of Severe Drought (D2) shrunk considerably.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Due to a multi-month precipitation deficit dating back to Fall of 2025, Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought was in place at the start of the month. However, well-above normal precipitation occurred during March, with the month finishing as one of the top 5 wettest in Lincoln. Lincoln recorded 6.16 inches of precipitation, more than double the monthly average. By mid-March, the drought had improved and was no longer classified as Severe (D2) across Logan County.

A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front moved across Central Alabama from late on March 11 into the early morning hours of March 12. After initially only producing a few areas of wind damage, the line quickly intensified east of I-65. Around 1 AM CDT, several trees were downed across Coosa and Tallapoosa counties. Scattered tree damage was also reported in Montgomery before activity quikcly ramped up after 2:30 AM CDT. Multiple areas of rotation within the line produced three EF-0 tornadoes across Pike, Barbour, and Russell counties, along with numerous instances of tree and structural damage from straight-line wind in these three counties along with Bullock and Lee. The line exited into Georgia by 4:30 AM CDT.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An area of damage was surveyed along John C Martin Rd to the south of Clayton and the damage was determined to be the result of a brief, EF0 tornado. The tornado touched down just east of a couple chicken houses where it damaged the roof of a metal outbuilding and ejected pieces of tin into a nearby field. The tornado continued east a short distance through the field then it crossed John C Martin Rd where multiple softwood trees were snapped and uprooted at the intersection of Hovey Rd and John C Martin Rd. A house across the street lost a few shingles and most of the windows were blown out on the front of the home. Several trees in the yard were snapped or uprooted. The tornado quickly weakened as it continued east-southeast into an open field where several large branches were snapped along a tree line then the tornado dissipated shortly after.

Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two separate storm chaser videos showed a brief EF-U tornado occurring in a field near Kensington Avenue and S 1000W Road in Kankakee Township. Swirl patterns identified in a field from Gray Sky satellite imagery were used to approximate the start and end locations of the tornado. There is no known damage that was caused by the tornado.

In addition to the thunderstorm outflow, isolated gradient wind gusts as high as 45 mph were noted across east-central Illinois, which also helped loft some dust. However, the worst visibility impacts were tied to the thunderstorm outflow. A Blowing Dust Advisory was issued.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported a plume of blowing dust impacting visibility along a gust front that was moving south from a cluster of thunderstorms over northern portions of Champaign County. Pictures showed this dust plume near Rantoul, then continuing south towards Thomasboro and southeast towards Flatville, with near zero visibility noted at both locations. A power pole was also leaning as a result of the associated winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree blew down onto a house along McClellan Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. Flooding continued in Athens through mid afternoon on the 18th while portions of Vinton County continued to experience flooding into the morning of the 19th. One to three inches of rain fell across parts of Washington, Jackson, and Meigs Counties while the rest of southeast Ohio generally received an inch or less. Severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds that downed trees and powerlines across southeast Ohio during the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Scattered trees fell down around the county. The most widespread damage occurred in the Oak Hill community where some trees fell on houses and approximately 1000 customers were without power.

Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over 2000 residents were without power from tree damage.

Along U.S. Route 42 near the Ohio River, several wooden electrical power lines were downed and extensive tree damage occurred. Just to the west of Tom Harris Road, a hillside had extensive tree damage as well. The tornado continued across rural areas east of Carrollton where additional damage occurred along State Route 36. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured wind gust at the Chanute Martin Johnson Airport ASOS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface frontal boundary stalled out over portions of Deep East Texas, Lower Toledo Bend Country, and into North-central and Northeast Louisiana during the early morning hours on June 20th, separating warm and very moist air near and south of the front from the slightly drier air to the north. A weak upper level disturbance traversed east atop the front throughout the morning through the early afternoon hours, which enhanced large scale forcing for the development of showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall. As this continued through the morning, the periods of heavy rain moved repeatedly over the same areas, which resulted in widespread amounts of 2-6+ inches falling over Deep East Texas, Central and Northeast Louisiana. This produced multiple reports of flash flooding across these areas before the storms weakened during the afternoon.||The following are storm total rainfall amounts across portions of North Louisiana: ||Desoto Parish: 4 miles northeast of Pleasant Hill: 4.78 inches.|Red River Parish: 2 miles south-southwest of Coushatta: 4.02 inches, 1 mile west-northwest of Hall Summit: 7.38 inches.|Lincoln Parish: Ruston: 4.21 inches, 1 mile North of Ruston: 5.07 inches.|Jackson Parish: 7 miles west-southwest of Chatham: 4.75 inches, 3 miles south-southwest of Jonesboro: 4.00 inches.|Ouachita Parish: 8 miles Southeast of Downsville: 4.58 inches, 7 miles west-southwest of Claiborne: 4.60 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water one foot deep covered Highway 155 between Martin and Coushatta.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning hours of June 13, 2026, severe thunderstorms tracked through eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa, producing hail and damaging wind gusts. The storms were driven by moisture return from a low-level jet impinging on a slowly sagging cold front. Elevated showers and thunderstorms developed over eastern Nebraska prior to sunrise before moving eastward into an environment characterized by sufficient instability and shear to support severe weather. Notable reports included quarter-sized hail (up to 1.00 inch in diameter) in and around the Omaha metro area���including Fremont (Dodge County), Douglas, and Sarpy counties in Nebraska, as well as Mills and Pottawattamie counties in Iowa. Measured wind gusts ranged from 58 to 60 mph, with an estimated wind gust of 70 mph recorded near Valley, Nebraska.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Official NWS Observation of a measured 58 mph wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: FM629 was closed between Bonnie View and Woodsboro.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed around Gadsden.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 11th slowed down a cold front moving through the area but also provided a focus for thunderstorm development. Strong instability, resulting from the warm temperatures and high moisture, ahead of the front fueled the rapid development of severe thunderstorms from the late afternoon into the evening hours. Thunderstorms initially developed over the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains where temperatures in excess of 100 degrees allowed updrafts to break through a capping inversion. Atmospheric flow was weak which allowed storms to move slowly and create torrential rainfall in some locations. Some roads within the city of Levelland (Hockley County) became impassable because of water over the road. The most significant thunderstorm developed over southern Lubbock County and moved southward producing severe wind gusts and wind damage throughout Lynn County. These winds caused minor but widespread damage throughout the towns of Tahoka and Wilson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary storm over the city of Levelland created heavy rainfall leading to excessive runoff. A report was received that portions of Texas Highway 114 were impassable within the city of Levelland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A photograph on social media showed hail in Meadow as large as golf balls.

The women were believed to be swimming when an incoming tide caught them unaware. Rescue swimmers were called out and pull them onto the shore. One was declared dead shortly after being rescued, with the other in critical condition before her death was confirmed the following Monday. Buoy 46042 off of Monterey Bay reported a wave height of 11 feet, with a west-northwest swell of 8.5 feet at 10 seconds and wind waves of 6.5 feet at 4.8 seconds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. The hot temperatures allowed storms to be high based producing mostly severe wind gusts. One of the more robust updrafts produced quarter size hail in the city of Lubbock. The most impressive storm of the evening was one that tracked near Slaton (Lubbock County). This storm generated a microburst with a peak wind gust of 110 mph measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet. A storm survey the next day revealed very localized damage around the mesonet site northeast of Slaton. Cotton crops were destroyed and mesquite trees were stripped. Additionally, irrigation pivots were damaged and partially rolled. A heavy gate damaged the fence surrounding the mesonet site but no damage to the sensors occurred. Later in the evening, a line of thunderstorms developed on an outflow boundary moving into the northwestern South Plains. These thunderstorms continued to produce intermittent severe wind gusts as they tracked across the northern South Plains into the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Memphis measured a severe wind gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided forcing for ascent, storms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. High atmospheric moisture content situated over saturated soils also created efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex as they moved into southwest Iowa.||As the severe complex traversed southwest Iowa, it produced several areas of severe weather. Isolated large hail up to quarter-size (1.00 inch) was reported. However, as the storms merged and grew upscale, straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 69 mph, which resulted in significant and widespread tree damage. Notable impacts included uprooted trees in Elliott, a mature walnut tree completely uprooted near Macedonia, and numerous large tree limbs snapped in Carson and Essex before the complex eventually tracked east and weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of thunderstorm wind gusts were estimated at 60-70 mph along with no power at a truckstop near Glenwood, IA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down along East 1800 North Road west of its intersection with IL-49 about 2 miles west-northwest of Fithian at 7:39pm CDT.  It tracked eastward along this road, significantly damaging several outbuildings before entering Kickapoo State Recreation Area where it snapped or damaged an estimated 250 trees with winds of up to 110mph.  The tornado continued eastward, then dissipated along Hungry Hollow Road just west of Danville at 7:53pm CDT.  Damage in Danville was determined to be from straight-line winds of 80-100mph.

One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated wind gusts of 75mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Several damaging wind reports and a tornado occurred across west central Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed just south of Highway 64 and west of Woodland W Road. It moved east-northeast, crossing Woodland W Road and Highway 64, where numerous trees were snapped or uprooted, some fell onto homes, power poles were snapped, and outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado then moved east across two neighborhoods just north of Highway 64. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped in these neighborhoods and some homes were damaged when trees or large limbs fell onto them. The tornado then turned southeast and crossed Highway 64 near the Highway 23 intersection, where large tree limbs were snapped and signs were damaged. It then crossed the Arkansas River and then Highway 23, and dissipated east of Santa Fe Trail and Aux Arcade Park Road, snapping numerous large tree limbs before it ended. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KSRX WSR-88D radar. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Lost Creek, a tree fell onto a house along East Main Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. Flooding continued in Athens through mid afternoon on the 18th while portions of Vinton County continued to experience flooding into the morning of the 19th. One to three inches of rain fell across parts of Washington, Jackson, and Meigs Counties while the rest of southeast Ohio generally received an inch or less. Severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds that downed trees and powerlines across southeast Ohio during the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Route 690 was closed due to flooding and State Route 681 was closed due to flooding beyond Hebbardsville Road. Several areas of flooding were observed in Athens with vehicles stuck in flood waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on a property just east of Clarks Creek where several trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado would continue east towards Baton Rouge Road, where several more hardwood trees had large branches broken off, with tree debris thrown onto both sides of the road. Additionally, a barn was completely destroyed in the same area. Sporadic tree damage continued along Baton Rouge Road, eventually leading to another barn where the walls completely collapsed and the roof was blown off. The damage to these outbuildings was consistent with |EF-1 damage, with maximum winds around 90 mph. Just a bit farther down the road, another outbuilding had its sheet metal roof completely ripped off, with pieces of sheet metal thrown about 50 yards into the nearby field. Some of the siding was also peeled off. ||The damage continued along portions of Baton Rouge Road, with extensive tree damage noted leading up to the intersection of Interstate 75. Most of the tree damage was primarily large branches that were broken off, but there was one hardwood tree that was uprooted. Just east of Interstate 75, additional tree and power pole damage occurred. ||The area of most concentrated damage occurred in several neighborhoods just east of U.S. Route 25. On Ridgelea Drive, there were multiple large, healthy trees that were uprooted and/or snapped at the base. On Humes Ridge Road, more large trees and wooden power poles were snapped. The most significant damage occurred near the end of the tornadic path on Waterworks Road, where a standalone, multi-car garage had the majority of its roof ripped off. Multiple sections of the garage had significant loss of its cinder block exterior walls, as well as some minor damage to the interior walls between car ports. Debris from the garage was spread out into the nearby field. Given the structural integrity of the garage, it was estimated that wind speeds up to 95 mph were observed in this part of the tornado track,| consistent with EF-1 damage. Finally, some minor tree damage was observed in the field just off to the east before the tornado ended.

Some of the more significant damage occurred near several neighborhoods south of Falmouth, where numerous trees were uprooted/snapped at the base, along with structural damage to several homes and outbuildings. Most of the observed damage from these buildings was a loss of roofing material, but there were a couple of outbuildings that had collapsed walls that led to a complete failure of the structure.|This type of damage is consistent with winds of 80-85 mph. There was additional tree damage in western portions of the county, as well as southeastern portions near McKinneysburg. When overlaying all of this damage with radar imagery, the likely cause of this damage was from straight-line winds as an enhanced surge in the winds created a bowing segment feature on radar, with the apex of this bow moving through the southern half of Pendleton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface frontal boundary stalled out over portions of Deep East Texas, Lower Toledo Bend Country, and into North-central and Northeast Louisiana during the early morning hours on June 20th, separating warm and very moist air near and south of the front from the slightly drier air to the north. A weak upper level disturbance traversed east atop the front throughout the morning through the early afternoon hours, which enhanced large scale forcing for the development of showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall. As this continued through the morning, the periods of heavy rain moved repeatedly over the same areas, which resulted in widespread amounts of 2-6+ inches falling over Deep East Texas, Central and Northeast Louisiana. This produced multiple reports of flash flooding across these areas before the storms weakened during the afternoon.||The following are storm total rainfall amounts across portions of North Louisiana: ||Desoto Parish: 4 miles northeast of Pleasant Hill: 4.78 inches.|Red River Parish: 2 miles south-southwest of Coushatta: 4.02 inches, 1 mile west-northwest of Hall Summit: 7.38 inches.|Lincoln Parish: Ruston: 4.21 inches, 1 mile North of Ruston: 5.07 inches.|Jackson Parish: 7 miles west-southwest of Chatham: 4.75 inches, 3 miles south-southwest of Jonesboro: 4.00 inches.|Ouachita Parish: 8 miles Southeast of Downsville: 4.58 inches, 7 miles west-southwest of Claiborne: 4.60 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water covered Rogers Road.

The storms were driven by moisture return from a low-level jet impinging on a slowly sagging cold front. Elevated showers and thunderstorms developed over eastern Nebraska prior to sunrise before moving eastward into an environment characterized by sufficient instability and shear to support severe weather. Notable reports included quarter-sized hail (up to 1.00 inch in diameter) in and around the Omaha metro area���including Fremont (Dodge County), Douglas, and Sarpy counties in Nebraska, as well as Mills and Pottawattamie counties in Iowa. Measured wind gusts ranged from 58 to 60 mph, with an estimated wind gust of 70 mph recorded near Valley, Nebraska.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 63 mph.

This storm produced a measured 58 mph wind gust in Mills County and caused damage to a garage door and machine shed in Pottawattamie County before weakening late in the evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed report of water covering Highway 35.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed around Fultondale, with several blocked roadways, including KC Dement Ave, Stouts Rd, and 34th St N.

Hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 11th slowed down a cold front moving through the area but also provided a focus for thunderstorm development. Strong instability, resulting from the warm temperatures and high moisture, ahead of the front fueled the rapid development of severe thunderstorms from the late afternoon into the evening hours. Thunderstorms initially developed over the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains where temperatures in excess of 100 degrees allowed updrafts to break through a capping inversion. Atmospheric flow was weak which allowed storms to move slowly and create torrential rainfall in some locations. Some roads within the city of Levelland (Hockley County) became impassable because of water over the road. The most significant thunderstorm developed over southern Lubbock County and moved southward producing severe wind gusts and wind damage throughout Lynn County. These winds caused minor but widespread damage throughout the towns of Tahoka and Wilson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Tahoka measured severe wind gusts from 2214 CST through 2225 CST. A peak gust of 76 mph was measured at 2219 CST. Minor, although extensive, damage was observed throughout the town of Tahoka. Damage mostly consisted of downed trees, damaged fences, and downed power lines. Downed trees obstructed several roadways throughout Tahoka and Wilson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple trees were downed near Whitney, including one blocking the roadway near U.S. Highway 11 at Frost Hollow Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An overall active pattern continued into June 2026 with daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received generally 3 to 8 inches of rain with the highest amounts favoring areas along and near the Tennessee River as well as areas near the Tennessee/Alabama border. It was also these areas that received more than their monthly normal precipitation while other areas continued to run a deficit. Fortunately, these repeated rounds of rain continued to improve drought conditions. For the first time since April 2026, none of Middle Tennessee was in extreme drought. About 11 percent of the area continued to be in severe drought, an improvement from 34 percent in May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions from May 2026 improved in June with severe drought conditions across most of Cumberland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were ranging between 75-79 mph for 10 min.

As this occurred, showers and thunderstorms developed and strengthened along this boundary as it continued southeastwards into the morning hours of June thirteenth with a few of these storms becoming strong in nature. This brought strong wind gusts to portions of the Albemarle Sound southeastwards to the Pamlico Sound and coastal waters near Oregon Inlet.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust was recorded on the Alligator Bridge XALI WeatherFlow station as thunderstorms moved through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Turkey measured a severe wind gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for thunderstorm development.
