EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down 2 miles southwest of Hoopeston about a half mile south of IL-9 and just east of North 1300 East Road at 7:44pm CDT.  The tornado overturned an irrigation pivot, then crossed IL-1 and damaged the roof of a tractor dealership.  As it skirted along the southern edge of Hoopeston, it damaged numerous trees and stripped shingles off a few homes.  The tornado then strengthened as it reached the intersection of IL-9 and North 1700 East Road where it snapped trees and damaged the roof of a home.  Further east, it flattened an outbuilding and damaged several more trees as it entered Cheneyville.  Significant damage to a couple buildings southwest of Cheneyville near the intersection of IL-9 and North 1900 East Road was determined to be rear-flank downdraft winds of up to 100mph.  The tornado dissipated southeast of the intersection of East 4200 North Road and North 2100 East Road at 7:52pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down at the Buckhannon Country Club, with some damage reported to the clubhouse.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. Flooding continued in Athens through mid afternoon on the 18th while portions of Vinton County continued to experience flooding into the morning of the 19th. One to three inches of rain fell across parts of Washington, Jackson, and Meigs Counties while the rest of southeast Ohio generally received an inch or less. Severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds that downed trees and powerlines across southeast Ohio during the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Route 349 was closed due to flash flooding near Lake Alma Road.

This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours and continued into the overnight hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado began just west of Martha Comer Drive, snapping several hardwood tree trunks before moving across the southern portion of a community college campus. The Kentucky Mesonet site on campus measured a wind gust of 114 mph. The tornado then tracked east and northeast across open field, eventually hitting several businesses along Kentucky Highway 9 (AA Highway), causing roof and structural damage. As the tornado approached East Maple Leaf Road, it quickly intensified. A couple of residences were severely damaged, including an outbuilding demolished with pieces and contents of the structure thrown between 100 to 200 feet. This included a 690 pound four wheeler and a large cinder block. A dual axle trailer jacked up on a block was pushed nearly 100 feet before being stopped by a cement barrier. A house suffered extensive roof damage. A property on the east side of East Maple Leaf Road was also heavily damaged with the debris in a convergent path. This included the roof and siding of a house, several snapped and uprooted hardwood trees, and a couple of hardwood fences that were posted well into the ground, that were pulled toward the circulation. Splatter was observed on the east and south sides of the home, further suggesting a cyclonic rotation. |The tornado then took a left turn toward the northeast as it snapped more trees and destroyed another portion of a fence. Additionally, on the southern side of the tornado, a couple of large barns were heavily damaged with both roofs a total loss, as outflow winds occurred on the south side of the tornado. As the tornado continued on a northeast track across a field, a metal outbuilding was pulled down a hill as the circulation neared. Additional tree damage was observed east of Hill City Road before the tornado dissipated. Sporadic tree damage was reported farther northeast toward the Ohio River as a result of outflow winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 30, 2026, a cold front extending from Minnesota into east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa interacted with an extremely unstable air mass featuring SBCAPE exceeding 4,000 J/kg. Strong capping suppressed widespread convection during the evening, allowing only a single storm to develop in southwest Iowa. This storm produced a measured 58 mph wind gust in Mills County and caused damage to a garage door and machine shed in Pottawattamie County before weakening late in the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet measured wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of excessive heat impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa from June 28 into June 30, 2026. The heat was supported by a strong mid- to upper-level ridge building into the central Plains. A warm front lifted northward across the area early on June 28, with temperatures rapidly rising in its wake. Daily high temperatures peaked in the upper 90s to low 100s, while southerly low-level flow ushered in dewpoints in the 70s. As a result, daily maximum heat index values peaked in the 105 to 115-degree range. In addition, little overnight relief was observed, with heat index values remaining at or above 75 degrees for at least 48 consecutive hours throughout the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Citizen Weather Observer Program (CWOP) measured peak heat index of 113 degrees within the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions remained across Stokes county through late June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, and February contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 20th to 30th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Standing water reported at the intersection of Texas State Highway 188 and County Road  85. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June saw repeated episodes of heavy rainfall interrupted by periods of dangerous heat. Weekly rainfall commonly ranged from 2 to over 8 inches, with localized flooding, saturated soils, and standing water occurring throughout the month. A tropical system during the third week of June produced another round of widespread heavy rain that further improved soil moisture, replenished stock tanks, and significantly improved pasture and rangeland conditions. These wet conditions repeatedly delayed hay harvest and other field operations. Despite the abundant rainfall, temperatures frequently reached or exceeded 100��F, with heat index values climbing to 105-110��F in some areas. By the final week of June, the first extended dry period in a while allowed fields to begin drying and agricultural activities to resume while drought conditions remained substantially improved due to the month's persistent rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to isolated D2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow-reinforced front moved into the area during the morning of June 22nd, and a dryline set up over west Texas. These features, combined with lift from a disturbance in the upper-level flow, yield thunderstorm development during the afternoon. One storm in rural Pecos County interacted with remnant surface vorticity from the decaying boundary and managed to produce a weak tornado. Another storm moved through Midland and produced up to ping-pong ball sized hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Park employees travelling on I-10 sent in a picture of a tornado in rural portions of Pecos County south of I-10. Other pictures from county EMS and from a nearby gas plant were received shortly after. The tornado tracked near the gas plant and a pipeline construction site. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed on Lister Ferry Rd and on Steele Station Rd.

The tornado began just south of County Road 325 N between County Road 400 E and 450 E where the roof of a barn was damaged. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drone footage from Cass County Emergency Management shows evidence of a tornado southeast of Lake Cicott. Dozens, if not hundreds, of trees were damaged by the brief tornado along with instances of property damage. The tornado appears to have begun over a wooded area near the termination of S CR 750 W (South of W CR 50 S). Here, a few trees were uprooted followed by an area of trees snapped near the base. Based on a convergent signature, the tornado appears to have curved quickly to the northeast, taking a few roof panels off a nearby outbuilding. Now approaching the bend in the road of W CR 50 S, the tornado appears to have intensified sharply with intense destruction and uprooting of trees, resulting in a clear convergent pattern. Nearby buildings appear to have avoided significant damage. On yet another sharp jaunt to the north, now headed to a farmstead, the tornado continued to destroy trees but also destroyed two barns, removed portions of roof off three other outbuildings, and completely destroyed a grain bin. Debris was gathered at the base of a nearby tree line. Aloft, a few large branches appear to have been snapped. Beyond this, trees are untouched suggesting the tornado lifted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An overall active pattern continued into June 2026 with daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received generally 3 to 8 inches of rain with the highest amounts favoring areas along and near the Tennessee River as well as areas near the Tennessee/Alabama border. It was also these areas that received more than their monthly normal precipitation while other areas continued to run a deficit. Fortunately, these repeated rounds of rain continued to improve drought conditions. For the first time since April 2026, none of Middle Tennessee was in extreme drought. About 11 percent of the area continued to be in severe drought, an improvement from 34 percent in May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from May 2026 improved in June with abnormally dry to moderate drought conditions across Perry County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours of June 5, 2026, severe thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across southeastern Saline County. Consecutive rounds of thunderstorms generated intense rainfall rates of 2.5 to 3.5 inches per hour, rapidly driving total estimated rainfall to between 5.00 and 7.00 inches. At 8:17 PM CST, emergency management reported 5.00 inches of rain and water flowing over multiple roads in this part of the county. At 9:35 PM CST, a public report indicated that Walnut Grove Creek was out of its banks. The following day, emergency management shared photos showing water- and mud-covered rural roads west of De Witt, along with flooded cropland. Roadways likely remained submerged into the early overnight hours.

A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down 3 miles southeast of Saybrook about a half mile north of the intersection of East 750 North Road and North 4100 East Road at 7:06pm CDT.  The tornado snapped a few large tree branches and peeled back the metal roof of an outbuilding before crossing into the National Weather Service Chicago County Warning Area (CWA) in southwestern Ford County just north of the Sangamon River at 7:07pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado began near Farm Road 1078, just to the northwest of Butterfield. NWS ground surveys concluded that the tornado path tracked to the east across Highway 37. A couple of old wooden power poles snapped or were brought down along Highway 37. Several uprooted trees and large branches snapped along the path. Sentinel 2 satellite data analysis revealed that the tornado continued to the northeast, crossing State Highway U, producing an intermittent path of tree damage about 6.6 miles long. Satellite data revealed the tornado was 350 yards at its widest point with estimated max winds of 85 mph.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 90mph touched down 1 mile east southeast of Fidelity. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 2, thunderstorm development was initiated by a weak backdoor cold front moving in from the northeast. The resulting activity was primarily concentrated within and surrounding the DFW Metroplex, leading to instances of marginally severe hail and strong to severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree limb was blown down onto a house, breaking the sunroof.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down near Lick Road around Tennerton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree fell on Power Lines on County Route 11/2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late on the night of June 18, coverage of showers and thunderstorms expanded in association with a cold front and a slow-moving shortwave trough. This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. As the front continued southward and the shortwave propagated eastward, a second round of showers and storms developed across Central Texas on Saturday, June 20. The primary hazard accompanying these storms was flash flooding, though a few instances of damaging winds were also reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media video showed numerous vehicles stalled in flood waters on Manana Dr at  I-35E in Dallas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 100 mph touched down southeast of the intersection of Sterns Road and Munger Road, in the Pratt's Wayne Woods Forest Preserve where one tree was blown down. The tornado quickly intensified and produced a concentrated area of damage at a shopping center at the intersection of Sutton Road and Stearns Road. Roofing material was peeled off of buildings, brick columns and metal fencing were blown out of a garden center and all of the gas pumps at a gas station were blown over. The tornado produced extensive tree damage as it moved northeast, north of Sterns Road. The tornado ended near Wilcox Drive, just east of the West Branch of the DuPage River.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a departing mid latitude upper trough, a lingering upper trough to the southwest of the Florida Keys, little or no convective inhibition and precipitation water above 2.1 inches resulted in concentrated heavy convective rainfall within the city of Key West.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS employees, members of the public, law enforcement and private industry streaming webcams verified extensive street flooding from heavy rainfall, with lowest streets with up to 2 to 3 feet of standing water.  At least one street closure and a few stalled vehicles were reports.  Flooding was most noted on North Roosevelt Boulevard near the Triangle intersection with the Overseas Highway, South Roosevelt down through Flagler Blvd., Flagler Avenue and several downtown poor drainage area streets.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 1.5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of excessive heat impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa from June 28 into June 30, 2026. The heat was supported by a strong mid- to upper-level ridge building into the central Plains. A warm front lifted northward across the area early on June 28, with temperatures rapidly rising in its wake. Daily high temperatures peaked in the upper 90s to low 100s, while southerly low-level flow ushered in dewpoints in the 70s. As a result, daily maximum heat index values peaked in the 105 to 115-degree range. In addition, little overnight relief was observed, with heat index values remaining at or above 75 degrees for at least 48 consecutive hours throughout the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KHNR AWOS recorded minimum temperatures above 75 degrees for at least 48 hours, paired with daily maximum heat index values peaking around 105 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought Conditions across Surry county through late June after several rounds of heavy rainfall. Drought conditions lingered however, because the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 20th to 30th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

Drought conditions lingered; however, after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June saw repeated episodes of heavy rainfall interrupted by periods of dangerous heat. Weekly rainfall commonly ranged from 2 to over 8 inches, with localized flooding, saturated soils, and standing water occurring throughout the month. A tropical system during the third week of June produced another round of widespread heavy rain that further improved soil moisture, replenished stock tanks, and significantly improved pasture and rangeland conditions. These wet conditions repeatedly delayed hay harvest and other field operations. Despite the abundant rainfall, temperatures frequently reached or exceeded 100��F, with heat index values climbing to 105-110��F in some areas. By the final week of June, the first extended dry period in a while allowed fields to begin drying and agricultural activities to resume while drought conditions remained substantially improved due to the month's persistent rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to isolated D2.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow-reinforced front moved into the area during the morning of June 22nd, and a dryline set up over west Texas. These features, combined with lift from a disturbance in the upper-level flow, yield thunderstorm development during the afternoon. One storm in rural Pecos County interacted with remnant surface vorticity from the decaying boundary and managed to produce a weak tornado. Another storm moved through Midland and produced up to ping-pong ball sized hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports from the public and from the media of up to ping pong ball sized hail on the southern and eastern sides of Midland. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed around Odenville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down in the vicinity of W 400 S and S 300 W on the southwest edge of Wabash. At this location, a number of wood power poles were snapped at the base. The tornado then raced northeast to Glendale Dr., McKibben St., and Barkley Dr. in Wabash where a number of homes of damaged. Homes lost shingles or even portions of the roof decking. Debris was lofted into nearby tree lines. One dual-axle fifth-wheel camper was tipped over. Insulation and dirt splatter was noted at a few different homes. Beyond Berkley Dr., damage was limited to instances of small limbs down in the neighborhood. Farther northeast, in the vicinity of Lafountaine Ave and W Waterworks Rd., an outbuilding was destroyed when its south-facing door appeared to be blown, in resulting in a collapse of walls and loss of roof panels. The tornado reached its peak intensity as it moved over properties on W Water Works road. Here, two injuries were reported as homes lost windows and roof decking, and a manufactured home was shifted several feet off its foundation. Dirt and insulation splatter was noted in these areas. Beyond S Meridian Rd., damage was once again limited to instances of trees or branches down. Powerlines were down near E Baumbauer Rd, where the tornado appears to have lifted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed southwest of Andrews, racing northeast toward Huntington. At least two properties on W Division Rd were impacted, as indicated by a loss of shingles, siding, and roof panels. Numerous trees were damaged as well, including trees snapped. Near the intersection of W 100 N and N 800 W, additional tree damage was observed and an outbuilding lost several roof panels. Along W 200 N, a number of trees were damaged at one property. Across the street, a mobile home lost its roof. The tornado appears to have lifted prior to reaching the Yake Subdivision, just south of the Wabash River. In the subdivision, isolated tree branches were down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of severe thunderstorm winds were observed from Levelland Municipal Airport to four miles south of Levelland. An Automated Weather Observing station measured a wind gust to 63 mph. A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site measured a wind gust to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall improved the Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) on June 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours of June 5, 2026, severe thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across eastern Cass county. Consecutive rounds of thunderstorms generated intense rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour, driving total estimated rainfall to between 2.00 and 4.00 inches. At 9:15 PM CST, a public report was received on social media of curb to curb flowing water near downtown Plattsmouth, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree knocked down a power line along County Road 16 in south Buckhannon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Siding was damaged on a mobile home in Burnsville.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on Union Hill Road, about six tenths of a mile north of Appalachian Highway, where a few hardwood trees were snapped and multiple limbs were broken off of trees. The tornado then moved through a heavily forested area towards the intersection of Lansing Road and Chenoweth Fork Road where more tree damage was noted. Tree damage continued in a concentrated path to the east-northeast along Chenoweth Fork Road before crossing Appalachian Highway and causing a fair amount of tree damage at a rest station on Meads Road. The damage noted in the first third of the tornado's path consisted of broken branches, snapped trunks, and uprooted mature trees. This was consistent with EF-0 and EF-1 damage. ||The tornado continued east through a forest with a large hillside that was not accessible by ground survey. This coincided with the first evidence of a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, Ohio radar. When the tornado came down the ridgeline just west of Elm Grove, the most significant damage indicators were noted. An entire section of hardwood forest, about 200-250 yards wide, was blown down. Drone photography and the ground survey confirmed all hardwood trees in this location were snapped, with none left standing. The estimate for this type of tree damage was around 115 mph, consistent with low end EF-2 damage.  ||Some higher-end EF-1 damage was observed as the tornado moved northeast off the hillside into Elm Grove, where the complete collapse of out buildings and barns occurred. Additionally, a significant portion of a roof off was lifted off of a house and large power transmission lines were snapped. After Elm Grove, the tornado turned southeast and caused additional damage near the intersection of State Route 772 and Appalachian Highway. The final evidence of tree damage was located on Sun Fish Creek Road, about a half mile south of Tennyson Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a morning cold front, clearing skies allowed for weak to moderate instability (500-1000 j/kg of CAPE) to build in across SW Idaho. With an upper trough just to the west, dynamics and kinematics were favorable for thunderstorm development. The 00z sounding that afternoon revealed a precipitable water value of 0.96 inches, well above the 90th percentile value of 0.83 inches. With high moisture values, heavy rain was a threat with any storms that developed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Timing estimated by MRMS, polygon focused on the area with the largest impact and intentionally kept broad. Numerous reports received of flooded roadways, some impassable; flooding also affected houses, public buildings, and infrastructure. The Caldwell Airport ASOS reported 1.06 inches of rainfall having fell in 15 minutes. A disaster was declared for Canyon County in the aftermath. There was an estimated 7 million dollars in damages to infrastructure.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a passing shortwave and a strong jet moving over western and central Wyoming brought numerous severe thunderstorms, with strong wind the main hazard from the storms. Some wind gusts reached hurricane force, with the strongest gust of 89 mph along Interstate 90 to the east of Buffalo in Johnson County. A 77 mph wind gust was reported in western Sublette County. Wind gusts over 58 mph also occurred in Fremont, Lincoln, Washakie, Park and Hot Springs Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts of 58 mph occurred in a rain shower over the Big Piney airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.25 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of excessive heat impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa from June 28 into June 30, 2026. The heat was supported by a strong mid- to upper-level ridge building into the central Plains. A warm front lifted northward across the area early on June 28, with temperatures rapidly rising in its wake. Daily high temperatures peaked in the upper 90s to low 100s, while southerly low-level flow ushered in dewpoints in the 70s. As a result, daily maximum heat index values peaked in the 105 to 115-degree range. In addition, little overnight relief was observed, with heat index values remaining at or above 75 degrees for at least 48 consecutive hours throughout the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KRDK AWOS recorded minimum temperatures above 75 degrees for at least 48 hours, paired with daily maximum heat index values peaking around 105-107 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June saw repeated episodes of heavy rainfall interrupted by periods of dangerous heat. Weekly rainfall commonly ranged from 2 to over 8 inches, with localized flooding, saturated soils, and standing water occurring throughout the month. A tropical system during the third week of June produced another round of widespread heavy rain that further improved soil moisture, replenished stock tanks, and significantly improved pasture and rangeland conditions. These wet conditions repeatedly delayed hay harvest and other field operations. Despite the abundant rainfall, temperatures frequently reached or exceeded 100��F, with heat index values climbing to 105-110��F in some areas. By the final week of June, the first extended dry period in a while allowed fields to begin drying and agricultural activities to resume while drought conditions remained substantially improved due to the month's persistent rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D1 by 6/9, ending inclusion in Storm Data.

Dry low-levels allowed several storms to produce strong downbursts, the strongest of which occurred in Seagraves, where damage to multiple buildings was reported.

A few thunderstorms managed to produce severe downburst winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet Station Belding 3NNW recorded several severe wind gusts, including a 75 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed in Carrollton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flood reported over Business Highway 77 north of Robstown on DriveTX interactive map. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line raced through northern Indiana and spawned numerous tornadoes. Most tornadoes were narrow and lasted less then 10 minutes. Additional areas of straight line wind damage were noted as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In an open area north of US 24 and east of State Route 9, an incredibly brief tornado appears to have touched down and impacted a single residence. Here, a two-story home completely lost its roof and debris was deposited into adjacent fields. Hardly any rafters remain and no roof decking is present. Intense dirt and insulation splatter was noted on the east and north side of the home. Additionally, a detached garage to the south-southeast of the home was demolished by the tornado. A property less then 500 yards to the northeast was not impacted, suggesting the tornado quickly lifted beyond 600 N.

Debris was lofted well northeast into the nearby fields. Debris was observed all the way to State Road 1 where additional minor tree and roof damage was observed. The tornado dissipated shortly after crossing State Road 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of very large severe hail affected the city of Levelland from 1918 CST through 1923 CST. Hail ranged in size from tennis balls to baseballs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mid level moisture pulled up ahead of an upper level disturbance over the western U.S. combined with intense daytime heating resulted in the development of high based showers and thunderstorms across west central New Mexico midday June 8th moving northeast across central New Mexico during the late afternoon and early evening hours. Little to no rainfall from these high based showers and thunderstorms reached the ground and instead resulted in erratic wind gusts and areas of blowing dust. Some of these virga showers and dry thunderstorms resulted in severe wind gusts at a personal weather station in western Albuquerque and at the Santa Fe Municipal Airport. The disturbance moved across the state on June 9th resulting in high based showers and storms across central New Mexico and wetter strong to severe storms across eastern New Mexico due to higher low level moisture across this part of the state. Severe wind gusts were observed at the Wild Rivers RAWS near Questa and at Conchas Lake State Park. Finally, very dry and gusty winds were observed across far western New Mexico with a brief high wind gust at Gallup Municipal Airport during the afternoon hours June 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at Santa Fe Municipal Airport measured a 71 mph wind gust caused by a virga induced microburst.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) and exceptional drought (D4) conditions across northeast Florida and southeast Georgia gradually improved through the month of June due to the shift to a more typical summertime sea breeze pattern bringing rainfall each day. The biggest impact was from the remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June which brought very deep tropical moisture, training storms and heavy downpours especially to southeast Georgia. 24 hour storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 2 to 10 inches from that event. This rainfall also helped the containment of local ongoing wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Despite some beneficial rainfall, Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued through the month of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An overall active pattern continued into June 2026 with daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received generally 3 to 8 inches of rain with the highest amounts favoring areas along and near the Tennessee River as well as areas near the Tennessee/Alabama border. It was also these areas that received more than their monthly normal precipitation while other areas continued to run a deficit. Fortunately, these repeated rounds of rain continued to improve drought conditions. For the first time since April 2026, none of Middle Tennessee was in extreme drought. About 11 percent of the area continued to be in severe drought, an improvement from 34 percent in May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from May 2026 continued in June across northeast Sumner County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few shingles were blown off a roof. Tree limbs that were 6 to 8 inch in diameter are downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement report of hail measured up to 1.75 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A number of organized thunderstorm complexes affected northwestern Arkansas during the month of June, which resulted in widespread heavy rainfall across the region. Most of the area received between five and fifteen inches of rain, which corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of average monthly rainfall amounts. As a result of this abundant, widespread heavy rainfall, severe (D2) drought conditions across portions of Carroll, Madison, Crawford, and Franklin Counties improved to abnormally dry (D0) drought conditions or better by the end of the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken band of thunderstorms developed across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 6th, as an upper level disturbance approached the region. Low level wind shear increased with the approach of the disturbance, and this wind shear combined with a moderately unstable air mass that had developed, resulted in some of the storms developing low level rotation, which supported the formation of three tornadoes across Sebastian and Crawford Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado developed in a large corn field north of Gun Club Road and east of Highway 59. It moved north-northwest across Hollis Lake Road, where a few trees were uprooted and numerous large tree limbs were snapped. It then moved across an oxbow lake, crossed Hale Farm Road, and dissipated. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KSRX WSR-88D radar. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 85 to 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Ellamore, a tree blew down onto Lantz Road.

This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of Ten Mile Creek rose out of its banks and flooded Ten Mile Creek Road. North of Minerva, portions of Four Mile Creek spilled out of its banks and flooded Four Mile Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rain occurred near Parkersburg in Wood County, where two to three and a half inches of rain resulted in flash flooding, impacted local roads and stranded vehicles. Additional areas of one to two inches fell across north-central West Virginia, as well as the southern coalfields. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds that downed numerous trees and powerlines across much of the state during the morning of the 18th. One notable area of damage was in southern Upshur County, where an NWS storm survey found significant swaths of tree damage indicative of up to 100 mile per hour straight line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed in and around Clarksburg and Bridgeport.
