EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Car submerged and stranded due to high water over road under bridge.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above normal temperatures and minimal precipitation continuing from late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of southeast AR. Through the month of June, D3 (Extreme Drought) and D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions expanded to affect Ashely and Chicot Counties as depicted on the U.S Drought Monitor. Average temperatures for the month ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal, and several daily temperature records were set especially late in the month. Observed precipitation values ranged from 50 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 10 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Chicot County intensified from D3 (Extreme Drought) to D4 (Exceptional Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough moving through the region combined with cooling temperatures aloft and daytime heating to facilitate shower and thunderstorm activity. A shower was strong enough to produce a cold-air funnel along the coast in addition to a short lived thunderstorm producing strong outflow winds in southwest Washington.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An unusually intense storm was able to generate a strong downdraft despite limited environmental support, which resulted in a narrow damage swath in Meadow Glade, WA in Clark County. NWS Portland conducted a damage survey in the affected area on Sunday, June 7. NWS storm surveyors found a small area at the  west end of the storm track which experienced heavier damage,  including a metal roof peeled back from an outbuilding and  multiple hardwood trees with trunks snapped multiple feet above  ground level. These damage indicators suggest a maximum wind speed  of just over 90 mph. As the storm moved east, associated wind  speeds weakened, producing minor damage including small downed or  broken tree limbs, lifted roof shingles, and damaged fences,  corresponding to wind speeds of 50-65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper-level trough moving through the region combined with cooling temperatures aloft and daytime heating to facilitate shower and thunderstorm activity. A shower was strong enough to produce a cold-air funnel along the northwest Oregon coast.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed on Morgan Rd, including one on a vehicle near County Road 13.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. With abnormally high amounts of atmospheric moisture, these thunderstorms were able to produce very heavy rainfall with rain amounts of five to seven inches reported across portions of Sumner and Robertson counties. This caused flash flooding for these areas, particularly in low-lying areas and those along area creeks. This MCS also produced severe thunderstorm winds which downed several trees and caused other minor damage before it weakened across southern Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain caused portions of the Parks subdivision in White House to flood with water up to the bottom of car doors, likely as a nearby creek overflowed. Extent of damages is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front backed south and westward through eastern and central NM during the early morning hours of June 14th. Abundant low-level moisture pushed in behind this front, reaching the Continental Divide. This provided fuel for thunderstorm development during the early afternoon hours of the 14th with on such severe thunderstorm producing severe wind gusts in Rio Rancho. Afternoon thunderstorms developed again over the northern mountains and along the central mountain chain of NM June 15th. There were reports of 8 inch tree branches down in Taos landing over power lines from severe thunderstorm wind gusts. Other thunderstorms advanced eastward off the Sangre de Cristo Mountains organizing into a line producing severe wind gusts through northeastern NM. This line of storms over northeastern NM eventually advanced all the way through east-central NM and into the TX Panhandle. Severe wind gusts reaching 60 mph or more were observed in Guadalupe County, including at Santa Rosa Lake State Park.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm outflow gusting to 60 mph at the Thompson Cattle Ranch ZiaMet station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed around Vestavia Hills and part of Hoover, including blocking one lane at Caldwell Mill and Camp Horner Road as well as a tree and power pole down along Rocky Ridge Rd at Lochridge. Additionally, a tree fell on a car on Indian Hill Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of a funnel cloud 4 miles east of Swanton.

A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter estimated wind gusts of 75mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 105 mph touched down along County Road E 2200 North, west of Route 23. The tornado may not have been fully condensed to the ground or consisted of intermittent touchdowns along the first two thirds of the path where only minor tree damage was noted. A photo from a storm chaser showed a couple of mesovortices crossing Interstate 55. Minor tree damage continued as the tornado moved through Odell and areas west of Route 47. Based on storm chaser videos, the tornado appeared to rapidly strengthen and widen while crossing Route 47. Sporadic tree damage continued along the path until utility poles were broken and leaning along E 3000 North Road and N 3100 East Road. Drone imagery showed swirl marks in fields west of N 3200 East Road. Several outbuildings and a garage were destroyed just east of N 3200 East Road and a house had a significant portion of its roof structure removed. Several farm buildings and a garage were destroyed just east of N 3300 East Road, south of Route 17. A large barn was tipped on its side. Significant tree damage also occurred. The porch roof on a house collapsed along Route 17 in Blair. A wall of a farm building was removed with debris blown into a field. The tornado continued northeast and ended in a field near railroad tracks, just south of the Livingston LaSalle County line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall supported gradually improving drought conditions across much of northwest Kansas in June. D2 Severe Drought impacted Cheyenne, Rawlins, and Thomas counties the first day of the month, with improvement noted thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted Graham county through the 8th, with improvement thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted Sheridan and Gove counties through the 22nd, with improvement thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted the southern halves of Greeley and Wichita counties through the 29th, with improvement thereafter. Finally, D2 Severe Drought to D3 Extreme Drought impacted Decatur and Norton counties the entire month. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from a little over one inch over western portions of Greeley county, to about ten inches over north-central Gove and south-central Thomas counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and one-half inches over western Greeley county, to about three and one-half inches over northeast Norton county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about one to four inches, highest over central and southeast portions of the county. These values are about one and one-half inches below average to one inch above average. Normal June precipitation across the county is about two and three-quarters of an inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) to severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across central and northern Minnesota during June 2026, with abnormally dry (D0) areas in Koochiching and St. Louis counties deteriorating into moderate and severe drought, while existing moderate drought across Aitkin, Cass, Crow Wing, and Itasca counties intensified to severe drought covering up to 97 percent of individual counties. High spatial variability in precipitation occurred across the region; while locations such as Leech Lake (5.55 inches) and Brimson 2S (5.76 inches) received above-average rainfall, substantial deficits elsewhere���most notably at International Falls Intl Airport (1.37 inches, 2.41 inches below average) and Pokegama Dam (2.53 inches, 2.10 inches below average)���allowed severe drought to establish a firm foothold across the area by the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions covered around 54 percent of Itasca County at the beginning of June, but conditions degraded further throughout the month. Moderate drought expanded to cover the entire county, while severe (D2) drought developed and expanded to around 82 percent coverage by the end of the month. The cooperative observers at Northome 3S, Grand Rapids Forestry Lab, and Pokegama Dam recorded 3.89, 3.66, and 2.53 inches of precipitation, respectively. These values were 0.34, 1.04, and 2.10 inches below average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over one thousand homes were without power as a result of nearby downed trees and power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th. This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia on the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeastward the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid-morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||Severe thunderstorms produced strong winds during this time, which downed trees and caused power outages across portions of northeast Kentucky on the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down in the central part of the county, including along Allcorn Road and Brushy Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a quasi-stationary front extending across southern Missouri and northwest Tennessee during the afternoon hours of June 13, 2026.  These storms were supported by SBCAPE values of 3000 to 4000 J/kg and 0-6km bulk shear values of around 30 knots. The storms formed into a line by late afternoon, with several reports of damaging winds. Slow-moving storms combined with precipitable water values around 2 inches to produce heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: East Mitchell Street in Trimble was closed due to a downed tree and electrical lines blocking the roadway.

At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated wind gust up to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms tracked across most of southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and portions of northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on June 10, 2026. Multiple measured wind gusts of 70+ MPH were reported as the storms moved across southern Wisconsin, resulting in widespread tree & power line damage. Several areas of structural damage also occurred, with subsequent damage surveys identifying two EF0 tornadoes near the communities of Lomira and Eden. Analysis conducted by the Storm Prediction Center identified the June 10 thunderstorm complex as a derecho.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter estimates 80 MPH wind gusts just west of Edgerton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening hours of May 31 and into the early morning of June 1, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped across northeast Nebraska and western Iowa became the focal point for strong to severe thunderstorm development. The environment along the boundary featured roughly 2,000 J/kg of instability and 30 knots of deep-layer shear, which proved sufficient to organize convection. Additionally, a dry sub-cloud layer yielded approximately 1,400 J/kg of DCAPE, promoting a severe downdraft threat alongside the hail risk.||As storms initiated and pushed southward overnight, radar signatures indicated the potential for several swaths of large hail and damaging winds, particularly across western Iowa. However, because the storms primarily traversed sparsely populated areas late at night, only a handful of severe weather reports were received. Quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail was estimated near the towns of Woodbine and Avoca, Iowa. The storms also produced a measured wind gust of 63 mph and localized tree damage in Pottawattamie County, Iowa. The complex continued tracking southward, eventually decreasing in intensity and weakening below severe limits during the early morning hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours of June 2, 2026, scattered, pulse-type thunderstorms developed and hail and heavy rainfall to portions of southeast Nebraska. Based on radar analysis, the most intense hail core tracked directly over Lincoln, Nebraska, resulting in a public report of quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail. In addition to the hail threat, these thunderstorms were highly efficient rainfall producers. The combination of intense rainfall rates and slow storm motions allowed a quick 2 to 3 inches of rain to accumulate across localized areas of southeast Nebraska.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread and consistent rainfall following a pattern change in mid-May led to reductions in drought severity across Central Alabama from late May into early June. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were downed along Highway 172 in Hackleburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front backed south and westward through eastern and central NM during the early morning hours of June 14th. Abundant low-level moisture pushed in behind this front, reaching the Continental Divide. This provided fuel for thunderstorm development during the early afternoon hours of the 14th with on such severe thunderstorm producing severe wind gusts in Rio Rancho. Afternoon thunderstorms developed again over the northern mountains and along the central mountain chain of NM June 15th. There were reports of 8 inch tree branches down in Taos landing over power lines from severe thunderstorm wind gusts. Other thunderstorms advanced eastward off the Sangre de Cristo Mountains organizing into a line producing severe wind gusts through northeastern NM. This line of storms over northeastern NM eventually advanced all the way through east-central NM and into the TX Panhandle. Severe wind gusts reaching 60 mph or more were observed in Guadalupe County, including at Santa Rosa Lake State Park.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Tucumcari Airport measured a 62 mph thunderstorm wind gust.

The event|began at approximately 7:30 PM EDT, when a cluster of showers|initiated in central Jefferson County, West Virginia. This|convective system tracked continuously northeastward into|Frederick County, Maryland, while exhibiting steady|intensification.||As the storm progressed east of Libertytown, Maryland, it|generated a localized zone of significant structural and tree|damage. The warm front lifted north Monday night, which brought the hot and humid weather further north and east to include northeast Wisconsin and the lakeshore with similar temperatures and dew points. The combination of hot temperatures and high dew points allowed heat index values to soar to 105 to 110 degrees both days. ||In addition to the hot temperatures, overnight lows only fell into the upper 70s to lower 80s Monday night (6/29) into early Tuesday morning (6/30), providing minimal relief from the hot temperatures. The heat wave broke when an area of showers and thunderstorms tracked through the area Tuesday afternoon into Tuesday evening (6/30).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures and high humidity caused heat index values to rise as high as 109 degrees during the afternoon on Monday and 108 degrees Tuesday afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wide tornado circulation occurred across southwest Dickinson County during the late evening of June 8th.  The tornado appears to have traveled southeast slowly.  The severe storm that produced the tornado had a very large and very strong low level mesocyclone which produced damaging inflow and outflow winds around the actual tornado itself.  This made finding the actual tornado path more difficult.  The actual tornado produced EF1 damage with winds to around 110 mph with some outbuidling damage and extensive tree damage noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This next tornado occurred as the previous tornadoes occluded and another one formed on the southern end of the initial mesocyclone. The estimated path and time are based on eye witness reports and radar imagery. The tornado remained in open country where little to no damage indicators exist and no damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pulled moist air into the region during the early portions of June 26th.  Morning clouds gave way during the afternoon, which allowed for the atmosphere to become more unstable. Thunderstorms initially developed in northeastern New Mexico and moved into the Panhandles during the evening and overnight of June 26th. As they encountered the moist, unstable air, they strengthened and organized into a fast-moving squall line. Damaging straight line winds were the main threat with these storms. A few storms ahead of the squall line were able to produce large hail but overall the atmosphere was not as conducive for large hail given the potential for melting to occur.

A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were downed across northern Chilton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rain across parts of central Illinois from the evening of June 10th into the pre-dawn hours of June 11th.  Rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches were common, with some locations exceeding 3.50.  Excessive rainfall rates associated with strong to severe thunderstorms during the evening of June 10th resulted in scattered instances of flash flooding across Knox, Peoria, Tazewell, McLean, and Sangamon counties.  In addition, sharp rises on area creeks and streams led to overland flooding in a few spots...most notably on the north side of Lexington in McLean County.  The flood waters gradually receded after sunrise on June 11th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vehicle stalled in waist-deep water on a roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak dryline formed during the day of the 30th and mixed eastward to the edge of the caprock. Convergence along the dryline, a weak short wave trough, and very hot temperatures contributed to convective initiation by mid-afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains. Storms repeatedly trained over Hall County producing intermittent severe winds gusts near Lesley (Hall County) for over an hour. Late in the afternoon additional thunderstorms developed in eastern New Mexico in the drier air and moved eastward into the South Plains. A very dry sub cloud layer allowed these storms to produce several severe wind gusts as they marched eastward towards the Interstate 27/US Highway 87 corridor. By the time storms reached Lubbock County late in the evening, they were moving very slowly which produced heavy rainfall over the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County). Numerous city roads on the south side of the city of Lubbock were inundated with water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Reese Center measured a wind gust to 68 mph at 2001 CST. At 2032 CST, an off duty NWS employee reported that several power poles were blown over south of Wolfforth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rainfall supported gradually improving drought conditions across much of northwest Kansas in June. D2 Severe Drought impacted Cheyenne, Rawlins, and Thomas counties the first day of the month, with improvement noted thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted Graham county through the 8th, with improvement thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted Sheridan and Gove counties through the 22nd, with improvement thereafter. D2 Severe Drought impacted the southern halves of Greeley and Wichita counties through the 29th, with improvement thereafter. Finally, D2 Severe Drought to D3 Extreme Drought impacted Decatur and Norton counties the entire month. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from a little over one inch over western portions of Greeley county, to about ten inches over north-central Gove and south-central Thomas counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and one-half inches over western Greeley county, to about three and one-half inches over northeast Norton county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about three and one-half inches to eight inches, highest over southwest portions of the county. These values are about one-half inch to five inches above average. Normal June precipitation across the county ranges from about two and one-half inches to a little over three inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) to severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across central and northern Minnesota during June 2026, with abnormally dry (D0) areas in Koochiching and St. Louis counties deteriorating into moderate and severe drought, while existing moderate drought across Aitkin, Cass, Crow Wing, and Itasca counties intensified to severe drought covering up to 97 percent of individual counties. High spatial variability in precipitation occurred across the region; while locations such as Leech Lake (5.55 inches) and Brimson 2S (5.76 inches) received above-average rainfall, substantial deficits elsewhere���most notably at International Falls Intl Airport (1.37 inches, 2.41 inches below average) and Pokegama Dam (2.53 inches, 2.10 inches below average)���allowed severe drought to establish a firm foothold across the area by the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions affected around 29 percent of Aitkin County at the beginning of June, but conditions degraded further throughout the month. Severe (D2) drought developed across the area, initially covering around 29 percent of the county before shrinking to around 18 percent by the end of the month, while moderate drought or greater expanded to cover around 64 percent. The CoCoRaHS observer at McGregor 7.3 N recorded 4.84 inches of precipitation, 0.24 inches above average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed in the roadway on US-250N at Mile Marker 4.0.

These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall that occurred during the morning of June 14th caused the James River at Springfield to reach moderate flood stage. This caused elevated stream flows at Lake Springfield. Four individuals went into Lake Springfield during the afternoon of June 14th and went over the Springfield Lake Dam where their devices were capsized. Three individuals drowned in the incident and the other had moderate injuries. A Flood Warning was in effect at the time of the incident.

A wake low produced high winds during the late morning and early afternoon of June 17th. Wind gusts between 45 mph and 55 mph with a few higher gusts brought down numerous tree limbs. Scattered thunderstorms produced heavy rain and localized flash flooding during the mid afternoon across southeast Cook County. Isolated thunderstorms moved across far northern Illinois during the late evening of June 17th and produced one brief tornado.

Basement flooding was also reported in Chicago Heights. A car was stalled in one to two feet of water in an underpass along Route 30 and South Halsted Street. In Park Forest, Orchard Drive was closed due to flooding at an underpass near North Street and video showed Andover Street flooded with approximately one foot of water east of Andover Court. Roadway flooding was reported in multiple locations in Thorton, Lansing and Calumet City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed within the vicinity of a strong mid-upper level shortwave trough and a surface low. One supercell tracked from southeast Minnesota through northeast Iowa and into southwest Wisconsin while maintaining is strength during the late afternoon. The storm evolved into a line as it trtacked through south central Wisconsin during the early evening and produced a swath of damaging winds and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of wind damage of around 9 miles long and 1.5 miles wide occurred with the rear-flank downdraft of a supercell thunderstorm that had a history of producing a tornado. Two farm properties sustained heavy outbuilding damage, with a barn wall blown out and roof pulled upward, a lean-to destroyed with sheet metal lofted into a nearby field, and a metal barn destroyed with sheet metal lofted and placed in trees by the church across the road. There were numerous hardwood trees snapped and uprooted along the path, and power poles were leaning in one location.

An isolated severe storm embedded in a line led to isolated wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northwest Pennsylvania. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northwest Pennsylvania, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters, particularly near the OH/PA border across Northwest Pennsylvania where a few tornadoes also occurred. At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief EF-1 tornado touched down in central Crawford County at approximately 4:28 PM EDT, south of Dibble Hill Road and east of Theuret Hill Road, and tracked southeast. The tornado snapped several large tree limbs near the point of touchdown before crossing Stoltz Road, where several large trees were uprooted and fell onto a detached garage. A power pole snapped and fell toward the northwest even as the tornado moved southeast. Leaves and hay debris were scattered and pasted across the east side of a barn and nearby structures, indicating rotational winds. Additional trees were snapped and uprooted south of the property and within a tree line to the east. Based on the damage, maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, yielding an EF-1 rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 75 yards. The National Weather Service Cleveland thanks the Crawford County EMA for its assistance during the storm survey.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of an estimated 60 mph wind gust accompanied by 1.00 inch hailstones.

Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Cowpasture River, which was observed to be below the 25th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County Road 44 / County Road 83 closed due to high water near Banquete.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were downed along U.S. Highway 278.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. This MCS also produced severe thunderstorm winds which downed several trees and caused other minor damage before it weakened across southern Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain caused flooding along Slaters Creek Road in Millersville. Extent of damages is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread thunderstorms initially developed across the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the second, fueled by abundant moisture and aided by a mid-level disturbance moving across the region. The slow-moving thunderstorms ingested deep and rich moisture, leading to widespread moderate to heavy rainfall. The large expanse of rain gradually built eastward across the Texas/New Mexico state line and into the western South Plains and Texas Panhandle through the evening hours. Additional storm development blossomed along a low-level boundary over parts of the central and southeastern South Plains late in the evening, before being overtaken by the initial activity to the west early in the morning on the third. Relatively weak vertical wind shear and modest instability limited overall storm strength but produced torrential rainfall. Where the heaviest rain fell, portions of Farm to Market Road 212 and US Highway 380 in eastern and northeastern Lynn County were flooded. Flooding was also observed in and around Brownfield (Terry County), as well over northwestern portions of Cochran County, including in some locations along Farm to Market Road 596 northwest of Morton (Cochran County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS storm survey revealed extensive flooding in eastern Lynn County from heavy rainfall late on the third into the early morning hours of the fourth. The most widespread flooding occurred along Farm to Market Road 212 north of US Highway 380. Standing water still covered parts of the roadway the next morning. There also existed further evidence that water covered a greater portion of the roadway by the mud left behind as the water receded. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 between Farm to Market 212 and Tahoka.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Childress measured a wind gust of 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were snapped along County Road 26 and County Road 331.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 66 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.

The tornado damaged an outbuilding and additional trees along East Oaks Road North, then crossed US-45 northeast of Frasca Field.  A few roofs were damaged near US-45 with more tree branches snapped further east before the tornado dissipated just west of the intersection of County Road 1850 and County Road 1900 at 7:30pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) to severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across central and northern Minnesota during June 2026, with abnormally dry (D0) areas in Koochiching and St. Louis counties deteriorating into moderate and severe drought, while existing moderate drought across Aitkin, Cass, Crow Wing, and Itasca counties intensified to severe drought covering up to 97 percent of individual counties. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions covered nearly 97 percent of Cass County at the beginning of June, but conditions degraded further throughout the month. Severe (D2) drought expanded rapidly to cover around 97 percent of the county, while moderate drought or greater expanded to cover 100 percent of the area by the end of the month. The cooperative observers at Gull Lake Dam, Leech Lake, and Cass Lake recorded 4.70, 5.55, and 3.39 inches of precipitation, respectively. High spatial variability in precipitation occurred across the region; while locations such as Leech Lake (5.55 inches) and Brimson 2S (5.76 inches) received above-average rainfall, substantial deficits elsewhere���most notably at International Falls Intl Airport (1.37 inches, 2.41 inches below average) and Pokegama Dam (2.53 inches, 2.10 inches below average)���allowed severe drought to establish a firm foothold across the area by the end of the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) drought conditions covered nearly 97 percent of Cass County at the beginning of June, but conditions degraded further throughout the month. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down along Route 28 near the West Virginia and Virginia state lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The atmosphere had a few impressive characteristics including mid-lapse rates of 7-7.5 C/km, DCAPE of at least 1000 J/kg, and surface based CAPE of 2000-4000 J/kg in the afternoon. A mid-level ridge, however, was too strong to support any serious and widespread storm development and the absence of shear prevented any storm organization. Even so, orographic lift caused a storm to form and briefly form a landspout in Wythe County. A survey was conducted, but no tornadic or wind related damage was found. PWAT values of 1.5-1.75 did contribute to torrential rainfall in the storms that did form, resulting in a Flood Advisory for Watauga.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photographs were shared on social media depicting a landspout along Interstate 81 near the community of Wytheville. A storm survey was sent to investigate further but no wind damage was found.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense complex of thunderstorms moved across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the late evening hours of June 20th into the morning hours of June 21st. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado developed and quickly intensified over one property. The brunt of the damage was to a double wide manufactured home that was bolted to a poured basement foundation. This home was lifted and completely taken apart with the frame bent and twisted. Unfortunately there was a fatality for this resident who was thrown in the field to the north of the property. Most of the debris from the home and two outbuildings was pushed to the northeast into an open field and could be found for six miles to the northeast. A neighboring house to the west had damage to the edge of the roof and siding from debris tossed into it, but there wasn't other damage to that property. The power pole was still upright, but the lines had been taken down. There were no remaining cedar trees on the north side of the property as viewed from satellite and street view which were part of the debris to the northeast.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail measured up to 1.50 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions continued across south central Virginia and Severe Drought Conditions continued across SW Virginia in June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, but also locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought conditions in Bedford county in late June  after a few rainfall events brought some rain to the county. Drought conditions lingered; however, after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 5th to 10th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Highway 286 flooded and closed near CR 18.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were downed on Mill Creek Rd and also on Highway 5.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread thunderstorms initially developed across the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the second, fueled by abundant moisture and aided by a mid-level disturbance moving across the region. The slow-moving thunderstorms ingested deep and rich moisture, leading to widespread moderate to heavy rainfall. The large expanse of rain gradually built eastward across the Texas/New Mexico state line and into the western South Plains and Texas Panhandle through the evening hours. Additional storm development blossomed along a low-level boundary over parts of the central and southeastern South Plains late in the evening, before being overtaken by the initial activity to the west early in the morning on the third. Relatively weak vertical wind shear and modest instability limited overall storm strength but produced torrential rainfall. Where the heaviest rain fell, portions of Farm to Market Road 212 and US Highway 380 in eastern and northeastern Lynn County were flooded. Flooding was also observed in and around Brownfield (Terry County), as well over northwestern portions of Cochran County, including in some locations along Farm to Market Road 596 northwest of Morton (Cochran County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS storm survey revealed extensive flooding along Farm to Market 596 in northwestern Cochran County. Numerous locations along this road showed evidence of previous water over the roadway. Standing water still existed on portions of the road the next morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports were received of hail in the city of Childress ranging in size from quarters to golf balls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Sandoval County Emergency Manager and a later survey by NWS Albuquerque showed that a flash flood debris flow drove large boulders across NM4 just south of Jemez Springs near the Fire Dept., with flash flooding impacts stretching from Madrid Road to the Jemez Historic Site. This closed the highway for a period of time, and caused one person to need assistance leaving their stuck vehicle. Heavy rainfall caused the flash flooding and was unrelated to the nearby McCauley Springs burn scar. Damage is an estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of severe to extreme drought conditions and multiple runs of critical fire weather conditions allowed two remote wildfires to rapidly grow during the last week of June 2026. The lightning caused Sacaton Fire began June 21st in a remote area of the Gila National Forest, while the Beehive fire began in a remote area of the Tusas Mountains June 26th, with both continuing into the month of July. While both fires produced some smoke concerns in the surrounding areas, neither was a threat to lives or property.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The lightning caused Sacaton fire was located in an extremely remote area of the Gila National Forest within the 2012 Whitewater-Baldy burn scar. The very rugged and remote area made fire suppression activities difficult. Combined with critical fire weather conditions, the fire was able to grow to 372 acres by the end of June, continuing into July.
