EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of offshore winds between high pressure over the northern Bering Sea and northwest portions of the Alaska Mainland and a low over the Gulf of Alaska combined with a very warm and dry airmass to produce critical fire weather conditions across parts of Southwest Alaska during the afternoon and evening hours on June 3rd, 2026.  Temperatures rose as high as 81 degrees (observed in King Salmon) with sustained winds as strong as 20 mph and minimum relative humidity values as low as 20%.  Similar conditions were observed over a smaller area close to the Alaska Range the next day (June 4th) close to Lake Iliamna.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: No significant new wildfire starts, but critical fire weather conditions were observed.  The Bethel ASOS recorded temperatures at or near 75F combined with sustained winds around 15 to 20 mph and relative humidity values between 20 and 25 percent.  Conditions meeting Red Flag criteria were observed between 3:30 PM and 6:30 PM AKST 6/3/26 at the ASOS site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines downed and a power outage in Minneapolis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pulled moist air into the region during the early portions of June 26th.  Morning clouds gave way during the afternoon, which allowed for the atmosphere to become more unstable. Thunderstorms initially developed in northeastern New Mexico and moved into the Panhandles during the evening and overnight of June 26th. As they encountered the moist, unstable air, they strengthened and organized into a fast-moving squall line. Damaging straight line winds were the main threat with these storms. A few storms ahead of the squall line were able to produce large hail but overall the atmosphere was not as conducive for large hail given the potential for melting to occur.

A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed on Mundy Road, County Road 23, and County Road 27 south of Livingston.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet measured wind gust of 67 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary boundary hovered over central Ohio, northern West Virginia, and southern Pennsylvania on June 27th and 28th, but eventually sank south of the area early on the morning of the 29th. ||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms continued to develop along and south of the front, depositing one to three inches of rain across much of the area. While the heaviest rain amounts fell in the southern coal fields, soils to the north had already been compromised by prior rounds of precipitation. Thus, an inch to an inch-and-a-half of rain was enough to spawn some flooding on roads in Harrison, Barbour, and Randolph counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Route 19 was closed from the old landfill to Sycamore Road due to high water from Sycamore Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Disturbances in the upper-level flow, coupled with upslope flow in the higher terrain, caused shower and thunderstorm development across west Texas and southeast New Mexico. Dry low-levels allowed several storms to produce strong downbursts, the strongest of which occurred in Seagraves, where damage to multiple buildings was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Members of the public posted pictures of several powerlines blown down onto State Hwy 115 on social media. The time of occurrence is estimated from radar. The maximum gust and the cost of damages is also estimated.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ongoing severe drought (D2) persisted across portions of southeast West Virginia, including: Boone, southern Braxton, Clay, Fayette, Kanawha, Lincoln, Logan, McDowell, Mingo, Nicholas, Raleigh, southern Roane, southern Wayne, and Wyoming counties.  Moderate drought (D1) also remained present just north and west of the D2 area. ||Significant improvements occurred during the second half of the month as multiple rounds of rain and storms produced four to eleven inches of rain that resulted in weekly category improvements. By the second week of the month, D2 was confined to Mingo, McDowell, and portions of Kanawha, Clay, Nicholas, Fayette, Raleigh, Wyoming, and Logan counties. Minimal improvements to D1 also occurred. In the third and fourth weeks of the month, both D2 and D1 eroded from all but McDowell, and parts of Wyoming and Raleigh counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down near the intersection of Banta Road and IL-26 east of the Illinois River at 4:56pm CDT.  The tornado tracked northeastward, damaging trees before reaching Columbia Road where several houses lost roofs and extensive tree damage occurred.  It then crossed into southern Marshall County west of Snag Creek Road at 5:02pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms. The tornado continued northeast until it ended in a field north of N 1475th Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate (D1) to severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across central and northern Minnesota during June 2026, with abnormally dry (D0) areas in Koochiching and St. Louis counties deteriorating into moderate and severe drought, while existing moderate drought across Aitkin, Cass, Crow Wing, and Itasca counties intensified to severe drought covering up to 97 percent of individual counties. High spatial variability in precipitation occurred across the region; while locations such as Leech Lake (5.55 inches) and Brimson 2S (5.76 inches) received above-average rainfall, substantial deficits elsewhere���most notably at International Falls Intl Airport (1.37 inches, 2.41 inches below average) and Pokegama Dam (2.53 inches, 2.10 inches below average)���allowed severe drought to establish a firm foothold across the area by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed along Parkway Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorm cells were observed training across the Flat Rock Community, located just northeast of the town of Mt Airy in Surry County. Cells began crossing the area at around 5:45 pm EDT, and continued passing across the area repeatedly until around 8:15 pm EDT before rainfall became light in intensity. Rainfall rates rose to as high as 5 inches per hour multiple times through the event. Despite dry antecedent conditions with D2: Severe Drought highlighted for the northern half of Surry County by the U.S. Drought Monitor, MRMS FLASH data estimated the rainfall reached the 142-year Average Recurrence Interval ceiling for a 3-hour duration in the Flat Rock area, with rainfall totals reaching 120 percent of the 3-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow was unimpressive however, reaching into the 300 to 400 cfs per mi^2 by around 8:00 pm EDT. The heavy rain produced runoff around 6 inches deep across Highway 103 from a nearby hillside drainage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Runoff from heavy rain was observed flowing across Highway 103 around 6 inches deep. No damage was observed to the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours of June 5, 2026, thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall triggered flash flooding across southern Richardson County. Consecutive rounds of thunderstorms generated intense rainfall rates of 1.50 to 3.00 inches per hour, driving estimated total rainfall to between 4.00 and 6.00 inches. As a result, the Big Nemaha River gauge at Falls City (FLLN1) rose above flood stage at 2:45 AM CST on June 5th. The gauge crested at 31.09 ft, consistent with moderate flooding, at 11:28 AM CST on June 5th. The gauge fell below flood stage at 2:45 AM CST on June 6th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: FM 70 flooded and closed near Highway 286.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were downed around Jasper.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. With abnormally high amounts of atmospheric moisture, these thunderstorms were able to produce very heavy rainfall with rain amounts of five to seven inches reported across portions of Sumner and Robertson counties. This MCS also produced severe thunderstorm winds which downed several trees and caused other minor damage before it weakened across southern Middle Tennessee.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm winds downed a tree onto a fence in Charlie Daniels Park in Mt. Juliet. Damages are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed off the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the sixth. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rich moisture advected into the region ahead of a dryline positioned across the south-central Texas Panhandle into the southwestern South Plains. Strong heating ahead of the dryline and a weak short wave trough aloft allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop across the central South Plains. A well mixed boundary layer allowed for storms to be high based and produce strong wind gusts. One Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Abernathy (Hale County) recorded severe wind gusts with the outflow well ahead of the parent thunderstorm. Weak flow allowed for storms to have little to no movement which produced heavy rainfall and flash flooding in Hockley County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports were received of a swath of hail on the northwest side of the city of Lubbock. Hail ranged in size from dime size to quarter size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Hackberry measured a wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pulled moist air into the region during the early portions of June 26th.  Morning clouds gave way during the afternoon, which allowed for the atmosphere to become more unstable. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down southwest of the intersection of Lovers Lane and North County Highway 12 about 2 miles southwest of Ipava at 5:17pm CDT.  Drone footage showed that the tornado initially touched down in a field, then tracked northeastward through a solar farm where it tossed a few solar panels.  It then damaged crops as it headed toward Ipava and eventually crossed Bernadotte Street just south of West Main Street.  Video showed a very weak tornado passing through Ipava: however, no damage was noted in the footage.  The tornado dissipated on the northeast side of Ipava near the intersection of East Mechanic Street and North Kinsey Street at 5:22pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downed tree was observed at the intersection of Stull Hill Road and Mountain Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. Flooding continued in Athens through mid afternoon on the 18th while portions of Vinton County continued to experience flooding into the morning of the 19th. One to three inches of rain fell across parts of Washington, Jackson, and Meigs Counties while the rest of southeast Ohio generally received an inch or less. Severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds that downed trees and powerlines across southeast Ohio during the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Upwards of 500 residents were without power due to several areas of tree damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: June brought drought relief to west Tennessee, but did not end the ongoing drought. Beneficial rainfall during the latter portion of the month helped stabilize or improve conditions in some areas, but substantial precipitation deficits remained. Continued warm temperatures and elevated evapotranspiration meant that sustained rainfall would be necessary to produce meaningful drought recovery heading into July.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 Severe Drought Conditions improved to D1 Moderate Drought conditions prior to the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 120 mph touched down in the Spears-Pioneer Woods Forest Preserve just north of 95th Street damaging trees. The tornado moved northeast causing damage to trees, utility poles and minor roof damage across northern Hickory Hills. The tornado crossed Interstate 294 and strengthened on the southeast side of Justice were two apartments had roofs fully removed near 83rd Street and Roberts Road. Six injuries occurred on the top floor of one of these apartment buildings. Another roof was removed from an apartment building near 79th Street and Oketo Avenue. Numerous other roofs suffered at least minor damage. Damage to trees and utility poles continued. The tornado was likely near its maximum width of 350 yards as it moved through this area of Bridgeview. The tornado weakened as it moved through the Clearing and Garfield areas of Chicago, though damage to roofs, siding and trees continued. The tornado then moved northeast, just north of Midway Airport while it continued to cause tree damage and minor roof damage to houses. The tornado ended near Leamington Avenue, just north of 52nd Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe thunderstorms tracked across portions of central and northeast South Dakota during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 3, generating high winds, large hail, and heavy rainfall.  ||One cluster tracked along the North Dakota border, where a personal weather station in Frederick recorded a peak wind gust of 84 mph. These high winds destroyed the football field scoreboard and a storage shed in Frederick, knocked down trees and a radio tower, downed power lines in Hecla, and snapped power poles and flipped an irrigation pivot six miles north of Britton. The city of Britton lost electrical power. Three additional weather stations in Marshall County clocked wind gusts in excess of 60 mph. ||A second storm cluster moved out of eastern South Dakota into the southern Glacial Lakes region. Quarter-sized hail occurred at several locations. Heavy rainfall topping out at 4.40 inches in Clear Lake resulted in water six inches deep running over roads and caused a creek near the golf course to overflow its banks. Across central South Dakota, storms produced hail ranging from penny to golf ball size south of Interstate 90.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning hours of June 13, 2026, severe thunderstorms tracked through eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa, producing hail and damaging wind gusts. The storms were driven by moisture return from a low-level jet impinging on a slowly sagging cold front. Elevated showers and thunderstorms developed over eastern Nebraska prior to sunrise before moving eastward into an environment characterized by sufficient instability and shear to support severe weather. Notable reports included quarter-sized hail (up to 1.00 inch in diameter) in and around the Omaha metro area���including Fremont (Dodge County), Douglas, and Sarpy counties in Nebraska, as well as Mills and Pottawattamie counties in Iowa. Measured wind gusts ranged from 58 to 60 mph, with an estimated wind gust of 70 mph recorded near Valley, Nebraska.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.00 inch in diameter. Reported received via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public measured wind gust of 74 mph along with tree damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from severe drought to moderate drought as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 100th to 200th percentile across much of SE West Virginia. Rainfall totals over the past 30 days ranged from 5.0 to 8.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread short-term improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to near normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Both Mercer and Monroe counties continued to remain in Severe drought as portions of those counties received rainfall totals closer to 3-4 inches over the 30 day period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought conditions in Mercer county by late June after repeated rounds of rainfall during the month of June. The previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 10.00-15.00 inches, which ended up being 75 to 90 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 30th to 70th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 30th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Bluestone River, which was observed to be below the 25th to 75th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report from mPING: Street/road flooding; Street/road closed; Vehicles stranded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed at Highway 31 and County Road 5 as well as along County Road 9.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rich moisture advected into the region ahead of a dryline positioned across the south-central Texas Panhandle into the southwestern South Plains. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser measured a wind gust of 64 mph in far southwestern Floyd County.

The heat wave broke when an area of showers and thunderstorms tracked through the area Tuesday afternoon into Tuesday evening (6/30).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures and high humidity caused heat index values to rise as high as 108 degrees during the afternoon on Monday and again on Tuesday.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gust measured by anemometer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pulled moist air into the region during the early portions of June 26th.  Morning clouds gave way during the afternoon, which allowed for the atmosphere to become more unstable. Thunderstorms initially developed in northeastern New Mexico and moved into the Panhandles during the evening and overnight of June 26th. As they encountered the moist, unstable air, they strengthened and organized into a fast-moving squall line. Damaging straight line winds were the main threat with these storms. A few storms ahead of the squall line were able to produce large hail but overall the atmosphere was not as conducive for large hail given the potential for melting to occur.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moisture associated with Tropical Storm Arthur approached Central Alabama on June 17 into June 18. On June 17, several showers and low-topped supercells developed over southeastern Central Alabama. One cell produced a well-defined funnel cloud in southeastern Lowndes County that was caught in at least two videos posted to social media. The next day, heavy rainfall near Chalkville led to a portion of Sweeny Hollow Rd being flooded.||In the wake of the remnants of Arthur passing through Central Alabama on June 18, a cold front entered the area and became stalled. On June 19, heavy rainfall became concentrated along a boundary along and south of the U.S. 80 corridor, leading to flooding issues in Pike and Lowndes counties. By June 20, the stalled front over Central Alabama reignited training thunderstorms along the U.S. 280 and I-22 corridors, with heavy rainfall of 2 to 5 inches causing flash flooding in the Birmingham metro area during the afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Prolonged heavy rainfall over the Birmingham metro area led to numerous instances of flash flooding after 2 to 4 inches of rainfall accumulation over the span of 4-5 hours. Flooding was observed in numerous areas of Jefferson County, including Birmingham, Hoover, Vestavia Hills, Cahaba Heights, Ensley, Adamsville, and Graysville.||Several portions of Columbiana Road in Vestavia Hills were flooded and closed. Nearby, Patton Creek flooded parts of U.S. 31/Montgomery Highway, resulting in temporary closure of the roadway and impacting businesses and shopping centers, including the area around the Vestavia Bowl. Little Shades Creek overflowed in this area as well, flooding the Loch Haven area and the Hoover Dog Park near Rocky Ridge Rd. Additionally, in Cahaba Heights, a tributary of Little Shades Creek caused flooding over Dolly Ridge Rd and in Meadowlawn Park.||In Ensley, Village Creek rose into minor flood stage (10 ft), topping out at 11.38 ft, while Valley Creek at Ave W also rose briefly to minor flood stage (12 ft), cresting at 12.39 ft. In North Birmingham, Interstate 65 was flooded between Finley Blvd and I-22, with several inches of standing or flowing water impeding traffic.||Across northwestern Jefferson County, closer to 4 to 5 inches of rain fell around Adamsville and Graysville, with numerous flooded and closed roadways. Floodwater entered a home along Cherry Ave on the east side of Graysville, forcing residents to evacuate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 10th, an inverted trough over the Atlantic Ocean waters adjacent to the northeast Florida and southeast Georgia waters developed coastal showers that moved onshore in the overnight into morning hours. Showers interacted with the land breeze creating a convergent line of heavy showers that caused flooding along the coast. Moist west-southwest flow then developed resulting in typical summertime sea breeze thunderstorms each afternoon into evening for the next several days. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. The hot temperatures allowed storms to be high based producing mostly severe wind gusts. One of the more robust updrafts produced quarter size hail in the city of Lubbock. The most impressive storm of the evening was one that tracked near Slaton (Lubbock County). This storm generated a microburst with a peak wind gust of 110 mph measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet. A storm survey the next day revealed very localized damage around the mesonet site northeast of Slaton. Cotton crops were destroyed and mesquite trees were stripped. Additionally, irrigation pivots were damaged and partially rolled. A heavy gate damaged the fence surrounding the mesonet site but no damage to the sensors occurred. Later in the evening, a line of thunderstorms developed on an outflow boundary moving into the northwestern South Plains. These thunderstorms continued to produce intermittent severe wind gusts as they tracked across the northern South Plains into the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Levelland measured a severe gust of 65 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for severe thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary forcing for ascent, thunderstorms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. Additionally, high atmospheric moisture content situated over already saturated soils generated efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex.||During the initial discrete phase, the dominant hazard was large hail, with hailstones measured up to 2.00 inches in diameter. The rotating updrafts also produced a couple of funnel clouds, including a photographed rope funnel near Hallam and another near Swanton, though they remained aloft, and no tornadoes were confirmed. As the storms merged into a larger complex, the primary threat shifted to damaging straight-line winds. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 68 mph, which resulted in localized thunderstorm wind damage across the region before the system eventually weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 0.75 inches in diameter. Report received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down near the intersection of Broadway Road and Springfield Road about 2 miles south of Groveland at 6:08pm CDT.  It tracked northeastward along the southern edge of Morton where it snapped numerous trees, some of which fell onto cars.  The tornado exited Morton near the intersection of East Jefferson Street and Tennessee Avenue and entered the Mayfair subdivision where it caused extensive tree limb damage and stripped shingles off a few homes.  It crossed I-74 about 1.5 miles east of the Washington Road overpass and damaged an outbuilding and a couple of farmsteads before crossing into Woodford County about 1 mile north of Deer Creek along Lakeland Road at 6:17pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado with estimated peak winds of 120 mph touched down just west of Hendricks Street and move through central Merrillville. The tornado quickly widened with numerous homes sustaining significant damage along W 64rd Avenue, 61st Place, 61st Avenue, and Grand Place, including removal of walls and roofing structures. Extensive tree damage also occurred. The tornado continued moving east along W 61st Avenue damaging houses with some garages destroyed. The tornado was likely at peak intensity as it moved near the Harrison Middle School, where the gymnasium roof was damaged. Numerous houses were damaged near Andrean High School, which suffered significant roof damage. Significant tree damage continued as the tornado crossed Interstate 65. A semi-truck was overturned just west of the interstate and the driver suffered minor injuries. Tree damage continued north of Lake George and the tornado ended near W 3rd Street and Ash Street. At least 200 buildings and houses were damaged with over 60 houses suffering major damage.

A cluster of severe thunderstorms moved through parts of north central North Dakota, including the Turtle Mountains area, before additional storms developed to the south in the James River Valley area. |The most significant damage occurred approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph. To the northeast, there was another property with approximately 15 to 20 oak trees that were damaged. |The other main area of damage occurred in Stutsman County, one mile west of Spiritwood. A 200 foot by 60 foot barn was blown over and dismantled. Based on photo and satellite imagery, barn was oriented west-east with 3 doors facing south. The storm was moving from south to north, which would be a favorable direction to funnel wind into the broad side of the barn with multiple doors, helping the barn collapse and push pieces into the tree row directly to the north. This is consistent with wind speeds of around 85 mph.|The highest measured wind gust was 62 mph near Zeeland in Mcintosh County and near Pettibone in Kidder County. The largest hail reported was golf ball sized, west of Belcourt in Rolette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to the size of quarters that lasted about 10 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Mostly near to above average precipitation supported steadily improving drought conditions across far southwest Nebraska, especially for Dundy County very early in the month, and by mid to late June for Hitchcock and Red Willow counties. Near to below average precipitation prevailed across portions of Red Willow County where drought persisted the longest. D2 Severe Drought only persisted through the 1st for Dundy County, with D2 Severe Drought to D4 Exceptional Drought persisting through mid to late June for the northeast half of Hitchcock County, and through the entire month for all of Red Willow County. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about two inches over northern Red Willow county, to a whopping ten inches over northwest Hitchcock county. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two and three-quarters of an inch over western Dundy county, to about three and one-half inches over eastern Red Willow county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about three inches to just over seven inches (near normal to about four inches above average), highest over far northeast portions of the county. Normal monthly precipitation across the county is near and either side of three inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active stretch of weather took shape across West Virginia from June 10th to the 12th amid several passing disturbances. Beginning on the morning of the 10th, overnight thunderstorm complexes across the Ohio Valley spilled into the state just after sunrise, containing heavy downpours. This resulted in high water issues across isolated spots in Lincoln, Putnam, and Kanawha Counties through the late morning hours before the departure of the first upper level disturbance.||A brief reprieve from the evening of the 10th to the morning of 11th was quickly interrupted by an approaching cold front that promoted diurnally showers and thunderstorms for the next two days. Thunderstorms developed early in the afternoon on June 11th across north-central West Virginia and tracked eastward into the mountains. Damaging winds associated with storms resulted in a swath of downed trees and power lines in these areas before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating. A similar setup took place the next day as the front slid through the forecast area, with storms developing around midday, this time across portions of central and southern West Virginia. More tree and power line damage occurred as a result, along with one instance of one inch hail. The cold front slipped through the entire area by the evening of June 12th, mitigating further showers and storms in the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One downed tree was observed at the intersection of Nutter Fork Road and Chips Run.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system traversed the Great Lakes Region on the night of June 17th, then continued across southern Ontario into southern Quebec on the 18th.  This system lifted a warm front north through the area during the early morning hours of the 18th, then pulled a cold front southeast into the area during the day.  Meanwhile, a strong shortwave trough helped steer a strong jet over portions of the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. ||Rain started to spread across southeast Ohio and over into western and north central West Virginia the evening of the 17th. Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours then tracked across this same area overnight before sinking southeast the morning of the 18th. While the bulk of precipitation departed southeast Ohio and northern West Virginia by mid morning, the lingering front combined with a feed of moisture from a Gulf system allowed showers and a few storms to persist across Northeast Kentucky, southern West Virginia, and southwest Virginia through the 18th. Precipitation finally came to an end on the morning of the 19th.||The heaviest rainfall occurred in Vinton and Athens counties, where three to five inches of rain resulted in flash flooding and impacted local roads and stranded several vehicles. Flooding continued in Athens through mid afternoon on the 18th while portions of Vinton County continued to experience flooding into the morning of the 19th. One to three inches of rain fell across parts of Washington, Jackson, and Meigs Counties while the rest of southeast Ohio generally received an inch or less. Severe thunderstorms also produced damaging winds that downed trees and powerlines across southeast Ohio during the morning of the 18th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous areas of power outages occurred due to storm damage.

The strongest and most organized thunderstorms moved across Ulster and Dutchess Counties where numerous reports of downed trees and wires occurred. More isolated thunderstorms also produced some downed trees across far northern Washington County and near North Creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires were downed blocking all lanes on NY 81 near CR 45 near Earlton. A member of the public also reported multiple branches and some snapped trees in the same vicinity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was knocked down on a private property.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several clusters of severe thunderstorms tracked across portions of central and northeast South Dakota during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 3, generating high winds, large hail, and heavy rainfall.  ||One cluster tracked along the North Dakota border, where a personal weather station in Frederick recorded a peak wind gust of 84 mph. These high winds destroyed the football field scoreboard and a storage shed in Frederick, knocked down trees and a radio tower, downed power lines in Hecla, and snapped power poles and flipped an irrigation pivot six miles north of Britton. The city of Britton lost electrical power. Three additional weather stations in Marshall County clocked wind gusts in excess of 60 mph. ||A second storm cluster moved out of eastern South Dakota into the southern Glacial Lakes region. Quarter-sized hail occurred at several locations. Heavy rainfall topping out at 4.40 inches in Clear Lake resulted in water six inches deep running over roads and caused a creek near the golf course to overflow its banks. Across central South Dakota, storms produced hail ranging from penny to golf ball size south of Interstate 90.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado developed in Dearborn County at 2314EST on Texas Gas Road, about 4 miles east of Dillsboro. It moved east and crossed Laughery Creek as  it entered Ohio County at 2317EST, about 2.8 miles southeast of Dillsboro. The tornado then moved across Laughery Creek, producing significant tree damage along and near Laughery Creek and in wooded areas along Hartford Pike, where numerous trees were snapped. Along Holmes Hill Road, more tree damage was observed along with the roof being lifted off an outbuilding. On Thuermer Hollow Road, more trees were damaged and a roof was lifted off a barn. Along State Route 56, additional roof damage to a barn and damage to large healthy trees were noted. Farther east on the Indiana side of the Ohio River, numerous trees were knocked down at a campground. The tornado crossed the Ohio River and entered into Boone County, Kentucky at 2325EST before it dissipated at at 2326EST, just across the Ohio River along Belleview Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave advancing through the Ohio Valley and Pennsylvania allowed for a complex of thunderstorms to develop across western Pennsylvania during the morning hours of June 10, 2026. Upscale growth of this complex continued into portions of central Pennsylvania where slightly more moisture and instability was in place, with CAPE values peaking between 2000-3000 J/kg during the afternoon hours across much of the region. Storms largely stayed below severe limits due to the lack of bulk shear; however, some strong-to-severe thunderstorms knocked down trees in northern York County. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall occurred during portions of Mifflin County, where ponding of water occurred due to a slow-moving thunderstorm ahead of this complex with additional rainfall occurring during the afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down a tree onto South York Road east of Dillsburg.

Numerous reports of wind damage were relayed to NWS Albany from 911 call centers and local law enforcement in Herkimer, Hamilton, Fulton, Montgomery, Saratoga, Schenectady, Albany, Rensselaer, and Columbia Counties. However, particularly hit hard was Montgomery County where extensive tree and wire damage was reported across portions of Fonda and Fultonville.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A report of a downed tree across NY Route 334 was reported to NWS Albany via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of June 29, 2026, into the early morning hours of June 30, severe thunderstorms moved across northern and eastern Nebraska, producing hail, damaging wind gusts, and a brief tornado. Storms developed along a cold front within a highly unstable air mass characterized by MLCAPE values exceeding 3,500 J/kg, DCAPE values over 1,500 J/kg, and steep lapse rates.||Two distinct rounds of severe weather impacted the area. The first round targeted far northeast Nebraska���primarily Knox and Cedar counties���between 5:00 PM and 8:00 PM CST. This initial round was dominated by a supercell that produced measured wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.||A second round of storms developed in east-central Nebraska later in the evening and tracked northeastward. This activity quickly consolidated into a severe convective cluster that produced damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado as it passed through Boone, Madison, Stanton, and Wayne counties. The complex intensified rapidly upon entering Madison County and the Norfolk area, producing widespread wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph. A personal weather station 2 miles southeast of Hadar recorded a peak gust of 101 mph, which destroyed a well-anchored carport. Multiple hail reports between 1.00 and 2.00 inches in diameter were also received. A brief, EF-0 tornado was also confirmed in Stanton County, with maximum estimated wind speeds of 85 mph. The system continued northeast into the overnight hours, producing severe wind gusts into northwest Iowa and southern Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions worsened across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions improved to Severe Drought in northwest North Carolina in the middle of June after the previous several months of March, April, and May recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 2.00-4.00 inches, and locally higher totals of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 10 to 25 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, April, and May contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 16th of June. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Laredo PD reported that the intersection of Ejido and Potomac was closed due to  flooding. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of northwesterly flow across Central Alabama aided the formation of a mesoscale convective system (MCS), which moved across the region during the afternoon of June 1. Gaining momentum while passing through the Tennessee Valley in North Alabama, a line of severe thunderstorms matured over Central Alabama as it moved southeastward. Surface-based CAPE values over 4000 J/kg were observed prior to the arrival of the MCS, with compressional heating raising temperatures into the mid 90s in many places. Aided by moist soils from days of rainfall, winds generally up to 60 mph blew down hundreds of trees across nearly every county in Central Alabama. Many trees fell on homes, vehicles, and power lines, or blocked roadways. Power outages were numerous, especially across parts of Jefferson and Shelby counties. The MCS gradually fizzled out as it reached southeastern Alabama.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed around Oneonta, and a carport was blown into the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed and tracked southeast through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of June 9, 2026. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 11th slowed down a cold front moving through the area but also provided a focus for thunderstorm development. Strong instability, resulting from the warm temperatures and high moisture, ahead of the front fueled the rapid development of severe thunderstorms from the late afternoon into the evening hours. Thunderstorms initially developed over the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains where temperatures in excess of 100 degrees allowed updrafts to break through a capping inversion. Atmospheric flow was weak which allowed storms to move slowly and create torrential rainfall in some locations. Some roads within the city of Levelland (Hockley County) became impassable because of water over the road. The most significant thunderstorm developed over southern Lubbock County and moved southward producing severe wind gusts and wind damage throughout Lynn County. These winds caused minor but widespread damage throughout the towns of Tahoka and Wilson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported hail up to quarter size in the city of Childress.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct rounds of convective development occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 23rd. The first occurred during the early afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle. This area of convection originated in southwestern Kansas into the Oklahoma and northern Texas Panhandles. A strong low level jet during the morning hours allowed this convection to blossom as it tracked southward through the eastern Texas Panhandle. A favorable environment existed out ahead of the storms during the early afternoon after the low level jet diminished. By the time the storms reached the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle they produced large hail in Childress (Childress County) and several severe wind gusts. The second round of thunderstorms developed off of an outflow boundary produced by the early afternoon convection. A very unstable air mass was present south of the boundary which was also characterized by strong deep layer shear. This allowed updrafts to develop into supercell thunderstorms, of which many became splitting supercell storms. The most intense thunderstorms remained anchored to this pre-existing boundary. One supercell thunderstorm tracked southward over Hockley County and produced baseball size hail along with substantial wind damage between Sundown (Hockley County) and Texas Highway 114. Additionally, a number of wake lows developed which produced several high wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photographs on social media showed hail in and west of Ralls along US Highway 62/82 ranging in size from quarters to half dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A Gulf low moved inland over the Alaska Panhandle along with a ridge over the Southcentral and the Al-Can border. These features allowed for easterly waves to move over the Susitna Valley and into the East Kuskokwim Valley. These easterly waves, further enhanced by an upper low dropping into Southwest Alaska, combined with warmer temperatures and ample moisture allowed for many thunderstorms to form over the Susitna Valley and the East Kuskokwim Valley. There were 2420 lightning strikes over the Susitna Valley and Talkeetna Mountains from thunderstorms on June 19. By 9:30 PM that day, six fires were confirmed over the Susitna Valley. In the Susitna Valley, the greatest concentration of lightning strikes was northeast of Skwentna around the Petersville area. In the East Kuskokwim Valley, there were many lightning strikes around Lime Village.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous lightning strikes from thunderstorms were observed around Lime Village during the afternoon hours of June 19. There were numerous fire starts but the Alaska Division of Forestry & Fire Protection (DFFP) immediately deployed aviation and ground assets to suppress the starts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Northeast Kansas continued to endure one of its worst stretches of severe storms in recent memory with another high impact wind and flood event.  A cluster of storms developed in north central Kansas and evolved into a bow echo.  The storms produced destructive winds in excess of 100 mph across parts of Ottawa county with a swath of winds of 75-95 mph causing damage from Dickinson county east along I-70 into Douglas County including the city of Topeka.  Widespread damage occurred due to the winds.  Torrential flooding rains of 2-3 inches per hour also plagued the area and produced damaging flooding across many areas during the night.   Two to six inches of rain fell over already saturated grounds causing the flooding.  There were also two documented tornadoes one in Dickinson county and a small tornado in Douglas County on the north side of the city of Lawrence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. The hot temperatures allowed storms to be high based producing mostly severe wind gusts. One of the more robust updrafts produced quarter size hail in the city of Lubbock. The most impressive storm of the evening was one that tracked near Slaton (Lubbock County). This storm generated a microburst with a peak wind gust of 110 mph measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet. A storm survey the next day revealed very localized damage around the mesonet site northeast of Slaton. Cotton crops were destroyed and mesquite trees were stripped. Additionally, irrigation pivots were damaged and partially rolled. A heavy gate damaged the fence surrounding the mesonet site but no damage to the sensors occurred. Later in the evening, a line of thunderstorms developed on an outflow boundary moving into the northwestern South Plains. These thunderstorms continued to produce intermittent severe wind gusts as they tracked across the northern South Plains into the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports were received of a swath of hail on the northwest side of the city of Lubbock. Hail ranged in size from penny to quarter size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of June 5, 2026, a stalled frontal boundary draped from southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa served as the focal point for thunderstorm development. As an approaching shortwave disturbance provided forcing for ascent, storms initiated along the boundary. The surrounding environment was characterized by strong deep-layer shear and robust instability, capable of supporting all severe hazards. High atmospheric moisture content situated over saturated soils also created efficient rainfall processes, elevating flash flooding concerns. These storms initially erupted as brief, discrete cells before rapidly undergoing upscale growth into a larger convective complex as they moved into southwest Iowa.||As the severe complex traversed southwest Iowa, it produced several areas of severe weather. Isolated large hail up to quarter-size (1.00 inch) was reported. However, as the storms merged and grew upscale, straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Multiple stations measured severe wind gusts peaking at 69 mph, which resulted in significant and widespread tree damage. Notable impacts included uprooted trees in Elliott, a mature walnut tree completely uprooted near Macedonia, and numerous large tree limbs snapped in Carson and Essex before the complex eventually tracked east and weakened.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system interacted with a highly unstable and sheared environment to produce a significant severe weather outbreak across central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of June 11th.  Scattered supercell thunderstorms initially developed west of the I-55 corridor along a pre-frontal trough during the afternoon.  One of these storms produced an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Woodford and Marshall counties and dropped tennis ball-sized hail (2.50 diameter).  Additional cells rapidly developed further west across southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri ahead of an advancing cold front.  These storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward into central Illinois during the evening.  Widespread damaging wind gusts of 60-70mph occurred with the line along and north of the I-72 corridor.  After storm surveys were completed, it was discovered an additional 8 tornadoes were embedded within the line...creating pockets of enhanced damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An areal photo showed a brief west-to-east tornado track in an open field south of East Randolph Road.  No damage was observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As an upper level low moved through the region, severe thunderstorms developed along a weak cold front that moved through North Dakota. Scattered showers and non-severe thunderstorms were ongoing during the morning before increasing in strength throughout the afternoon. A cluster of severe thunderstorms moved through parts of north central North Dakota, including the Turtle Mountains area, before additional storms developed to the south in the James River Valley area. |The most significant damage occurred approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph. To the northeast, there was another property with approximately 15 to 20 oak trees that were damaged. |The other main area of damage occurred in Stutsman County, one mile west of Spiritwood. A 200 foot by 60 foot barn was blown over and dismantled. Based on photo and satellite imagery, barn was oriented west-east with 3 doors facing south. The storm was moving from south to north, which would be a favorable direction to funnel wind into the broad side of the barn with multiple doors, helping the barn collapse and push pieces into the tree row directly to the north. This is consistent with wind speeds of around 85 mph.|The highest measured wind gust was 62 mph near Zeeland in Mcintosh County and near Pettibone in Kidder County. The largest hail reported was golf ball sized, west of Belcourt in Rolette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Private weather station reported wind gusts up to 59 mph.

A cluster of severe thunderstorms moved through parts of north central North Dakota, including the Turtle Mountains area, before additional storms developed to the south in the James River Valley area. |The most significant damage occurred approximately 4 miles northeast of Belcourt. Multiple buildings were damaged at a collection of properties in this area. A garage on the southwest side of the damage area lost a section of its roof that video and drone footage show was blown northeast across the property. The other main building with damage is a residential home at the center property that lost a significant portion of its roof ripped off. On the north and east side of this property, there were multiple hardwood trees damaged, some snapped about halfway down, but all generally extending to the northeast. A utility truck was parked at the center property and was facing south when the storm came through. A two by four plank of wood went through the windshield and both occupants of the truck had minor injuries. At the eastern property in this group, a shed collapsed and was blown into the edge of a wooded area to the northeast. Drone footage shows numerous trees damaged in this wooded area, extending a few hundred feet northeast of the buildings on the property. Winds were estimated at 95 mph. To the northeast, there was another property with approximately 15 to 20 oak trees that were damaged. |The other main area of damage occurred in Stutsman County, one mile west of Spiritwood. A 200 foot by 60 foot barn was blown over and dismantled. Based on photo and satellite imagery, barn was oriented west-east with 3 doors facing south. The storm was moving from south to north, which would be a favorable direction to funnel wind into the broad side of the barn with multiple doors, helping the barn collapse and push pieces into the tree row directly to the north. This is consistent with wind speeds of around 85 mph.|The highest measured wind gust was 62 mph near Zeeland in Mcintosh County and near Pettibone in Kidder County. The largest hail reported was golf ball sized, west of Belcourt in Rolette County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail estimated to be golf ball sized. Public report relayed by broadcast media.
