EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued, and worsened across Stokes county through April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued in the Palo Duro Canyon area into April and degraded further into Extreme Drought (D3) by the middle to latter portions of the month. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the area. In total, Palo Duro Canyon measured less than one tenth of an inch and ended the month 1.4 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 3.1 inches below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down and blocking traffic on Big Sugar Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought continued or worsened for the majority of the region throughout the month of April. This, combined with many days of breezy to gusty wind conditions, resulted in a number of wildfires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Sargent wildfire  developed in northwest Baker county, northern Osceola National Forest on April 2, 2026 around 350 PM EDT. The smoke plume extended northward affecting local roads near the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge and into Waycross, GA. On April 3rd, the Florida Forest Service reported the Sargent Fire quickly grew to about 4,000 acres moving into Columbia and Clinch counties. The highway between Fargo, GA and John Bethea State Forest in Florida was closed (Highway 2 in Florida and Highway 94 in Georgia). The majority of the fire was burning in Florida but it had crossed into southern Georgia. On the evening of April 3rd, the fire was now estimated at 2,720 acres and 50% contained following improved mapping. On April 5th, Florida Highway 2 and Georgia Highway 94 were now only closed at night due to potential low visibility from fog and smoke. Light rain on April 5th and 6th was not enough to help put out the fire. On April 11th, the fire was 81% contained at 2,489 acres. On April 15th, reburn in the swamp occurred due to hot and dry weather. On April 20th, the acreage increased to 2,523 acres due to spotfires which are caused by flying sparks or embers carried by the wind from an existing fire and ignite a new fire. No structures were threatened. Breezy winds, extreme to exceptional drought conditions, lack of beneficial rain, and remaining heavy fuels continued elevated fire activity through the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of scattered tree, power line, and structural damage across northern Jefferson County. This included many uprooted and snapped trees, power lines down, and fallen trees on vehicles especially in Waterloo and Watertown. Eight power poles were snapped on East Clarkson Rd. in Waterloo.  A farm on highway B east of Johnson Creek suffered severe silo damage, and a grove of trees were knocked down nearby.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail northeast of Menomonee Falls.

At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa.  Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hardwood tree trunks snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of May saw below normal precipitation through the Four Corners region and portions of the central highlands of New Mexico, while areas along the Rio Grande Valley, southwestern, and eastern NM saw near to above normal precipitation. Mean temperatures trended near to slightly above normal through western NM and near to slightly below normal across eastern NM. This led to a modest expansion of extreme drought conditions across western NM and portions of the eastern plains of NM along the TX border. Gaps of severe drought through the northern mountains were filled in. Due to ongoing drought conditions and record low snowpack the previous winter, the Rio Grande dried up through the Albuquerque metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme and severe drought persisted over the northern and southern portions of the zone respectively.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon of the 15th saw a repeat of the previous day's activity. Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 15th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Several wildfire starts occurred on the afternoon of the 15th although none of these wildfires caused any known damage. The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Post measured severe wind gusts from 1838 CST through 1843 CST. A peak wind gust of 65 mph was measured at 1839 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quasi-stationary surface boundary draped west to east across the northern peninsula and an approaching upper-level disturbance created an environment of favorable shear and instability that produced 2 EF-0 tornadoes near Hudson and Shady Hills in Pasco County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm exhibiting supercell characteristics for multiple hours while offshore moved ashore with a tornado estimated to have touched down around 1814 UTC (2:14 PM EDT) near Hudson in Pasco County, while continuing to exhibit a rotational signature via |KTBW WSR-88D and TTPA TDWR. Damage was initially observed along Saltwater Blvd, where a tree branch was snapped and fell onto a power line. Additional damage points were noted further east along Saltwater Blvd, with two homes suffering partial roof damage or loss. Additional homes suffered various degrees of roof, lanai or carport damage at points northward across Puffin, Heron and Curlew Lanes, while tree damage was noted across nearby Osprey and Gull Lanes. The tornado then crossed U.S. Hwy 19 before the radar signature became increasingly disorganized shortly thereafter, and it is likely that the tornado dissipated sometime around 1819 UTC (2:19 PM EDT) between Whitby Road and Lakeshore Blvd after traveling for just over one mile. Maximum peak wind of 85 mph.

A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.

Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down across Red Bud Drive near Lake Deerwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In May 2026, New Hampshire saw noticeable short-term improvements in drought conditions, though deep groundwater deficits continued to pose a challenge across the state. Soaking rains in mid-May provided widespread relief, particularly across the northern mountains and foothills. Over a single week ending May 19, the coverage of Severe Drought (D2) in New Hampshire dropped significantly from 36% down to 20.5%. The mid-May rain events successfully replenished surface topsoil moisture, restored streamflows, and boosted lake and reservoir levels back toward seasonal baselines. However, extended precipitation deficits over the preceding 90 days, particularly across southern New Hampshire, kept deeper hydrologic systems under stress. Deep groundwater aquifers respond on a much slower, lagging timeframe, meaning the water table remained significantly lower than long-term historical averages for May. Consequently, several groundwater monitoring wells across southern and central New Hampshire continued to record below to much-below normal levels.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on April 28 had less than 1% (0.62%) of Coos County in Severe Drought (D2), but by the end of May severe drought was completely cleared (0%), with Moderate Drought (D1) reduced to less than 1% (0.52%) and 75% Abnormally Dry (D0). May rainfall averaged 5.45 inches, well above normal by 1.77���. However, one wet May wasn't enough to wipe out extended long-term shortfalls: the 12-month period ending May 2026 still had a multi-month precipitation deficit of more than 5 inches.

Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated time and location of tornado based on reports received from emergency management and radar interpretation.

The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST. Sea-breeze boundaries along the Middle Texas Coast served as a focus for thunderstorm development during the afternoon. While upper-level winds were relatively weak, sufficient instability and moderate deep-layer shear supported organized convection capable of producing damaging wind gusts. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across northeast Georgia. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal. Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, as May rainfall wound up 150 to 200% of normal. Some locations across the Piedmont received around 300% of normal May rainfall. Drought category was reduced to moderate-to-severe across the area by the start of June.

Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 64 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to two inches in diameter damaged homes and vehicles, and covered the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms occurred across Central Alabama during the late morning to early afternoon of May 22. Enough shear and instability were present to promote the development of small, low-topped supercells within a tropical environment. A few of these cells produced brief rotation, and three brief tornadoes occurred in Marengo and Tuscaloosa counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado touched down just north of Interstate 20/59 nearly 2 miles east of exit 89 in a largely open field with a few trees here and there, one of which was uprooted. Numerous video recordings on social media showed a lowering cloudbase and nebulous funnel cloud crossing the interstate, with what looked like a very narrow drill bit tornado finally touching down. From there, the tornado moved north, crossing Union Road, where minor damage occurred to a double wide manufactured home and the first hint of a debris signature appeared. The tornado then traversed inaccessible forests and fields and intensified before reaching K and R Road, where several hardwood and softwood trees were snapped or uprooted. Only minor damage occurred to any homes on the street. The tornado then turned more northeasterly, crossed Bama Rock Garden Road where a carport was tossed and a home sustained other minor damage and crossed Charles Brook Rd, snapping and uprooting several trees. The tornado dissipated over inaccessible forest somewhere beyond Charles Brook Rd. Maximum winds were estimated at 95 mph.

Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from less than two inches over western Cheyenne county, to about seven to eight inches over southern Yuma and northern Kit Carson counties. Normal monthly precipitation amounts range from about two inches over southwest Cheyenne county, to about three inches over northeast Yuma county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about three inches over northeast portions of the county (about one-quarter to one-half inch above average), to around eight inches over southern and southwest portions of the county (four to five inches above average). Normal monthly precipitation amounts are about two and three-quarters of an inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A northwest flow aloft was in place across the Four State Region during the morning of May 10th, developing on the east side of an upper level ridge of high pressure over the Rockies and Desert Southwest. A shortwave trough embedded in this flow regime traversed the Oklahoma/Texas Panhandle during the early morning hours, before moving into East Texas by late morning and North Louisiana during the afternoon. Diurnal heating contributed to an unstable air mass by late morning/early afternoon, with the approaching trough helping to enhance large scale forcing for the development of scattered severe thunderstorms across portions of East Texas and North Louisiana, where multiple reports of large hail and damaging winds were received. These storms eventually exited the region by late afternoon with the departure of this disturbance aloft.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A chicken truck was blown over in Hainesville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure system sat north of Maine, as a low pressure moved northeast into the region. Favorable cold air damming set up led to temperatures at, or around, freezing throughout the state. Precipitation began to move in late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. Warm mid-layer temperatures move in with associated warm front, transitioning snow in the northern regions over to mixed precipitation. Snow transitioned to sleet, sleet to freezing rain, and freezing rain to rain throughout Thursday. Transition to mixed precipitation began before sunrise from Central Highlands to Northwest Aroostook County, and then over to northern Aroostook when the sun rose. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in the north, and 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet. A trace - 0.05 inches of freezing rain in the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Downeast region. A trace - 0.75 inches of sleet fell in the Central Highlands region. Sleet fell on top of snowfall, which had resulted in messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 1-3 inches of snow fell in Central Penobscot. Co-Op observer reported 0.7 inches of sleet in Lincoln.

Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Critical fire weather conditions resulting from strong and very dry windy conditions allowed for the Sparks and Crow Creek Wildfires to rapidly grow. The Sparks Wildfire, discovered April 28th, grew eastward in extreme western Quay County near NM Highway 156. The Sparks Wildfire threatened structures, but no damage has been reported and came under control April 29th. The Crow Creek Wildfire was discovered in Colfax County north of Maxwell, NM along NM Highway 445 April 29th. It rapidly grew northward toward U.S. Highway 64 closing the highway, and coming under control April 30th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Crow Creek Wildfire was discovered in the afternoon of April 29th near NM Highway 445 north of Maxwell. The fire quickly grew to an estimated 1,200 acres making wind-driven runs north toward U.S. Highway 64, closing the highway between Colfax Tavern and Raton Municipal Airport. No structures were impacted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee late in the evening of April 27, 2026, and into the early morning hours of April 28th. A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front, but the first round was scattered thunderstorms ahead of this line. The thunderstorms preceding the main line produced large hail and damaging wind gusts while the line of thunderstorms was mainly responsible for scattered wind damage. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering 100% of Colorado Zone 023 - San Juan River Basin. With the 4/8 US Drought Monitor update, the area of Extreme (D3) Drought was reduced to 75%, with Severe (D2) Drought now covering 25% of the zone. With the 4/29 update, Extreme (D3) Drought was further reduced to 10% coverage, with Severe (D2) Drought now covering 90% of the zone. Drought impacts at this point are limited to reduced winter tourism due to the poor winter snowpack. The Colorado State Climatologist has referred to this year's winter snowpack as historically poor. Additionally, concern is increasing over the impact of the drought on the upcoming summer wildfire season. There is also concern over water availability for home irrigation, farming, and ranching.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor indicated approximately 70% of Colorado Zone 001 - Lower Yampa River Basin was under Exceptional (D4) Drought, with the remaining 25% under Extreme (D3) Drought. With the 4/29 US Drought Monitor update, the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought was reduced to 30% coverage, while 70% of the zone was now under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions. These conditions remained unchanged through the end of the month. While no direct impacts from the drought were yet observed, increasing unease among those living and working in this zone has been noted. People are becoming increasingly concerned about water availability through the summer, and what the ongoing drought might mean for summer wildfires. There is also concern over drinking water availability and sourcing. With the lack of snowmelt, water quality is poorer than in typical years. The city of Rangely also has specific concerns regarding water flow rates and level, as they draw water directly from the White River, and if water levels are too low and flow too weak, it becomes impossible to draw water reliably.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High surf conditions led to an incident on April 2, 2026, at Poza Las Mujeres Beach in Manati, Puerto Rico. Two individuals from Bayamon, PR, a 23-year-old woman and a 24-year-old man, were walking along a rock formation near the natural pools when a wave swept the man into the ocean. While Emergency Management personnel successfully rescued the woman, the search for her companion continued for two days. Authorities recovered the man's body in a nearby area two days after the incident. However, two rescue divers were injured attempting to retrieve the body after being struck by a large wave, thrown against rocks, and swept away by strong rip currents. The divers suffered various fractures and trauma and had to be rescued by helicopter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two rescue divers were injured at La Poza de las Mujeres after being struck by a large wave, thrown against rocks, and swept away by strong rip currents during a recovery operation. The divers suffered various fractures and trauma. The incident occurred amid adverse marine conditions and strong surf, hampering recovery efforts for a 24-year-old male who was swept away by currents on Thursday. The injured divers were rescued from the water by a police helicopter (FURA) and transported to a medical center in stable condition.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Surface shortwave troughing allowed for ample lift in an environment with increasing instability as skies began to clear out during the early afternoon hours. Sufficient deep-layer shear across the region allowed for some thunderstorm development with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms across much of southern Pennsylvania during the late afternoon and evening hours. Thunderstorms across south-central Pennsylvania during the late afternoon hours gradually pulsed up to severe limits, causing an area of tree and building damage in Franklin County before a similar instance occurred in Adams County with a small barn collapse. Residual convection from western Pennsylvania began moving into portions of central Pennsylvania during the evening hours, causing isolated tree damage in Somerset County along with some damage in Bedford County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees near residences on Snider Road west-southwest of Chambersburg. Reports also indicated a small building collapse in the vicinity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of minor weather disturbances moved through the region from April 9th through the 11th. These combined with increased moisture to bring showers and storms to the region. With enough wind shear available in the atmosphere, some of these storms brought severe wind gusts to the region. Dry and windy conditions were in place on April 9th and that helped drive the spread of a wildfire known as The Smooth Eddy Incident which was over 500 acres. Additionally, the Purple Monster Wildfire would be sparked due to dry lightning in Oldham County on the evening of April 9th. That fire would go on to burn 1,911 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Purple Monster wildfire sparked the evening of April 9th about 9 miles north of Vega, TX due to dry lightning.  Gusty winds out of the thunderstorm would aid in the fire spread, as well as critically dry fuels and still low overall RH values. Part of the fire was on rugged and would be a challenge to tackle, and the fire would go on to burn 1911 acres before being contained.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The eastern part of Deaf Smith County started April in Moderate Drought (D1) and the remainder of the county continued into April in Severe Drought (D2) as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. However, this area of Moderate Drought quickly eroded within the first week and became Severe Drought. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured around three quarters of an inch in the west to around one tenth of an inch in the east. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather outbreak unfolded across central and north-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening of Friday (4/17). The event was triggered by a surface low-pressure system and cold front across the upper Midwest. ||NWS storm surveys confirmed 2 tornadoes that resulted in structural damage. A tornado formed 3 miles northwest of Glandon around 4:44 PM CDT and tracked into southeast Lincoln County producing EF-1 damage before dissipating around 4:55 PM CDT. Another tornado formed 3 miles west-southwest of Ringle in Marathon County around 4:46 PM CDT and dissipated around 5:03 PM CDT 5 miles southwest of Hogarty. This tornado produced EF-3 damage and destroyed 13 homes, produced major damage to 25 homes, with 101 homes reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. An estimated $8.2 million worth of damage was reported from the tornado. ||Beyond the tornadic threat, the storms produced isolated large hail up to half dollar size and damaging winds. Heavy rainfall was another impact, with localized totals ranging from 1 to 4 inches. These torrential downpours caused flash flooding, particularly in Marshfield where 2.65 inches of rain fell and multiple vehicles were reported stranded in deep water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed about 3 miles west-southwest of Ringle, east of Kronenwetter near Martin and Creek Road, at about 4:46 PM CDT. The tornado moved northeast, crossing highway 29 and downing hundreds of trees. It then moved through neighborhoods along and near River Road from Shady Lane to north of Clubhouse Road.  In this area, dozens of homes suffered significant roof damage, with failures of attached garages common. At least three homes in this area had complete removal of their roofs with failure of all external walls and several interior walls, consistent with EF-3 damage. Hundreds more trees were downed in this area, with many snapped near the base. Multiple sheds and outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado continued northeast, closely following the Eau Claire River, and dissipated between Gold Dust Road and County Road Z, 5 miles southwest of Hogarty, at about 5:03 PM CDT. The tornado destroyed 13 homes, produced major damage to 25 homes, with 101 homes reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. An estimated $8.2 million worth of damage was reported from the tornado. Total path length is estimated to be 13.53 miles long, with a width of 600 yards. Peak wind estimated to be around 145 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Occluding low pressure system to the north moves east, further into Canada. Associated warm front moved through the state Tuesday evening, March 31st, and associated cold front moved through Maine quickly behind it on Wednesday, April 1st. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th into the early morning hours on April 26th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and extreme North Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across parts of extreme North Louisiana in addition to isolated damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar size hail reported in Mooringsport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.

After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quasi-stationary surface boundary draped west to east across the northern peninsula and an approaching upper-level disturbance created an environment of favorable shear and instability that produced 2 EF-0 tornadoes near Hudson and Shady Hills in Pasco County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The development of a second circulation became apparent west of Shady Hills around 20 minutes after the circulation associated with the Hudson tornado weakened, and it is estimated that a tornado touched down near Gladwin Avenue to the west of East Road |at approximately 1843 UTC (2:43 PM EDT). Damage from this tornado consisted largely of snapped tree limbs and branches, although a large tree was uprooted and downed onto a mobile home along Eden Avenue near the intersection of East Road. The tornado moved very slowly east and east-southeast while appearing to exhibit a bit of a binary interaction with the remnant circulation that produced the Hudson tornado that was located to its east, before radar indicated it likely dissipated around 1848 UTC (2:48 PM EDT), less than one mile from where it is estimated to have touched down. Maximum peak wind of 85 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Electrical Transmission Lines (ETL)/wood poles leaning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. As the severe squall line pushed across the Missouri River into western Iowa during the mid-to-late evening hours of May 17, it maintained its intensity and continued to produce damaging straight-line winds. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. On May 18th, storms which initially developed as scattered cells over southern Illinois merged into a line across southern Indiana. This line of storms had a modest amount of instability and vertical wind shear to support it, with temperatures in the upper 80s and dewpoint temperatures in the upper 60s supporting 1500-2000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Scattered wind damage was observed across southern Indiana, with the greatest concentration of damage occurring in Dubois and Washington County, where several trees were blown down. Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms later in the evening would also lead to a few occurrences of flash flooding, especially along tributaries of the Blue River in Washington County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down along Indiana State Road 160 near its intersections with Franklin School Road and Conway Church Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down on Highway 96 between Bronson and Pineland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Pictures sent in of several roads inundated with about 1 foot of water on Main Street. Water up to the foundations of some buildings in Port O'Connor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station XWLD Wildcat measured gusts up to 41 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed social media report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter. Time estimated with radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 3.5 to 4-foot diameter tree was blown down across Stringtown Road near Hopedale.

Atascosa, Bastrop, Blanco, Caldwell, De Witt, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Karnes, Maverick, Wilson, and Zavala Counties stayed in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 20.6 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were still below normal conservation levels. Lake Travis rose 5.7 feet but was 11.1 feet below normal. Canyon Lake remained the same as in April and was 22.3 feet below normal. Lake Amistad dropped 0.7 feet and was 69.8 feet below normal. Medina Lake rose 0.3 feet but was still 87.1 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) to much below (<10%) normal on the Medina and Blanco Rivers; below normal on the lower Colorado River; and below normal to normal (25%-75%) on the lower Guadalupe and San Marcos Rivers. All other rivers were normal to much above normal (90%-95%).

Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media photo was received showing baseball-size hail along U.S. Highway 43 between Forkland and Demopolis.

This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were uprooted in Kirbyville.
