EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

An early season spring storm brought a period of freezing rain and snow to portions of western and central MN, and rain and storms to southern and eastern MN from Friday, March 6th into Saturday, March 7th. Storms were intense enough to produce occasional thundersnow and thundersleet during the evening of the 6th. Total snow accumulations were generally under an inch, and the greatest ice accretion reported by trained observers was around 0.1 in portions of western and central MN. A CoCoRaHS observer also noted around 0.1 in Fairmont of Martin County. Temperatures did not warm above freezing until later in the day on the 7th, resulting in a slower recovery from the light icing and snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A CoCoRaHS observer reported freezing rain with a thin layer of ice covered in snow on the morning of the 7th. The ASOS at nearby KSTC also noted a couple of hours of light freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The lack of rainfall during winter 2025/2026 resulted in a continuation of drought conditions across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley to begin March. D2 (Severe Drought) to D3 (Extreme Drought) was common to start March, with a small area of Exceptional Drought (D4) across the Brush Country.  Additionally, the area saw deepening/expansion of these categories and the month we on. From the last week in February to the first week of March, D4 (Exceptional Drought) increased across 8% of the area from 18% to 26%, and the combination of D2 to D4 increased from 91 to 97% of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions continued across a portion of central and southern Jim Hogg County, with D3 (Extreme) elsewhere, through the 2nd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.

At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter measured a 66-mph peak straight-line convective wind gust from a line of thunderstorms about one-mile NNW of Martin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Tuesday, March 31st, warm, moisture-rich Gulf air surged into the Northeast ahead of a nearly stationary front, placing the region in a favorable warm-sector environment for severe thunderstorms.  The combination of greater instability, strong wind shear, and abundant moisture ultimately led to severe thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon and evening. Daytime clearing likely increased instability, while both cooler incoming air and strong winds aloft supported organized storms capable of producing large hail, and damaging winds.

Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across North Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed across Hart Road northeast of Campti.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to D2 and D3 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 6, 2026, severe thunderstorms brought large hail to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 and D3 drought.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved into McCurtain County, Oklahoma, late in the evening on March 10th. Circulations were embedded within this line of thunderstorms,  with one of which producing an EF2 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 118 mph that began on Old Golden Highway, resulting in snapped trees and the loss of shingles to a local residence. The tornado then continued east, reaching Thomas Road near the intersection of Old Golden Highway where more trees were snapped and uprooted and a barn/shed experienced damage to the roof. The tornado then began to pick up in intensity as it moved across Oak Hill Road where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. As the tornado then continued northeast towards Rhoden Road, it caused significant damage to a family residence, resulting in the collapse of most exterior walls and an injury to the occupant who had to be airlifted to the hospital. Trees were then uprooted and fell onto this residence, causing additional damage. Next door to this home, significant damage was found to other structures as well as additional tree damage. Just before reaching Rhoden Road, another residence was damaged, where areas of the roof were uplifted, multiple trees were snapped and uprooted, and the neighboring barn experienced significant roof damage. The tornado then moved north/northeast of the road, pushing a small outbuilding off of its foundation and snapping and uprooting more trees before lifting as it crossed Highway 3.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees downed across Highway 371 in Laneburg.

Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.

During and after a period of heavy snowfall which totaled 6.0 inches at Worthington, visibility was reduced to near zero at times with blowing snow.  State and federal highways were closed during the height of the blizzard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of eastern Oklahoma experienced above average precipitation during April, with widespread five to eight inches of rainfall occurring across the area, and up to about twelve inches falling locally. This corresponded to 150 to 300 percent of monthly average precipitation occurring across much of the region. However, portions of eastern Oklahoma only received between 75 and 90 percent of monthly average precipitation amounts. As a result of the widespread rainfall across much of the region during the month, drought conditions improved across much of the area, with only portions of Wagoner, Cherokee, Mayes, and Choctaw Counties remaining in severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. The far eastern portion of Choctaw County remained in extreme (D3) drought conditions through the month. Monetary damage estimates as a result of the drought were not available.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and powerlines were reported across Palatka along 3rd Ave, Horseman Club Rd, South State Rd 19, Bardin Rd, Silver Lake Dr, West River Rd and Kelley Smith Ranch Rd. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Fire started during the late evening hours of March 26th approximately 2 miles north of Ashby. Strong northerly winds pushed the fire quickly to the south and south-southwest across western portions of Grant County. Ashby and Hyannis were evacuated during the night of March 26th. By the time the fire was contained on March 31, a total 36,004 acres of rangeland was consumed in Grant and Garden Counties along with two homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire initiated shortly after midnight MDT of March 26th approximately 2 miles north of Ashby. Aided by strong northerly winds, the fire raced to the south consuming approximately 34,748 acres in Grant County. Ashby and Hyannis were evacuated the night of the 26th. Four primary structures were consumed in the fire along with fencing and 3 outbuildings.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Fire started during the afternoon hours of March 12th approximately 9 miles south of Kilgore. This fire tracked east, then south due to a wind shift. By the time the fire was fully contained on the 23rd a total of 17,229 acres were consumed in the fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire started approximately 9 miles south of Kilgore during the afternoon hours of March12th. West winds initially pushed the fire east. By evening, a cold front shifted the winds to the north, forcing the fire south. By the time the fire was totally contained on the 23rd, a total of 17,229 acres of rangeland was consumed. One primary residence was consumed in the fire, along with one cabin and three outbuildings. Approximately 10 head of livestock were lost in the fire.

The thunderstorms caused a tornado, damaging winds, flash flooding and significant hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a closed upper low across the Baja Peninsula transitioned to an open wave and moved to the northeast, widespread convection developed from western-north Texas into much of Oklahoma during the evening of the 10th. Strong surface heating in the afternoon contributed to strong instability and, combined with increasing deep-layer wind shear, yielded an environment capable of organized thunderstorms. The most impactful storm of the event was a supercell thunderstorm that develop across west-central Oklahoma and tracked across the greater Oklahoma City metropolitan area, producing large to very large hail and a weak tornado. By mid-evening, a developing quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) produced sporadic (yet intense) thunderstorm wind damage across portions of far southern Oklahoma.

An upper level system brought showers and thunderstorms during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th across the combined Panhandles. The thunderstorms impacted the northeast but the state of the atmosphere was conducive for strong winds aloft to come down to the surface with even some of the lighter showers and storms. This created a few wind gusts exceeding 58 mph. The next morning, on the 11th, the upper level system brought high winds to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles which created wind gusts upwards of 71 mph early in the morning hours.

A negatively tilted upper-level trough began to deepen as it moved from the northern Rockies into the Middle Mississippi Valley on Sunday afternoon, driving a potent cold front eastward. Mid-level heights also began to fall Sunday afternoon as impressive kinematics overspread the region. Moderately steep mid-level lapse rates greater than 7 C/km, along with SBCAPE values of 750-1200 J/kg and storm relative helicity values upwards of 300 m2/s2 developed ahead of the cold front. An impressive line of storms formed along and ahead of the cold front, producing a half dozen weak tornadoes, 75+ mph wind gusts, and large hail across the Mid-South.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Damage to a porch and garage door. A fence and large tree branches were knocked down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front provided lift while marginal atmospheric parameters were in place for scattered severe thunderstorms. The cold front ignited storms after 10 AM in southwest Tennessee with CAPE values on the order of 700-1200 J/kg, effective bulk wind shear values of around 30 kts, and mid-level lapse rates around 6-6.5 C/km. These parameters increased during the afternoon with peak heating. Thankfully, the front was clear of southwest Tennessee, and only a few thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed trees across a bridge on Indian Creek Rd. Bridge is impassable.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low amplitude shortwave and accompanying 40 kt speed max approached the Mid-South and allowed lapse rates to steepen above 7 C/km. Ahead of this activity, the Mid-South housed around 750 J/kg of SBCAPE and bulk shear in excess of 45 kts. Small, organized clusters impacted the Mid-South in the late afternoon and brought damaging winds and large hail. Heavy rain showers ahead of the thunderstorm activity also brought on an urban flash flood threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water flowing over roadways in downtown Marietta.

Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Continued D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes and large to giant hail as they moved across northern Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of March 10th. Included in the 9 total tornadoes in northeast Illinois that day is an EF-3 which tracked from the south side of Kankakee into Newton and Jasper counties in Indiana and devastated a portion of Aroma Park. There were two primary corridors of large hail; one extending from northern Will County into the city of Chicago, which produced hail upwards of 4.8 inches in diameter, and another from central Livingston County extending east across Kankakee County. Nearly a dozen individual reports of hail greater than 4 inches came out of this southernmost corridor, and a 6.6 inch hailstone found in Kankakee is pending as the new Illinois state record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of central and eastern Kankakee County before moving into northwest Indiana. The most notable damage caused by this tornado in Kankakee County occurred in the Aroma Park area. This tornado began just north of W 3000S Road southwest of Kankakee, IL, about one mile east of State Route 115. The tornado intensified while traveling east-northeastward into the far southern section of the city of Kankakee in the vicinity of Route 45, where concentrated higher end EF-1 tree damage and structural damage was observed. The tornado intensified further while moving across E 2500S Road, destroying a two-story home and several metal farm buildings, consistent with EF-3 caliber wind speeds. Concentrated extreme tree damage was noted, with numerous large hardwood trees snapped, stubbed, or uprooted despite lacking leaves, likely due to extensive debris lofting in the area.|After crossing I-57 and the Kankakee River, the tornado rapidly increased in size, producing a swath of significant damage in and near northern portions of Aroma Park. In this area, multiple homes were heavily damaged to an estimated EF-2 intensity. The tornado's peak width occurred here and was estimated to be approximately 1550 yards. Ground survey and aerial imagery suggests that the tornado further intensified as it tracked east-southeast before crossing the Kankakee River again. Within a narrow 150-200 yard wide section along S. Sandbar Road to the northeast of Aroma Park, three homes were completely destroyed, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds, and multiple others were heavily damaged and rendered uninhabitable. A heavy pickup truck parked in front of the garage of one of the destroyed homes was moved over 100 feet into a ditch next to the driveway, possibly being spun around the remnants of a small tree before reaching the ditch. In addition, on the other side of Sandbar Road, a crossover type SUV appeared to have been rolled onto the adjacent property and deposited onto a pile of debris just north of a heavily damaged residence. Along the swath of the most intense structural damage, concentrated extreme tree damage was noted, with numerous large hardwood trees snapped, stubbed, or uprooted despite lacking leaves, likely owing to extensive flying debris. Along Sandbar Road and through the Kankakee Elks Golf Course, the tornado's width was estimated at near 1500 yards. The tornado then continued generally east to east-northeast towards the Indiana state line, downing numerous additional trees, causing occasional structural damage, and flipping irrigation pivots as it moved just north of the communities of Wichert and Hopkins Park. The tornado continued on its destructive path into Newton County, Indiana where it caused additional EF-3 damage before eventually lifting west of De Motte in Jasper County. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Aroma Park and the other two in Newton County, Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of Newton and northwest Jasper Counties, most notably the community of Lake Village. After forming and causing EF-3 damage in Kankakee County, Illinois, this tornado crossed into Newton County between W 800 N Road and W 900 N Road near N 650 W Road. Upon entering the county, the tornado destroyed multiple outbuildings and significantly damaged multiple homes. On N 600 W Road, multiple homes were completely destroyed with debris blown clear of the foundations, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds. Nearby forested areas had almost all trees snapped or uprooted with some trees remaining standing with only stubs of a few large branches remaining, likely due to extensive lifted debris. Multiple homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was destroyed along N 500 W Road and along and near N 400 W Road. As the tornado crossed US-41 into the south side of Lake Village, it widened to approximately 1100 yards while damaging the roof and canopy of a gas station and a nearby retail building. Further north along N 300 W Road, multiple blocks of homes had significant roof damage and almost all trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado continued eastward into a wooded area near the Lugene Links Golf Course, where a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted. As the tornado neared W 950 N Road and N 150 W Road, a few homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was completely destroyed. The tornado continued to produce damage to trees and outbuildings as it traveled northeastward through mainly rural portions of northern Newton County and northern portions of Roselawn. The tornado continued into Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Kankakee County and the other two near Lake Village.

Along South Pass in the Wind River Mountains, the maximum gust was 111 mph. The high wind resulted in roads closing to high profile vehicles for several hours, impacting transportation. The passing cold front was accompanied by a period of moderate to heavy snow that further hampered transportation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High wind occurred in portions of Natrona County. Some notable gusts included 76 mph at Scenic Drive and 67 mph at the Natrona County airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex, multi-day weather system moved across the region bringing rounds of wind, snow, and when combined, blizzard conditions. Strong winds aloft brought a round of high winds to the region beginning late on the 11th through the 12th. A low pressure system with a cold front pushed south through the 12th, ending the high wind threat, but bringing a heavy snow threat to the mountains and lower elevations of North-Central MT. The front then stalled, continuing periods of heavy snow through the 14th when gusty winds developed across the I-15 and MT Highway 200 corridor which led to blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter measured a storm total of 9 inches on the 14th. There were a few other heavy snow reports ranging between 9 to 14 inches for storm total.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter 2026 led to the continuation and expansion of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of March. Rainfall amounts during March only averaged around 2 inches, which was only half or less the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with the above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well.

Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across Southwest Arkansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed on Champagnolle Road just northeast of El Dorado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Early morning convection and persistent cloud cover in southeast Georgia limited the severe threat due to a lack of diurnal instability. Pre-frontal convection developed in northeast Florida around 12 PM then strengthened and converged into a line as it moved eastward toward the northeast Florida coast between 1-2:45 PM. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser shared pictures of a tree down across FL 206 near Hamilton Ave. Time was estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracks east over New England, and south of the Gulf of Maine on Sunday evening. Warm front with associated low pressure stays over the Maine gulf  Sunday evening into night. Snow moves in Sunday morning and continues into Sunday evening. Temperatures were teetering just below freezing, so this system was generally a wet, heavy snowfall. Highest totals fell Sunday evening, in northern Somerset and Piscataquis  counties, roughly 7 inches, with localized higher spots at higher elevations. Bangor region and interior Downeast generally saw 3-6 inches of snow. Downeast coast received roughly 2-4 inches. Snow moved out by mid-morning on Sunday.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 6-8 inches of snow fell in Northern Piscataquis Sunday into Sunday evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A pair of cold fronts brought abnormally cold temperatures on March 17th and 18th. The cool temperatures over the warmer lake waters of both Lake Erie and Lake Ontario setup a lake response off of the lakes, but conditions over and lee of Lake Ontario were more favorable. Lake Effect snow developed on the morning of March 17th northeast of the lakes. By the mid morning, the lake band off of Lake Ontario dropped south, focusing on Oswego County for the remainder of the day and into the early morning of the 18th. Oswego County received the most snow as the lake band oscillated back and forth north to south. ||Notable snowfall amounts include: 13.4 inches in Fulton, 10.0 inches in Altmar and 9.2 inches in Palermo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 95 mph and max width of 200 yards entered Washington Parish from Tangipahoa Parish just northwest of the intersection of LA 1057 and LA 450. The tornado strengthened, uprooting trees and snapping large branches and the tops of trunks as it reached LA Hwy 10 and moved into Sylvest Rd. Additional tree damage was identified downstream of the surveyed end point of this tornado via high resolution satellite imagery which evidently dissipated prior to it reaching LA Hwy 16, west of Franklinton.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong EF-1 tornado touched down south of Hwy 570 near Moak Rd in Pike County, MS. This tornado rapidly strengthened and grew in size as it tracked to the east-northeast causing destruction of a wood frame farm outbuilding and increasingly significant treefall as it crossed Kodiak Ln and Magnolia Pisgah Rd. While there was a high proportion of treefall associated with this tornado in this area, a significant portion was due to uprooted trees from soft soils due to recent heavy rainfall. As such, maximum sustained winds were estimated near 110 mph despite the heavy deforestation. This level of heavy deforestation spanning approximately 375 yards wide at peak width continued across Hwy 570 to Dye Ln where tree damage rapidly became less significant. It's estimated that this tornado rapidly lifted as it crossed Magee Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 62 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large scale spring storm brought a round of heavy snow to the Upper Mississippi Valley from Saturday, March 14th through Sunday, March 15th. The footprint of the greatest totals stretched from southeast MN into central WI, where many places saw at least a foot of snowfall. The heavy snow combined with strong northwesterly winds resulted in reduced visibilities, often at one mile or less in the heaviest hit areas. Persistent blizzard conditions were most widespread in southern Minnesota, severely deteriorating road conditions. This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by MNDOT for much of the southern portion of the state, including the closure of the southbound lanes of I-35 near Albert Lea.||The highest snowfall reports were:|19.0 inches in Zumbrota, MN (Goodhue).|16.9 inches in Rosemount, MN (Dakota).|16.0 inches in Pine Island, MN (Goodhue).|14.8 inches in Elko New Market, MN (Scott).|14.5 inches in Lakeville, MN (Dakota).|14.5 inches in Prior Lake, MN (Scott).|14.0 inches in western Bloomington, MN (Hennepin).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around 2 to 4 inches of snow fell from Saturday night into Sunday morning. The highest report was 4.1 inches in Long Prairie. The snow was heavy at times, impacting visibility and driving conditions Sunday morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: After snowing for much of the afternoon, a trained spotter at Bonanza reported 2.5 inches of snowfall as of 1645 EST. Later in the evening, a trained spotter reported a measured snow total of 4.0 inches near Bays Branch at 2013 EST.  Meanwhile, an NWS employee 3 miles WSW of Prestonsburg measured 1.2 inches at 2003 EST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening of Thursday March 5th, a supercell thunderstorm tracked out of northern Oklahoma and into southern Kansas. As the storm crossed into Kansas, the rotation strengthened and eventually produced a couple of tornadoes over western Sumner County. One tornado damaged a few farm outbuildings, multiple trees and overturned a pumpjack. It was rated an EF-2. The other tornado damaged farm outbuildings and utility poles. Thankfully there were no injuries or fatalities. The storm produced damaging straightline winds as well. ||Additional storms developed across central Kansas with up to nickel to quarter sized hail reported. There were storms with winds around 60 mph as well including one that damaged a cedar tree.

A strong upper level jet was positioned over the Pacific Northwest from March 8 through 13. As it mixed down to the lower levels, it brought periods of high winds sustained in the 30 to 40 mph range and gusts up to 70 mph for portions of the region. It was followed by a cold front that brought snow amounts ranging from 2 to 9 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer reported 9 inches of snow 6 miles south of Huetter. Other reports were 8.5 inches near Hayden Lake and 7 inches near Post Falls.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northerly winds were sustained as high as 48 mph 3 miles south-southeast of Lake Park and 44 mph at Spirit Lake. A period of light freezing rain totaled up to a tenth of an inch near Lake Park. After a change to snowfall which totaled 5.3 inches 3 miles south-southeast of Lake Park, 4.7 inches at Milford, and 4.5 inches in Spirit Lake, visibility was reduced to near zero at times with blowing snow. Travel was not advised over most roadways during the height of the blizzard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme to exceptional drought conditions combined with dried available fuels resulted in a wildfire developing across northeast Florida. High dispersions and gusty winds at the end of March especially assisted in the spreading of the new wildfire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On March 23rd, Alachua County Sheriff's Office reported that a small brush fire that ignited near S County Road 325 near Cross Creek. This fire quickly grew in size to 134 acres by the end of the month thanks to very favorable fire weather conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April saw below to well below normal precipitation across a majority of New Mexico, with the exception of a small area of the northwestern mountains. The average temperature anomaly was also generally 1 to 5 degrees above normal over nearly all of the state. This led to a notable expansion of extreme drought conditions over northeastern NM, and severe drought conditions over the eastern plains. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: New Hampshire faced a pronounced north-south divide in precipitation amounts during April 2026. Northern New Hampshire benefited from wetter short-term precipitation patterns and a gradual snowmelt, which yielded localized improvements in overall drought intensity and shallow groundwater conditions. Conversely, coastal and southern areas faced substantial precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This poor spring recharge actively drove drought degradation, prompting the reintroduction of Moderate Drought (D1) across southern New Hampshire. Groundwater levels across regional monitoring networks remained critically low, heavily constrained by long-term moisture deficits. Despite minor surface-level recoveries in soil layers and small reservoirs, water levels in waterways underperformed expectations, with streamgages finishing the month exhibiting below-normal to much-below-normal streamflows. No flooding or significant runoff events were reported anywhere in the state, mirroring the quiet hydrologic conditions seen throughout the region. Overall drought conditions improved in the north, and worsened in the south.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Coos County averaged 4.51 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 1.22 inches above normal. The USDM denoted significant drought improvements during the month, with the March 31 USDM having 41% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 58% in Moderate Drought (D1), but by April 14 the D2 dropped to 0.6%. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South Texas saw intermittent rounds of beneficial rainfall through April that provided short-term drought relief and improved topsoil moisture, but long-term drought impacts remained evident across much of the region. In the South district, heavy rains temporarily greened up rangelands, improved forage availability, and stabilized livestock conditions, though low stock tank levels, depleted subsoil moisture, and continued supplemental feeding highlighted ongoing hydrologic stress. Crop conditions generally improved with moisture, supporting emergence and development of corn, sorghum, cotton, hay, citrus, and specialty crops, but uneven stands, delayed planting, irrigation dependence, and lingering drought-stressed soils continued to limit recovery potential. Across the Coastal Bend, rainfall was more variable, with some areas receiving several inches while others remained dry, resulting in uneven improvement to pasture and crop conditions. Corn and sorghum showed recovery where rain occurred, though drought stress, failed stands, replanting concerns, and poor forage availability persisted in drier locations. Overall, recent precipitation improved short-term crop and grazing outlooks across South Texas, but sustained rainfall will be needed to fully recharge soils, support dryland crop development, and maintain pasture recovery heading into the warmer months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Improvement to just D2 drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.||The second supercell developed northwest of Seward, Nebraska, and tracked northeastward to Wahoo, Nebraska, before gradually weakening as it approached the northern side of the Omaha metropolitan area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 8 tornadoes were confirmed across southeast Louisiana, including 2 with path lengths exceeding 10 miles. Well over a dozen additional reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down On HWY 51 and Arcola Rd.

This led to a widespread travel advisory issued by WISDOT for the majority of western WI, including the temporary closure of I-94 south of Eau Claire.||The highest snowfall reports were:|20.5 inches near Augusta, WI (Eau Claire).|19.0 inches in Pepin, WI (Pepin).|18.5 inches in Durand, WI (Pepin).|16.0 inches in Cadott, WI (Chippewa).|15.2 inches 7 miles S of Altoona, WI (Eau Claire).|15.0 inches in Lund, WI (Pepin).

The DOT issued a travel advisory on Sunday due to the blizzard conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southern stream shortwave phased with a digging northern stream upper trough over the OH/TN valleys the night of 3/11 into the morning of 3/12 bringing a strongly forced system into the forecast area. The environment ahead of this system was characterized by sufficient instability with MLCAPE values around 500 J/kg, 0-1km SRH values of 100-200 m2s2 and 0-6km shear of 60 knots. This environment combined with strong forcing supported a QLCS line that moved across the forecast area during the morning hours. Several damaging wind reports and a few tornadoes occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of siding blown off of 5 separate houses near the intersection of Garcia Dr and Brainard Ave in Fort Gordon.

During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.

A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rockcastle County dispatch reported a tree blown down along North Wilderness Road (US-25) in the 10500 block.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the central US overnight on the 14th into the 15th, resulting in a first round of snowfall across northern Michigan on the morning of the 15th. There was a break for part of the day of the 15th, though some areas closer to Manistee transitioned to sleet/freezing rain at times. Another round of precipitation moved in during the evening and overnight hours going into the 16th as the strengthening low pressure center crossed southern Michigan, resulting in feet of snow across the UP and parts of northwest Lower Michigan/Tip of the Mitten. This transitioned to several inches of sleet across parts of north central Lower Michigan, and significant icing across northeast Lower and central Lower Michigan. Additional wraparound snow and lake effect snow continued during the day of the 16th, resulting in additional blowing/drifting snow and whiteout conditions. Snow drifts as high as 4-7 feet, to even as high as a single story house, were reported. Widespread travel difficulties and stops across the area due to the heavy snow and sleet, with additional tree and infrastructure damage due to ice accretion resulting in the Michigan governor declaring a state of emergency for Alcona, Alpena, Missaukee, Ogemaw, Roscommon, and Wexford counties in northern Lower Michigan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Near-blizzard conditions were observed at KCIU on the 16th, with winds gusting 25-35mph and visibilities of a quarter mile or less off and on for several hours. Snowfall totals across the county were around 10 inches in the city of Sault Ste. Marie, MI to as high as 31 inches near Pickford. State offices were proactively closed for the 16th due to the anticipated conditions. Michigan State Police rescued an escaped horse on M-129 near Sault Ste. Marie during the near-blizzard conditions, but all parties, including the horse, were uninjured.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning and afternoon hours of April 15th, 2026, an upper-level wave ejected northward into the central Plains, pushing an attendant surface low pressure system from southeast Nebraska northeastward into central Iowa. This system pulled a warm sector northward into eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, interacting with a weak convergent boundary draped generally along and just north of the Interstate 80 corridor. Driven by afternoon high temperatures peaking in the 70s, instability increased through the day, with a narrow ribbon of surface-based CAPE (SBCAPE) values exceeding 2,500 J/kg wrapping into the mid-Missouri River Valley. Under the influence of this unstable and highly sheared environment, two elevated severe supercells tracked across eastern Nebraska into southwest Iowa.||The first severe cell tracked generally from Schuyler, Nebraska, east-northeastward into Dunlap, Iowa. This storm produced several reports of quarter-sized (one inch in diameter) hail along its track. As the storm moved through Harrison County, Iowa, it intensified further, producing golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) and wind-driven hail damage in Dunlap.||The second supercell developed northwest of Seward, Nebraska, and tracked northeastward to Wahoo, Nebraska, before gradually weakening as it approached the northern side of the Omaha metropolitan area. Notable severe reports from this storm included two-inch in diameter hail south-southwest of Dwight, Nebraska, and golf-ball-sized hail (1.75 inches in diameter) within Dwight itself, which resulted in visual damage to residential vinyl siding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated at 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 15, 2026, strong non-thunderstorm wind gusts impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. During the morning hours, a deepening mid-level trough moved into the region and intensified an existing surface low pressure system. This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. This deep mixing tapped into a potent 60 to 70 knot jet descending on the backside of the system, efficiently transferring momentum to the surface and resulting in multiple measured wind gusts in the 58 to 64 mph range.||Additionally, the combination of snowfall and gusty winds reduced visibility to under a quarter mile for extended periods across portions of northeast Nebraska. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. Further south, across the rest of eastern Nebraska, intermittent snow bands dropped 0.5 to 2 inches of snow, resulting in more sporadic reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KLNK ASOS measured wind gust of 60 mph at the Lincoln Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.

A strong cold front moved through the southeast US as a deep mid/upper level trough shifted eastward from the lower Mississippi valley into the deep south.  Ahead of the front, there was ample instability, low level helicity, and shear with cool temperatures aloft. A tornado watch was in effect for much of northeast Florida and southeast Georgia on March 16, 2026. Then, a squall line along the cold front swept across northeast Florida bringing damaging straight line winds ranging from 45 to 70 mph between 1:30 - 4:30 PM. Convection shifted off the coast by 5 PM.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Environmental conditions favorable for a QLCS (Quasi-Linear Convective System) tornado event developed across southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening hours of March 11th. An upper-level storm system moving east from Texas overspread a very moist and increasingly unstable air mass in place across the region. At the same time, intense low-level wind shear and strong atmospheric spin developed as southerly winds strengthened ahead of an approaching line of storms with bowing segments.||The combination of rich Gulf moisture, strong low-level atmospheric spin, and a fast-moving line of thunderstorms created an environment supportive of embedded rotating circulations along the leading edge of the QLCS. As that line moved west to east across the local area, several rapidly developing tornadoes formed within these circulations. A total of 6 tornadoes were confirmed across southwest Mississippi and multiple  reports of damaging straight-line winds were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak estimated winds near 105 mph and max width of 300 yards touched down near Johnston Chapel Rd. A broadly defined area of uprooted and damaged trees was identified via high resolution satellite imagery near the beginning of this path which continued east-southeast across Old Brookhaven Rd and Interstate 55. This damage was corroborated by a storm report with pictures of numerous uprooted trees near Chapel Dr. The tornado began to strengthen and increase in size with complex multi-vortex behaviors evident according to the damage path present after crossing I-55. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted along US Hwy 51, Rollingwood Drive, and Johnston Station Rd. Additional tree damage was surveyed near Lakeside Drive on Southwest Mississippi Community College campus. The tornado continued east destroying a cinderblock dugout at North Pike High School. More tree damage was also identified on Barrett Drive and Jaguar Trail. Scattered pockets of wind damage were evident via ground survey across Barnett Rd and L.D. White Rd, but the most cohesive damage points representative of a tornado damage path were evident to the southeast as the multi-vortex tornado continued to produce patches and swaths of tree damage on high resolution satellite imagery near Hwy 570 and and River Ridge Rd. The tornado damage path evidently became incoherent after crossing River Ridge Rd and it's estimated the tornado lifted prior to reaching Hwy 44.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind caused roof siding to rip off of a home 2 miles from US Route 127 near Hustonville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tekamah ASOS measured wind gust of 68 mph.

Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

This intensification caused a considerable tightening of the regional pressure gradient, resulting in strong northwest winds that overspread the area from the late morning through the remainder of the day. Behind the departing surface low, strong cold air advection steepened low-level lapse rates. Although snowfall totals peaked at just 3.5 inches in northern Cedar County, this was sufficient to produce several hours of blizzard conditions in the region. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system deepens over Maine on Monday evening, as low approaches from the northwest by Tuesday. Steep pressure gradient over the region and upper-level jet, helps to support strong winds in northern and eastern Maine. Wind gusts predominantly peaked over northern and eastern Maine overnight Monday into Tuesday morning. Winds generally 55-60mph over Downeast region, and generally 35-50mph in more inland regions. Plethora of downed trees, primarily in Penobscot, Washington, and Hancock counties. Roughly 3,000 people lost power during this event, most of which were in Hancock county.

At the surface, a cold front drifted southeastward across Lake Ontario, southern ON, and southern Lower MI toward Lake Erie during the early afternoon through late evening of the 31st. Ahead of the front, several lines of multicell thunderstorms and a discrete supercell persisted generally eastward across northern OH during the late afternoon through the late evening of the 31st. Some of these storms produced sporadic straight-line convective wind damage, two mesovortex-related tornadoes, and small hail. The ambient environment of these storms included weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. It appears the development of a southwesterly to west-southwesterly low-level jet and resulting enhanced surface-based ESRH coinciding with favorably-low mixed layer LCL's contributed to the development of the two tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Ashtabula County Airport ASOS recorded a 63-mph peak straight-line convective wind gust from a line of thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapid thunderstorm initiation developed during the afternoon on March 15th as strong ascent occurred when a cold front interacted with a plume of returning surface moisture. Modest surface dew points in the lower to middle 60s amid steep mid-level lapse rates supported 1000-2000 J/kg of MUCAPE. 50+ knots of deep-layer shear also favored storm organization with a mixed mode of supercells and line segments. The surging nature of the front promoted rapid upscale growth into a QLCS before spreading eastward across the Red River Valley and into the Ark-La-Tex region. Strong low and mid-level shear between 200-300 m2/s2 supported embedded supercells, along with QLCS wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were recorded across East and Northeast Texas.
