A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms bringing numerous trees down the New River Valley and the Piedmont of Virginia. A gradient of negative omega values (upward motion) across southwest Virginia was noted as the storms passed, likely keeping the storms active in spite of crossing over the Appalachians. This storm episode is notable as gusty winds from the storms' outflow resulted in wind damage in areas that did not meet warning criteria. One was strong enough to knock over a tent in Bedford, killing 1 and injuring 22 at an outdoor event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down and on a power line near the Walmart Neighborhood Market. A power line was also reported down and caught a tree on fire on Hollyhock Road NW.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant flash flooding reported in Homer with Highway 79/Main Street covered by swift moving water, leading to a high water rescue of two people pulled from a stalled vehicle in floodwaters at least two feet deep in a nearby grocery store parking lot.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted northern Oklahoma on the 13th and early morning hours of the 14th. The first featured a slowly decaying line of thunderstorms during the early morning of the 13th, producing a few observations of severe winds and wind damage. Later in the afternoon, a pair of supercell thunderstorms developed along a remnant outflow boundary across the region. Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Blackwell (BLAC) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed numerous trees across central and southern Johnson County into Franklin area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with path length of 11.94 miles and a path width of 200 yards began in Johnson county with 2.47 miles of it within Johnson county. The tornado had a peak wind  of 105 mph with peak winds of 90 mph within Johnson county. Within Johnson county, impacts were limited to tree damage and several farms and structures with minor damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above normal temperatures and minimal precipitation continuing from late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of northeast LA. Through the month of May, D2 (Severe Drought) and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions expanded to affect all of our northeast LA parishes as depicted on the U.S Drought Monitor. Average temperatures for the month ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 50 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 10 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in West Carroll Parish intensified from D2 (Severe Drought) to D3 (Extreme Drought) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy downpours occurred across central MS and south MS during the afternoon hours of May 25. These downpours lead to multiple roads to be flooded and one fatality.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The 200 block of McGilvary Road was flooded over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with path length of 6.64 miles and a path width of 300 yards began in eastern Vigo County. Within Vigo county the peak width was 75 yards, path length of 2.14 miles and peak winds of 95 mph. The peak winds were 110 mph after it moved into Clay county. Damage within Vigo county was limited to tree damage along East Dallas Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of June, D0 (Abnormally Dry) D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Adams County to Lowndes County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Attala County decreased from D1 (Moderate Drought) to D0 (Abnormally Dry) as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This long-track EF-2 tornado developed about 5 miles east of Waukon during the late afternoon hours and trekked east-southeast through Allamakee County resulting in significant tree damage and some structural damage. The tornado eventually reached the Mississippi River just north of Harpers Ferry, where it crossed into Crawford County, Wisconsin near US Lock and Dam No. 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This strong and long-tracked EF-2 tornado began about 5 miles east of Waukon and continued east-southeast causing a continuous path of tree damage all the way to the Misssissippi River near Lock and Dam 9. The tornado also damaged farm outbuildings and a few residences. Extensive tree damage along Waterville Road formed the basis for the EF-2 rating for this tornado. The tornado crossed the Mississippi River and continued east into Wisconsin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.

An unsettled weather pattern unfolded across the Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians for the start of June amid a stalled frontal boundary and building heat and humidity. This combination allowed for daily storm initiation across the Midwest that eventually tracked into Ohio and northern West Virginia. On June 6th and 7th, storms tracking into the area reached Harrison and Taylor Counties late in the evening and caused tree and power line damage before dissipating with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Grafton, a tree blew down onto Addison Street.

Otherwise, high pressure influenced the lowlands and maintained quiet weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed trees and power lines in the community of Gary resulted in local power outages.

Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 18, 2026, an approaching upper-level shortwave trough and associated cold front crossed the NWS Buffalo region, interacting with a developing warm sector to trigger scattered showers and severe thunderstorms. According to NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions, early-morning clouds and showers along a warm front initially limited heating, but afternoon boundary-layer destabilization yielded 1,000 to 1,500 J/kg of MUCAPE���particularly across the Western Southern Tier. The Storm Prediction Center outlined a Marginal Risk for severe weather, noting that 0���6 km bulk shear values near 45 knots and steep low-level lapse rates would support multi-cell storm structures capable of producing localized damaging wind gusts. Meanwhile, the Weather Prediction Center noted a subdued flash flood threat; although warm-cloud depth and precipitable water values over 1.25 inches fueled heavy downpours, fast storm motion kept rainfall progressive enough to prevent widespread flooding. Following the cold frontal passage, convective activity waned overnight as cooler air over Lake Erie initiated early-season lake effect rain bands and a lingering potential for waterspouts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of trees down, and trees and wires down across the Town of Clyde.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees and wires down near the intersection of South Dakota Road and Sarah Furnace Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked wires down onto Bald Eagle Mountain Road east of Beech Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This episode is part 1 of 2 from two rounds of severe weather that occurred during the late evening of June 9th into the early morning of June 10th. ||Widespread wind damage occurred across western Minnesota during overnight storms which had moved in from the Dakotas. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were three separate downed tree reports in the Mount Airy area. One was at the intersection of Rockford Street and Old Highway 601 near Iglesia Misionera Cristo Vive Mount Airy. Another was at the intersection of Lambert Farm Trail and Rockford Street. The last was at the intersection of Rockford Street and Smith Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown onto a powerline at east Knox Rd. and Day St, resulting in a power outage.

Additional thunderstorms developed in the afternoon of June 2nd in a similarly unstable summer airmass.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to 1 inch in diameter was observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires were downed near Poultney Street and Broadway in the Village of Whitehall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported wind gusts up to 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by the Automated Surface Observing System site 3 miles north-northwest of Sioux Falls at Joe Foss Field.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large high pressure system parked over the Mississippi River Valley, bringing several days of hot, southerly flow across the region. From the afternoon of June 28 to the evening of June 29, the combination of heat and humidity, boosted by recent rain, created dangerous conditions. Some heat index values exceeded 105 to 110 degrees in and near northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous heat index readings reached a brief afternoon peak as high as 105 degrees at Elkton, 103 degrees at Brookings, and 102 degrees near Volga.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits (107F) combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet measured wind gust of 73 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video of street flooding on Barton Avenue in Luling.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A well-defined damage path of an EF-0 tornado was identified on high-resolution satellite imagery over rural, inaccessible parts of southeast St. Charles Parish. The tornado touched down near Bayou des Allemands and tracked north-northwest over rural, inaccessible marshland. While the majority of damage along this path was marsh vegetation, a narrow swath of trees were evidently damaged/displaced which is the basis for its EF-0 rating. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several streets across Poplarville were impassable due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. High precipitable water (PWAT) values of 1.7+ inches within the unstable environment supported strong downdrafts capable of isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of Northwest Louisiana along with a few reports of localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees downed along Highway 615.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 11, 2026, a severe flash flood event impacted Carroll County, New Hampshire, devastating numerous roads in the town of Madison and surrounding areas. The event was driven by a slow-moving warm front interacting with an unstable and moist airmass. This setup allowed a cluster of deep convection to train continuously over the region, producing extreme localized rainfall rates that peaked at an estimated 4 inches per hour. Total accumulations reached 5.47 inches near Albany and a public report of 4.45 inches in Madison, qualifying the deluge as a 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) event. The extreme flooding was heavily exacerbated by saturated antecedent soil conditions left behind by a remarkably wet May, which had already seen double its typical rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain over steep terrain resulted in Salins Rd and Appenvel Way was being closed at due to flooding at the intersection.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Putnam (PUTN) Mesonet observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was reported down along Newsome Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated Extreme (D3) to widespread Severe (D2) drought continued across Southwest Arkansas through the first half of June, before tapering back to Severe (D2) drought as appreciable rainfall helped to ease drought conditions. June monthly rainfall totals ranged significantly from 5-10 inches across Southwest Arkansas with isolated lesser amounts in parts of Union County, generally near and northeast of El Dorado. As a result, drought conditions continued to improve throughout the month with the additional rainfall. Despite the improvement, all of this rainfall was not enough to completely erode the severe drought across the vast majority of Southwest Arkansas, which persisted through the end of the month.

Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across Caldwell and La Salle parishes in East-central Louisiana through the first ten days of June, before improvement to drought was observed as widespread 5-8 inches of rain fell across these areas. Improvement to soil moisture as well as streamflow was observed across East-central Louisiana, with ag producers reporting improvement to stock pond levels and greenup of pastures. Beneficial rain continued into the first half of July, with additional improvement to drought conditions observed.

A cold front moved slowly southward through the Mid-Atlantic, triggering scattered thunderstorms with heavy rainfall rates and severe weather. While shear was not very high (<30 knots), the atmosphere was considerably unstable with SBCAPE values of at least 2000 J/kg. Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms that reached as far south as North Carolina. One storm in particular sent a swath of trees and power lines down in Mount Airy of Surry County. This storm formed and intensified after crossing the Blue Ridge and shortly dissipated in Stokes County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Five fallen tree reports. Two separate reports along Perry Taylor Road near Mt. Airy. Another tree was down near the intersection of McKinney Road and Old Hwy 601. The final two were also along McKinney Road.

Low level lapse rates and mid-level lapse rates were up to 8.5 C��/km and  6.5��C/km, respectively, in the Piedmont. All these parameters, combined with DCAPE values of 1000-1400 J/kg, resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms bringing numerous trees down the New River Valley and the Piedmont of Virginia. A gradient of negative omega values (upward motion) across southwest Virginia was noted as the storms passed, likely keeping the storms active in spite of crossing over the Appalachians. This storm episode is notable as gusty winds from the storms' outflow resulted in wind damage in areas that did not meet warning criteria. One was strong enough to knock over a tent in Bedford, killing 1 and injuring 22 at an outdoor event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mPing reported hail the size of a dime at Village Oaks Town Homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 27th afternoon to early evening, a stationary west-east frontal boundary combined with a very moist column and forcing from a short wave trough over the Middle Mississippi Valley, to produce heavy to extreme rainfall rates over Sullivan and Greene Counties, and later Martin County.  Resultant flash flooding was considerable during the afternoon east of Sullivan through the Linton area.  Less impactful early evening flash flooding occurred in Martin County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy thunderstorm rainfall of up to 2.50 inches in under 2 hours, produced flash flooding in central Martin County that crossed US Highway 50 near Stiles Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple cars were stalled in high water in and around Haynesville, including Highway 79 covered in high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted northern Oklahoma on the 13th and early morning hours of the 14th. The first featured a slowly decaying line of thunderstorms during the early morning of the 13th, producing a few observations of severe winds and wind damage. Later in the afternoon, a pair of supercell thunderstorms developed along a remnant outflow boundary across the region. Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A personal weather station observation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 6th afternoon to early evening, a moist column combined with dynamic lift from an approaching cool front to produce numerous to widespread training thunderstorms over northern portions of central Indiana.  While most cells were generally sub-severe, isolated damaging winds were most organized in Warren County and most intense at the Muncie airport.  More noteworthy was the quasi-parallel nature of the approaching boundary to the moist conveyor's axis, which produced multiple roudns of heavy rain over several zones, and considerable flash flooding in portions of Warren County and Fountain County where up to an estimated 7.00 inches of rain fell. This severe weather event would be the first of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several tree limbs downed by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with path length of 11.94 miles and a path width of 200 yards began in Johnson county and continued into Shelby county with 9.47 miles of it within Shelby county. The tornado had a peak wind of 105 mph with peak winds. Within Shelby county, the most intense damage happened along homes near 600W and 75W with several homes impacted along with widespread tree damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with path length of 6.64 miles and a path width of 300 yards began in eastern Vigo County before moving into Clay county. Damage within Clay county included significant damage to a 100 year old brick barn and several homesteads in western Clay county along 200S.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined effects of persistent above-normal temperatures and minimal precipitation starting in late April 2026 resulted in mounting drought impacts across portions of much of northern, southern and central Mississippi. Through the month of June, D0 (Abnormally Dry) D1 (Moderate Drought), D2 (Severe Drought), and D3 (Extreme Drought) conditions, as depicted on the U.S. Drought Monitor, expanded to affect areas generally from south of a line from Adams County to Lowndes County. D4 (Exceptional Drought) conditions developed through northwest portions of the area including portions of Bolivar County and Washington County. Average temperatures for the month in these areas ranged from 2 to 4 degrees F above normal. Observed precipitation values ranged from 45 percent of normal to lower than 25 percent of normal. Soil moisture values continued to worsen through the month, with subsoil moisture values between 20 to 30 percent below normal for much of the affected area. This placed a severe stress on pastures for livestock and began to reduce expected yield from row crops. Pine plantations and Christmas tree farms experienced severe losses especially among younger trees. Streamflows on creeks and rivers were reduced.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions in Carroll County decreased in intensity from D3 (Extreme Drought) to D2 (Severe Drought).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large thunderstorm complex developed in south central South Dakota in the early morning hours of June 29th and tracked northeast across the state, finally exiting into southeast North Dakota and western Minnesota during the mid morning hours. Extreme winds were observed with this system. Two separate weather sensors recorded extraordinary peak wind gusts of 131 mph: the South Dakota State University mesonet station located at the Highmore Municipal Airport and a personal weather station three miles east-southeast of Holabird. These winds knocked down trees and damaged structures across portions of central and northeast South Dakota. Ground zero was the town of Highmore (population of roughly 650 residents) in Hyde county where up to 80 to 90 percent of residences and commercial buildings experiences some form of wind damage, with a number of vehicles and farm implements also being tipped and tossed.  Residents at Highmore Health, the towns nursing home had to be evacuated due to damage to the facility. There was no loss of human life and injuries reported were due to post-storm cleanup operations. 3 horses died due to these high winds. Cost of debris cleanup in Hyde county alone topped out at 1.4 million dollars. ||Electrical infrastructure was severely disrupted, causing $2.4 million in utility distribution damage across Hyde and Hand counties. Power was knocked out to 1,072 residents in Hyde County (94% of the county). Power generation was heavily impacted; at least 20 wind turbines were damaged or destroyed at the Triple H and North Bend wind farms, with replacement costs estimated at $50 million.||Day County suffered extensive damage, particularly around Andover, where straight-line wind speeds reached 100 mph. Extensive tree stands were leveled, grain bins dented, and buildings damaged at the Andover Threshing Grounds. Day County power damage reached $18,000, leaving 487 residents without electricity. A brief EFU tornado was confirmed near Andover.||Even as the storm system departed, wrap around high winds caused additional tree damage in areas that had just missed out on thunderstorm wind damage, with several trees and limbs down in parts of Aberdeen, and a peak wind gust measured on a personal weather station of 88 mph in the town of Westport (Brown county).||Governor Rhoden requested a Presidential Disaster Declaration to assist with damage cleanup and repairs for Hyde, Hand, Hughes, Buffalo and Stanley counties including Lower Brule and Crow Creek reservations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon sea breeze, combined with a weak upper level disturbance approaching the Lower Texas Coast, triggered two bands of slow-moving thunderstorms that dropped more than 3 of rainfall in a short period of time.  One band, across the west half of Brownsville, created localized flash flooding with water between 2 and 3 feet in some areas. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A slow moving thunderstorm with torrential rainfall dropped 3.64 in about an hour across west Brownsville, just south of Los Ebanos Blvd. and west of Barnard Road. Similar rainfall likely occurred in a flood-prone intersection along the IH-69E frontage road and shopping centers at E. Price Blvd, where video from social media showed cars stuck in knee deep water.  An NWS employee reported over a foot of water with difficult to near-impassible driving along Wild Rose Lane, west of Business 77 (Central Blvd.).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 29th into early July 2026, a stacked subtropical ridge built northward from the Mississippi Delta through most of North America's eastern half, with its center nearly stationary near the Tennessee Valley.  Corresponding surface high pressure aligned from the Gulf coast to New England promoted light to moderate southwesterly breezes into central Indiana which maintained dewpoints usually in the 73-78 degree range and daily high temperatures in the low 90s.  Resultant daily maximum heat indices were generally 100-109 degrees, with several, mainly central to southern central Indiana zones, reaching heat indices of 110-113 on June 29th and/or 30th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A stretch of excessive heat began on the 30th with a peak heat index value of 105F recorded at the Columbus AWOS. This event continued into July.

Each day yielded developing showers and thunderstorms across the Midwest and travelling eastward along the front before dissipating after sunset. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 18, 2026, an approaching upper-level shortwave trough and associated cold front crossed the NWS Buffalo region, interacting with a developing warm sector to trigger scattered showers and severe thunderstorms. According to NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions, early-morning clouds and showers along a warm front initially limited heating, but afternoon boundary-layer destabilization yielded 1,000 to 1,500 J/kg of MUCAPE���particularly across the Western Southern Tier. The Storm Prediction Center outlined a Marginal Risk for severe weather, noting that 0���6 km bulk shear values near 45 knots and steep low-level lapse rates would support multi-cell storm structures capable of producing localized damaging wind gusts. Meanwhile, the Weather Prediction Center noted a subdued flash flood threat; although warm-cloud depth and precipitable water values over 1.25 inches fueled heavy downpours, fast storm motion kept rainfall progressive enough to prevent widespread flooding. Following the cold frontal passage, convective activity waned overnight as cooler air over Lake Erie initiated early-season lake effect rain bands and a lingering potential for waterspouts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of trees down across the town of Scio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto Mix Run Road.

Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked wires down on Villa View Drive near Rouzerville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees onto wires near Forest Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief EF-0 tornado occurred during the early evening of June 14th. The maximum wind speed was estimated to be 75 mph and the tornado had a maximum path width of 15 yards. Minor damage to trees was noted along PA-872 in Homer township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees snapped on Patterson Run Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down at the intersection of Perch Road and Grassy Creek Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on IL-29 south of Cedar Hills Dr.

Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six two-foot diameter trees were blown down and shingles were peeled off a roof.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Halls Pond Road in the Town of Hebron.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mott NDAWN reported wind gusts up to 68 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by the South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 4 miles east of Irene.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of trees down, blocking Highway 48 south of Essex, IA. Wind gusts were estimated at 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gause Boulevard in Slidell impassable due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. High precipitable water (PWAT) values of 1.7+ inches within the unstable environment supported strong downdrafts capable of isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of Northwest Louisiana along with a few reports of localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water covered multiple roads in Homer.

Throughout June 2026, New Hampshire experienced short-term drought relief driven by soaking rains, though long-term groundwater deficits persisted in the southern half of the state. Spurred by a remarkably wet May and continued rainfall in June, total drought coverage in New Hampshire fell from a high of over 68% Severe Drought (D2) in late 2025 to 35.9% total drought (D1���D2) by June 23. Northern and western New Hampshire saw drought designations completely erased due to localized rainfall exceeding 150���200% of normal. D2 Severe Drought covered 3.2%���10.9% area in the state, confined mostly to southern Rockingham and Hillsborough counties along the Massachusetts border and the Seacoast. Despite geographical shrinkage, lingering Moderate (D1) and Severe (D2) drought areas overlapped with higher-density southern counties. As a result, approximately 75% of New Hampshire's residents (997,000 people) remained within a classified drought zone in late June. Deep subsurface water tables, reduced in the drought of 2025, lagged considerably due to slow infiltration rates in thicker surficial aquifers and long-term rainfall deficits. Well monitoring confirmed several southern New Hampshire wells remained in the Below to Much Below Normal categories.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first microburst occurred over the open water of  Lake Winnipesaukee shortly after 4:00 PM on June 18th. Based on damage reports this likely occurred in the vicinity of Round and Welch Islands in Gilford, New Hampshire. There were pictures of trees snapped on Round Island and reported damage on parts of Welch Island. The microburst continued unimpeded by friction towards Sandy and Cow Islands in Tuftonboro, New Hampshire. There were at least three camps damaged by tree falls on Sandy Island. On the southwest side of Cow Island there was significant tree damage. At least three additional camps were damaged by falling trees, as well as at least two docks that sustained damage. An estimated 1,500 trees, mostly softwood, were either snapped or uprooted by the winds. The open water and lack of friction likely allowed this microburst to expand beyond on the accepted definition of areal extent.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down near the intersection of Pratt Road and Moser Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A remnant outflow boundary extended roughly west-to-east from North Central Texas into Northeast Texas and far Northwest Louisiana early in the afternoon on June 2nd, with a separate convective outflow boundary analyzed to the north across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. South of this secondary outflow boundary, temperatures were in the lower 90s F with lower to mid 70s dew points supportive of strong buoyancy characterized by MLCAPE values 3000-3500+ J/kg. High precipitable water (PWAT) values of 1.7+ inches within the unstable environment supported strong downdrafts capable of isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, thunderstorms increased in coverage through the afternoon along these boundaries with several damaging wind reports recorded across parts of East Texas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Boat dock canopy covering was destroyed on Lake Tyler East.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A small complex of showers and thunderstorms drifted south into McCurtain County Oklahoma and the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas during the early morning hours of June 12th, near a weak cold front and attendant upper level disturbance. This front, coupled with the weak disturbance aloft and weak low level forcing along the lead gust front, maintained these storms as they entered the northern sections of the region, and produced strong, gusty winds near 50 mph across Sevier and Howard Counties in Southwest Arkansas. These winds resulted in a few isolated downed trees near De Queen, Lockesburg, and Dierks around daybreak on the 12th, before diminishing later that morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down and blocked Highway 70 about two miles west of De Queen. The nearby ASOS at the De Queen Helms Sevier County Airport measured a peak wind gust of 52 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the 27th afternoon to early evening, a stationary west-east frontal boundary combined with a very moist column and forcing from a short wave trough over the Middle Mississippi Valley, to produce heavy to extreme rainfall rates over Sullivan and Greene Counties, and later Martin County.  Resultant flash flooding was considerable during the afternoon east of Sullivan through the Linton area.  Less impactful early evening flash flooding occurred in Martin County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme thunderstorm rainfall up to 5.00-6.00 inches in under 4 hours from east of Sullivan to south of Bloomfield, produced flash flooding in Linton, Lyons and Switz City.  In Linton, vehicles stalled out, a child swept away by water was rescued, and railroad ties floated through town.  Additionally, a culvert was washed out in Greene County on County Road 475 West, while Indiana Route 54 was flooded out in Sullivan County east of Sullivan.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weak EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 88 mph was spawned during the evening hours of June 23, 2026, from a quasi-linear convective line segment passing through and near the community of Plain Dealing. A vast majority of the damage was to trees with many hardwood and softwood trees being uprooted along the path. Sporadic softwood tree snaps throughout the assessed path of nearly 5 miles long garnered the peak wind speed of 88 mph for the tornado. Many power lines were downed in the path of the tornado, but the survey team determined that most of this occurrence was due to trees and tree limbs falling on the lines. It is also important to note that there were other sporadic instances of tree damage throughout northern Bossier Parish was due to the severe line of thunderstorms moving through during the evening, but the assessed tornado damage featured much more concentrated damage along a path.

Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
