EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Putnam County EF-1 tornado crossed over into Morgan County where it caused further minor tree damage.  The tornado had weakened to an EF-0 before entering Morgan County with estimated max wind speeds of 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with path  length 1.37 miles and maximum width 100 yards moved through mostly rural areas of Brown county. The peak winds were 100 mph with the tornado causing extensive tree damage and mainly roof damage to a couple buildings.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct clusters of severe thunderstorms impacted central and northeast South Dakota during the afternoon and evening of June 4. In the northeast, severe storms generated large hail up to golf ball size five miles south-southeast of Cottonwood Lake and nine miles southeast of Tulare. The Huron Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) 12 miles east-southeast of Sunshine Bible Academy recorded a peak wind gust of 86 mph.||A separate cluster of storms tracked through mainly central and south central South Dakota producing peak wind gusts of 71 mph and 68 mph at the South Dakota Department of Transportation Road Weather Information System (RWIS) stations six miles southwest of the Joe Creek Recreation Area and nine miles north-northwest of Vivian, respectively.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball-sized hail was reported nine miles southeast of Tulare.

On June 10, 2026, a warm front pushing across the NWS Buffalo region tapped into a hot, humid airmass with dewpoints in the upper 60s and 70s, setting the stage for organized summer convection. As a mid-level disturbance tracked over the Great Lakes, multi-cell thunderstorm clusters formed over Western New York and consolidated into linear segments, prompting SPC Severe Thunderstorm risks for damaging wind gusts and hail. Simultaneously, atmospheric precipitable water levels near 1.5 inches triggered localized heavy downpours up to 1.5 inches per hour, leading to WPC Marginal Excessive Rainfall risks and minor urban flooding in low-lying areas. Convective activity waned overnight with the loss of diurnal heating, giving way to cold air advection behind the cold front that fueled early-season lake-induced instability and marine hazards across Lakes Erie and Ontario.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Barcelona Harbor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. The Aberdeen City Forester reported the cost for just tree cleanup on city property (including boulevards) topped out at $14,585. ||Six miles south of Goodwin, multiple irrigation pivots were twisted by intense winds. Major power outages affected 5,849 customers in Brown County, 1,106 in Hamlin County, and 64 in Deuel County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down into a yard in Curwensville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down multiple trees between Glen Hope and Madera, including one down across State Route 53.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked down trees and wires on West Street in Warren.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Ahead of an approaching cold front and aided by leading shortwave-induced ascent, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked across southeastern Ohio and western Pennsylvania producing wind damage, several tornadoes, and a few instances of large hail. Moist southerly flow pulled upper 50s to low 60s dew points with surface temperatures in the mid 70s allowing for sufficient destabilization up to 1500 J/kg of MLCAPE, 35-40 knots of effective shear, and 50-150 m2/s2 of 0-1 km SRH to support an all hazards threat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees snapped and uprooted across Keisterville with concentrated damage behind  the Post Office.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This episode is part 1 of 2 from two rounds of severe weather that occurred during the late evening of June 9th into the early morning of June 10th. ||Widespread wind damage occurred across western Minnesota during overnight storms which had moved in from the Dakotas. The strongest wind report was observed in Lac Qui Parle County at 83 mph near Marietta, MN. One tornado was caught on camera overnight near the Kandiyohi and Pope County line, but no damage was reported, leaving its rating as EF-U (Unknown). As the line of storms continued east, wind gusts decreased to 30-40kts in most areas. However, several emergency managers areas reported downed trees within their municipalities. A few downbursts did occur northeast of the Twin Cities metro area, with tree damage being reported from St Paul up towards Shoreview and White Bear Lake and then all the way up to Forest Lake and Chisago City.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind gusts downed trees and powerlines in Hancock. AWOS station Morris Municipal Airport measured a 60mph thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado developed 4 miles north of Mattoon and tracked|southeast, damaging trees, homes, and electrical transmission|lines as it crossed US Highway 45. It intensified as it reached|County Rd 700E, uprooting large hardwood trees and lifting the|roof off a single family residence. It continued east-southeast|from there, crossing Interstate 57 where it flipped a semi,|resulting in one injury. It then heavily damaged a few farm|outbuildings and trees on the western outskirts of Charleston. It|continued eastward through the north side of Charleston, causing|damage at the fairgrounds, a few outbuildings, an elementary school, and trees|throughout town before lifting 2 miles east of Charleston along|Illinois 16.

Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-scale mid-level trough nudged out into the Northern Plains while a strong frontal boundary moved out across the Dakotas. Storms initiated with up to 3000 J/kg elevated CAPE near a surface boundary. Storms quickly organized into a linear system with short bowing segments which produced gusts of 60 to 75 mph. A large trailing stratiform precipitation shield developed featuring a strong wake-low an hour or two after the strong thunderstorm outflow winds with gusts up to 70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gust was measured by a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site 8 miles east of Alpena.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS survey team concluded an EF-1 tornado tracked from Evelyn Ave towards Woodhaven Dr and Roberta Grove Blvd. Several businesses in the Lynn Park Shopping Center (at the corner of Prospect Ave and Grand Caillou Rd) sustained damage to almost every window and had partially collapsed interior walls and their roof. HVAC equipment on the roof was thrown northward onto the ground from these businesses. 4 homes had partial to significant roof loss. One home had an exterior wall collapsed. Several carports were significantly damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado that began in Hancock County entered Harrison County at Deschamp Road. The tornado then evidently weakened and the damage path become more intermittent until it reached the Wolf River where another swath of trees was rated low-end EF-1. The tornado damage path became intermittent once more after crossing the intersection of Cemetery and Steel Bridge Rd. The tornado then evidently reached its third peak as an EF-1 tornado as it crossed Cemetery Rd and MS Hwy 53 where swaths of trees were damaged and uprooted. The tornado then rapidly dissipated as it continued northeast and it's estimated to have lifted prior to reaching Herman Ladner Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front bisected Minnesota which had produced thunderstorms during the pre-dawn hours of Friday, June 5th, 2026. Storms redeveloped that afternoon across western MN along this same stalled boundary and producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.

An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Buffalo (BUFF) Mesonet observation.

A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in the Piedmont of Virginia. A swath of wind damage was reported in Franklin County which included one report a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down in the Drakes Branch Community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Old Minden Road was closed due to high water over the roadway between Benton Road and Gould Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-6+ inches fell over Southern McCurtain County Oklahoma from the morning through the evening, contributing to areas of flash flooding. An isolated severe thunderstorm also developed over this area during the evening hours on the 23rd before diminishing. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across McCurtain County Oklahoma along with an isolated damaging wind report.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Living Land Road was flooded in multiple locations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening mesoscale convective system (MCS) advanced east southeast into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours on June 24th, just north of an outflow reinforced frontal boundary which extended from Northeast Texas into North Central Louisiana and eastward into Mississippi. Behind the MCS, showers and thunderstorms increased in coverage from North Louisiana into Southwest Arkansas. Wind profiles in the 925-850 millibar layer showed some modest strengthening into the 25-30 knot range from the south southwest, helping to remove lingering lower level convective inhibition centered near 850 mb. Low level flow overrunning the surface boundary set up a convergence axis in the 925-850 millibar layer, aligned from Southeast Oklahoma into Northwest Louisiana. This zone of convergence focused increasing coverage of elevated thunderstorms throughout the morning, beneath increasingly diffluent flow aloft in the 300-400 millibar layer. The convergence axis was aligned with a gradient in MLCAPE of 500 to 1500 J/kg noted to the southwest of the axis. Precipitable water (PWAT) values ranged from 1.7 to near 2 inches across the region. As a result, hourly rainfall rates of 1 to 2+ inches occurred within areas of training storms with localized rainfall totals of 2 to 6+ inches common across Southwest Arkansas. Thus, numerous reports of flash flooding were recorded throughout the morning into the mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was reported to be entering 8-10 homes on North Main Street in Nashville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a tree.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An area of mainly sporadic tree damage was|found across Kokomo from near Berkley Road, along and near west|Sycamore street, to Crown Point Cemetery. Additional Tree damage|was found along east Sycamore street, near Wildcat Creek.||All of this damage was found to be due to straight line winds, as|all damage was blown down in a east to east-northeast direction.|Wind gust that caused the damage are estimated to be in the 80-90|MPH range with a peak gust of 95 MPH possible.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three trees downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several tree limbs snapped by thunderstorm wind gusts in town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One downed tree was observed along Long Ridge Road.

Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked wires down along Westminster Drive near Tire Hill.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 70 mph, knocked down numerous trees and power lines down in Middlecreek Township. This included a large tree down that blocked portions of Barron Church Road for multiple hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree onto a house in Warren.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from severe drought to moderate drought as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 100th to 200th percentile across much of SE West Virginia. Rainfall totals over the past 30 days ranged from 5.0 to 8.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread short-term improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to near normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Both Mercer and Monroe counties continued to remain in Severe drought as portions of those counties received rainfall totals closer to 3-4 inches over the 30 day period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought Conditions improved from Severe drought to Abnormally dry conditions as several rainfall events resulted in 30 day percent-of-normal rainfall averaging in the 110th to 125th percentile range across Eastern Greenbrier County. Rainfall totals ranged from 4.0 to 6.0 inches. The rainfall resulted in widespread short-term improvements in soil moisture and stream flows, bringing most back to just below normal levels after being categorized as below normal to much below normal in the months prior. Soil moisture improved to the 70th to 80th percentile based off the NASA Sport LIS 0-100 cm soil moisture percentile, while stream flows improved to the 75-90th percentile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Large scale upper level troughing with two separate embedded upper level lows progressed across the region late June. The colder core, which actually ended up being the southern of the two, moved across Southwest Montana and resulted in snow levels falling to below 6,000ft at times as heaviest precipitation moved over the area. Heavy snow developed near and above pass level in northwest Beaverhead County, resulting in nearly 2 feet of snow near the peaks close to the ID border.||Meanwhile further north under the second upper low, a strong surface low ended up developing near the Hi-Line, which resulted in strong winds in a few zones before the surface low filled/weakened. ||Strong upper level support further north resulted in widespread heavy rains, with additional upslope forcing along the Rocky Mountain Front, which resulted in some flooding in Glacier NP June 29.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Late morning June 29 reports were received that water in Swiftcurrent Lake was approaching the bottom of the bridge connecting Many Glacier Hotel to Many Glacier Road, and that several trails and campsites had already been closed in the Many Glacier Valley due to flooding from heavy rain and a small contribution from snowmelt. Many Glacier Hotel was ultimately evacuated after MBRFC forecast crest information was received. Numerous trails were closed in the Many Glacier Valley, with it being noted that water was flowing down several trails.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.

With estimated wind speeds of approximately 120 mph, |the storm caused moderate damage to outbuildings and trees, along with minor structural impacts to single-family residences. The tornado continued to the southeast where it caused major roof damage to a two-story house, rolled an SUV, damaged an outbuilding, and snapped several large hardwood trees. Moving southeast toward |E 1700th Ave, the storm snapped the top of another large hardwood |and stripped shingles from a single-story residence, with further |tree damage reported just north of that location. East of N 700th |St, more tree damage occurred alongside shingle damage to a mobile |home. As the tornado tracked further along E 1700th Ave, it damaged |another outbuilding, two grain bins and additional trees before |finally lifting approximately 0.25 miles east of N 800th St.

Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado touched down in rural Jasper County, about 2.5 miles southwest of Rose Hill. Tree damage was noted along N 1050th St, with trunks snapped on several hardwood trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed near the intersection of Route 153 and Beattie Hollow Road in the Town of Salem.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large-scale mid-level trough nudged out into the Northern Plains while a strong frontal boundary moved out across the Dakotas. Storms initiated with up to 3000 J/kg elevated CAPE near a surface boundary. Storms quickly organized into a linear system with short bowing segments which produced gusts of 60 to 75 mph. A large trailing stratiform precipitation shield developed featuring a strong wake-low an hour or two after the strong thunderstorm outflow winds with gusts up to 70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gust was measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The week leading up to the Fourth of July brought a punishing, multi-day stretch of extreme heat to the Mid-South. A massive mid-level ridge of high pressure parked itself directly over the Tennessee River Valley, creating a persistent heat dome over the entire Mid-South. Under this stagnant high-pressure system, daytime heating worked in tandem with tropical moisture surging up from the Gulf. This combination created dangerously muggy air, pushing dew points into the mid-to-upper 70s���and occasionally near 80��F���making the atmosphere feel as suffocating as it was hot.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The daytime hours maximum heat index was within the triple digits combined with limited cooling at night with an overnight low in the mid to upper 70s.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the last two days of June, a favorable synoptic weather pattern brought extreme heat to portions of northeast Iowa as ample moisture resulted in remarkably high dewpoints. Consequently, heat indices soared well above 100 degrees with numerous locations seeing heat indices of 110 to 115 degrees or even higher in some locations. June 29th was the hottest day but extreme heat persisted into the 30th where heat indices in excess of 100 degrees were still common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of extreme heat moved into the region during the end of June with widespread heat indices over 100 degrees. On June 29th, heat indices ranged from 105 to 109 degrees across the county during the afternoon and early evening. The highest heat index observed in the county was 109 degrees in Oelwein. On June 30th, continued heat indices over 100 degrees persisted throughout much of the daytime hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level low pressure system associated with Post-Tropical Storm Arthur pushed slowly through the area resulting in several rounds of thunderstorms over the coastal waters.  Some of these storms produced strong downburst winds over the waters resulting in several marine thunderstorm wind events.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet site at Mid-Lake measured wind gust at 44mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Approximately half a foot of water on Highway 24 north of US Highway 90 in Gray. A car is stalled in the water.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-0 tornado touched down near Bayou la Cache, east of Chauvin, LA in Terrebonne Parish and tracked northeast toward Montegut, LA. High resolution satellite imagery depicted a defined swath of tree damage beginning over inaccessible areas which aligned with a tornado debris signature on Climavision V014. The damage path grew to a maximum width of 200 yards and peaked in intensity over inaccessible forest west of Blue Jay St as it enroached on neighborhoods near Crochetville Rd. The tornado gradually weakened and decreased in size as it moved over southern parts of Montegut, near Crochetville Rd where mainly minor tree damage was noted. It is estimated that this tornado dissipated near Willow Aly and Bayou Terrebonne.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado tracked across parts of St. Charles and Jefferson Parishes, affecting the community of Avondale, LA. This tornado began over the Salvador Wildlife Management Area as evidenced by a well-defined 15-20 yard wide path of damage to marsh vegetation oriented southwest to northeast that was collocated with an intensifying area of rotation on both TMSY and KHDC. This damage path gradually broadened and fluctuated in intensity causing minor damage to trees as it traveled over uninhabited and inaccessible marsh areas. The tornado damage path evidently became larger and more noticeable again near Bayou Verret. A clear path of tree damage was evident on high resolution satellite imagery spanning to approximately 300 yards wide with numerous trees damaged or displaced as the tornado exited St Charles Parish and crossed into Jefferson Parish 1.35 miles south of Highway 90 along Bayou Verret.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The damage path of a brief EF-0 tornado was identified via high resolution satellite imagery in northwest Harrison County. This tornado caused predominantly damaged to trees over inaccessible areas between West Wortham and McHenry roads. This focused damage path closely aligned with a strong tornado vortex signature that crossed through the area. The tornado apparently lifted as it crossed McHenry Rd as no other damage could be identified as the circulation lifted northward.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down on a power line in Millard.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface cold front bisected Minnesota which had produced thunderstorms during the pre-dawn hours of Friday, June 5th, 2026. A strong low-level jet which had supported this development weakened, thus allowing for gradual clearing and building instability during the daytime hours. A suitable environment for severe thunderstorms was realized across the eastern Dakotas and western Minnesota as precipitable water values exceeded 1 inch and dew points crept into the 60s.  Storms redeveloped that afternoon across western MN along this same stalled boundary and producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of penny size hail provided via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure located over western Nebraska featured a northward progressing warm front that extended as far as the Minnesota and Iowa border. On June 7th, 2026, this warm front proceeded into southern Minnesota which produced tropical-like precipitable water values exceeding 1.75 inches and dew points near 70 degrees. With sufficient instability in place, storms developed in the wake of the passing warm front.  Very heavy rainfall rates between 1.75 to 2.0 inches per hour produced localized flooding in Steele County. Two intersections were closed by law enforcement due to the flooding, and another rural intersection one mile south of Steele Center (CR-45 and 88th St) was closed due to moving water over the road.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall caused flooding at the intersection of 4th Ave SW and 3rd St SW. County dispatch advised that the intersection was closed off. Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor radar analysis recorded rainfall rates between 1.75 to 2 inches per hour in a short duration of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At 10:45PM on June 19, 2026, the Iron fire ignited on private land northwest of Eureka in Juab county, Utah. Given exceptionally hot, dry, and windy conditions through much of its early life, it would go on to grow rapidly through the next few days while exhibiting extreme fire behavior as it grew across portions of Juab, Utah, and Tooele counties (encompassing portions of public zones 102, 106, and 115). Thankfully, no structures were harmed with no reported injuries or fatalities. This fire has been contained as of July 3, 2026 and reached a total of 41,842 acres.

An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freedom (FREE) Mesonet observation.

A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in the Piedmont of Virginia. A swath of wind damage was reported in Franklin County which included one report a tree falling onto a house.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down near the intersection of Fall Creek Road and Kentuck Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley bordering Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Northeast Texas, and into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours of June 19th, with a warm, very moist and unstable air mass present across East Texas along and south of the front. An upper level disturbance traversed atop the front during the morning and early afternoon hours, enhancing large scale forcing for the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along and south of the front. Given the very moist air mass in place, these storms were very efficient rainfall producers, with widespread rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling over Central and Northern Red River and Bowie Counties in Northeast Texas. These excessive rainfall amounts in a short period of time resulted in reports of flash flooding across these areas, particularly in the Detroit and Dekalb areas with multiple roads flooded and water entering homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water entered several homes and buildings in Detroit. Report from mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley of Northeast Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and into extreme Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning hours of June 23rd, which focused areas of repeated showers and thunderstorms as an upper level disturbance shifted east-southeast atop the front. A very warm and moist air mass resided near and south of the front, which contributed to increased storm intensity and rain rates with areas of heavy rainfall falling over extreme Northeast Texas and North Louisiana during the morning. Widespread rainfall amounts of 2-10+ inches fell over portions of North Louisiana during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the evening through the morning hours on the 24th, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-4+ inches falling. These storms also spawned an isolated tornado near Plain Dealing during the evening of the 23rd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed on Highway 170 in Vivian.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 9th evening, a moist and unstable airmass across central Indiana interacted with an approaching upper-level disturbance resulting in severe thunderstorms. Thunderstorms initially developed in western and northwestern central Indiana after 6:00 PM EST before organizing into line segments that tracked eastward across the region through the late evening and overnight hours.||Strong straight-line wind gusts were produced by the severe thunderstorms. Peak measured wind gusts reached 61 mph at the Purdue University Airport in Tippecanoe County and 63 mph at the Indianapolis Regional Airport in Hancock County. The severe winds caused broad impacts across Tippecanoe, Vigo, Clay, Morgan, Hendricks, Hancock, and Johnson counties, primarily consisting of downed trees, large tree limbs, and localized power line damage that created temporary roadway obstructions.||Repeated convective activity and heavy rainfall totals between 2.5 and 4 inches subsequently impacted eastern portions of the area during the early morning hours of June 10. This heavy rain led to localized flash flooding across roadways in Decatur County, though no building inundation or water rescues were reported before floodwaters receded. This severe weather event would be the second of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limbs downed by thunderstorm wind gusts. Minor flooding on roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 11th evening, a cold front interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass across central and northern Indiana, initiating a fast-moving severe convective line. The synoptic setup supported widespread straight-line wind damage and embedded mesovortices as the squall line tracked eastward through the region between 7:59 PM EST and 10:32 PM EST.||Five tornadoes touched down across Warren, Carroll, Johnson, Shelby, and Randolph counties during the event. Four brief EF-0 tornadoes produced peak winds between 70 mph and 85 mph, causing tree damage and minor agricultural impacts. The most significant tornado was an EF-1 that tracked nearly 12 miles across Johnson and Shelby counties, generating peak winds of 105 mph that damaged several homes, outbuildings, and trees.||Widespread straight-line winds produced the majority of the severe impacts as the line moved across more than a dozen counties. Measured wind gusts frequently ranged from 59 mph to 67 mph, with localized straight-line winds estimated up to 95 mph in Howard County. Damage across the region included widespread downed trees and power lines, overturned commercial vehicles on major highways, and structural damage to roofs, barns, and outbuildings. This severe weather event would be the third of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts across a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.

During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree branch downed and shingles blown off by thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of storms initially generated hail mainly to the size of quarters across portions of central South Dakota, then organized into a line and increased speed. This resulted in high winds across northeast South Dakota during the late evening and early overnight hours. A peak wind gust of 90 mph was recorded by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) mesonet station 4 miles north of Altamont, with a 78 mph wind gust recorded on a personal weather station 9 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 77 mph on a personal weather station in Faulkton and a 74 mph gust at the SDDOT station near Ree Heights (Hand County). ||Intermittent wind damage was reported across much of northeast South Dakota, with reports of peeled roofs and lost tiles, blown in garages and trees down. In the city of Aberdeen and surrounding area, several of these trees landed on vehicles. The Aberdeen City Forester reported the cost for just tree cleanup on city property (including boulevards) topped out at $14,585. ||Six miles south of Goodwin, multiple irrigation pivots were twisted by intense winds. Major power outages affected 5,849 customers in Brown County, 1,106 in Hamlin County, and 64 in Deuel County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A resident 2.5 miles east of Castlewood relayed photos of a damaged metal shed and multiple downed trees.

A surface trough and low-level jet combined with a very moist and unstable air mass that led to severe thunderstorm development along the triple point of a surface low in west central North Dakota. Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon in southwest North Dakota, with additional storms in the far northwest. Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.

Storms gradually moved to the north-northeast through the evening in a primarily cluster storm mode. The area of most significant damage was in Ward and McHenry Counties. In the town of Sawyer in Ward County, the Emergency Manager reported damage from powerful thunderstorm wind gusts that resulted in power outages, trees on roads, and a large tree that fell onto a house and made a hole in the roof. Northeast of Deering in McHenry County, there was significant damage to a homestead due to thunderstorm wind gusts. A barn on the property had roof panels ripped off and some collapse of the wood frame structure for the roof. Damage in both of these locations were consistent with wind speeds around 90 mph. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, a few miles west of Fortuna in Divide County. One tornado occurred with these storms, and was reported approximately 3 miles east of Noonan in Divide County. It was a very brief tornado and caused no known damage, so has been rated EF-Unknown by NWS policy.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hebron NDAWN station reported wind gusts up to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the South Hills of Charleston, a tree was blown down at the intersection of South Ruffner Road and Shady Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A decaying band of precipitation moved across the Ohio River into West Virginia early in the morning of the 22nd, then additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms made their way across the area during the day and into the night. Precipitation eventually tapered off from west to east following the frontal passage overnight into the morning of the 23rd. ||Strong to severe storms that developed during the day downed trees and powerlines across parts of the area. Flash flooding from the excessive rainfall in southeast West Virginia stranded vehicles, prompted water rescues, entered some homes, washed out a few bridges, and impacted numerous roads. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding observed in 7600 Block of Laurel Creek Road near Clothier. People were stuck in homes with no power in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered late morning and early afternoon hour showers and thunderstorms continued to exhibit upscale growth into a broken line of strong-to-severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours of June 11, 2026. Environmental analysis during the late afternoon hours across central Pennsylvania exhibited ample instability (with SBCAPE values exceeding 3000 J/kg across the entire region), steep low-level lapse rates, and ample DCAPE values exceeding 1000 J/kg. While shear was not the most sufficient, ample instability allowed for storms to continue in a broken line as they shifted eastward across the region through the evening hours. Widespread wind damage was reported along the broken line of thunderstorms, with numerous trees down across much of the forecast area south of the Interstate 80 corridor. Across areas north of the Interstate 80 corridor, scattered instances of wind damage were reported, with the most widespread in Lycoming County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked trees down throughout Berlin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms began to develop during the early afternoon hours across northwestern Pennsylvania with the passage of a potent shortwave diving southeastward out of the Great Lake region on June 6, 2026. Storms gradually trended upscale with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms beginning to form by the afternoon hours within an environment with ample instability (2000 J/kg of CAPE) and bulk shear (30 knots) in place across northwestern Pennsylvania. Wind damage was observed in portions of Warren County during the early afternoon hours before storms across northern Pennsylvania began to weaken. Additional development to the south continued to exhibit upscale growth with more favorable shear and instability in place given less cloud cover, with two broken lines of thunderstorms gradually congealing into one solid line across eastern Pennsylvania. These lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage between the Interstate 80 and 78 corridors. Further south, a bowing segment across southwestern Pennsylvania continued into Somerset County producing destructive wind damage near Somerset. This bow exhibited some weakening as it progressed further east, but continued to produce considerable tree damage across portions of Bedford and Fulton Counties before weakening further.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms, producing wind gusts estimated near 70 mph, knocked down multiple wires in and around Confluence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a tree down onto US-6 near Ludlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the afternoon and evening of June 11th producing wind damage, localized flooding and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong long track tornado with estimated peak winds of 165 mph touched down in far southeast Lake County and crossed into far southwest Porter County where it quickly intensified. Widespread tree damaged including snapped and uprooted trees occurred along the entire path of the tornado in Porter County. Just east of Route 231 there was a swath of trees where nearly every tree trunk was snapped. Along S 625 W Road, a few farm outbuildings were destroyed and a house suffered roof damage. Several farm buildings, a garage and a manufactured home were destroyed along W 1000 S Road just west of S 500 W Road. Another house suffered major roof damage. A barn and farm outbuildings were destroyed just east of S 475 W Road. Farm buildings and grain bins were destroyed near S 350 W Road. Large trees were snapped and uprooted in this area. The tornado continued moving northeast and strengthened and widened as it moved north of Route 8. The tornado was likely at peak intensity as it moved across eastern Porter County. Several homes were destroyed and two separate sets of high-tension power trusses were sheared apart and collapsed. Significant scouring of the ground and crop damage also occurred. The tornado moved into LaPorte County just north of Slocum Ditch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low and surface cold front combined with a very unstable airmass resulted in severe thunderstorms across western and central North Dakota. Supercell thunderstorms initially produced very large hail before transitioning to a linear storm mode, which led to widespread significant thunderstorm wind gusts. The largest reported hail was 3 inches in diameter, occurring southwest of Medora in Billings County. Measured wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common as storms moved across western and central North Dakota. The area with the most significant wind damage occurred across Stark, Morton, Mercer, and McLean Counties. In a swath from Dickinson, to Hebron, to Beulah, to Douglas Bay, to west of Garrison, damage from thunderstorm wind gusts led to winds estimated from 80 to 100 mph. The strongest measured wind gust came from a personal weather station just east of Beulah that reported a gust of 103 mph. Damage included campers turned over, large trees downed, roof damage, power outages, garages destroyed, vehicle damage, siding damage, and dented grain bins.
