EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Delayed public report received via social media of hail measured up to 1.25 inches in diameter near Cook, NE. Time estimated with radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Highway CC was closed at a low water area due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of  upstate South Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. Despite the very warm and dry conditions, occurrence of large wildfires was limited, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was instituted in late March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued through April as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured 0.2 inches in the far northwest to 1.2 inches of rain in the eastern half. Hartley County ended the month about 0.3-0.8 inches below normal for much of the county, however, the locations that saw higher rain amounts actually ended the month around 0.2 inches above normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 1.4 to 2.3 inches below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree was uprooted onto power lines near the intersection of Florence Street and Camp Street in Kilgore, causing power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken band of supercell thunderstorms developed across Southeast Oklahoma late in the afternoon on April 28th, with this convection being largely focused along an outflow boundary and warm front lifting northward. The downstream air mass on the western edge of an earlier cold pool in far Southwest Arkansas adjacent to Southeast Oklahoma was still recovering with MLCAPE values rebounding to 2500-3500 J/kg. This recovering air mass coupled with an environment featuring 50-55 knots of effective bulk shear and effective storm-relative helicity (SRH) of around 200 m2/s2 supported the continuation of these supercells. As a result, a few reports of damaging wind gusts were recorded across parts of Southwest Arkansas during the late afternoon on April 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees downed across the county, some of which were located along U.S. Highway 371 near Lockesburg and on Elm Drive in Lockesburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D0 conditions worsened to D2 and persisted for the rest of April.

A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported a small downed tree with thunderstorms in Elk Grove. Nearby wind gusts measured 42 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout April, drought conditions worsened significantly across the entirety of the Oklahoma Panhandle. The region started the month entrenched in Severe Drought, but persistent moisture deficits drove a widespread expansion of Extreme Drought as the weeks went on. The prolonged dry spell not only depleted ground moisture but also dried out vegetation, creating dangerous fire weather conditions.||Measurable precipitation was thoroughly lacking. Total rainfall amounts across the three counties hovered between a mere 0.2 inches and 0.8 inches. While Beaver County managed to see slightly more rain than the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle, it still only amounted to less than one inch. All three counties ended April with noticeable short-term deficits. However it is long-term deficits that truly highlight the compounding dryness over the first third of the year. The region faced 120-day deficits ranging from 2.5 inches up to 4.5 inches. The ongoing lack of rainfall left fuels incredibly dry across the landscape. In Texas County specifically, these parched conditions set the stage for fire ignition; when dry thunderstorms rolled through the area, lightning strikes sparked wildfires in the vulnerable, dried-out vegetation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened across the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. The month began with the region in Severe Drought (D2) but by around the 21st of the month, Extreme Drought (D3) expanded into much of Cimarron County from the west. The region continued to see a lack of significant rainfall during the month. Rainfall amounts of around 0.25 inches to 0.3 inches fell during the month. However, Cimarron County ended April with precipitation deficits of around 1.0 to 1.2 inches. Precipitation deficits over the past 120 days were 2.5 to near 3 inches.

Large hail up to tennis ball size occurred with the strongest thunderstorms, as well as isolated damaging wind.

Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches over this period. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches. The National Operational Hydrologic Remote Sensing Center estimated 2 to over 4 feet of snow above 5000 feet, with 3 to 6 inches down to around 4000 feet from April 10th through 12th. There were extended periods of chain controls along the mountain highways due to heavy snow. Over 100 vehicles were stuck on Highway 88 in Amador County at one point due to the winter storm. Interstate 80 had periods of closures and holding of traffic due to heavy snow and spinouts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multi-month precipitation deficit from Fall of 2025 to February of 2026 led to widespread Severe Drought (D2) conditions developing across central Illinois. A continued active pattern led to the eradication of Severe Drought area-wide early in April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms brought intense storms to the region during the late evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The storms delivered a severe combination of damaging wind gusts, large hail, and an isolated tornado. Moving through the state in the overnight hours, a line of storms impacted Jasper and Newton counties with heavy rain, wind, and lightning. Early morning video documented significant tree damage and downed power lines near 1st and Schifferdecker in Joplin. Widespread wind damage tore the roof off the Joplin Parks and Recreation building and leveled several metal outbuildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and power poles and lines were reported down near Zora and Peace Church Roads. Trees from 18 to 24 inches in diameter were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the early evening of the 27th, ahead of a cold front moving into the region. The strongest thunderstorms produced hail up to penny size.

A broad area of mostly elevated strong to severe thunderstorms developed and shifted southward across Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex along an advancing cold front throughout the day on April 29th. Modest low-level warm air advection atop a slightly stable, near-surface layer managed to sustain the convection within a more moderately unstable and strongly sheared environment aloft. As a result, the environment remained favorable for embedded supercell structures capable of large hail. Given the relatively closer proximity of the southernmost storms to the surface front, the threat for severe wind gusts also continued southeast toward the boundary. As a result, numerous reports of large hail were recorded across parts of East Texas along with an isolated report of damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported in Judson.

A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing a ruler-measured hailstone was shared on social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING. The event time was adjusted based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of North Louisiana through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 2 to 4 inches across much of North Louisiana, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

High pressure system sat north of Maine, as a low pressure moved northeast into the region. Favorable cold air damming set up led to temperatures at, or around, freezing throughout the state. Precipitation began to move in late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. Warm mid-layer temperatures move in with associated warm front, transitioning snow in the northern regions over to mixed precipitation. Snow transitioned to sleet, sleet to freezing rain, and freezing rain to rain throughout Thursday. Transition to mixed precipitation began before sunrise from Central Highlands to Northwest Aroostook County, and then over to northern Aroostook when the sun rose. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in the north, and 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet. A trace - 0.05 inches of freezing rain in the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Downeast region. A trace - 0.75 inches of sleet fell in the Central Highlands region. Sleet fell on top of snowfall, which had resulted in messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation moved through Northwest Aroostook county. Began as 3-6 inches of snow, before mid-level warm front transitioned precipitation to mixed precipitation. Roughly 1-1.5 inches of sleet fell in the morning. Trained spotter recorded 1.5 inches of sleet in Madawaska. A trace to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Survey teams found substantial wind damage to trees and a few structures in the community of Piggott. Tree damage was relatively widespread, with numerous uprooted and downed trees. Minor structural damage and a few downed utility lines were also noted. The damage swath was approximately one mile wide, mainly affecting the northern side of town, with trees and debris blown to the southeast, consistent with an intense rear flank downdraft. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at around 80 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KTCC ASOS measured a 58 mph thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the evening of June 10th.  Scattered wind damage was observed along and north of the I-72 corridor, with the most concentrated damage focusing across portions of Menard, Logan, Sangamon, and Macon counties where the cells interacted with an existing outflow boundary from earlier storms.  Six tornadoes touched down within this corridor, including an EF-1 tornado that tracked across Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport and the north side of Springfield.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down along Moore Road about 3 miles west of Abraham Lincoln Capital Airport at 11:04pm CDT.  It tracked eastward across the airport, lofting 6,000lb aircraft hangars and rolling an enclosed trailer.  The tornado then struck the Animal Protective League animal shelter on Taintor Road where it uplifted the roof and collapsed the east wall of the building.  As it continued across the north side of Springfield, numerous trees were damaged or snapped and a few homes sustained siding and shingle damage.  The tornado then moved across Camp Butler and into Mechanicsburg where it caused additional tree and building damage before dissipating about 5 miles east of Mechanicsburg just north of the Sangamon River at 11:30pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough lifted northeast from the Ohio Valley into the lower Great Lakes during the evening of June 9, 2026 through the early morning hours of June 10, 2026. Showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a nearly stationary front in southern lower Michigan and intensified across northern Ohio with the approach of the shortwave late in the evening. Thunderstorms with intense rainfall rates slowly moved east across Sandusky County, Ohio with PWAT values near 2 inches and weak deep layer shear. Total rainfall amounts of 2.5 to 4 inches fell across Sandusky County, Ohio over a two to three hour period, with instantaneous rainfall rates of 3 to 5 inches per hour at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads closed due to creeks/streams overflowing their banks and flowing across the roadways due to previous heavy rainfall. Locations include CR-260 at Fuller Creek, OH-412 between CR-232 and CR-238, and CR-294 between US-6 and CR-247.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported down and blocking a road in town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of Southwest Arkansas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged around 3 to 4 inches across much of Southwest Arkansas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from pea to quarter size covered the ground in the Noonday area.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Craig county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 8.00-10.00 inches, which ended up being 75 to 90 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Johns Creek, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout April, drought conditions worsened significantly across the entirety of the Oklahoma Panhandle. The region started the month entrenched in Severe Drought, but persistent moisture deficits drove a widespread expansion of Extreme Drought as the weeks went on. The prolonged dry spell not only depleted ground moisture but also dried out vegetation, creating dangerous fire weather conditions.||Measurable precipitation was thoroughly lacking. Total rainfall amounts across the three counties hovered between a mere 0.2 inches and 0.8 inches. While Beaver County managed to see slightly more rain than the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle, it still only amounted to less than one inch. All three counties ended April with noticeable short-term deficits. However it is long-term deficits that truly highlight the compounding dryness over the first third of the year. The region faced 120-day deficits ranging from 2.5 inches up to 4.5 inches. The ongoing lack of rainfall left fuels incredibly dry across the landscape. In Texas County specifically, these parched conditions set the stage for fire ignition; when dry thunderstorms rolled through the area, lightning strikes sparked wildfires in the vulnerable, dried-out vegetation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened across the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. The month began with the region in Severe Drought (D2) but much of Beaver County was encompassed in Extreme Drought (D3).  The region continued to see a lack of significant rainfall during the month, with Beaver County seeing more rainfall than the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle during the month. Rainfall amounts of around 0.2 inches to 0.7 inches fell during the month. However, Beaver County ended April with precipitation deficits of around 1.3-1.8 inches, with a very localized exception in the far northwest part of the county where deficits were around 0.4 inches. Precipitation deficits over the past 120 days were 3.5 inches to 4.5 inches and near 5 inches in the far southern part of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken band of supercell thunderstorms developed across Southeast Oklahoma late in the afternoon on April 28th, with this convection being largely focused along an outflow boundary and warm front lifting northward. The downstream air mass on the western edge of an earlier cold pool in far Southwest Arkansas adjacent to Southeast Oklahoma was still recovering with MLCAPE values rebounding to 2500-3500 J/kg. This recovering air mass coupled with an environment featuring 50-55 knots of effective bulk shear and effective storm-relative helicity (SRH) of around 200 m2/s2 supported the continuation of these supercells. As a result, a few reports of damaging wind gusts were recorded across parts of Southwest Arkansas during the late afternoon on April 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed across Buck Range Road, blocking all lanes of traffic.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread showers and storms pressed through southeast Ohio on the first day of April ahead of a cold frontal passage. Strong to severe thunderstorms were first noted shortly after midday along the border of Kentucky and West Virginia, with more quickly infiltrating Ohio by peak heating hours. Storms grew strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts, 1 to 1.5 inch hail stones, and heavy downpours. Aside from numerous reports of large hail across Washington County, downed trees and power lines were observed, along with an isolated instance of flash flooding in Marietta. Storms pressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia by the middle of the evening, bringing the severe weather threat to an end for southeast Ohio.

An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 13th, a large trough of surface low pressure aligned from the central Plains to Ontario, combined with a very large surface ridge occupying the Deep South to the Atlantic Seaboard, to produce a strong surface pressure gradient across the Midwest.  Additionally, a small mid-level short wave trough, lifting from the Middle Mississippi Valley to the southern Great Lakes, induced a low-level jet stream over Indiana that produced 50-60 mph winds within 5,000 feet of the surface.  These very strong to marginally severe winds mixed down as gusts, including an observed 64 mph gust at the KIND Indianapolis Airport very early on the 13th.

A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.

This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was reported down blocking the road on Missouri Highway 17 and K Highway.

A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local business reported approximately quarter size hail in Dunlap, IA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 26th, near a warm front as an upper level disturbance approached the region from the west. The atmosphere across eastern Oklahoma became very unstable during the afternoon and early evening and the deep-layer wind shear was strong with the approach of the upper level disturbance. Some of the thunderstorms were able to develop into supercells due to the favorable combination of instability and wind shear. Several tornadoes and large hail up to quarter size occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado was observed by several storm chasers. It remained over open country with no known damage. The path details were based on the storm chaser observations and radar data.

A series of heavy precipitation events resulted in record setting and historic flooding on several rivers across northeast Wisconsin from the middle to late part of April. The heavy rainfall especially impacted the Wolf River basin, leading to record setting flooding for the Wolf River at Shiocton and the Wolf River at New London. Record flooding also occurred on other rivers over northeast Wisconsin, including the Embarrass River. ||The river flooding resulted in tremendous disruptions to daily life for those living along and near the Wolf River and Embarrass River. Evacuations occurred in the towns of Shiocton and New London for multiple days. Power and gas were shutoff in these areas as flood waters impacted many homes and businesses. The peak of the flooding along the Wolf River occurred from April 16 through April 21.  Flooding then moved downstream on the Wolf River, impacting the Fremont area. Over 150 homes were affected, with damages estimated over $4 million.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread low-land flooding occurred in Outagamie County, resulting in considerable flood damage along the Wolf River and Embarrass River to 52 homes and $4.6 million of damage. Evacuations occurred in the towns of Shiocton and New London for multiple days.  Power and gas in these areas were shutoff as flood waters impacted many homes and businesses.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong upper level troughing diving southeastward from central BC toward southern AB/SK resulted in a sharp transition to strong zonal flow aloft across the Northern Rockies April 7. Favorable timing of the system, arriving during the day, allowed for daytime mixing to translate stronger gusts to the surface in many areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Montana mesonet station Brady NE measured sustained winds averaging 41 mph over 60 minutes. Additionally, Montana mesonet station Fairfield N measured a 61 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued into April as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured 0.07 inches of rain in the southeast part of the county to near 0.8 to one inch in the far northwest part of Potter County. Potter County ended the month about 1.5 inches below normal in the southeast part of the county to around one third of an inch below normal in the northwest part of the county. The 120 day departure below normal was around 2.5 inches in the west to 3.5 inches in the east. A little bit of the southern and eastern part of Potter County was in Moderate Drought (D1) in the beginning of the month but this was quickly replaced by Severe Drought by mid month. Another week or two later, the eastern part of the county was degraded even more into Extreme Drought (D3) and remained this way through the rest of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure system sat north of Maine, as a low pressure moved northeast into the region. Favorable cold air damming set up led to temperatures at, or around, freezing throughout the state. Precipitation began to move in late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. Warm mid-layer temperatures move in with associated warm front, transitioning snow in the northern regions over to mixed precipitation. Snow transitioned to sleet, sleet to freezing rain, and freezing rain to rain throughout Thursday. Transition to mixed precipitation began before sunrise from Central Highlands to Northwest Aroostook County, and then over to northern Aroostook when the sun rose. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in the north, and 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet. A trace - 0.05 inches of freezing rain in the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Downeast region. A trace - 0.75 inches of sleet fell in the Central Highlands region. Sleet fell on top of snowfall, which had resulted in messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation moved through Northeast Aroostook county. Began as 3-6 inches of snow, before mid-level warm front transitioned precipitation to mixed precipitation. Roughly 1-1.5 inches of sleet fell in the morning. NWS employee recorded 1.3 inches of sleet in Castle Hill. A trace to 0.05 inches of freezing rain. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Northeast Texas during the evening with reports of widespread damaging wind gusts along with a handful of large hail reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees uprooted along U.S. Highway 67 east of Mount Vernon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Bath county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Cowpasture River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Interstate 55 was flooded near Trigg Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The KGUP ASOS measured a 58 mph thunderstorm wind gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa.  Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail occurred for 5 to 10 minutes, largest briefly up to ping-pong ball size.

A round of severe thunderstorms and flash flooding occurred as a strong cold front approached and tracked across southern WI. More specifically, supercell thunderstorms developed from northeast IA into southwest WI and far southern WI during the late afternoon and evening hours. Eventually these storms transitioned to a squall line which had a number of tornadoes associated with it, as it tracked through southeast Wisconsin.  Flash flooding affected much of the same region especially in Janesville. Many large hail reports and a small number of downburst damaging wind reports were also received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado started near 6 Mile Rd west of Raynor Ave and tracked to the northeast, ending in southern Milwaukee county.  Possible that this tornado merged with the other one directly to the south.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There was extensive river flooding along the Wisconsin River, Fox River, and Rock River in southern Wisconsin in April. The river levels were above normal after 5 inches of rain fell over the 5 days, and then another episode of heavy rain of 3 to 5 inches occurred on April 17th. In addition, vegetation was still fairly dormant so the grass was not able to soak up much of the rainfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of  upstate South Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. Despite the very warm and dry conditions, occurrence of large wildfires was limited, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was instituted in late March.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across north central and northwest North Carolina in early and late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21th of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows. A couple snowfall events in late February contributed to some relief in streamflows and areawide drought conditions; however, precipitation totals still fell short, and overall lead to some minor Severe Drought Expansions across the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued, and worsened across Watauga county through April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Watauga River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50-60 knots knocking down trees and wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The storm came in two waves, initially on April 3rd with the heaviest snow across north central South Dakota where Mahto recorded 8.2 inches of snow, 7 inches in Bowdle and 6.5 inches 7 miles west southwest of Hillsview (McPherson county). There was a short duration break for most areas during the late afternoon/evening before wrap around snowfall dropped into north central and northeast South Dakota between the late evening and early morning of April 4th. Snowfall rapidly dropped in intensity by the late morning of April 4th. A grand total of 14 inches was recorded near Artas and 3 miles southwest of Greenway, while the EM of Dewey County estimated 12 inches of snow for Timber Lake, with 12 inches also estimated in Hecla (Brown County). ||Corson and Dewey County Sheriff and Emergency Management issued a No Travel Advised for the counties at 1045 am. Because of mild temperatures in March and early April, most roads stayed ice free during this system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A resident near the town of Artas and the COOP observer 3 miles southwest of Greenway both recorded a total of 14 inches snowfall. The COOP observer in the town of Pollock recorded a total of 10 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms, initially elevated, developed by late morning on April 18th as a cold front rapidly undercut a moist and unstable air mass across East Texas. Mid-level lapse rates averaged near 8 degrees C/km while effective deep-layer shear was on the order of 50-60 knots. Although the risk for large hail was generally the the primary hazard with the most intense thunderstorms, a localized risk for severe wind gusts also accompanied the strongest thunderstorm cores. As a result, numerous reports were documented with large hail across parts of East Texas while a few isolated reports of damaging wind gusts were also noted later in the event as surface-based thunderstorms began to evolve within a more linear convective mode.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging from pea to quarter size covered the ground on the south side of Tyler.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Northern Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across Howard and Hempstead Counties in addition to damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees downed along Yorks Chapel Road near Highway 355. There were also some chicken houses damaged near Ferguson Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D0 rapidly deteriorated to D2 and persisted through the end of April.

A low-pressure system tracking through southern Wisconsin and northern Michigan brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the early morning through around midday on Thursday (4/02) before changing over to rain by the afternoon. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet fell across much of north-central Wisconsin with one quarter to one half of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. Over 65,000 customers were reported without power during the worst part of the storm. A 56 year old man died on the interstate in Brown County as a result of the slippery roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest sleet total in Langlade County was 1 inch in Antigo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding from heavy rain on Westbound Interstate 80 at Penryn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS Albany received a report of large tree limbs down blocking one lane on NY-22 in Amenia via an email from NY Alert.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail near Blue Mounds. Time confirmed via radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.

A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media report of a 200 pound well lid blown off. The location is approximate, and the event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across portions of the far southeastern portions of the CWA in Oregon and southern Howell Counties. Through the month the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southern Missouri shrank significantly. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri continued to experience (D3) Drought conditions. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, only small areas of Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year if any occurred or were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While some rainfall did occur, below the monthly average rainfall occurred for most of the county, which produced continued dry conditions. This allowed drought to remain Extreme (D3) to Severe (D2) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous low-pressure system and cold front pushed through the Plains and the Ozarks, interacting with a warm, moist air mass as a strong upper-level trough and a veered wind profile created high wind shear and instability. This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An National Weather Service survey concluded an EF1 tornado touched down southwest of Warsaw, crossing the lake, and tracking just east of Highway 65. The tornado flipped several mobile homes resting on blocks, damaged signs and roofing associated with stores along Highway 65, and created a pattern of tree damage including many uprooted or snapped, surveyed through in-person and Sentinel-2 satellite surveys. The tornado tracked for a little over 6 miles with a path width of 200 yards and maximum wind speeds of 90mph.

Several trees were uprooted in a cyclonic pattern and multiple other trees and limbs were damaged along the tornado's path. A window on a home was broken and two outbuildings suffered damage. Along the slightly over 7 mile track of the tornado maximum winds were 90mph with a width of 300 yards.

Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of streets from Sussex toward Menomonee Falls.
