A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1 inch in diameter near Humboldt, NE.

This allowed the trailing cold front to sweep generally southeastward across northern OH and northwest PA toward southern OH and southwestern PA. Along and ahead of the front, clusters of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across interior northern OH and generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage and marginally-severe hail in Marion, Morrow, and Holmes Counties. These thunderstorms occurred in a relatively-warm and moist sector comprised of weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate effective bulk shear.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was knocked down on the Union University campus.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

Very dry antecedent conditions resulted in areas of blowing dust and reduced visibility across central and southern NM. Winds tapered off during the late evening and overnight hours as stronger winds aloft slowly exited east of the state.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering 100% of Colorado Zone 006 - Grand Valley. Drought conditions remained unchanged through the end of the month. While direct impacts from the drought have not been noted as yet, there is increasing unease among those who live and work in the zone over what the drought could mean for summer wildfire season. There's also concern over water availability through the summer for irrigation and home use. Some local HOAs are estimating water will no longer be available for home use or irrigation by August. Drinking water providers in the Valley are also concerned over water quality. Some source water from the Grand Mesa snowmelt, which has a higher water quality than water sourced from the Colorado River. At this rate, the Grand Mesa snowpack is in such poor shape that most water providers expect to have to use river water to provide drinking water. There's also concern about being able to draw from the Colorado River at all due to low flow and low water levels. Drawing from the river also has water rights concerns, as much of the water through the Colorado River in the Grand Valley is already allocated to areas downstream.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

Severe Drought conditions expanded into SE West Virginia after the previous three months of December, January, February, and early March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New, and Greenbrier River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Western Greenbrier county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 10.00-15.00 inches, which ended up being 75 to 90 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Greenbrier River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was reported over Baseline Boulevard at several low water areas.

This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down on the Natchez Trace Parkway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low-pressure system tracking through southern Wisconsin and northern Michigan brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the early morning through around midday on Thursday (4/02) before changing over to rain by the afternoon. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet fell across much of north-central Wisconsin with one quarter to one half of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. Over 65,000 customers were reported without power during the worst part of the storm. A 56 year old man died on the interstate in Brown County as a result of the slippery roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest ice totals across Waupaca County included 0.31 inches near Sheridan and 0.25 inches in Clintonville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid and upper level jet at the base of a disturbance over the western U.S. moved over New Mexico during the day April 26th. Deep daytime mixing tapped into these stronger winds aloft by mid morning resulting in strong to high wind gusts across much of central and eastern New Mexico. Very dry antecedent conditions resulted in areas of blowing dust and reduced visibility across central and southern NM. Some showers were observed across northwest and north central New Mexico with one of these showers resulting in a brief 59 mph wind gust at Gallup Municipal Airport. Winds tapered off during the late evening and overnight hours as stronger winds aloft slowly exited east of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at Tucumcari Regional Airport measured a brief high wind gust of 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Exceptional (D4) Drought as covering approximately 35% of Colorado Zone 009 - Grand and Battlement Mesas, with 55% of the zone under Extreme (D3) Drought, and 10% under Severe (D2) Drought. Drought conditions remained unchanged for much of the month. With the 4/29 US Drought Monitor update, the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought was reduced to 15% coverage, with 70% of the zone now under Extreme (D3) Drought, and 15% under Severe (D2) Drought. Impacts thus far from the drought have been limited to economic losses due to the lack of snowpack, mainly focused on tourism and the one ski area in the zone. The Colorado State Climatologist has referred to the 2025-2026 winter as historically bad. Those who live and work in the zone are beginning to be concerned with what the drought means for the summer wildfire season. Additionally, there is concern over water quality and availability as many who live in this zone draw their water from water stored from snowmelt.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions persisted through the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Highway E was closed at the Little Niangua River due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.25 inches in diameter near La Vista, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed a tree completely blocking North Lowell Road in the area of Camelot Road in Windham.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: It was determined that there was a second microburst just northeast of the first, along the path of the mesocyclone. There was no visible damage to the backlands of Cow |Island, so the NWS Storm Damage Survey Team estimates the second microburst began somewhere just north of Barbers Pole channel before Tuftonboro Neck. This microburst was smaller in areal extent but more intense. Another 1,500 trees, again mostly softwood, were estimated to have been snapped or uprooted. These also caused the majority of the damage observed. There were five vehicles damaged, two of which were total losses. In addition, there were five cabins or outbuildings attached to summer camps that were destroyed and at least another twelve that were damaged by falling trees. Near the Sandy Island Dock several people escaped with minor cuts and scrapes when two trees fell through the shelter they were under. In a nearby parking lot a tree fell onto a car causing one minor hand injury in which medical attention was not necessary.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Much of South-Central Texas received greater than normal rainfall in June leading to maintenance and improvement in the ongoing drought. Hays County improved from Extreme (D3) Drought to Severe (D2) Drought. Bastrop, Travis, and Wilson Counties remained in D2. The Edwards Aquifer level rose 3.6 feet but was still 16.7 feet below normal. Lake Travis rose 2.2 feet but was 8.9 feet below normal. The 7-day average streamflow was below (10%-24%) normal on the lower Colorado River; and below normal to normal (25%-75%) on the lower San Antonio and upper Colorado Rivers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As developing Tropical Storm Arthur moved along the middle Texas coast (June 17) and as a degenerated low pressure system along the Louisiana Coast (June 18), very hot air descended on the southern tip of Texas, with record extreme heat index, or feels-like, temperatures for the entire region on the 18th.  The high heat index values held on into June 19th, before unsettled weather brought slightly lower temperatures and pockets of rain by the 20th, which ended the short but brutal window of extreme heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of hot temperatures near of just above 100 degrees and high humidity, a remnant of rainfall associated with tropical moisture as Tropical Storm Arthur began to form, created heat index values estimated to be between 111 and 114, with a peak of 115, in inland Willacy County.  Observed data from Valley International Airport (Harlingen, about 8 miles south of the county line) and Brooks County Airport (near Falfurrias) were used as proxy data for this area.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hottest feels-like day in modern history occurred on June 18th across Zapata County, as searing heat combined with remnant high humidity from early week's rain to produce extreme heat of 116F or higher for 8 hours. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief tornado touched down in central Crawford County near Leimbach Road at approximately 4:29 PM EDT. The tornado touched down west of Leimbach Road and north of Double Hill Road, then moved generally east-southeast. Damage consisted primarily of snapped and uprooted trees. Several trees were snapped near the point of touchdown, and a falling tree clipped and damaged a well-constructed detached garage. As the tornado crossed Leimbach Road, several large hardwood trees were uprooted. The fallen trees were oriented toward the northeast, consistent with the localized tornadic wind field despite the tornado's overall east-southeast movement. Based on the observed damage, maximum wind speeds were estimated at 95 mph, yielding an EF-1 tornado rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards and produced a short, intermittent damage path before dissipating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes. This included a long-track significant (EF-2) tornado that impacted portions of southern Atoka County with the easternmost supercell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado began near South Bluebird Lane, where a few homes sustained minor roof damage and a large tank was knocked over and rolled. The tornado snapped several trees as it crossed South Park Lane, just north of the West Voca Road intersection. The tornado then paralleled West Voca Road where tree and minor roof damage was noted eastward towards U.S. Highway 69. The tornado then crossed U.S. Highway 69 and Old U.S. Highway 69 just north of Caney, where trees were snapped and uprooted. The tornado continued to the southeast, damaging trees and outbuildings along east Allison Road. The most significant damage occurred near the intersection of Allison Road and Forest Hill Road, where a mobile home was destroyed and other homes received varying degrees of roof damage. The tornado also bent several large metal high-tension power poles east of this intersection along Allison Road. Further to the east, a house along South Sawmill Road lost a significant portion of its roof. Another concentrated area of damage was noted near the East Cottonwood Road and South Iron Stob Road intersection, where several homes, barns and at least one camper were significantly damaged. Two additional residences along East Cottonwood Road experienced light damage as the tornado began to dissipate, just west of Oklahoma State Highway 109A. ||In addition to the tornado, very strong straight-line winds just south of the tornado path caused significant damage in and near Caney. In addition to widespread damage to trees, roofs and outbuildings, an anchored 20-ft storage unit was completely destroyed on the southwest side of town. Maximum wind speeds associated with this wind damage are estimated to be as high as 100-105 mph, similar to portions of the tornado track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Extreme (D3) drought lingering across portions of the far southeastern portions of the CWA in Oregon and southern Howell Counties. Through the month the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southern Missouri shrank significantly. Despite the rainfall, portions of south central Missouri continued to experience (D3) Drought conditions. Elsewhere, drought conditions saw improvement across portions of southwestern Missouri. By the end of the month, along with the Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) Drought conditions, only small areas of Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year if any occurred or were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: While some rainfall did occur, below the monthly average rainfall occurred for most of the county, which produced continued dry conditions. This allowed drought to remain Severe (D2) to Abnormally Dry (D0) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water resulted in road closures along County Route 16 near Point Pleasant.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. These initial isolated cells primarily produced large hail. The storms then developed into a training complex which brought heavy downpours. Total rainfall accumulated between 1 and 4 inches, triggering flash flooding and rapid rises in local streams.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: State Highway P was closed at Lindley Creek due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down on Greenbrook Parkway in Southaven.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball sized hail was reported in a mainly rural area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northern Illinois during the evening of April 2nd producing wind damage and three tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS damage survey confirmed that a brief EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 105 mph impacted a few properties along Ridge Road in southern Ogle County. One house had two-thirds of its roof removed by the tornado and several trees were damaged by the tornado as well.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCV approaching from the Upper Ohio Valley began tracking into Ohio during the late afternoon and evening hours where a more favorable environment over western and central Pennsylvania allowed for a cluster of severe thunderstorms. Ample shear in the realm of 40 to 50 knots, CAPE values between 1000 to 1500 J/kg, and increasing low-level moisture allowed for an increase in severe potential as thunderstorms entered central Pennsylvania during the evening hours. An initial cluster of thunderstorms began to split the border between New York and Pennsylvania, with ample low-level shear allowing for broad rotation within these storms. Multiple instances of tree damage were observed in McKean County, with an observed 60 mph wind gust in Potter County. A secondary cluster of thunderstorms later in the evening caused isolated tree damage in both Cameron County and Elk County. This cluster of thunderstorms weekend slightly downwind of the Allegheny Plateau, moving through sparsely populated areas of northern Clinton, northern Lycoming, Potter, and Tioga counties before moving into eastern Lycoming County. In eastern Lycoming County, multiple instances of damage to structures were reported north of Williamsport with multiple instances of tree damage observed before thunderstorms shifted east of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph, knocked down a large tree onto the roadway in the 1800 block of State Route 42 west of Lungerville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

Occluding low pressure system to the north moves east, further into Canada. Associated warm front moved through the state Tuesday evening, March 31st, and associated cold front moved through Maine quickly behind it on Wednesday, April 1st. Downeast region saw some snowfall early Tuesday morning, and alongside the warm front, mid-level warm air advection created a prime environment for some sleet development. Precipitation began as snow in the north, freezing rain/sleet in the Central Highlands, and rain Downeast. As the cold front quickly swept through the region, temperatures tanked, and resulted in more mixed precipitation. By the time the system fully moved through the region by Wednesday, roughly, 1/2 to just under 1 inch of sleet fell in Aroostook county. Roughly 0.1 to 0.25 inches of freezing rain fell in southern Aroostook, Piscataquis and northern Penobscot counties. Event began in March. System resulted in messy travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 2-3 inches of snowfall fell during the evening of the 31st. Frenchville ASOS reported a trace of freezing rain on April 1st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed low pressure system moved across the region, creating a deformation zone that brought winter weather conditions to the Northern Rockies. The primary synoptic driver of the precipitation was an advancing frontal boundary that moved through the area during the morning and day of Thursday April 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation began as a frontal passage that moved through around 0700MST on April 2, bringing snowfall rates of nearly two inches per hour to the Discovery Ski Area. Snow continued into April 3, resulting in storm total accumulations of ten inches at Discovery and five and a half inches northwest of Anaconda. Roadway conditions deteriorated, leading to significant travel impacts on April 3. At 0239MST, chains were required for towing units on Interstate 90 between mile markers 228 and 241. A crash resulted in a right lane closure on US Highway 12 westbound at mile marker 29.5 at 0305 MST (indirect). Additionally, spun-out semi-trucks forced a right lane closure on Interstate 90 eastbound at mile marker 232 around 0355MST (indirect). At Georgetown Lake, snowfall began around 0600MST on April 2, accompanied by wind gusts near twenty miles per hour and road temperatures dropping to thirty-two degrees, before tapering off by 0300MST on April 3. Snow eventually tapered off at Homestake Pass by 0830MST.

All of these areas improved to Severe Drought (D2) on March 24th, with further improvement occurring on March 31st when the area of D2 decreased to only portions of Carroll County near and north-northwest of Camden, and extreme north-centeral Tippecanoe County.||This final patch of D2 across central Indiana's northern-most one percent, lingered amid very heavy rainfall of 2.20 to 3.60 inches during a one-week period through the early morning of April 7th.  The corresponding weekly update saw this area undergo a rare two-intensity-level downgrade to D0 (Abnormally Dry).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief EF-0 tornado dropped from locally lower ceilings within a bookend vortex embedded in the QLCS near Cecil Harden Lake, 1.3 miles southeast of the Hollandsburg community.  The bookend vortex crossed the lake, spawning the weak spin-up one-quarter mile south of the lake's southeastern shoreline;  along its 900-foot track, the tornado then crossed residential roads East Mallard Drive and South Ebert Drive, before ending 400 feet south of the lake's shore.||Drone imagery showed clear convergence of downed trees in a grove between Meadows Lane and Mallard Drive;  30 to 40 additional trees were either uprooted or snapped along the path.  Incident structural damage was limited to minor siding loss.  The tornado's damage was mainly vegetation, with peak ind gusts of 85 mph for the event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level disturbance moved across the northern and central Rockies during the day on April 23rd resulting in some strong wind gusts across the Sangre de Cristo Mountains before sunrise before spreading east to the adjacent highlands across northeast and east central NM mid to late morning as daytime mixing commenced. This resulted in a period of high winds at Clines Corners during the late morning hours. These strong winds helped the Tusas Wildfire near Sapello, NM, that started April 22nd, grow to 233 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Tusas Wildfire began along NM Highway 266 between mile markers 3 and 4 west of Sapello, NM. The fire grew northeastward into surrounding hills located in an area surrounded by but not included within the 2022 Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon burn scar. The fire grew in a critical fire weather environment April 23rd before coming under control April 24th, burning a total of 233 acres. No structures were reported destroyed or damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: We had a few wildfires that occurred in early April.  A couple in Hutchinson County (North and South Twin), and another Fire in Potter County (Meadow View).  The fires ranged from 365-1262 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dry spring continued across Middle Tennessee during April 2026. Precipitation amounts were generally 3 to 5 inches across with most of this rain recorded during the last week of the month. While these rain amounts were higher compared to the past couple months, it was still below normal for the month. Drought conditions worsened through the month of April. By the end of the month, all of Middle Tennessee was in at least severe drought with about 38 percent of this classified as extreme drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Abnormally dry conditions from March 2026 worsened in April with severe drought conditions developing across DeKalb County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of North Louisiana through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 2 to 4 inches across much of North Louisiana, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Alleghany county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Jackson River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: April 2026 was a deeply challenging month for North Mississippi as a multi-season drought dramatically intensified. State climatologists noted that February 2026 had already broken records as the single driest February in Mississippi history, and April provided no relief. Instead of bringing typical spring showers to recharge the water table, April brought scorching temperatures and a severe spring recharge gap. By the end of the month, North Mississippi stood as one of the primary focal points of agricultural and hydrological distress in the Deep South. With nearly the entire state under moderate-to-exceptional drought conditions, North Mississippi's critical agricultural sectors faced immediate, severe operational strain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D0 conditions worsened to D2 and persisted through the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Glens Falls ASOS reported a gust of 62 mph via an updated METAR.

A tornado, isolated damaging wind, and large hail up to two inches in diameter occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.

A surface cold front moved across Minnesota during the early morning of April 17th which ultimately produced two rounds of thunderstorms.  The first line of storms was associated with a warm front which produced quarter size hail across south-central Minnesota mid-morning. The secondary and stronger line of storms tied to the cold front itself moved through in the early afternoon across eastern MN. This line produced a swath of large hail measuring from quarter size up to ping pong ball size hail in Cannon Falls (Goodhue County) which ended up being the largest measured hailstone from this event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report received via NWS Chat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to quarter-size in Northwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

On the evening of April 15th, a line of thunderstorms tracking east over Lake Erie intensified as they tracked onshore into northwestern Pennsylvania, Chautauqua County and Southern Erie County. As the storms continued east they became severe, causing two tornadoes in Cattaraugus County along with damaging wind gusts across a large chunk of the Western Southern Tier. The thunderstorms were associated with a Mesoscale Convective Vortex, that per usual for these types of setups, had plenty of shear to support the development of a tornado or two. Due to the lower instability values along with showers and increased cloud cover ahead of and behind the primary line, additional thunderstorms weren't able to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service in Buffalo investigated storm-related damage from a rotating thunderstorm within a line of storms that affected the area southeast of Machias in Cattaraugus County on April 15th. The National Weather Service storm survey team investigated the damage in the area and confirmed damage consistent with an EF-0 tornado with estimated peak winds of 75 mph.||Several trees uprooted in multiple directions shortly after the intersection of Tug Hill Road and Gulf Hill Road. Primary residence had a window blown in the upper most story of the house, with a secondary residence loosing a few roof shingles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Anomalously dry conditions persisted across much of central Pennsylvania through April 2026, with severe drought persisting across portions of southern Pennsylvania with slight expansion into southeastern Pennsylvania towards the latter portions of the month due to lack of widespread rainfall, with month-to-date precipitation values generally one inch below average for the month of April across the southeastern half of Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across southern Fulton County through April 2026. Some light rainfall through the middle of month allowed for slight expansion of the severe drought with more beneficial rainfall not coming until the final week of April 2026. A Drought Warning remained in effect by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection for the entire month with voluntary water restrictions in place across portions of the county.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drier than average conditions over the course of multiple months lead to the addition of severe (D2) drought across conditions persisted across much of eastern Lancaster County during the second half of April 2026. Drier than average conditions were observed throughout the first half of the month with generally light rainfall across the region with slightly more beneficial rainfall coming in the final week of the month. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado touched down in northern Poinsett County early in the morning on Tuesday, April 28. The tornado occurred over an open field and no damage was reported. Since no damage indicators were found, this tornado is rated an EF-Unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.

Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Cherry Fire ignited around 10:30 a.m. on Friday, June 26, 2026, near Weiss Highway and Cherry Creek in Juab County, Utah. It subsequently merged with the nearby Maple Peak Fire, which had started the night before. Given exceptionally hot, dry, and windy conditions through much of its early life during a PDS Red Flag Warning day, it would go on to grow fast and rapidly through the next few days while exhibiting extreme fire behavior as it grew across portions of Juab, Utah, and Tooele counties (encompassing portions of public zones 101, 102, and 115) eventually reaching the ongoing Iron fire. Thankfully, no structures were harmed with no reported injuries or fatalities. This fire has been contained as of July 9, 2026 and reached a total of 34,252 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably strong mid-level shortwave trough progressed across Northern New England on June 18th.  This brought deep layer shear that allowed for high potential storm structure organization into line segments.  The forcing combined with deep moisture allowed for robust convection, with bowing line segments transiting across Central and Southern New Hampshire.  Convective wind gusts along with a few areas of microburst wind damage brought down 1000s of trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed a tree and wires blocking Brook Rd. in New  Hampton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A decaying thunderstorm produced a wind gust of 62 mph at the Santa Fe Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed over northern Illinois during the pre-dawn hours of June 6th, then dropped southeastward into central Indiana as the morning progressed.  The storms skirted through Vermilion County with gusty winds and rain, but no reports of severe weather or flooding.  By late afternoon, thunderstorms began re-developing along the residual outflow boundary...with cells continuously back-building over portions of Vermilion County into the evening.  Very heavy rainfall occurred in a small portion of the county from Bismarck to the northern edge of Danville.  The Danville Airport (KDNV) measured 6.41, while an observer 1 mile west-northwest of the airport received 7.50.  The heavy rain falling on already wet soils led to flash flooding during the evening, with residual flooding lingering into the morning of June 7th.  Water rescues had to be performed near Stoney Creek on the southeast side of Danville as the creek overflowed its banks and flooded a few homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water was flowing across several county roads near the Vermilion Regional Airport (KDNV), along North Bowman Avenue between Danville and Bismarck, and in the town of Bismarck.  One vehicle was stranded in high water.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado touched down at approximately 4:51 PM EDT on Sunday, June 14, 2026, along Lippert Road, just east of the intersection with Mallory Road in Crawford County. The tornado tracked east along Lippert Road, causing significant damage to one residence, including roof damage, the loss of an attached porch, damage to four vehicles, displacement of an RV approximately 50 feet, and damage to a garage roof. An additional six homes sustained minor damage, including damage to roofs, siding, and windows. As the tornado continued east, numerous trees were blown down, blocking driveways and roadways. Several large limbs snapped and fell onto a barn and a nearby home. The tornado gradually weakened and dissipated northwest of the intersection of Lippert Road and Vincent Road. Based on the observed damage, maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, resulting in an EF-1 rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards. This first round of storms left behind an outflow boundary extending from eastern Arkansas across the Memphis metropolitan area into north Mississippi. Storms ignited along this boundary during the late afternoon and evening hours, fueled by strong instability and an upper-level trough overspreading the region. There were several additional reports of large hail and damaging winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe storms tracked across eastern IA, northwest IL, and northeast MO during the afternoon and evening of April 17.  Widespread wind gusts between 60-80 mph (isolated 80-100 mph), large hail up to teacup size, and several tornadoes were reported.  ||The most significant damage occurred in Lena, IL where many homes and outbuildings were damaged, trees uprooted, and power lines downed by an EF2 tornado.  Very strong straight-line winds also were documented in parts of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A high-end EF2, possible multi-vortex, tornado with estimated peak winds around 130 mph started along Highway 20, southwest of Lena IL, and tracked through Lena before lifting just southwest of Orangeville. The tornado caused significant damage to trees along its path, including uprooting and snapping trees. When the tornado begun it immediately caused EF1 damage to trees, gaining strength to an EF2 tornado snapping many power poles southwest of Lena. The tornado turned to the right, into town causing a lot of roof damage and tree damage. A lot of houses had shingle and siding damage. The most significant damage occurred on Grove Street, where three houses lost their entire roof structure. Two of the homes experienced partial exterior wall collapses. Damage in this area is consistent with 130 MPH winds. In Lena, the damage footprint in Lena is approximately 1250 yards wide. As the tornado moved to the northeast, damage to farm structures was noted. Even towards the end of the path, the tornado was causing EF1 damage to trees.

Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.

A severe weather outbreak unfolded across central and north-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and early evening of Friday (4/17). The event was triggered by a surface low-pressure system and cold front across the upper Midwest. ||NWS storm surveys confirmed 2 tornadoes that resulted in structural damage. A tornado formed 3 miles northwest of Glandon around 4:44 PM CDT and tracked into southeast Lincoln County producing EF-1 damage before dissipating around 4:55 PM CDT. Another tornado formed 3 miles west-southwest of Ringle in Marathon County around 4:46 PM CDT and dissipated around 5:03 PM CDT 5 miles southwest of Hogarty. This tornado produced EF-3 damage and destroyed 13 homes, produced major damage to 25 homes, with 101 homes reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. An estimated $8.2 million worth of damage was reported from the tornado. ||Beyond the tornadic threat, the storms produced isolated large hail up to half dollar size and damaging winds. Heavy rainfall was another impact, with localized totals ranging from 1 to 4 inches. These torrential downpours caused flash flooding, particularly in Marshfield where 2.65 inches of rain fell and multiple vehicles were reported stranded in deep water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds downed trees and power lines southwest of Phelps. The time of this report is an estimate based on radar data.

Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail near Ridgeway. Time confirmed via radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down across the road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history. The wildfire was difficult to contain because of hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought, breezy winds and lack of rain across southeast Georgia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. On April 25th, the fire grew to 9,578 acres per overnight infrared flight mapping.  Evacuation areas were expanded to the Brantley���Wayne County line due to the fire movement to the north and northeast, while evacuations and road closures on the southern portion of the fire have been lifted. Wayne County issued Mandatory Evacuations for the area from the Brantley County Line at Wire Rd to Post Rd, to Ten Mile Rd and all areas in between. The fire was 13,745 acres and 7% contained. The fire produced 150-foot flame lengths during a significant run toward Browntown Road. The blaze was a plume-dominated wildfire, a rare occurrence that happened on multiple days during the fire. On April 26th, a Mandatory Evacuation was issued for the entire community of Manningtown, off of Browntown Road by Wayne County Emergency Management. Infrared mapping showed the fire at approximately 20,933 acres with 7% containment. Without precipitation, the fire was very active again with wind driven movement to the northeast and east until the wind shifted in the afternoon with the sea breeze. At 5 PM, Wayne County EM announced the fire had crossed into Wayne county. At 8 PM, an isolated thunderstorm moved over the fire bringing rain amounts of 0.4 to 0.8 inches. This amount of rain did not extinguish the fire, but briefly decreased the extreme fire behavior. On April 28th, the fire was 22,600 acres and 32% contained. On April 30th, roads from Browntown south of Murphy Road and HWY 32 were opened. The fire was 22,532 acres and 37% contained. More smoke occurred on April 30th in bay vegetation due to hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought and lack of rain. A new fire started north of the Hwy 82 Fire in Wayne County that was approximately 40 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region.
