EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front moved through northeast Pennsylvania on Sunday, April 19th, ushering in a much colder air mass. Temperatures dropped into the mid-20s to lower 30s overnight and remained well below normal through Tuesday, April 21st. This event occurred before the Frost Freeze program was even underway for the season, but due to how far below freezing some areas reached, this unfortunately led to costly crop damage in northeast Pennsylvania.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado that began west of Ponca City moved back crossed a bend of the Arkansas River moving back into Kay County from Osage County. This tornado moved through a rural area of bottomlands along the Arkansas River. No known damage occurred in this area before the tornado crossed the Arkansas River again into Osage County. See Storm Data from NWS Tulsa for the documentation of this tornado in Osage County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The storm came in two waves, initially on April 3rd with the heaviest snow across north central South Dakota where Mahto recorded 8.2 inches of snow, 7 inches in Bowdle and 6.5 inches 7 miles west southwest of Hillsview (McPherson county). There was a short duration break for most areas during the late afternoon/evening before wrap around snowfall dropped into north central and northeast South Dakota between the late evening and early morning of April 4th. Snowfall rapidly dropped in intensity by the late morning of April 4th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Northern Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across Howard and Hempstead Counties in addition to damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees downed along and near County Road 14 and County Road 306 east of Columbus.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across portions of eastern Nebraska through the month of April. However, there was some slight improvement through the month with only small departures from average precipitation in many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions were present in the extreme northwest corner of the county at the beginning of April. By the end of the month, conditions had improved significantly, erasing severe drought entirely and reducing the moderate (D1) drought coverage from 68 percent down to under 8 percent. The cooperative observer at Beatrice 1N recorded 4.57 inches of precipitation (1.69 inches above average). The CoCoRaHS observers at Barneston 0.3 N and Wymore 8.1 Ssw recorded 3.21 and 3.74 inches of precipitation, respectively. These values were 0.12 inches below and 0.41 inches above average.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to widespread showers and storms pressed through southeast Ohio on the first day of April ahead of a cold frontal passage. Strong to severe thunderstorms were first noted shortly after midday along the border of Kentucky and West Virginia, with more quickly infiltrating Ohio by peak heating hours. Storms grew strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts, 1 to 1.5 inch hail stones, and heavy downpours. Aside from numerous reports of large hail across Washington County, downed trees and power lines were observed, along with an isolated instance of flash flooding in Marietta. Storms pressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia by the middle of the evening, bringing the severe weather threat to an end for southeast Ohio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail in Black Earth. Time confirmed via radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The location is approximate.

Severe thunderstorms developed across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening of the 26th, near a warm front as an upper level disturbance approached the region from the west. The atmosphere across eastern Oklahoma became very unstable during the afternoon and early evening and the deep-layer wind shear was strong with the approach of the upper level disturbance. Some of the thunderstorms were able to develop into supercells due to the favorable combination of instability and wind shear. Several tornadoes and large hail up to quarter size occurred with the strongest thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This was a satellite tornado that occurred simultaneously with a portion of the Foraker tornado, and was witnessed by numerous storm chasers. It remained over open country with no known damage.  The path details were based on the storm chaser observations and radar data.

The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Exceptional (D4) Drought as covering 100% of Colorado Zone 008 - Central Colorado River Basin. Drought conditions in this zone remained unchanged through the end of the month. Drought impacts in this zone are mainly in economic losses due to poor winter tourism, as many towns have ski area or other winter-sports oriented businesses. Additionally, there is growing concern over what the lack of snow and the drought means for the summer wildfire season.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of streets and sidewalks mainly in northwest Milwaukee County, including stranded vehicles in floodwaters. Some reports of basement flooding in northern Milwaukee County. Pictures and videos provided.

Two separate personal weather stations on the south and southeast sides of town recorded a 72 mph and a 73 mph gust.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms passed through the region for nearly the entirety of April 27th. The afternoon round was expected to be the most volatile, with an environment primed for high-end severe weather reflected by an areawide SPC Moderate Risk. What culminated was widespread large to giant hail, wind damage, and two tornadoes in Missouri.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief EF-1 tornado touched down in southwestern Monroe County near Route M and Highway 151. The primary damage caused by this tornado was a farm just south of Highway 151. Numerous large tree limbs were broken on the property with one tree limb pointed to the west. One farm building was collapsed on the western side of the barn. The eastern facing part of the building which was attached to the cement slab was still standing, while the western facing part of the building had completely collapsed. Due to this, we estimated slightly below the expected wind speed which also matched the surrounding tree damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Braman Tornado: Numerous spotters and chasers observed this tornado develop in western Kay County. The initial damage occurred near 140th Street and Earth Road where a tree was uprooted and a farm house suffered roof damage. The tornado continued generally east breaking a power pole on 124th Street south of Earth Road and destroying a barn and damaging more power poles and trees near Earth Road east of 124th Street. The first of two satellite tornadoes developed in this area near Earth Road between 124th and 108th. The primary tornado moved north, then looped back around to an easterly movement as the motion of both the primary tornado and the satellite tornado was influenced by the Fujiwhara effect.||As the primary tornado moved east-northeast after this interaction, a barn was destroyed along Earth Road east of 108th Street, and a number of trees and power poles were damaged along 76th Street near Fork Road. As the tornado was crossing the Chickaskia River, a second satellite tornado developed and rotated around this primary tornado. The tornado continued east snapping power poles along 60th Street, and destroying two barns and more power poles along 44th Street just south of the city limits of Braman. The survey and mobile radar data from the Doppler on Wheels project show that the tornado made another loop just southeast of Braman and east of US-177, then moved southeast damaging trees along Fork Road east of 29th Street before dissipating.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Enid Tornado initially developed near or on the southwest portion of Vance Air Force Base and moved east-northeast crossing over the southern edge of the runway complex, but remaining south of the majority of structures on the base. However as the tornado crossed US-81, it moved through the Gray Ridge Estates neighborhood where most of the houses in the neighborhood sustained damage, and many destroyed or receiving significant damage. Damage to at least three homes in this neighborhood was rated EF4. ||After moving northeast out of this neighborhood, the tornado moved through open land. Although the tornado continued moving through areas without structures, damage done to trees east of Leona Mitchell Blvd and north of Fox Drive was significant. At least one tree was debarked, and a hardwood tree was pulled from the ground and displaced 20 feet to the east. Farther northeast, significant ground scouring and severe tree damage was observed as the tornado crossed E0455 Road and South 16th Street. At Southgate Road, a number of structures were destroyed including two metal buildings, a warehouse and an outbuilding. An RV parked in this area was picked up and the chassis of this RV was found about 305-310 yards northeast of its origination point. Damage was rated EF4 in this area as well.||The tornado moved through more open land damaging trees as it approached S 30th Street. Radar and damage patterns indicate that the tornado moved in a loop briefly just southwest of South 30th Street and Rupe Road. A home was destroyed (EF4) and a number of other structures and trees were destroyed or heavily damaged along South 30th Street. Coming out of the loop, the tornado moved southeast across S 30th Street thereby continuing in relatively open land as opposed to moving northeast toward a d neighborhood on the southeast side of Enid. A farmstead was hit at S 42nd Street and Rupe Road destroying a barn, damaging the house and trees on the property.||Crossing Rupe Road, radar indicated the tornado likely moved in a loop again northeast of Rupe Road and S 42nd Street, before moving southeast and east and dissipating near Boggy Creek just west of Woodring Airport.||Despite the intensity of this tornado, there was only one injury that required transport.||Scientific notes: Researchers at the National Severe Storms Laboratory and the University of Illinois performed a variety of calculations to estimate the potential wind speed of the tornado. Two researchers performed a treefall pattern analysis to match the observed pattern of treefall to a simulated pattern from a vortex model. One researcher used this method to determine a probabilistic wind speed distribution from treefall near Southgate Road using six different sets of constraints. The calculated median maximum 3-second velocity in all of these six experiments was over 205 mph, and the interquartile range of two of these six experiments was completely over 200 mph. ||A second researcher also performed a treefall analysis with a Monte Carlo simulation slightly adjusting the input variables. Taking the runs with the lowest 0.5% error, a median estimated maximum wind velocity of 94 m/s (210 mph) was calculated.||A third researcher made calculations of the 300 yard displacement of the RV near Southgate Road using simulations with a 3-dimensional vortex model that does include modeled vertical motion of the tornado, again using a Monte Carlo simulation. Of the simulations that provided the closest match the displacement of the RV, the maximum winds of these simulations were 91-97 m/s (204-217 mph).||Based on these engineering calculations that included both 3-dimensional vortex modeling (including vertical motions) and 3-second averaging wind speed averaging consistent with the EF-scale values, it is very highly likely that this tornado produced winds that would be classified as an EF5 tornado in the vicinity of Southgate Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.

Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of National Weather Service ground surveys, radar data, and Sentinel-2 satellite data concluded that an EF0 tornado briefly occurred approximately 2 miles south of White Church. A short 0.6-mile confined path of trees were damaged just east of State Route 17.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low-pressure system tracking through southern Wisconsin and northern Michigan brought a wintry mix of freezing rain and sleet to the region from the early morning through around midday on Thursday (4/02) before changing over to rain by the afternoon. Around 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet fell across much of north-central Wisconsin with one quarter to one half of an inch of freezing rain accumulation across central and portions of east-central Wisconsin. Over 65,000 customers were reported without power during the worst part of the storm. A 56 year old man died on the interstate in Brown County as a result of the slippery roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The highest ice totals across Shawano County included 0.30 inches in Wittenberg and 0.25 inches in Shawano.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system made its way into the Bering Sea early Wednesday morning (4/22), bringing widespread snow, mixed precipitation, and strong winds to Western Alaska and portions of the Western/Central Interior. As the low moved inland, a front moving northeast off the low brought predominantly snow to the Seward Peninsula and YK Delta with 2 to 8 of total accumulations. This system was able to support gusty winds up to 60 mph and easily created widespread blowing snow conditions to much of the West Coast. By the time the front made its way into the Interior, a rain/snow mix of around 2 to 6 fell in addition to strong southerly gap winds through both Isabel and Windy Pass. Winds gusted anywhere between 65 to 75 mph through the passes, creating difficult travel conditions along the Parks and Richardson Highway. Effects from this system subsequently diminished by the weekend (4/25 through 4/26), resulting in a steady warming trend as upper level southerly flow set up over the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Point Lay AWOS site (PPIZ) reported blizzard like conditions at 05:35 AKDT on 4/23 and continued through 13:05 AKDT on 4/23. Blizzard criteria was met at 08:35 AKDT on 4/23. A peak observation was reported at 06:00 AKDT on 4/23 with snow, freezing fog, less than 1/4 miles visibility, and 33 mph winds gusting to 40 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A protracted period of abnormally dry weather that began in autumn of 2025 and continued through the winter culminated in extreme drought conditions across much of western North Carolina by early spring. Monthly precipitation was anywhere from 25 percent to 75 percent of normal for seven consecutive months beginning in September 2025. The September through March period was one of the top 5 driest on record across much of the area. Portions of the Piedmont saw their driest September-through-March on record. Unusually warm weather in March and April of 2026 further contributed to evolving drought conditions. Both months were among the top 5 warmest on record at most major climate sites across the region. By early April, streamflow across the region was 25 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture levels were extremely low and only poor-to-fair crop conditions were reported during the critical spring planting period. The dry and warm conditions enhanced the wildfire danger across the region, but large wildfires were few and far between, likely due to a statewide burn ban that was initiated in late March. By the end of April, drought status had been upgraded to exceptional across portions of the Piedmont.

An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of North Louisiana through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 2 to 4 inches across much of North Louisiana, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

Snow transitioned to sleet, sleet to freezing rain, and freezing rain to rain throughout Thursday. Transition to mixed precipitation began before sunrise from Central Highlands to Northwest Aroostook County, and then over to northern Aroostook when the sun rose. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in the north, and 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two large trees were blown down.

A second round of storms later on produced isolated wind damage, including some damage north of Geneseo, IL that was due to straight-line winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The storm came in two waves, initially on April 3rd with the heaviest snow across north central South Dakota where Mahto recorded 8.2 inches of snow, 7 inches in Bowdle and 6.5 inches 7 miles west southwest of Hillsview (McPherson county). There was a short duration break for most areas during the late afternoon/evening before wrap around snowfall dropped into north central and northeast South Dakota between the late evening and early morning of April 4th. Snowfall rapidly dropped in intensity by the late morning of April 4th. A grand total of 14 inches was recorded near Artas and 3 miles southwest of Greenway, while the EM of Dewey County estimated 12 inches of snow for Timber Lake, with 12 inches also estimated in Hecla (Brown County). ||Corson and Dewey County Sheriff and Emergency Management issued a No Travel Advised for the counties at 1045 am. Because of mild temperatures in March and early April, most roads stayed ice free during this system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP observer in Eureka reported a storm total of 7.8 inches, with a total snowfall of 7.7 inches submitted by a resident 7 miles west southwest of Hillsview.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There was extensive river flooding along the Wisconsin River, Fox River, and Rock River in southern Wisconsin in April. The river levels were above normal after 5 inches of rain fell over the 5 days, and then another episode of heavy rain of 3 to 5 inches occurred on April 17th. In addition, vegetation was still fairly dormant so the grass was not able to soak up much of the rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Fox River in Waukesha rose to a Moderate flood stage. Water touched the base of Barstow St bridge and Bank St bridge. Corrina Blvd, Buckley St, W Main St, Riverwalk Dr, and parts of Dunbar Ave flooded. Grede Park, Glacial Drumlin Trail, Fox Riverwalk, and Frame Park flooded. Floodwaters affected yards of homes near Bethesda Park.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Northern Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across Howard and Hempstead Counties in addition to damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball size hail reported just north of Washington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms moved across lower Michigan late on April 13th into the early morning hours of April 14th.  Large hail was common with limited damaging winds. Moderate to heavy rain occurred along with some localized inconvenient flooding with one to three inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported quarter to half-dollar size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Charlotte county in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Roanoke River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms moved across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois and produced 50+ mph winds, causing some areas of damage to trees, roofs, and a few outbuildings.  The line of very gradually fading storms produced surges of straight-line wind damage. These were most pronounced to the immediate south of mesovortices (small scale circulations within the thunderstorm line that can in themselves result in tornadoes). Based on the nature of damage, observations, and radar, these reflect 65-80 mph wind gusts.||Two main areas of damage that experienced enhanced wind surges were:  1.) Kalona, IA (Washington Co)  and 2.) the east-southeast side of Iowa City (Johnson County).||A third area of isolated wind damage from Miles to Sabula, IA (Jackson County) was a little different in that it was much more of an outflow surging from decaying storms, but again straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Out building roof and walls damaged along with a grain bin. The time was estimated using radar data.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding at Interstate 80 eastbound and Norwood Avenue.

A line of thunderstorms developed across portions of central and south-central Kansas during the afternoon and evening hours of April 23rd. Several landspout tornadoes occurred as this line of thunderstorms moved across portions central and south-central Kansas.

The Texas Panhandle experienced a stark and worsening drought throughout April. While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. Most counties recorded less than half an inch for the entire month, with several seeing less than one tenth of an inch. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The bulk of Lipscomb County was in Moderate Drought (D1) to start April with the exception of the far southeast portion of the county which was in Severe Drought (D2). By the middle of the month, the entire county was in Severe Drought, and Extreme Drought (D3) moved in quickly and expanded across the far north and southeast portions of the county by the end of the month. This worsening drought was due to the lack of continuous, significant rainfall. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. In total, the county measured one quarter of inch or less of precipitation. Lipscomb County ended the month about 1.7-2.3 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 3.5 inches below normal in the much of the county to over 5 inches below normal in the south to southeast portion of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous low-pressure system and cold front pushed through the Plains and the Ozarks, interacting with a warm, moist air mass as a strong upper-level trough and a veered wind profile created high wind shear and instability. This set the stage for supercellular development that evolved into bowing line segments. This setup brought destructive straight-line wind gusts of 60-70 mph, with isolated gusts reaching up to 75 mph. Hail up to 2 inches occurred and 5 tornadoes touched down in Benton and Morgan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A home was struck by lightning causing a structure fire on the south side of Versailles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours of April 28th, a stalled cold front served up a quick burst of strong thunderstorms around northeast Kentucky. One of these stronger storms were noted to have passed over Olive Hill in Carter County, where a few trees and power lines were blown down along one of the local roadways. Activity quickly moved east of the state border for the rest of the morning timeframe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April began with abnormally dry conditions (D0) in the southern part of West Virginia as well as a portion of the northeast mountains. D0 expanded across much of the area by the second week of the month, while portions of the northeast mountains and southern WV degraded to moderate drought (D1). Further degradation occurred for the third week of the month, with D1 spreading into all but Wood and Pleasants Counties, and severe drought (D2) developing in McDowell, Raleigh, Wyoming, eastern Boone, southern Fayette, southeast Kanawha, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, eastern Webster, and much of Pocahontas and Randolph counties. By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. The last week once again had rainfall accumulations between half and one and a half inches with pockets around two inches. Nevertheless, rounds of precipitation did not achieve high enough amounts or long enough duration to impede the ongoing drought.||All six climate sites in West Virginia registered below normal precipitation for the month. Beckley was nearly two tenths of an inch below normal, Charleston and Clarksburg were between six and seven tenths of an inch below normal, and Huntington, Parkersburg, and Elkins ranged from one and a quarter to around one and an eighth inches below normal. Despite the overall dryness, enough rain fell on the 29th of the month to break the existing daily precipitation record at Charleston.||Impacts from the drought included hauling water for livestock, supplemental feeding for livestock due to slow pasture growth, and slow crop growth.

By the last week of the month, D2 expanded to encompass more of eastern WV, including Fayette, McDowell, Nicholas, Pocahontas, Raleigh, Wyoming, southeast Braxton, eastern Logan, eastern Mingo, southern Upshur, and much of Boone, Clay, Kanawha, Randolph, and Webster counties. Meanwhile, only minor expansions of D1 and D0 occurred in the northwest part of the state.||A half inch to an inch of rain fell across much of the area during the first week of April, though there were some pockets of up to an inch. Little to no rain accumulated in the second week. Rain totals for the third week ranged from an inch or less in the mountains and north-central WV to half an inch or less in west and southwest WV. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 1 inch diameter hail near Sun Prairie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Vance Air Force Base (KEND) observation. Wind gust associated with a nearby tornadic circulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail measured up to 1.50 inches in diameter in Beatrice, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening of April 2nd, 2026,  and early spring supercell thunderstorm event spread across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. This brought several swaths of damaging wind, large hail, and several tornadoes to both Iowa and Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began in far eastern Whiteside County just north of Fulfs Road and just west of the Whiteside-Lee county line, where satellite imagery showed the beginning of a narrow southwest-northeast path of disturbed soil through farm fields. Drone footage taken along Mound Hill Road in Lee County revealed swirl marks in the field to the west that aligned with the path that was evident in the satellite imagery, confirming that the tornado remained on the ground continuously as it tracked into Lee County. The tornado crossed Mound Hill Road, downing a number of power poles and impacting a property on the east side of the road. The tornado reached its peak intensity here, destroying multiple outbuildings and snapping several trees at this property. The tornado left additional swirl marks in a field to the northeast of the property before causing damage to trees, a residence, and a metal outbuilding along and just south of Lenox Road. As the tornado reached Timber Creek Road, it caused damage to a barn, at least one power pole, and several trees. On the north side of the road, the tornado pushed an old barn off of its foundation into a grain leg, causing the grain leg to collapse. A concrete silo was also toppled at the same location. The tornado then continued northeastward, causing tree and roof damage at a property along Peek Home Road, then damaging an outbuilding, a house, and more trees at a property at Penrose Road and Swarts Road. The tornado produced its last instance of damage at the Hey Tree Service facility along U.S. Route 52/State Route 26 southeast of Woosung before dissipating prior to reaching the Ogle County line. Straight-line wind damage was also observed to the south and east of the tornado's track.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and a few power lines were knocked down across southern Benton County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail to the size of tennis balls was reported, damaging several roofs and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half dollar sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid and upper level jet at the base of a disturbance over the western U.S. moved over New Mexico during the day April 26th. Deep daytime mixing tapped into these stronger winds aloft by mid morning resulting in strong to high wind gusts across much of central and eastern New Mexico. Very dry antecedent conditions resulted in areas of blowing dust and reduced visibility across central and southern NM. Some showers were observed across northwest and north central New Mexico with one of these showers resulting in a brief 59 mph wind gust at Gallup Municipal Airport. Winds tapered off during the late evening and overnight hours as stronger winds aloft slowly exited east of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station at Little Burro on White Sands Missile Range measured high wind gusts up to 76 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system made its way into the Bering Sea early Wednesday morning (4/22), bringing widespread snow, mixed precipitation, and strong winds to Western Alaska and portions of the Western/Central Interior. As the low moved inland, a front moving northeast off the low brought predominantly snow to the Seward Peninsula and YK Delta with 2 to 8 of total accumulations. This system was able to support gusty winds up to 60 mph and easily created widespread blowing snow conditions to much of the West Coast. By the time the front made its way into the Interior, a rain/snow mix of around 2 to 6 fell in addition to strong southerly gap winds through both Isabel and Windy Pass. Winds gusted anywhere between 65 to 75 mph through the passes, creating difficult travel conditions along the Parks and Richardson Highway. Effects from this system subsequently diminished by the weekend (4/25 through 4/26), resulting in a steady warming trend as upper level southerly flow set up over the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Donnelly Dome USARRAY mesonet site (K24KX) reported a wind gust of 73 mph at 00:10 AKDT on 4/23. These strong wind gusts continued for 15 minutes until 00:25 AKDT on 4/23.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were knocked down in the city of Saint Francis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid and upper level jet at the base of a disturbance over the western U.S. moved over New Mexico during the day April 26th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month of April saw weather closer to that expected for the time of year. While temperatures did end up being, on average, warmer than normal, the departures were significantly less compared to the month of March. The mountains saw a few solid snowfalls during the month, as well as some precipitation across the lower elevations. Areas north of I-70 generally fared the best. Locations in this region did see some improvement in drought conditions. Areas south of I-70 generally remained the same or worsened slightly.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the beginning of the month, the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought as covering approximately 10% of Colorado Zone 011 - Central Gunnison and Uncompahgre River Basin, with 45% of the zone under Severe (D2) Drought, and 45% of the zone under Moderate (D1) Drought. Drought conditions remained unchanged through much of the month. With the 4/29 US Drought Monitor update, Extreme (D3) Drought was reduced to 5% coverage, with Severe (D2) Drought now covering 50% of the zone and 45% of the zone still under Moderate (D1) Drought. While this zone has done better than most as far the drought is concern, those who live and work in the zone are still becoming uneasy over how the drought could impact them going forward. There's concern over the upcoming wildfire season, as well as water allocations from reservoirs in the zone and availability of water for irrigation, farming, and ranching.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms pressed through West Virginia on April 1st as a cold front progressed overhead. The first notable storm kicked things off shortly after midday in Wayne County, with large hail and damaging wind gusts that resulted in local power outages. Additional storm damage progressed through the state over the course of the afternoon and evening as more development occurred ahead of the frontal passage. In addition to the downed trees and power lines, heavy downpours accompanying storms in the Parkersburg area led to street flooding along several roads in the city. The loss of daytime heating brought the severe threat of storms to an end that evening.

A southward moving cold front tracked across central MN and northwest WI early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN west-central WI. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms across west-central WI. A few thunderstorms produced large hail measuring as large as 1.25 in diameter as well as localized flash flooding in southern Eau Claire County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported water flowing over the roadway along Lowes Creek Rd just west of State Highway 93.

A severe weather episode, with widespread reports of large to very large hail and a tornado, impacted portions of northern Oklahoma during the afternoon and evening of the 17th. Numerous supercells developed along a trailing cold front, with strong wind shear and instability promoting hail sizes as large as tennis ball to just smaller than softball with multiple thunderstorms. A more organized supercell also produced a tornado on the south side of Ponca City, continuing into portions of Osage County (see NWS Tulsa writeup for more information). Additional thunderstorm activity continued into the late evening and early morning hours of the 18th, focusing along a southeastward advancing cold front. This portion of the event featured mainly occasional damaging wind gusts and small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hailfall near the intersection of U.S. Highway 81 and Oklahoma Highway 45.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Below average precipitation and above average temperatures contributed to worsening drought across northwest Kansas during April 2026. D2 Severe Drought expanded south to include most of the area by mid to late April, with D3 Extreme Drought expanding south to include central and northern portions of the area by late April. Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about one and one-half inches to one-half inch. Normal monthly precipitation ranges from one and eight-tenths to two and four-tenths.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Monthly precipitation amounts ranged from about four-tenths of an inch to a little over one inch, highest over far northwest portions of the county. Precipitation deficits ranged from about one inch to one and eight-tenths of an inch below average. Normal monthly precipitation across the county ranges from about one and eight-tenths of an inch to two and one-quarter of an inch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of minor weather disturbances moved through the region from April 9th through the 11th. These combined with increased moisture to bring showers and storms to the region. With enough wind shear available in the atmosphere, some of these storms brought severe wind gusts to the region.  Dry and windy conditions were in place on April 9th and that helped drive the spread of a wildfire known as Mary 15 to almost 900 acres.  Additionally, the Lightning Roll Wildfire would be sparked due to dry lightning in Beaver County on the evening of April 9th.  That fire would go on to burn 2,412 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure system sat north of Maine, as a low pressure moved northeast into the region. Favorable cold air damming set up led to temperatures at, or around, freezing throughout the state. Precipitation began to move in late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. Warm mid-layer temperatures move in with associated warm front, transitioning snow in the northern regions over to mixed precipitation. Snow transitioned to sleet, sleet to freezing rain, and freezing rain to rain throughout Thursday. Transition to mixed precipitation began before sunrise from Central Highlands to Northwest Aroostook County, and then over to northern Aroostook when the sun rose. Mixed precipitation transitioned to rain by afternoon. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in the north, and 1 to 1.5 inches of sleet. A trace - 0.05 inches of freezing rain in the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Downeast region. A trace - 0.75 inches of sleet fell in the Central Highlands region. Sleet fell on top of snowfall, which had resulted in messy clean up period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 2-4 inches of snow fell in Northern Penobscot, with areas of 4-6 inches of snow in the northwest. Co-Op observer measured 0.5 inches off sleet in Millinocket.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and through the evening on April 24th as a cold front advanced from Southeast Oklahoma into the Ark-La-Tex. Intersecting this front was an outflow boundary, which moved west southwest out of Arkansas toward Northeast Texas and Northern Louisiana. This same boundary was slow in advancing and showed signs of stalling across Southeast Oklahoma just ahead of the cold front. Low-level shear in this area was sufficient to support strong updrafts with 0-1 km storm-relative helicity (SRH) over 100 m2/s2. The air mass was very moist and unstable with deep-layer shear around 50 knots, further aiding storm longevity. As a result, numerous severe thunderstorms developed across Northeast Texas during the evening with reports of widespread damaging wind gusts along with a handful of large hail reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roof damage was observed to a metal outbuilding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As developing Tropical Storm Arthur moved along the middle Texas coast (June 17) and as a degenerated low pressure system along the Louisiana Coast (June 18), very hot air descended on the southern tip of Texas, with record extreme heat index, or feels-like, temperatures for the entire region on the 18th.  The high heat index values held on into June 19th, before unsettled weather brought slightly lower temperatures and pockets of rain by the 20th, which ended the short but brutal window of extreme heat.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hottest feels-like day in modern history occurred on June 18th across Jim Hogg County, as searing heat combined with remnant high humidity from early week's rain to produce extreme heat of 116F or higher for more than 9 hours. Peak values exceeded 120 for several hours in the mid to late afternoon, with an absolute peak of 126.08F at 2:15 PM CDT.  There were no known heat-related fatalities, though data will be researched in the future.  Ambient temperatures were around 100 during the time of peak heating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another widespread thunderstorm and severe weather period impacted the southern one-half of Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas on the evening of the 25th. This event included several supercell thunderstorms across this area, including a cyclic tornadic supercell that moved in areas south of Wichita Falls, Texas into Archer and Clay Counties. Several other (generally brief) tornadoes occurred with storms across south-central and southeastern Oklahoma, though signal of residual inhibition and numerous storm interactions on the cool side of a quasi-stationary boundary generally limited low-level mesocyclone organization and longevity. Large hail and sporadic wind damage also occurred with storms across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Soon after the previous tornado dissipated, storm spotters and chasers observed another tornado that developed in the same area. This tornado became a large tornado and moved very slowly. KFDR radar data suggests that it may have moved in a loop, but the tornado occurred over open rangeland and no specific damage was reported so the tornado path is estimated.

While a few isolated showers and storms moved through the area, the vast majority of the region suffered from a severe lack of continuous, meaningful precipitation. The month was defined by the complete erasure of lower-level drought categories and an aggressive expansion of Extreme Drought (D3) as long-term moisture deficits deepened.||Precipitation was incredibly sparse. A few lucky, localized areas in the northern portions of the Texas Panhandle managed to catch 1 to 1.5 inches of rain from passing storms but this was the exception rather than the norm.  The majority of the Panhandle finished April anywhere from 0.5 to over 2 inches below normal. The isolated spots in that saw heavier showers actually finished the month 0.2 to 0.4 inches above normal, though this did little to dent the overarching dry pattern.||However, it 120 day precipitation totals truly highlight true severity of the situation. Deficits broadly ranged from 2.5 to 4.5 inches below normal across the region. This remains the reason behind the growing drought across the region. This drought combined with dry fuels and windy conditions to help fuel wildfires across the area during the month.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought (D2) continued into April as the area still lacked any significant precipitation. This lack of rain continued through much of the month, but there were a few showers and storms that moved through the county. However, Hansford County ended the month about one half of an inch to 1.4 inches below normal. The 120 day departure from normal was around 2.5 inches below normal in the west to 3.5 inches below normal in the east. The bulk of the county remained in D2 drought through the month but far southern parts of Hansford County creeped into Extreme Drought (D3) near the middle to end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous supercell thunderstorms developed late in the evening on April 25th along a warm front extending from southern Oklahoma into western Arkansas, well ahead of an advancing cold front and dry line upstream over the Texas/Oklahoma panhandles. The environment farther downstream across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Northern Louisiana was very unstable and strongly sheared. This environment favored a continuation of severe thunderstorms and the potential for new supercell development. Nocturnal low-level cooling and capping were increasing, which generally kept the primary threat as large hail. However, given the persistent low-level shear, any surface-based thunderstorms also had the potential to produce some isolated damaging wind gusts. As a result, numerous reports of large and even very large hail were documented across Howard and Hempstead Counties in addition to damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Baseball size hail reported in Hope.

Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, and March contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions expanded into Wythe county in mid April after the previous several months of January, February, and March recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 21st of April. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 5th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A spring storm brought rain, mountain snow and thunderstorms to interior northern California in early to mid April. Gusty winds with a line of thunderstorms on April 11th between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM led to numerous reports of tree damage and power outages in the Greater Sacramento Area and into the adjacent Sierra foothills, with measured wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph observed. There were also numerous reports of roadway flooding. A touchdown of an EF-U tornado occurred from 2:05 PM to 2:06 PM on April 12th near Vina, CA. There were also reports of severe hail in thunderstorms. Heavy mountain snow brought major travel impacts to the Sierra Nevada from April 10th through 12th. UC Berkeley Central Sierra Snow Lab measured 42.6 inches of heavy snow. Kirkwood Ski Resort measured 41 inches of heavy snow. Wind gusts in the Sierra were measured generally between 45 and 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding at Watt Avenue.

Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 2 inch diameter hail southeast of Arena. Time confirmed via radar data.

A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail and damaging wind gusts.||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of hail estimated up to 1 inch in diameter in Falls City, NE.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms moved across the Ozarks from April 14 to 15, 2026, and brought intense multi-hazard weather. The system advanced in two primary waves driven by escalating atmospheric instability. Unseasonably warm air pushed temperatures into the mid-80s. Strong southern winds gusted between 30 and 40 mph, injecting high humidity into the region. The initial round of storms were discrete supercell thunderstorms which formed over the Ozark Plateau. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe storms, proceeded by isolated supercells produced significant severe weather as an intense system swept across the Ozarks on Monday, April 27th.  A potent line of storms brought immense straight-line winds, very large hail and several tornadoes. High winds, up to 80mph, snapped large tree branches, downed power lines, and caused considerable structural damage to mobile homes and roofs.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to 3 inches in size was reported in a mainly rural area. Damage occurred to a home, several outbuilding and a few vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A police vehicle was rolled over and off Interstate 22 near exit 18 due to very strong straight-line winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree uprooted by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid and upper level jet at the base of a disturbance over the western U.S. moved over New Mexico during the day April 26th. Deep daytime mixing tapped into these stronger winds aloft by mid morning resulting in strong to high wind gusts across much of central and eastern New Mexico. Very dry antecedent conditions resulted in areas of blowing dust and reduced visibility across central and southern NM. Some showers were observed across northwest and north central New Mexico with one of these showers resulting in a brief 59 mph wind gust at Gallup Municipal Airport. Winds tapered off during the late evening and overnight hours as stronger winds aloft slowly exited east of the state.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at Las Vegas Regional Airport measured high wind gusts up to 63 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary frontal boundary was draped across northern NY east across central VT and New England during the afternoon of April 16th. A weak area of low pressure was traversing this frontal boundary as well. Temperatures and dewpoints were summerlike along and south of the boundary allowing for thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon and evening hours.||Several thunderstorms contained gusty winds in excess of 40 mph, but only a few storms were severe. One storm in Williamstown produced a low-end EF1 tornado and golf ball size hail. This same storm produced quarter size hail in East Orange.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Storm Survey found EF1 tornado damage 2 SSE of the town of Williamstown. Maximum winds 90 MPH. A roof of a small farm building and a house were damaged as well as an old, small sugarhouse collapsed with numerous sheered tree tops and uprooted trees in saturated soils.

Convective activity died down past sunset.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An extended period of below normal rainfall coupled with much above normal temperatures from Fall 2025 into Winter/Spring 2026 led to the continuation of severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions from the U.S. Drought Monitor across much of East and Northeast Texas through the month of April. Rainfall amounts during April only averaged between 3 to 4 inches across much of East and Northeast Texas, slightly below the normal amount of rainfall for the month. Coupled with the consistently below normal rain observed since Fall 2025, considerable hardships from area agricultural producers continued, as pastures had become dormant early, forcing farmers to provide hay and other supplemental feed much earlier than normal, as well as water as multiple ponds had dried up. An increase in wildfires also persisted, with above normal temperatures continuing the drying of fuels. Streamflow from area creeks and bayous also fell below to much below normal as well. As a result, severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought only persisted and further expanded during the month of April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant multi-day severe weather event affected the Mid-South as a deepening surface low and cold front traversed the central United States. On April 27, 2026, a northward-lifting warm front introduced tropical moisture, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s and lower 70s. This environment, supported by a strong 500 mb jet streak, produced MLCAPE values exceeding 2,500 J/kg and effective bulk shear values often surpassing 40 knots.||The event unfolded in several phases. Starting late Monday, April 27, supercells across southern Missouri and northern Arkansas consolidated into a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS). This MCS tracked southward through Tuesday morning, bringing damaging winds, large hail, and two weak tornadoes. On Tuesday, a secondary shortwave trough triggered two additional rounds of severe weather. The first occurred late Tuesday afternoon into the early evening, featuring organized convection with bowing line segments that produced damaging winds, large hail, and a weak tornado in northeast Arkansas. The second round developed immediately after the first round had moved into Middle Tennessee and north Alabama, bringing further damaging winds from Tuesday evening through early Wednesday morning, along with locally heavy rainfall that caused flash flooding. By early Wednesday morning, April 29, the cold front exited the region, ending the threat and returning the area to cooler, drier conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were knocked down at Holly Grove Road and Liberty Church Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several supercells formed across southeast Kansas moved into and across southwest Missouri, bringing very large hail to the area. The most prolific hail-producing storm was a left-moving supercell that split as it moved into Barry County in Missouri, tracking north-northeast through Lawrence, Christian, Greene, Dallas, Webster, Laclede, and Camden counties, producing severe hail for two hours and twenty minutes.||This storm reached peak intensity as it reached Aurora and tracked across northwest Springfield, bringing a large swath of significant severe hail the size of baseballs (2.75 inches) to as large as 4.75 inches (slightly larger than a grapefruit, or around the size of a CD) across the Springfield metropolitan area. Hail was retrieved and measured at 4 inches in diameter at the NWS Springfield office, even after 30 minutes of melting. Widespread damage across the path of this storm was reported to vehicles, homes, businesses, vegetation, and utility infrastructure, including significant damage around the Springfield-Branson National Airport. An emu at Dickerson Park Zoo was killed by the hail, with another animal left in veterinary care, and numerous people were treated in area hospitals for injuries sustained from the hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 2nd's early evening, an upper level short wave disturbance crossing the Middle Mississppi Valley, and associated 1000-mb surface low pressure tracking quickly from Iowa to Wiscomsin, placed central Indiana within its warm sector.  The conditional set-up for severe weather included steep 0-3 km lapse rates, and corresponding DCAPE values of 500-800 J/kg extending along and just east of the Wabash Valley.  A resultant quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) crossed western central Indiana, producing widely scattered damaging straight line winds.  The system's overall high cloud base mitigated any tornado production except where a brief EF-0 was spawned in Parke County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.
