EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oxford County averaged 4.28 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.70 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 77% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 23% in Moderate Drought (D1), with a reduction in D2 to 57% and D1 to 19% by the end of the month. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 8 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed dozens of trees across Lawrence County. One tree was downed onto powerlines.

Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intensifying upper storm system instigated a period of severe thunderstorms across much of the WFO Norman Forecast area during the evening of the 1st. A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Androscoggin County averaged 3.943 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.35 inches above normal. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2), with no change throughout April. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 10 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe thunderstorms produced flooding and marginally severe hail in the early morning of April 15th across far northern Illinois.  Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of northern Illinois during the evening of April 15th producing localized wind damage, hail and flooding.

In response to a powerful upper-level trough barreling into the Central Plains, digging further south and deepening in the process, an area of low pressure at the surface also strengthened as it shifted east across Kansas and eventually into Illinois by the end of the day on the 15th. The accompanying surface cold front and resulting strong pressure gradient allowed legitimate High Wind criteria conditions to overtake the entire forecast area, with sustained winds commonly 35-45 MPH with gusts 55-65 MPH, and even a few localized 70+ MPH gusts. The brunt of the highest wind gusts occurred mainly during the 10AM-4PM CDT timeframe, with reports more scattered in nature outside of that period. Across south central Nebraska, some of the highest gusts included the following: 74 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located two miles west of Doniphan; 71 MPH, measured by the Hastings Airport ASOS; 67, measured by mesonet stations located three miles north-northeast of Kearney  as well as seven miles west-southwest of Ragan; 66 MPH, measured by the Grand Island Central Nebraska Regional Airport ASOS.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained speeds near 40 MPH and wind gusts exceeding 50 MPH were common throughout the day. The peak measured wind gust was 61 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located three miles west-southwest of Carleton, which also measured a separate gust of 58 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An organized line of storms was able to tap into a favorable environmental shear profile to produce several swaths of significant wind damage, as well as a few tornadoes across south central Mississippi.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began near Pleasant Hill Drive and Elm Lane in southeastern Lincoln County and tracked eastward, crossing MS Highway 583 in the Ruth community. It then continued along Greenwood Road and Raiford Trail, crossing Primitive Drive in the Bristerville community, then across Monument Trail and Junction Lane before crossing into southwestern Lawrence County near the Verna community. It crossed Holmesville Road and paralleled Verna Road before lifting near Excell Boyd Road. Along the path, countless trees were snapped or uprooted, some in large swaths, multiple outbuildings sustained damage, utility poles were damaged, a mobile home sustained roof and skirting damage, and a site built home sustained minor wind damage. The maximum wind speed of this tornado was 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell near Martin Creek Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report from a social media photo of a large tree limb down in town. Time estimated based on radar. Wind speeds were estimated at 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||A strong to severe thunderstorm initially tracked across Montgomery County, producing a combination of damaging winds and large hail. The storm initially dropped quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail near Stanton before an Iowa DOT mesonet station 3 miles north of Villisca measured a peak wind gust of 64 mph. As the storm moved over and around Red Oak, reported hail sizes increased. Widespread quarter-size hail within the city quickly gave way to golf ball-size (1.75 inches) hail southwest of town reported by emergency management, 2.00-inch hail measured by a storm chaser to the east-southeast, and baseball-size (2.75 inches) hail reported via mPING just 3 miles south of Red Oak.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 1.00 inch in diameter received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rain and mountain snow showers moved across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening of May 4th. Widespread snow then formed over the mountains and northern foothills during the early morning hours of May 5th and continued for most of the day. Across the lower elevations (below 6000 feet), precipitation type was mainly rain through the morning of the 5th and slowly began to turn over to snow during the afternoon. Snow then continued through the night of the 5th and early morning hours of the 6th. The heaviest snow occurred across the foothills and mountains of Boulder and Larimer Counties where 18 to 36 inches of snow fell. Areas west of I-25 to the base of the foothills received 4 to 12 inches, heaviest near the foothills. Main impact was broken tree branches on deciduous trees, some of which fell on powerlines leading to sparse power outages. Power outages topped 50,000 overnight the 5th and early morning the 6th. Denver International Airport (DIA) had over 700 flight delays and 40 cancellations for May 5th and May 6th. Numerous schools were closed on May 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRahs and trained spotters reported 4 to 12 inches of snow. The heavy wet snow led to many broken tree branches and limbs, a few of which fell onto vehicles and homes. Broken branches also fell onto powerlines, leading to some power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions expanded into SE West Virginia after the previous three months of  February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with pockets of 8.00-10.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd to 5th percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 19th of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New, and Greenbrier River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon of the 15th saw a repeat of the previous day's activity. Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 15th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Several wildfire starts occurred on the afternoon of the 15th although none of these wildfires caused any known damage. The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Automated Surface Observing System at Lubbock International Airport measured severe wind gusts from 1712 CST through 1725 CST. A peak wind gust of 69 mph was measured at 1712 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions across Cumberland County from April 2026 continued in May.

The tornado began to curve towards the southeast as it underwent the occlusion process, shrinking from a stovepipe appearance to a rope as it quickly moved over farmlands and turbines. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several slow-moving thunderstorms developed across the southern Nebraska Panhandle and northern Nebraska Panhandle, bringing hail, tornadoes, and torrential rain fall with flooding occuring in Kimball and Dawes Counties. No verification occurred in southeast Wyoming.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Management and storm chaser videos documented a brief tornado. The tornado lasted approximately 30 seconds before dissipating. No damage was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong surface low deepened as it moved through North Dakota, leading to high non-thunderstorm wind gusts. By the early afternoon, the strong winds were producing blowing dust and significantly reduced visibility across western North Dakota, with a Blowing Dust Warning and Blowing Dust Advisory issued for much of western and central North Dakota. Visibility was under one quarter of a mile at times. The strongest wind gust reported was 76 mph near Crosby in Divide County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Grenora NDAWN station reported gusts up to 69 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust was measured by AWOS station KAGZ at Wagner.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Friday night into Saturday, May 8-9, 2026, strong to severe thunderstorms in association with atmospheric disturbances initially developed across Zapata County on the 8th, before redeveloping as a single severe thunderstorm that waxed and waned between Starr and Cameron County on May 9th. Large hail was initially reported in Starr County just after daybreak on the 9th, before the storm re-strengthened in Hidalgo and Cameron County by mid-morning. The episode culminated into a microburst that caused structural damage to roofs, traffic lights, fences, homes, trailers, and power poles as well as trees in central Cameron County. There were 3 injuries, two requiring hospitalization, where poorly constructed mobile-type homes were destroyed.||At least 45,000 customers were without power at peak or just after the storms crossed the populated IH-2 corridor from near McAllen to east of Harlingen, one of the more widespread outages in recent memory.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported hail up to 0.75 inches in diameter on Bluebird St in Roma, TX.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A frontal boundary south of Interstate 10 slowed and stalled near the coast while successive midlevel disturbances crossed the Lower Mississippi Valley. Deep moisture pooled along the boundary, with precipitable water values near 2 inches, supporting efficient rainfall and repeated rounds of thunderstorms. Morning storms produced large hail and damaging winds. Additional storms trained across portions of the Interstate 10 and 12 corridors, causing flash flooding in the Baton Rouge and Hammond areas. During the afternoon, stronger storms reached the New Orleans metropolitan area, lower Mississippi River parishes, and adjacent coastal waters, producing damaging winds, and large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video on social media showed quarter sized hail in Greensburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave brought about windy thunderstorms across much of southern MT. In it's wake, a cold front crossed the area, and strong winds behind the front persisted well into the 14th. Non-convective gusts up to 80 mph were observed, with convective gusts up to 80 mph observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KLVM Livingston gusted to 69 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across portions of northern and central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 8th, spreading southward into southern Oklahoma and western-north Texas through the evening. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions remained across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions expanded into northwest North Carolina in early and late May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions expanded, and worsened across Surry county through early May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm survey revealed a tornado developed and moved northeast across far northeast Nemaha county damaging older farm outbuidlings and barns and snapping large tree limbs.  The tornado appears to have continued into southeast Nebraska.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong instability and weak wind shear led to scattered multi-cell thunderstorms across central and southern Oklahoma on the afternoon and evening of the 26th. One of these storms produced wind damage near Hobart in Kiowa County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The roof was partially removed from a home east of Hobart in association with a small thunderstorm. Storm chasers in the area observed a well-developed gustnado (or perhaps a landspout) in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado moved into Juneau County from Vernon County where it intensified quickly and hit a residence at EF-3 intensity, destroying the home's above ground level. As the tornado moved east, it produced significant tree damage before weakening in intensity as it approached State Road 80, where it damaged a few more homes and several outbuildings. The tornado continued northeast, dealing intermittent tree and structural damage at EF-1 intensity along its path until it dissipated just west of Overgaard Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure passing to the south of the UP brought mixed wintry precipitation to the UP on the 2nd and 3rd. Some locations experienced mostly snow and sleet while other locations saw freezing rain on top of sleet and yet more others saw just freezing rain, causing Ice Storm conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The CO-OP observer GDCM4 reported at least a glaze of ice with a frozen anemometer. Additional reports from the public included slick road conditions and ice accumulation on elevated surfaces such as trees and vehicles. Estimates elsewhere in the county were in excess of 0.25 inches. Key impacts: road closures, hazardous travel.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Oklahoma during the late afternoon of April 24th, then congealed into a partially organized cluster of storms as they moved southeast across the ArkLaTex region during the evening. The storms continued to strengthen and evolved into a more organized mesoscale convective system within northwest flow aloft as they approached the local area. The MCS moved across coastal Mississippi on the early morning hours of April 25th, producing a couple of tornadoes along with areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain caused street flooding around Hwy 90/Courthouse Rd area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved across the area and brought heavy snow, especially to the  mountains. The heaviest snow fell in the Tetons, where there were many reports of over a foot of new snow with a maximum amount of 25 inches at the top of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort. Other notable amounts included 20 inches in the Salt and Wyoming Range, 15 inches in the Bighorn Range, 14 inches in the western Wind River Range and 12 inches on Casper Mountain. Lesser amounts fell in the lower elevations. However, in northern Johnson County, a combination of snow and wind gusting to 50 mph brought closures of Interstates 25 and 90 for a time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL site, 12 inches of new snow fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of precipitation. The first round produced mixed precipitation across the county. The second round fell as mostly wet heavy snow that melted on contact with the ground. Snow accumulations measured 1 to 2 inches across the NW portion of the county. The ASOS Station at St. Cloud Airport measured a tenth of an inch of freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/2). Low pressure swept across Minnesota and Wisconsin from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across western Wisconsin observed a mix of rain/snow/freezing rain/and sleet. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the evening hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day and produced several hours of freezing precipitation. Given concerns of heavy icing, Ice Storm warnings were issued for portions of western WI. On early April 2nd, law enforcement dispatches in Dunn, Chippewa, and Eau Claire Counties reported downed trees and powerlines due to icing.  The thickest ice accretion report was located in St. Croix County of measuring 3/8 inches thick 2 miles NNE of Woodville. ||A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived April 3rd and persisted into early April 4th. Given that the low's track kept western WI within the warm sector of this system, the precipitation type was mostly rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS Observers measured an inch of snow across the county. Additionally, observers 2 to 6 miles south of Ellsworth, reported sleet and freezing rain with ice accumulations of 0.13 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: From April 24 to April 27, daily thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening, triggered by a dryline and a meandering frontal boundary. These long-lasting supercells were fueled by a highly unstable and sheared environment, resulting in several tornadoes, damaging winds, and very large hail. Two fatalities occurred on April 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager reported quarter sized hail in downtown Pottsboro.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds blew down one tree along Old Courthouse Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intensifying upper storm system instigated a period of severe thunderstorms across much of the WFO Norman Forecast area during the evening of the 1st. Storm development occurred both along a quasi-stationary boundary across northern Oklahoma and along an accelerating Pacific Front from far western Oklahoma into western-north Texas. A mix of supercells and a well-developed quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) yielded reports of large to very large hail and wind damage across portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The report was relayed through mPING. The event time was adjusted based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The final day of a prolonged stretch of severe weather potential (beginning on the 23rd) yielded another round of significant hail, winds and tornadoes across southern Oklahoma into portions of north Texas. A pair of intense supercells (one southeast of Wichita Falls, Texas and another from near Sulphur, Oklahoma to Atoka, Oklahoma) produced large to very large hail, damaging wind gusts and several tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limbs were blown down at Lake Arrowhead State Park. The event time is estimated based on radar observations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first of several days of severe weather across the WFO Norman Forecast Area featured intense thunderstorms (supercells) across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 23rd. An emerging upper trough and sharp dryline facilitated development of scattered intense supercell thunderstorms across portions of northern Oklahoma, with reports of large to very large hail, thunderstorm wind damage and several tornadoes. In addition to a family of well-documented tornadoes from east of Medford, Oklahoma (Grant County) to near Braman, Oklahoma (Kay County), a violent tornado impacted areas around Vance Air Force Base and the south/east extents of Enid, Oklahoma. This tornado prompted a rare Tornado Emergency, the first in the WFO Norman Forecast Area since May 19th, 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An image showing a ruler-measured hailstone was shared on social media. The location is approximate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oklahoma City Will Rogers International Airport (KOKC) observation. Wind gust associated with a nearby tornadic circulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cumberland County averaged 3.39 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.57 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 28% in Extreme Drought (D3) and 72% in Severe Drought (D2) and 8% in Moderate Drought (D1). By the end of April the extreme drought had been eliminated, shifting to moderate drought which now represented 100% of the county. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 12 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

Large hail and winds in excess of 70mph were associated with this bowing segment as it dove east-southeastward from South Central Missouri into the Bootheel. A more intense pocket of wind known as a macroburst produced winds up to 100mph across portions of Ripley County from southeast of Doniphan to south/southwest of Naylor, uprooting dozens of trees and damaging several structures and multiple vehicles.||For the Carter-Ripley-Butler corridor, environmental parameters included: MLCAPE of 1000-2000J/kg, DCAPE of 500J/kg, very strong effective bulk shear of 60-70kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 6-7C/km.

Moving east-southeast, damaging wind impacted the Oxly community and locations near and south of the Naylor community. In Oxly, dozens of trees were snapped or uprooted, causing damage to outbuildings and downing power lines. To the south and west from Naylor to Hemenway, a grain bin rolled hundreds of yards and a large farm outbuilding was shifted off its foundation. A child sustained minor injuries when they were struck by debris. Along the damage path, hundreds of trees were snapped, uprooted or lost large limbs. An accompanying surface cold front pushed southeast across the region during the daytime hours, ending up across far southeastern portions of the local forecast area by mid-late afternoon. Scattered thunderstorms developed along this frontal boundary roughly between 3-4 PM CST, having plenty of deeper layer shear to work with and MLCAPE around 1000-1500 j/kg. A few storms strengthened enough to drop large hail across portions of Thayer and Fillmore counties between 4-7 PM CST. The largest hail reported was around Bruning, which had golf ball to tennis ball size hail.

Maximum winds were estimated at 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A two day period of active weather prevailed over West Virginia from May 19th to the 20th amid an advancing cold front. Beginning on the 19th, one sub-severe thunderstorm spilled into Wood County from activity that progressed through southeast Ohio, which resulted in some downed tree limbs. The more impressive round of storms took shape on the 20th as the front encroached on the Central Appalachians. Storms initially tracked into  the southwest portions of West Virginia around peak heating and remained active throughout the course of the evening. Damaging wind gusts associated with storms resulted in a slew of downed trees and power lines across the state. A 60 mile per hour gust was recorded outside of Elkins by a trained spotter as a strong storm swept through. Additionally, storms crossing through the Kanawha Valley grew tall enough to produce large hail for a brief period of time. On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Evidence of a high-end EF-1 (110mph) tornado was found in south- central Victoria County. In between, several manufactured homes on Jared Rd, Lexie Ln, and York Rd suffered significant roof damage, broken windows, and scattered debris correlated to circulation of a tornado. One manufactured home was completely destroyed along Jared Rd. The tornado track was found to be around 1.1 miles long and a width of around 400 yards, spanning from 2:02-2:06pm CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very dry spring led to the development of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought in the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. With an extra prolonged period of dryness and abnormally warm temperatures both in May and leading up to May, drought impacts were felt quite a bit. Not only were crops not surviving spring planting, but grasses remained abnormally dry and dormant for this time of year. This lead to extreme wildfire conditions as temperatures reached the upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small section of northern Dallam and Sherman counties up against the Oklahoma Panhandle started the month of May in Extreme Drought (D3). The rest of Dallam and Sherman, and all of Hartley and Moore, counties started the month in Severe Drought (D2). Around half way through the month all of Dallam, the northwest two thirds of Hartley and just about all of Sherman had degraded to D3. Rain events just started to pick up across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles which spared the area of D2 from D3 until later in the month. By month's end Moore County fell into D3 while a good portion of Dallam, Sherman, and north-central Hartley improved back to D2. The entire area kept a 120 day deficit around 1 to 4. This late into the spring, crop and other agricultural damage had already been done.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a near-record dry April, the impacts of months-long precipitation deficits as high as 18 resulted in extreme to exceptional drought conditions lingering into May across western North Carolina. Many pastures and hayfields were rated poor-to-very poor, resulting in forage shortages. Crop stress affected soybeans, delayed or reduced planting for corn and other crops, and lowered vegetable yields. Reservoirs, lakes, and streams were well below normal (e.g. Fontana Lake around 18 feet below normal). Mandatory or voluntary conservation measures were in place in multiple systems, and  some ponds and smaller supplies were critically low. Fire danger remained abnormally high and the wildfire season extended into May across the mountains, although the threat steadily decreased during the first half of the month owing to greenup and a continued statewide burn ban. A transition to a very wet pattern finally brought some relief late in the month, especially to the Blue Ridge, the foothills, and the southern Piedmont, where May rainfall wound up 125 to 175% of normal. Drought category was reduced to severe across much of these areas by the start of June.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Friday night into Saturday, May 8-9, 2026, strong to severe thunderstorms in association with atmospheric disturbances initially developed across Zapata County on the 8th, before redeveloping as a single severe thunderstorm that waxed and waned between Starr and Cameron County on May 9th. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 95 mph tracked across portions of northern Walthall County, near Enon, MS. This tornado began near L. L. Coon Rd where high resolution satellite imagery showed areas of damaged/displaced trees on a confined path that tracked southeast toward MS Hwy 44. The tornado strengthened to EF-1 strength as it moved into Willie Cothern Rd where it uprooted trees, lifted metal roofing off a porch, and snapped a swath of tree trunks on private property. The tornado turned more eastward as it crossed MS Hwy 583 where it damaged shingles on a church and uprooted and snapped a few trees. Minor tree damage continued eastward across New Home Church Road with plenty of tree debris across the road. The tornado then restrengthened some over inaccessible forested areas south of New Home Church Rd where patches of heavier tree damage/displacement was identified on high resolution satellite imagery. This tree damage gradually became more minor again near Hope Rd and Dee Toney Rd. Numerous small trees were leaning in a confluent pattern with large branches down near MS Hwy 27. Minor tree damage continued with uproots and large branches predominantly occurring along the damage path on Jordan, Sauls, and Dan Holmes roads. This tornado continued east-southeast into Marion County, within the NWS Jackson area of responsibility, where additional EF-0 and EF-1 tree damage was identified by ground survey. It's estimated that the tornado finally lifted near Circle Bar Road after being on the ground for approximately 13 miles and 24 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions remained across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions expanded into northwest North Carolina in early and late May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions expanded, and worsened across Stokes county through early May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Dan River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Oklahoma during the late afternoon of April 24th, then congealed into a partially organized cluster of storms as they moved southeast across the ArkLaTex region during the evening. The storms continued to strengthen and evolved into a more organized mesoscale convective system within northwest flow aloft as they approached the local area. The MCS moved across coastal Mississippi on the early morning hours of April 25th, producing a couple of tornadoes along with areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 90 mph touched down at 30th Street and Brookwood Ave. where large branches were down on several trees. Similar damage occurred as the tornado tracked to the southeast across Pass Road and 28th Street. The tornado continued to the southeast and reached peak intensity of 90 mph near the intersection of 5th Avenue and 25th Street where a few trees were snapped. One hardwood tree was hollow inside and the other snap was very high. Numerous large branches were also removed from several trees near this intersection. The tornado then continued to the southeast crossing Gulf Avenue near 24th Street producing sporadic tree damage. The tornado then crossed the railroad just west of Hewes St. where additional large branches were removed from several trees all the way to Beach Blvd. Numerous trees were observed to have lost large branches between Roberts Ave. and Centennial Plaza on Beach Blvd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Kennebec County averaged 3.73 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.25 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2), and there were no changes to the designation during the month. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 10 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a tree onto a road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong Spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/2). Low pressure swept across Minnesota and Wisconsin from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across western Wisconsin observed a mix of rain/snow/freezing rain/and sleet. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the evening hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day and produced several hours of freezing precipitation. Given concerns of heavy icing, Ice Storm warnings were issued for portions of western WI. On early April 2nd, law enforcement dispatches in Dunn, Chippewa, and Eau Claire Counties reported downed trees and powerlines due to icing.  The thickest ice accretion report was located in St. Croix County of measuring 3/8 inches thick 2 miles NNE of Woodville. ||A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS Observers measured one quarter to three eighths of an inch of ice accumulation from freezing rain 2 miles NNE of Woodville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This strong EF-2 tornado began in rural portions of Olmsted County east of Viola where it damaged some farm outbuildings as it moved northeast. As the tornado approached the Wabasha County line, it strengthened and significantly damaged a farmstead, removing large sections of the roof and other portions of the home and outbuildings. It then continued northeast into Wabasha County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms moved across most of far northern Illinois during the evening of April 14th producing large hail, wind damage.  Flash flooding also occurred in parts of the Chicago metro area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread street and basement flooding was reported across much of northern Chicago, including Edison Park, Norwood Park, Jefferson Park, Rogers Park, Edgewater, Uptown, Forest Glen, North Park and West Ridge. Lakeshore Drive was flooded near Montrose Beach. The underpass on Interstate 94 at Pratt Avenue in Lincolnwood was flooded. In Edison Park, cars were reported stalled with water up to their bumpers.  Multiple roads and viaducts were flooded in Rosemont and near O'Hare Airport, including along portions of Interstate 90.  Rainfall amounts included 3.46 inches in Harwood Heights; 2.66 inches in Rogers Park; 2.59 inches in Park Ridge and 2.56 inches in Lincolnwood. Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 2.43 inches, which was a record 24 hour total for April 14th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved across all of northern Illinois during the evening of April 17th producing several tornadoes and wind damage.  Large hail occurred across parts of northwest Illinois and flooding occurred across parts of northeast Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado began near the intersection of Freeport Road and Bates Road southeast of Harrison, initially downing several tree branches at and near a small cemetery. The tornado produced additional tree damage as it tracked eastward along Roscoe Road before entering the west side of Roscoe and reaching its peak intensity as it tracked through the Hawks Point, Crystal Hills, and Oxford Commons subdivisions. There, multiple homes had portions of their roofs torn off or damaged and had sections of siding and fascia peeled off. A few homes also had their garage doors blown in, leading to parts of their garage walls getting blown out in a few cases. Numerous trees were also uprooted or damaged in these subdivisions. The tornado then continued eastward, knocking down several power poles along Gleasman Road and damaging a nearby farm outbuilding before crossing the Rock River. East of the Rock River, the tornado continued to cause extensive tree damage. Multiple additional houses sustained roof and fascia damage from the tornado as well. The tornado appeared to dissipate just as it reached the Winnebago-Boone County line. Extensive straight-line wind damage was also observed in close proximity to the tornadic circulation, particularly along its southern flank.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong system moved across the Great Basin into northern UT with a strong cold front sweeping through the area starting in the extreme late evening hours of 4/21/26, persisting into the early morning hours of 4/22/26. Numerous strong wind gusts were observed across northern UT, particularly across most valley locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front traversed across northern UT in the early morning hours bringing numerous wind gusts in excess of 58mph at sites such as South Mountain, UDOT SR-201 at I-80, and Pacificorp Kennecott Rd. Lake Point. The highest observed wind gust within this forecast zone was measured to be 70mph at the South Mountain site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of rain/freezing rain mix which lasted several hours each. CoCoRaHS observers across the county reported a light glaze of ice on non-paved surfaces.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the low to mid 60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2000J/kg in West Kentucky with DCAPE of 1100J/kg, 0-6km shear of 30-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from the Purchase Area of West Kentucky were a mix of hail and straight-line wind damage. Numerous wind damage reports were received in Carlisle, Graves, and Marshall Counties. Meanwhile, hail up to 2 in diameter accumulated on surfaces in Sharpe and produced damage to siding and windows. Power outages were highest in Lyon (25%), Livingston (15%), and Ballard (8%) Counties at their peak. Past the Lakes area, severe weather reports were entirely straight line wind damage with the worst of the damage occurring in Hopkinsville where numerous trees and power lines were downed and a few homes were damaged. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between May 28 and June 4, 2026, a very slow-moving upper-level low-pressure system  over Montana tapped into moisture from the Gulf of America, bringing heavy and widespread precipitation to western Montana. Prior to this event, several locations had already received significant moisture in May, leaving soils saturated and mountain runoff elevated. The combination of intense rainfall and ongoing snowmelt led to swollen rivers, and overwhelmed small streams, and flooded local irrigation canals. Intense thunderstorms brought heavy rain-rates in Sanders County resulting in mudslides.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread high water affected the Flathead River basin. Anticipating heavy rainfall, operators at the Hungry Horse Dam opened the spillway gates at 1137MST on May 28 to manage reservoir capacity, causing significant downstream rises. On Friday morning, May 28, the City of Columbia Falls temporarily closed the back portion of River's Edge Park to the public due to early inundation. The Flathead River at Columbia Falls (CFMM8) crested at 13.78 feet with a discharge of 46,400 CFS on the evening of May 29, remaining above the minor flood stage of 13.0 feet. A subsequent NWS flood survey on June 1 at 1025MST documented high water completely surrounding private residential properties near the confluence of the South Fork and Middle Fork of the Flathead River. Floodwaters fully encircled a home 1 mile west of Hungry Horse, though the water had not yet breached the structural foundation or entered the living spaces at the time of the inspection.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm positioned over the Eddy basin dropped between 1.41 and 1.60 inches of rain in less than 1.5 hours. This high-intensity rainfall fell on steep terrain, rapidly saturating soils and triggering multiple mudslides on the mountainside north of Highway 200. The resulting debris flow rushed down the slope 2 miles east-southeast of Eddy, uprooting at least one large tree and dislodging a boulder the size of a small car. The massive boulder and associated mud slide debris slid directly into the roadway, completely blocking traffic between mile markers 63 and 64. The local fire department and state road crews responded to manage traffic and clear the slide area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

Extreme Drought conditions remained across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions expanded into northwest North Carolina in early and late May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oxford County averaged 4.28 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.70 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 77% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 23% in Moderate Drought (D1), with a reduction in D2 to 57% and D1 to 19% by the end of the month. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 8 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplifying mid- to upper-level trough, combined with above-normal moisture, maintained an unstable, wet pattern. With previous rain left saturated soils and elevated rivers, heavy rainfall quickly lead to urban flooding, small stream flooding, river flooding, landslides and flash flooding. Significant flooding occurred in Las Piedras, particularly, where several houses where flooded and flash flooded following heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding affected at least 16 families in Las Piedras following heavy rainfall. One residence reported approximately 3 feet of water inside the home, resulting in significant damage to personal belongings, including beds, furniture, clothing, and toys. Rainfall totals of 5 to 6 inches were reported across the area, leading to flooding of homes and surrounding properties. Above mentioned totals fell within a matter of hours, leading to river overflow and significant Water accumulation. Nearby, the Rio Gurabo USGS river gauge reached flood stage at 16.09 feet at 1:45 PM AST. The information was provided by local emergency management officials.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois and West Kentucky compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri.||In Northwest Kentucky, during the late evening, MLCAPE remained elevated ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 1000-2000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-6, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C.||Reports from West Kentucky primarily came from an intensifying line of storms entering the Western Coal Fields area from the northwest. The most significant damage came from a surging portion of the line with an embedded supercell that resulted in two tornadoes: 1. an EF-0 tornado which crossed from northeastern Hopkins County into McLean County, and 2. an EF-1 tornado which caused damage from southeast of Rumsey to north of Livermore in McLean County. A swath of straight-line winds accompanied the first tornadic circulation. The tornadoes damaged numerous trees, some electrical lines and power poles, and a few homes and outbuildings. Several other straight-line wind damage reports were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed across KY-1078 between KY-35 and US-60 east of Henderson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Southern Missouri during the early to mid afternoon hours on April 16th. These storms became severe with large hail, eventually morphing into a more linear structure with the threat switching over to primarily damaging winds as the storms moved into the Lakes area and Southern Pennyrile of West Kentucky. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the mid-60s during the afternoon hours. Clearing behind morning showers allowed for SBCAPE values to reach 2500J/kg in Southeast Missouri with DCAPE of 900J/kg, 0-6km shear of 35-40kts, and mid-level lapse rates of 7C/km.||Reports from Southeast Missouri were primarily hail based. The largest hail occurred in the town of Advance which had numerous reports of golf ball to tennis size hail and a couple reports of baseball size hail, producing damage. Straight line wind damage was observed with a supercell in Bollinger County, downing a tree and damaging a barn roof.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Powerlines were downed south of Marble Hill as a supercell moved eastward through Bollinger County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In response to a powerful upper-level trough barreling into the Central Plains, digging further south and deepening in the process, an area of low pressure at the surface also strengthened as it shifted east across Kansas and eventually into Illinois by the end of the day on the 15th. The accompanying surface cold front and resulting strong pressure gradient allowed legitimate High Wind criteria conditions to overtake the entire forecast area, with sustained winds commonly 35-45 MPH with gusts 55-65 MPH, and even a few localized 70+ MPH gusts. The brunt of the highest wind gusts occurred mainly during the 10AM-4PM CDT timeframe, with reports more scattered in nature outside of that period. Across south central Nebraska, some of the highest gusts included the following: 74 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located two miles west of Doniphan; 71 MPH, measured by the Hastings Airport ASOS; 67, measured by mesonet stations located three miles north-northeast of Kearney  as well as seven miles west-southwest of Ragan; 66 MPH, measured by the Grand Island Central Nebraska Regional Airport ASOS.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained speeds near 40 MPH and wind gusts exceeding 50 MPH were common throughout the day. The peak measured wind gust was 61 MPH, measured by a mesonet station located six miles west of Cowles, which also measured a gust of 58 MPH. Gusts between 58 and 60 MPH were measured by a mesonet station located five miles north of Inavale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hardwood tree branches broken (1-3 inch diameter).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21. Isolated flash flooding also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media post showed widespread flooding over County Road 2015.
