EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell in the Joinerville community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Amateur radio report of power out in parts of Red Oak, IA with power poles down and tree damage. Wind speeds were estimated at 70-75 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||A strong to severe thunderstorm initially tracked across Montgomery County, producing a combination of damaging winds and large hail. The storm initially dropped quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail near Stanton before an Iowa DOT mesonet station 3 miles north of Villisca measured a peak wind gust of 64 mph. As the storm moved over and around Red Oak, reported hail sizes increased. Widespread quarter-size hail within the city quickly gave way to golf ball-size (1.75 inches) hail southwest of town reported by emergency management, 2.00-inch hail measured by a storm chaser to the east-southeast, and baseball-size (2.75 inches) hail reported via mPING just 3 miles south of Red Oak.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 2.75 inches in diameter received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of hail estimated up to 0.75 inches in diameter. Report received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rain and mountain snow showers moved across eastern Colorado during the afternoon and evening of May 4th. Widespread snow then formed over the mountains and northern foothills during the early morning hours of May 5th and continued for most of the day. Across the lower elevations (below 6000 feet), precipitation type was mainly rain through the morning of the 5th and slowly began to turn over to snow during the afternoon. Snow then continued through the night of the 5th and early morning hours of the 6th. The heaviest snow occurred across the foothills and mountains of Boulder and Larimer Counties where 18 to 36 inches of snow fell. Areas west of I-25 to the base of the foothills received 4 to 12 inches, heaviest near the foothills. Main impact was broken tree branches on deciduous trees, some of which fell on powerlines leading to sparse power outages. Power outages topped 50,000 overnight the 5th and early morning the 6th. Denver International Airport (DIA) had over 700 flight delays and 40 cancellations for May 5th and May 6th. Numerous schools were closed on May 6th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRahs and trained spotters reported 4 to 8 inches of snow. The heavy wet snow led to many broken tree branches and limbs, a few of which fell onto vehicles and homes. Broken branches also fell onto powerlines, leading to some power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across north central Oklahoma during the early afternoon of the 8th, along a cold front approaching the region from the northwest. The thunderstorms spread across eastern Oklahoma during the mid afternoon and evening. The atmosphere became moderately unstable during the afternoon ahead of the cold front in eastern Oklahoma, and deep-layer wind shear increased across the region with the approach of an upper level disturbance. The combination of moderately strong instability and strong deep-layer wind shear resulted in some thunderstorms evolving into supercell thunderstorms, the strongest of which produced large hail up to three inches in diameter and damaging wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms were initially transient and struggled to become organized due to a lack of deep layer shear across the region. However, numerous outflow boundary formed which initiated new convection and were able to take advantage of a moist and unstable atmosphere. Hail as large as tennis balls were observed in Hale County. The numerous outflow boundaries created enough shear to generate several landspout tornadoes across the area. None of the many landspout tornadoes caused any known damage. Additionally, merging storms in southeastern Hale County produced torrential rainfall which led to flash flooding of roads and fields north of Petersburg.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Brownfield measured a wind gust of 58 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A two day period of active weather prevailed over West Virginia from May 19th to the 20th amid an advancing cold front. Beginning on the 19th, one sub-severe thunderstorm spilled into Wood County from activity that progressed through southeast Ohio, which resulted in some downed tree limbs. The more impressive round of storms took shape on the 20th as the front encroached on the Central Appalachians. Storms initially tracked into  the southwest portions of West Virginia around peak heating and remained active throughout the course of the evening. Damaging wind gusts associated with storms resulted in a slew of downed trees and power lines across the state. A 60 mile per hour gust was recorded outside of Elkins by a trained spotter as a strong storm swept through. Additionally, storms crossing through the Kanawha Valley grew tall enough to produce large hail for a brief period of time. A swath of 1 to 1.75 inch hailstones were observed from Putnam and Logan Counties over to Kanawha and Clay Counties. The severe risk subsided as the sun began to set for the evening and the cold front began its passage through the forecast area.

On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hardwood tree branches broken (1-3 inch diameter).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist air combined with the influence of a dryline located across the eastern portion of the Texas Panhandle. This resulted in the development of an isolated thunderstorm during the evening of May 9th. With enough cold air present in the upper atmosphere, this allowed for large hail to grow within the storm and fall across portions of eastern Texas Panhandle. Additional storms developed during the early morning hours of May 10th along a southward moving cold front. These early morning storms produced hail between 1 and 1.5 over the northeastern combined Panhandles.

A few short lived thunderstorms formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle on the evening of May 13th. One of these storms was exiting Gray County as it was dissipating and the environment left behind helped cause a heat burst in Gray County, which led to gusts around 60 mph. The next day, May 14th, scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region. Finally, on the evening of the 15th, showers and thunderstorms developed over the northwest combined Panhandles. These storms also produced severe wind gusts across portions of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A couple of gusts to 59 and 60 mph occurred between 2111CDT and 2130CDT at the mesonet location one mile to the east northeast of Mclean, likely from a heat burst behind dissipating thunderstorms.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured by a personal weather station.

A tornadic supercell developed near or along the Kenedy/Kleberg County line during the evening of May 20, 2026. The storm tracked southeastward through Kenedy County before weakening just offshore Kenedy County that evening. A large hail and a very high wind gust (possible tornado) was reported as the supercell moved southeast and crossed Laguna Madre toward the nearshore Gulf waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Texas Coastal Oceanic Observation System platform at Rincon del San Jose, within Laguna Madre about one-third north of the Willacy/Kenedy County line, recorded a peak gust to 93 mph (80.86 knots) at 730 PM CDT.  This location is used as a proxy to the nearby land mass in Coastal Kenedy County, and based on the intensity of the supercell, it is certain that similar wind gusts occurred at this location. It is possible that the event produced a tornado - but lack of ground truth observations or a survey (in a very remote area accessible only by water craft) as well as the duration of the strong and shifting winds (nearly 20 minutes), as well as no sharply lowered surface pressure, suggest a rear-flank downburst as the strongest winds were from the north/northeast.

CZ_NAME: LAGUNA MADRE FROM 5NM N OF PT MANSFIELD TO BAFFIN BAY TX
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tornadic supercell developed near or along the Kenedy/Kleberg County line during the evening of May 20, 2026. The storm tracked southeastward through Kenedy County before weakening just offshore Kenedy County that evening. Large hail was reported over northern Kenedy, with very high wind (possible tornado) reported at the Rincon del San Jose Texas Coastal Oceanic Observing Network (TCOON) platform, near the Land Cut along Laguna Madre.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: TCOON site at Rincon del San Jose measured a wind gust of 93 mph at 730 PM CDT, with changing wind directions.  Gale force winds (34 knots or higher) arrived at approximately 721 PM, and soon reached Storm force (50.54 knots) at 724 PM.  Winds peaked at 80.86 knots at 730 PM and remained near storm force (46.65 knots) at 736 PM before finally dropping just below Gale force (33.24 knots) at 742 PM.  There was no known damage, including to the platform, as of this writing.

Extreme Drought conditions remained across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions expanded into northwest North Carolina in early and late May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 27, 2026, an upper-level shortwave trough and an associated deepening surface low-pressure system tracked across the Midwest. South of the low's path, a sufficiently unstable warm sector surged into central Indiana, characterized by rich boundary-layer moisture and strong low and deep layer wind shear. This setup supported multiple rounds of severe convection resulting in numerous damaging wind gusts or large hail reports. Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed multiple trees.

Areas across western Wisconsin observed a mix of rain/snow/freezing rain/and sleet. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the evening hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day and produced several hours of freezing precipitation. Given concerns of heavy icing, Ice Storm warnings were issued for portions of western WI. On early April 2nd, law enforcement dispatches in Dunn, Chippewa, and Eau Claire Counties reported downed trees and powerlines due to icing.  The thickest ice accretion report was located in St. Croix County of measuring 3/8 inches thick 2 miles NNE of Woodville. ||A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived April 3rd and persisted into early April 4th. Given that the low's track kept western WI within the warm sector of this system, the precipitation type was mostly rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS Observer 3 miles NNE of Stockholm measured two tenths of an inch of ice accretion.

The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail that was 0.88 inch in diameter was observed near Stewartsville, VA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Knox County averaged 4.21 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.17 inches above normal. It was the driest June through April stretch on record with deficits near a foot. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2), which was reduced to 85% by the end of the month. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 12 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

Three tornadoes also occurred between Jackson and Morgan Counties, along with flash flooding in Knox and Marion Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||A strong to severe thunderstorm initially tracked across Montgomery County, producing a combination of damaging winds and large hail. The storm initially dropped quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail near Stanton before an Iowa DOT mesonet station 3 miles north of Villisca measured a peak wind gust of 64 mph. As the storm moved over and around Red Oak, reported hail sizes increased. Widespread quarter-size hail within the city quickly gave way to golf ball-size (1.75 inches) hail southwest of town reported by emergency management, 2.00-inch hail measured by a storm chaser to the east-southeast, and baseball-size (2.75 inches) hail reported via mPING just 3 miles south of Red Oak.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 1.75 inches in diameter southwest of Red Oak, IA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe Drought conditions continued in Alleghany county in early May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, which ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Jackson River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon of the 15th saw a repeat of the previous day's activity. Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 15th combined with mid-level moisture to create numerous high-based thunderstorms. The lowest levels of the atmosphere were very dry which allowed for most of the rainfall to evaporate before reaching the surface. The rapidly sinking air near thunderstorms resulted in strong to severe gusts upon impacting the ground. The intense winds also kicked up copious amounts of dust creating brief brownouts in localized areas. Several wildfire starts occurred on the afternoon of the 15th although none of these wildfires caused any known damage. The Cherokee Fire within the canyon of Briscoe County burned a total of approximately 3,222 acres. The Ox Bow Fire started in rural Hall County northeast of Turkey burned approximately 1,000 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Chainey Mountain Fire also started in Hall County near the Childress County line and burned approximately 1,200 acres before being contained on the 16th. The Baylor Creek Fire started just northeast of the Chainey Mountain Fire and burned 195 acres crossing the Hall/Childress County line. The last known wildfire for the day began in Motley County called the Comanche Fire. This wildfire burned approximately 1,991 acres before being contained on the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Slaton measured severe wind gusts from 1751 CST through 1752 CST. A peak wind gust of 63 mph was measured at 1752 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a very dry April, conditions improved for Middle Tennessee during May 2026. The second half of the month was particularly active with above normal precipitable water values resulting in daily rounds of showers and thunderstorms. By the end of the month, most of Middle Tennessee received 5 to 10 inches of beneficial rainfall with the highest amounts falling over the southern and eastern half of the area. Most of Middle Tennessee received 75 to over 100 percent of monthly normal precipitation. This rain did help improve drought conditions. By the end of the month, about 34 percent of the area was classified as at least severe drought - an improvement from 100 percent in April. About 5 percent of this was classified as extreme drought which was down from about 38 percent in April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought conditions across Perry County from April 2026 improved in May. Severe drought conditions were present across the northern half of the county with moderate drought conditions across the south.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Electrical Transmission Lines (ETL)/wood poles broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Continued dryness in May, led to deterioration of drought conditions for much of western and north central Nebraska. There was one pocket of drought improvement across far southwestern Nebraska. By the end of May, 87 percent of western and north central Nebraska was in extreme (D3) or exceptional (D4) drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over most of Custer County, extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted through the end of May. Over far southeastern portions of the county, extreme (D3) drought conditions, improved to severe (D2) drought conditions by the end of the month. Across northwestern portions of Custer County, severe (D2) drought conditions deteriorated to extreme (D3) drought conditions by the end of May. At the Broken Bow Airport, 2.65 inches of precipitation was reported in May. This was 1.30 inches below the normal of 3.95 inches. The cooperative observer at Broken Bow 2W reported 2.69 inches of precipitation for May. This was 1.34 inches below the normal of 4.03 inches. The cooperative observer at Callaway 8WSW reported 2.36 inches of precipitation for May.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few short lived thunderstorms formed in the eastern Texas Panhandle on the evening of May 13th. One of these storms was exiting Gray County as it was dissipating and the environment left behind helped cause a heat burst in Gray County, which led to gusts around 60 mph. The next day, May 14th, scattered thunderstorms moved across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms lacked the instability and shear to produce large hail, but the nature of a dry surface layer allowed for storms to produce severe winds in excess of 60 mph across the region. In addition, these storms produced very little rainfall and lightning induced numerous fires across the region. Finally, on the evening of the 15th, showers and thunderstorms developed over the northwest combined Panhandles. These storms also produced severe wind gusts across portions of the area.

A very dry spring led to the development of Extreme (D3) to Exceptional (D4) drought in the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. With an extra prolonged period of dryness and abnormally warm temperatures both in May and leading up to May, drought impacts were felt quite a bit. Not only were crops not surviving spring planting, but grasses remained abnormally dry and dormant for this time of year. This lead to extreme wildfire conditions as temperatures reached the upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Much of Hutchinson, Roberts, and Hemphill counties were in Exceptional Drought (D3) at the start of the month. Conversely much of Hansford, Ochiltree, and Lipscomb counties started the month in Severe Drought (D2). With a continually growing deficit in rainfall, the cluster of counties that included Hansford, Ochiltree, and the northwestern half of Lipscomb fell into D3. An area of Exceptional Drought (D4) developed over the southeastern half of Lipscomb, all of Hemphill, and the southeastern half of Roberts County. Areas that developed D4 had a 120 day rainfall deficit of 5 to 8 while the areas with D3 had a 4 to 5 deficit.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level trough moved into the Rockies on May 18, with southwest flow aloft over the Missouri Ozarks. A cluster of thunderstorms pushed southeast into portions of central Missouri, bringing heavy rainfall and flash flooding to St. Clair, Benton, and Camden counties. Additionally, a low level jet axis extending from the Gulf through eastern Kansas strengthened overnight into May 19 while interacting with the upper level trough and a surface front. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Small hardwood tree limbs broken (up to 1 inch diameter).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21. Isolated flash flooding also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of water over roadways from DriveTexas. Time estimated by radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms occurred ahead of a frontal boundary on May 22-25. However, on May 25, a mesoscale convective system developed west of the area and enhanced the low level wind field.  This resulted in two tornadoes across the tri-state area. One tornado affected the Villa Tasso area in Walton county in Florida, and the other tornado affected Houston and Henry counties in Alabama.  Both tornadoes were rated EF1.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado initially touched down just north of U.S. 84 near Cowarts in Houston County, damaging trees and outbuildings. A pool screen was damaged at a home along Omussee Road, with additional tree and minor damage to homes. The tornado damaged the WDHN television station as it crossed Highway 52, breaking windows and damaging the roof. The tornado continued north-northeast downing trees and causing minor structural damage before moving into Henry County at County Road 22 and Buckhead Drive. The most severe damage was along County Road 15 where two homes were heavily damage. One home was destroyed. This home separated from the concrete foundation, slid, and then collapsed. The damage is consistent with an EF1 tornado with maximum winds of approximately 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In May 2026, New Hampshire saw noticeable short-term improvements in drought conditions, though deep groundwater deficits continued to pose a challenge across the state. Soaking rains in mid-May provided widespread relief, particularly across the northern mountains and foothills. Over a single week ending May 19, the coverage of Severe Drought (D2) in New Hampshire dropped significantly from 36% down to 20.5%. The mid-May rain events successfully replenished surface topsoil moisture, restored streamflows, and boosted lake and reservoir levels back toward seasonal baselines. However, extended precipitation deficits over the preceding 90 days, particularly across southern New Hampshire, kept deeper hydrologic systems under stress. Deep groundwater aquifers respond on a much slower, lagging timeframe, meaning the water table remained significantly lower than long-term historical averages for May. Consequently, several groundwater monitoring wells across southern and central New Hampshire continued to record below to much-below normal levels.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The USDM on April 28 had 95% of Strafford County in Severe Drought (D2), and conditions remained mostly unchanged through the end of May at 95% Severe Drought (D2) and 5% Moderate Drought (D1). May rainfall averaged 5.81 inches, well above normal by 2.24���. However, one wet May wasn't enough to wipe out extended long-term shortfalls: the 12-month period ending May 2026 still ranked as the 10th driest on record, leaving the area with a multi-month precipitation deficit of more than 9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dispatch center reported a couple of different flooded roads in Le Mars including portions of Holton Dr as well as 5th Ave. Several social media photos also showed significant, but localized, street flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

Deep moisture and sufficient instability supported efficient rainfall as successive storms moved north and northeast over soils saturated by repeated rainfall during the previous several days. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.

A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Storms weakened as they headed into northwest Iowa during the evening but still produced some hail up to ping-pong ball size and strong thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions remained across north central North Carolina, and Exceptional Drought conditions expanded into northwest North Carolina in early and late May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Yadkin, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, and January, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the New River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Oklahoma during the late afternoon of April 24th, then congealed into a partially organized cluster of storms as they moved southeast across the ArkLaTex region during the evening. The storms continued to strengthen and evolved into a more organized mesoscale convective system within northwest flow aloft as they approached the local area. The MCS moved across coastal Mississippi on the early morning hours of April 25th, producing a couple of tornadoes along with areas of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 95 mph touched down just north of the intersection of Ohio Ave. and Polk St. in Gulfport. The tornado quickly tracked to the south causing sporadic tree damage that consisted primarily of large tree limbs being blown off of trees as tracked southward between Wisconsin Ave. and West Railroad Ave. The tornado continued south-southeast across US Hwy 49 with visible damage observed to commercial businesses in this area. Large branches and snapped trees were observed between 34th St. and 28th St. At the intersection of 28th St. and 22nd Ave. two metal buildings had their garage doors blown out as the tornado continued south-southeast. At the intersection of Pass Road and 22nd Ave. a large hardwood tree was completely uprooted. The tornado then crossed Pass Road and produced additional tree damage in the form of large branches and a few snapped trees. The snapped trees were either dead and diseased, so the windspeed was lowered to 90 mph to account for this. As the tornado crossed the railroad track, minor damage to a home in the form of a few removed shingles was observed on 3rd St. The tornado then moved offshore near the intersection of Beach Blvd. and Pratt Ave.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cumberland County averaged 3.39 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.57 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 28% in Extreme Drought (D3) and 72% in Severe Drought (D2) and 8% in Moderate Drought (D1). By the end of April the extreme drought had been eliminated, shifting to moderate drought which now represented 100% of the county. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 12 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event which produced two rounds of precipitation. The first round produced mixed precipitation across the county. The second round fell as mostly wet heavy snow that melted on contact with the ground. Snow accumulations amounted to less than one inch across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted central, south-central, and southeast Kansas from the morning hours of April 26th through the early morning hours of April 27th. Several reports of large hail and damaging winds were relayed; the largest hail size was three inches near Cherryvale, and the strongest wind gusts were in Oswego with 85-95 mph winds which damaged many trees in town. In addition, a few tornadoes occurred across southeast Kansas. The strongest tornado was an EF2 in Montgomery County with damage to two homes along with many trees and some outbuildings; unfortunately one resident was injured in this tornado.

A quasi-stationary front drifted into northern Virginia, supported aloft by a weak upper level trough, provided instability for a few severe thunderstorms to develop. Lapse rates of around 6-7 degrees C/km and CAPE values between 1000-2000 J/kg were observed, in addition to afternoon surface temperatures in the 80s, triggered thunderstorms that produced large hail along the Blue Ridge into the Piedmont.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: WSET relayed a report of hail one inch in diameter near Forest, VA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolific tornado outbreak occurred during the afternoon on April 17th, with 5 tornadoes occurring in southeast Minnesota. Two were EF-2 intensity, one of which was highly visible from Rochester, Minnesota as it tracked from Stewartville to Marion, Minnesota, resulting in numerous homes being damaged. Some of these homes were rendered uninhabitable. Additionally, the storms that produced these tornadoes also brought up to golf ball sized hail in the Rochester area and surrounding communities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This strong EF-2 tornado began on the northeast side of Stewartville resulting in damage to several homes. The tornado then moved northeast through rural areas of Olmsted County while being highly visible on MNDOT cameras and from Rochester. This tornado eventually crossed I-90, hitting a semi-trailer and injuring the occupant, before moving northwest of Simpson. A farmstead near Simpson took a direct hit from the tornado where a single-wide manufactured home was rolled and farm outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado continued northeast into a neighborhood along Marion Road where several homes were rendered uninhabitable due to a collapse of their exterior walls and roof. Numerous other residences sustained window, roof, and outbuilding damage as well. The tornado continued through this neighborhood before dissipating along Timberidge Court between Rochester and Marion. Two more individuals were also injured in this area while sheltering in their home from the tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In Maine, hydrologic conditions varied significantly by region. The upper Kennebec and Androscoggin basins received above normal precipitation, which provided some localized relief. However, southern portions of the state experienced severe dryness, with monthly precipitation deficits exceeding two inches. This underperforming spring supported limited improvements in Maine���s drought, however the extreme drought (D3) was reduced to severe drought (D2).  Although early-month snowmelt and spring rains temporarily buoyed soil moisture, reservoirs, and shallow water tables, groundwater storage remained low. Regional monitoring wells, such as those in Oxford and Eustis, remained within the Below Normal (10th���25th percentile) or Much Below Normal (5th���10th percentile) categories, reflecting a deeply stressed system. By the end of April, no flooding had occurred, and the vast majority of waterways finished the month flowing at below-normal to much-below-normal rates.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sagadahoc County averaged 4.49 inches of precipitation in April, approximately 0.55 inches below normal. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2), with no change in designations during the month of April. Precipitation deficits since the beginning of the drought remained around 11 inches. The drought was primarily defined by subsurface groundwater deficits and lower than normal reservoir levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong spring system brought a variety of precipitation types to the region early April (4/1 to 4/4). Low pressure swept across Minnesota from the SW to the NE with warmer air south of the low's core and colder air north.  Areas across the northern half of Minnesota observed mainly heavy snow, whereas the southern half of Minnesota saw a combination of liquid and frozen precipitation types. This system produced two waves; the first wave arrived during the afternoon hours of April 1st and lasted into the following day. Temperatures throughout the vertical profile supported several hours of a rain/freezing rain/snow mix with CoCoRaHS observers reporting a glaze of ice over non-paved surfaces during the morning hours of April 2nd. A lull of activity followed the first wave of precipitation. The second wave arrived early April 3rd and persisted into April 4th.  During the daylight hours, the precipitation type was mainly rain but phased to freezing rain and snow overnight.  Winter weather headlines were issued with strong concerns towards icing and travel impacts. The highest snowfall totals (between 4 to 7 inches) were confined to north-central MN and farther northward. As for icing, most areas observed between a light glaze of ice accumulation to near a tenth of an inch.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter weather event produced two rounds of rain/freezing rain/snow mix which lasted several hours each. CoCoRaHS observers in neighboring counties reported a light glaze of ice on flat non-paved surfaces.

A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri. ||In Southern Illinois, during the early evening, MLCAPE was quite high ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 2000-3000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-7, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C. Warm moist air lifted dew points into the mid-60s during the afternoon hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a six-month respite (since early-September 2025) with no worse than Moderate Drought (D1) assigned to any portion of this 24-county South Central Nebraska area by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM), unfortunately March 2026 brought a steadily worsening drought situation back into the spotlight as much of the area not only spiraled into Severe Drought (D2), but also Extreme Drought (D3). This marked the first D3 within the area in 10 months (since May 2025) and marked the highest areal coverage of D3 in at least 2.5 years (since Sept. 2023). These rapid degradations not only stemmed from an incredibly dry March, but also from the inevitable consequence of cumulative dryness that had been building for six months...as October 2025-March 2026 ranked among the Top-4 driest October-March periods on record across most of the area (see below for more detailed precipitation info).  Breaking down the significant changes in county-level USDM drought categories during March, the month opened with the vast majority of the 24-county domain assigned either D1 (mainly counties along/north of Interstate 80) or Abnormally Dry/D0 (most places south of I-80). Only a small sliver of the area (around 2 percent of it) was void of all drought categories whatsoever...mainly southeast Thayer County. As March unfolded, degradation came swiftly, with portions of several counties designated D2 on the very first USDM issuance of the month, and a steadily expanding introduction of D3 arriving just a few weeks later. As a result, the end-of-March categorical breakdown stood as follows (in order of drought severity): 1) roughly 52% of South Central Nebraska featured D3 (most prevalent within counties along/north of I-80)...2) approximately 32% of real estate contained D1...3) around 15% of the area was in D1 (almost entirely within southern-most counties along the Kansas border)...4) the remaining sliver of the area (far southern Thayer/Nuckolls counties) was allotted D0. ||Turning to the dire precipitation details, and starting with the longer-term dryness (including a pronounced lack of snow) that defined Oct. 2025-March 2026, this six-month stretch registered among the Top-4 driest on record across South Central Nebraska. More specifically, based on a mix of observations from over 100 NWS and NeRAIN/CoCoRaHS observers along with some radar estimation, the majority of the 30-county area (roughly 80% of it) measured merely between 1.65-4.45...only 25-67% of normal. The highest concentration of amounts 2-or-less focused within primarily far northern and western counties, particularly: Dawson, Gosper, Furnas, Valley, Greeley, Buffalo. Citing six-month totals from just a few longtime NWS Cooperative Observer sites, the Canaday Power Plant (near Lexington) incredibly registered just 0.87 (17% of normal...driest on record), Arcadia 2W reported only 1.29 (21% of normal...driest on record) and Elwood 8S tallied just 1.36 (25% of normal...driest on record). At the Tri Cities airports, October-March ranked between the 2nd-4th driest on record, with totals ranging from 1.69 (Kearney) to 2.68 (Hastings). The only part of the area where precipitation amounts were even remotely close to normal (but still below it)...with at least 5...focused within portions of Thayer and Nuckolls counties. Drilling down to March itself, while October-February were dry enough, March truly brought things to a whole other level. In fact, the majority of South Central Nebraska measured somewhere between a paltry trace and 0.27 (essentially zero to 20% of normal). In fact, around 96% of the 24-county area observed LESS THAN ONE-FOURTH NORMAL March precipitation. Among the very driest of the dry, the following NWS stations were just a few of several that received a paltry trace for the month: Cambridge, Elwood 8S, Beaver City and Orleans 2W. In the Tri Cities, the airports registered just 0.12-0.14. Even the wettest parts of the domain were still significantly below normal, including totals of 0.63 at Hebron, 0.36 in St. Paul, and 0.35 at Belgrade. Needless to say, the significant dryness that spanned the end of 2025 into the start of 2026 set the stage for not only a rough start to the 2026 agricultural growing season in South Central Nebraska (meager soil moisture profiles) but also sparked an above-average early-spring wildfire threat. In addition to several smaller fires across the 24-county area, portions of southwestern Dawson County were ravaged by the massive Cottonwood Fire that ignited on March 12th in far southeastern Lincoln County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21. Isolated flash flooding also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media post showing a foot of water flowing over County Road 798.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured gusts up to 58 mph by the KLRD AWOS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May 2026 was a month of dramatic, high-stakes climatic shifts for North Mississippi. The month began with the region locked in the grip of a multi-season moisture deficit that peaked in intensity by mid-month. For the first few weeks, an aggressive early-summer evaporation engine baked the region's topsoil, threatening to derail the spring planting season entirely.||However, the final third of the month brought a significant and much-needed atmospheric pattern shift. A series of massive storm complexes pushed heavy convective rainfall across the Deep South, breaking the multi-month dry spell. While these late-May deluges stabilized crashing topsoil moisture, climatologists quickly warned that the rain fell too fast to fully heal the deeply depleted subsoil and groundwater reserves.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D4 Exceptional Drought and D3 Extreme Drought persisted the entire month across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought large hail and damaging wind gusts to eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the late afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2026. Through the afternoon, moisture pooled along a surface front, with an upper-level shortwave initiating convective development. Surface-based instability (SBCAPE) of 2000 to 2500 J/kg materialized across the region. This instability, combined with 35 to 40 knots of deep-layer (0-6 km) bulk shear, initially favored discrete supercell development. Atmospheric soundings revealed fairly dry low levels, which enhanced the threat for severe, damaging wind gusts as the convection transitioned into an outflow-dominated regime. Additional storms developed along the boundary across far eastern Nebraska into the evening hours before the entire line eventually became outflow-dominant and weakened.||Several notable severe weather impacts were reported across southwest Iowa and eastern Nebraska during the event, primarily driven by damaging wind gusts and hail. The most significant wind damage occurred in southwest Iowa, where gusts estimated between 60 and 75 mph caused structural and agricultural damage. A measured gust of 74 mph was recorded by the Red Oak, IA AWOS, which correlated with amateur radio reports of downed power poles, tree damage, and widespread power outages in the city. In Mills County, severe winds blew over farm augers and moved grain wagons near Randolph, while structural damage to roofing and siding was reported further east in Stanton. Alongside the wind threat, severe hail up to 1.00 inch in diameter (quarter-sized) was widely reported across the region, including instances in Cass, Seward, Washington, and Douglas counties in Nebraska���with one 1.00-inch hail report coming directly from an NWS employee in Valley, NE.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: KRDK AWOS measured wind gust of 74 mph at the Red Oak Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||A strong to severe thunderstorm initially tracked across Montgomery County, producing a combination of damaging winds and large hail. The storm initially dropped quarter-size (1.00 inch) hail near Stanton before an Iowa DOT mesonet station 3 miles north of Villisca measured a peak wind gust of 64 mph. As the storm moved over and around Red Oak, reported hail sizes increased. Widespread quarter-size hail within the city quickly gave way to golf ball-size (1.75 inches) hail southwest of town reported by emergency management, 2.00-inch hail measured by a storm chaser to the east-southeast, and baseball-size (2.75 inches) hail reported via mPING just 3 miles south of Red Oak.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm chaser report of hail measured up to 2 inches in diameter along with photo of two separate hailstones at this size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21. Isolated flash flooding also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of one water rescue from partially submerged vehicle in the city of Alice.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell near the Turnertown community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) and Severe (D2) drought continued across North Louisiana throughout the month of May, as below normal rainfall remained a common theme across the area since early Fall 2025. May monthly rainfall totals ranged from 2-4 inches across Northwest Louisiana, and from 4-8+ inches across the West-central and North-central Louisiana.  Thus, the drier areas observed amounts that were 50-75% of their normal monthly rainfall, with the wetter areas observing near to as much as two times their normal monthly rainfall. Despite the wetness across much of these drought stricken areas, little runoff was produced given the long term dryness and thus, ag producers continued to struggle with delayed and little greenup, requiring feed to be provided to their livestock, much below normal to dry stock pond levels and thus, water had to be brought in, a culling of their cattle herds, as well as much below normal streamflow across the area rivers, bayous, and creeks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser reported the tornado was first visible in an open field west of 466th Avenue and north of 291st Street. The tornado moved slowly southeast toward a farmstead at the intersection of 466th Avenue and 291st Street where minor tree damage was reported. The primary circulation then broadened as the tornado turned more eastward and at times exhibited smaller brief vortices. Additional minor tree damage occurred before the tornado lifted in the vicinity of 291st Street and 467th Avenue. The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated peak wind of 75 mph and an estimated average path width of 50 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed in open fields near the intersection of 625 Avenue and 725 Road in Johnson county at 3:05 PM CST, and moved quickly east before entering Nemaha county. The tornado damaged many trees, flipped pivots, and destroyed at least two large farm sheds. The damage along the track was somewhat sporadic at times, and this concentrated area of tornado damage was embedded within a much broader area of 60 to 80 mph winds in the downdraft regions of the parent thunderstorm. The peak width of the tornado was determined where it traveled through a long line of trees and gave evidence to the most intense focused zone of winds being approximately 200 yards wide. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 97 mph. The tornado continued into Nemaha county before dissipating at 15:11 PM CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions were introduced across south central Virginia in late April after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 6.00-8.00 inches, with locally lower totals of 4.00-6.00 inches. This ended up being 50 to 75 percent of normal for that period, with locally lower percentiles in the 25 to 50 percent of normal. These continued dry conditions combined with the dry fall and early winter conditions leading up to below average rainfall in November, December, January, February, March, and April contributed to a continued decline in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 10th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the James, Roanoke, New, and Dan River basins, which were all observed to be around the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme Drought conditions Expanded into Charlotte county in May after the previous several months of February, March, and April recorded precipitation totals of 4.00-6.00 inches, which ended up being 25 to 50 percent of normal for that period. These dry conditions combined with the dry fall conditions leading up to below average rainfall during the winter months, contributed to a rapid decrease in groundwater and soil moisture in this region, where observed values for each had fallen to at or below the 5th percentile for groundwater, and 2nd percentile for soil moisture in the first 0-100 cm based off the NASA SPoRT LIS data estimated on the 1st of May. Streamflows similarly decreased across the area. This included the Roanoke River, which was observed to be below the 10th percentile per the USGS WaterWatch website and, in some cases, were near record-low flows.
